C. |title=Advances in Agronomy Volume 42 |publisher=[[Academic Press]] |doi=10.1016/s0065-2113(08)60522-2 |isbn=978-0-12-000742-4 |access-date=2023-02-23|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref> especially in subsistence [[smallholding]]s areas<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ghosh-Jerath |first1= Suparna |last2=Kapoor |first2=Ridhima |last3=Ghosh |first3=Upasona |last4=Singh |first4=Archna |last5=Downs |first5=Shauna |last6=Fanzo |first6=Jessica |year=2021 |title=Pathways of Climate Change Impact on Agroforestry, Food Consumption Pattern, and Dietary Diversity Among Indigenous Subsistence Farmers of Sauria Paharia Tribal Community of India: A Mixed Methods Study |journal=Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems |volume=5 |article-number=667297 |doi=10.3389/fsufs.2021.667297 |pmc=7613000 |pmid=35811836 |doi-access=free |bibcode= 2021FrSFS...567297G }}</ref> such as sub-Saharan Africa.<ref name="ta"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jamnadass |first1=R.H. |last2=Dawson |first2=I.K. |last3=Franzel |first3=S. |last4=Leakey |first4=R.R.B. |last5=Mithöfer |first5=D. |last6=Akinnifesi |first6=F.K. |last7=Tchoundjeu |first7=Z. |date=2011-09-01 |title=Improving livelihoods and nutrition in sub-Saharan Africa through the promotion of indigenous and exotic fruit production in smallholders' agroforestry systems: a review |url=https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/cfa/ifr/2011/00000013/00000003/art00007 |journal=International Forestry Review |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=338–354 |doi=10.1505/146554811798293836|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Research with the leguminous tree ''[[Faidherbia albida]]'' in Zambia showed maximum maize yields of 4.0 tonnes per hectare using fertilizer and inter-cropped with the trees at densities of 25 to 100 trees per hectare,<ref>{{cite web |title=Turning the tide on farm productivity in Africa: an agroforestry solution |url=http://www.worldagroforestry.org/newsroom/highlights/turning-tide-farm-productivity-africa-agroforestry-solution |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100620163751/http://worldagroforestry.org/newsroom/highlights/turning-tide-farm-productivity-africa-agroforestry-solution |archive-date=20 June 2010 |last=Langford |first=Kate |publisher=[[World Agroforestry Centre]] |access-date=2 April 2014 |date=8 July 2009}}</ref> compared to average maize yields in Zimbabwe of 1.1 tonnes per hectare.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bayala |first1=Jules |last2=Larwanou |first2=Mahamane |last3=Kalinganire |first3=Antoine |last4=Mowo |first4=Jeremias G. |last5=Weldesemayat |first5=Sileshi G. |last6=Ajayi |first6=Oluyede C. |last7=Akinnifesi |first7=Festus K. |last8=Garrity |first8=Dennis Philip |display-authors=5 |date=1 September 2010 |title=Evergreen Agriculture: a robust approach to sustainable food security in Africa |url=http://www.evergreenagriculture.net/sites/default/files/Evergreen%20Agriculture%20Garrity%20et%20al%20Food%20Security.pdf |journal=Food Security |volume=2 |issue=3 |pages=197–214 |doi=10.1007/s12571-010-0070-7 |s2cid=12815631 |archive-date=21 October 2012 |access-date=25 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021144226/http://evergreenagriculture.net/sites/default/files/Evergreen%20Agriculture%20Garrity%20et%20al%20Food%20Security.pdf}}</ref>

=== Hillside systems ===

A well-studied agroforestry hillside system is the Quesungual Slash and Mulch Agroforestry System in [[Lempira Department]], [[Honduras]]. This region was historically used for [[slash-and-burn]] [[subsistence agriculture]]. Due to heavy seasonal floods, the exposed soil was washed away, leaving infertile barren soil exposed to the dry season.<ref name="ayarza1">{{Cite book |chapter-url=http://www.iwmi.cgiar.org/Publications/brightspots/PDF/Latin_America/QSMAS_Case_study_Honduras.pdf |title=Comprehensive Assessment Bright Spots Project Final Report |last1=Ayarza |first1=M. A. |last2=Welchez |first2=L. A. |year=2004 |editor-last=Noble |editor-first=A. |chapter=Drivers effecting the development and sustainability of the Quesungual Slash and Mulch Agroforestry System (QSMAS) on hillsides of Honduras |access-date=14 January 2018}}</ref> Farmed hillside sites had to be abandoned after a few years and new forest was burned. The UN's FAO helped introduce a system incorporating local knowledge consisting of the following steps:<ref name="FAO 2001">{{Cite book |title=Conservation Agriculture: Case Studies in Latin America and Africa |publisher=[[FAO]] |year=2001}}</ref><ref name="Pauli Barrios 2011">{{Cite journal |last1=Pauli |first1=N. |last2=Barrios |first2=E. |last3=Conacher |first3=A. J. |last4=Oberthür |first4=T. |year=2011 |title=Soil macrofauna in agricultural landscapes dominated by the Quesungual Slash-and-Mulch Agroforestry System, western Honduras. |url=http://dapa.ciat.cgiar.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/02/2011_Soil_macrofauna_in_agricultural-Elsevie.pdf |journal=Applied Soil Ecology |volume=47 |issue=2 |pages=119–132 |via=Elsevier |doi=10.1016/j.apsoil.2010.11.005 |bibcode=2011AppSE..47..119P |s2cid=18732880 |access-date=6 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160324135912/http://dapa.ciat.cgiar.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/02/2011_Soil_macrofauna_in_agricultural-Elsevie.pdf |archive-date=24 March 2016}}</ref>

# Thin and [[Pruning|prune]] hillside [[secondary forest]], leaving individual beneficial trees, especially [[Nitrogen fixation|nitrogen-fixing]] trees. They help reduce [[soil erosion]], maintain [[soil]] moisture, provide shade and provide an input of nitrogen-rich [[organic matter]] in the form of litter.
# Plant maize in rows. This is a traditional local crop.
# Harvest from the dried plant and plant [[bean]]s. The maize stalks provide an ideal structure for the climbing [[bean]] plants. [[Bean]] is a [[Nitrogen fixation|nitrogen-fixing]] plant and therefore helps introduce more [[nitrogen]].
# [[Pumpkin]]s can be planted during this time. The plant's large leaves and horizontal growth provide additional shade and moisture retention. It does not compete with the [[bean]]s for sunlight since the latter grow vertically on the stalks.
# Every few seasons, [[crop rotation|rotate the crop]] by grazing cattle, allowing grass to grow and adding [[soil organic matter]] and nutrients (manure). The cattle prevent total [[reforestation]] by grazing around the trees.
# Repeat.

=== Kuojtakiloyan ===

The ''[[kuojtakiloyan]]'' of [[Mexico]] is a jungle-landscaped polyculture that grows [[avocado]]es, [[sweet potatoes]], [[cinnamon]], [[Prunus salicifolia|black cherries]], {{ill |Inga spuria |es |lt=cuajiniquil}}<!--both the latin and local names are possibly=''[[Inga vera]]'' but needs verifying-->, [[citrus fruits]], [[gourd]]s, [[macadamia]], [[mango]]es, [[banana]]s and [[sapote]]s.<ref name="Moreno-Calles 2013">{{cite journal |last1=Moreno-Calles |first1=A. I. |last2=Toledo |first2=V. M. |last3=Casas |first3=A. |year=2013 |title=Los sistemas agroforestales tradicionales de México: Una aproximación biocultural |url=http://www.scielo.org.mx/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S2007-42982013000400001 |journal=Botanical Sciences |volume=91 |issue=4 |page=383}}</ref>

[[File:Café_bajo_sombra_-_49465736457.jpg |thumb|[[Shade-grown coffee]] (''[[Coffea arabica]]'') in Sierra Norte of Puebla]]

[[File:Café_bajo_sombra.jpg |thumb|''Kuojtakiloyan'']]

''Kuojtakiloyan'' is a [[Sierra Puebla Nahuatl|Masehual]] term that means 'useful forest' or 'forest that produces', and it is an agroforestry system developed and maintained by indigenous peoples of the [[Sierra Norte de Puebla|Sierra Norte]] of the [[Puebla|State of Puebla]], [[Mexico]]. It has become a vital fountain of resources (food, medicinal herbs, fuels, [[floriculture]], etc.) for the local population, but it is also a respectful transformation of the environment, with its [[biodiversity]] and [[nature conservation]]. The ''kuojtakiloyan'' comes directly from the ancestral [[Nahuas|Nahua]] and [[Totonac|Totonaku]] knowledge of their natural environment.<ref name="lm">{{Cite news |last=Toledo |first=V. M. |date=2016-08-02 |title=La madre de todas las batallas |language=es |work=La Jornada: Opinión |url=https://www.jornada.com.mx/2016/08/02/opinion/015a1pol |access-date=2021-07-09}}</ref>

The ''kuojtakiloyan'' is a jungle-landscaped [[polyculture]] in which [[avocado]]s, [[sweet potatoes]], [[cinnamon]], [[Prunus salicifolia|black cherries]], [[Inga|chalahuits]], [[citrus fruits]], [[gourd]]s, [[macadamia]], [[mango]]es, [[banana]]s and [[sapote]]s are grown.<ref name="lm"/><ref name="Moreno-Calles 2013" /> In addition, a wide variety of harvested wild edible mushrooms and herbs (''[[quelite (disambiguation)|quelites]]''). The ''[[Heliocarpus appendiculatus|jonote]]'' is planted because its fiber is useful in basketry, and also [[bamboo]], which is fast growing, to build cabins and other structures. Concurrently to ''kuojtakiloyan'', [[Shade-grown coffee|shade coffee]] is grown (''café bajo sombra'' in [[Spanish language|Spanish]]; ''kafentaj'' in Masehual). Shade is essential to obtain high quality coffee.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Toledo |first1=V. M. |last2=Moguel |first2=P. |year=2012 |title=Coffee and sustainability: The mul- tiple values of traditional shaded coffee |journal=[[Journal of Sustainable Agriculture]] |volume=36 |issue=3 |pages=353–377 |doi=10.1080/10440046.2011.583719 |bibcode=2012JSusA..36..353T}}</ref> The local population has favored the proliferation of the [[stingless bee]] (''pisilnekemej'') by including the plants that it pollinates. From bees, they get honey, pollen, wax and [[propolis]].<ref name="lm"/>

=== Shade crops ===

With shade applications, crops are purposely raised under tree canopies within the shady environment. The understory crops are shade tolerant or the overstory trees have fairly open canopies. A conspicuous example is [[shade-grown coffee]]. This practice reduces weeding costs and improves coffee quality and taste.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Arboles en cafetales |url=https://repositorio.catie.ac.cr/handle/11554/453 |access-date=11 February 2024 |date=11 February 1999 |publisher=[[Centro Agronómico Tropical de Investigación y Enseñanza]] |isbn=978-9977-57-331-1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Muschler |first=R. G. |date=1 August 2001 |title=Shade improves coffee quality in a sub-optimal coffee-zone of Costa Rica |journal=Agroforestry Systems |volume=52 |issue=3 |page=253 |doi=10.1023/A:1011863426305 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2001AgrSy..52..253M}}</ref> In [[Sumatra]], agroforestry systems mixing [[Coffea canephora|robusta coffee]] with [[durian]] and [[papaya]] serve as vital buffers for protected areas such as the [[Gunung Leuser National Park]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kauffman |first1=J. Boone |last2=Adame |first2=Maria Fernanda |last3=Adinugroho |first3=Wahyu Catur |last4=Anshari |first4=Gusti |last5=Basuki |first5=Imam |last6=Donato |first6=Daniel |last7=Gangga |first7=Adi |last8=Murdiyarso |first8=Daniel |last9=Ritonga |first9=Rasis Putra |last10=Warren |first10=Matthew |last11=Novita |first11=Nisa |date=2025-10-01 |title=Total ecosystem carbon stocks of tropical peat forests and greenhouse gas emissions from their disturbance |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378112725003482 |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |volume=593 |article-number=122840 |doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2025.122840 |bibcode=2025ForEM.59322840K |issn=0378-1127|doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Alley cropping ===

{{main|Alley cropping}}

With alley cropping, crop strips alternate with rows of closely spaced tree or hedge species. Normally, the trees are pruned before planting the crop. The cut leafy material - for example, from ''[[Alchornea cordifolia]]'' and ''[[Acioa barteri]]'' - is spread over the crop area to provide nutrients. The hedges serve as windbreaks and reduce erosion.<ref name="Tripathi-Psychas-1992"/> In tropical areas of North and South America, various species of ''[[Inga]]'' such as ''[[Inga edulis|I. edulis]]'' and ''[[Inga oerstediana|I. oerstediana]]'' have been used for alley cropping.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://theecologist.org/2005/feb/20/rainforest-saver |title=The Rainforest Saver |work=The Ecologist |first=Daniel |last=Elkan |date=20 February 2005}}</ref> [[Weed control]] is inherent to the practice, providing mulch and shade.<ref name="Tripathi-Psychas-1992">{{cite book |last1=Tripathi |first1=Bansh R. |last2=Psychas |first2=Paul J. |title=The AFNETA Alley Farming Training Manual |publisher=[[Alley Farming Network for Tropical Africa]] (AFNETA) |date=1992 |hdl=10568/49807 |volume=1 - Core course in alley farming |isbn=978-131-074-X |oclc=29771935 |publication-place=[[Ibadan]] |pages=xi+180 |s2cid=130266228}} [[AGRIS]] id [http://agris.fao.org/agris-search/search.do?recordID=XF2016015795 XF2016015795]. {{hdl |20.500.12478/5101}}.</ref>

=== Syntropic systems ===

[[File:Un luxuriant jardin syntropique en Dordogne.jpg|thumb|A temperate Syntropic system in [[Dordogne]] France, including heavily mulched [[Common sunflower|sunflower]] plants]]

Syntropic farming, syntropic agriculture or syntropic agroforestry is an [[Organic farming|organic]], [[permaculture]] agroforestry system developed by [[Ernst Götsch]] in Brazil.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Andrade |first1=Dayana |last2=Pasini |first2=Felipe |last3=Scarano |first3=Fabio Rubio |date=August 2020 |title=Syntropy and innovation in agriculture |journal=Current Opinion in Environmental Sustainability |volume=45 |pages=20–24 |doi=10.1016/j.cosust.2020.08.003 |bibcode=2020COES...45...20A}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-07-30 |title=In syntropic agriculture, farmers stop fighting nature and learn to embrace it |url=https://news.mongabay.com/2020/07/in-syntropic-agriculture-farmers-stop-fighting-nature-and-learn-to-embrace-it/ |access-date=2024-04-13 |website=Mongabay Environmental News}}</ref> Sometimes systems of this type are called '''successional agroforestry systems''' or '''SAFS''', a broader concept originating in Latin America.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Steinfeld |first1=Jonas P. |last2=J.J.A. Bianchi |first2=Felix |last3=Luiz Locatelli |first3=Jorge |last4=Rizzo |first4=Rodnei |last5=Eduarda Bispo de Resende |first5=Maria |last6=Ramos Ballester |first6=Maria V. |last7=Cerri |first7=Carlos E.P. |last8=Bernardi |first8=Alberto C.C. |last9=Creamer |first9=Rachel E. |date=December 2023 |title=Increasing complexity of agroforestry systems benefits nutrient cycling and mineral-associated organic carbon storage, in south-eastern Brazil |journal=Geoderma |volume=440 |article-number=116726 |doi=10.1016/j.geoderma.2023.116726 |bibcode=2023Geode.44016726S |doi-access=free}}</ref> The system focuses on replicating natural systems of accumulation of nutrients in ecosystems, replicating [[secondary succession]], in order to create productive forest ecosystems that produce [[food]], [[ecosystem service]]s and other [[forest product]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-04-01 |title=Are syntropic agroforestry systems microclimatically similar to tropical forests? |url=https://www.researchsquare.com/ |access-date=2024-04-13 |website=researchsquare.com |language=en}}</ref>

The system relies on several processes:

* Dense planting mixing perennial and annual crops
* Rapid cutting and composting of fast growing pioneer species, to accumulate nutrients and biomass<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Murta |first1=Johnny Rodrigues de Melo |last2=Brito |first2=Gleicon Queiroz de |last3=Mendonça Filho |first3=Sérgio Fernandes |last4=Hoffmann |first4=Maurício Rigon |last5=Salemi |first5=Luiz Felippe |date=October 2021 |title=Understanding the effect of an agroforestry system with high litter input on topsoil permeability |url=https://bsssjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/sum.12647 |journal=Soil Use and Management |language=en |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=802–809 |doi=10.1111/sum.12647 |bibcode=2021SUMan..37..802M |url-access=subscription}}</ref>
* Creating greater water retention on the land through improving penetration of water into soil and plant water cycling

The systems were first developed in tropical Brazil, but many similar systems have been tested in temperate environments as soil and ecosystem restoration tactics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cossel |first1=Moritz von |last2=Ludwig |first2=Heike |last3=Cichocki |first3=Jedrzej |last4=Fesani |first4=Sofia |last5=Guenther |first5=Ronja |last6=Thormaehlen |first6=Magnus |last7=Angenendt |first7=Jule |last8=Braunstein |first8=Isabell |last9=Buck |first9=Marie-Luise |last10=Kunle |first10=Maria |last11=Bihlmeier |first11=Magnus |last12=Cutura |first12=David |last13=Bernhard |first13=AnnSophie |last14=Ow-Wachendorf |first14=Felicitas |last15=Erpenbach |first15=Federico |display-authors=5 |date=December 2020 |title=Adapting Syntropic Permaculture for Renaturation of a Former Quarry Area in the Temperate Zone |journal=Agriculture |volume=10 |issue=12 |page=603 |doi=10.3390/agriculture10120603 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2020Agric..10..603C }}</ref>

Syntropic systems have documented benefits including increased soil water penetration,<ref>Pereira, Sabrina Mendes, Maurício Rigon Hoffman, and Luiz Felippe Salemi. "[https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Luiz-Felippe-Salemi/publication/379261699_Soil_physical_properties_in_a_oxisol_under_a_syntropic_agroforestry_system_row_versus_inter-row/links/6602119aa4857c796282c359/Soil-physical-properties-in-a-oxisol-under-a-syntropic-agroforestry-system-row-versus-inter-row.pdf Soil physical properties in an oxisol under a syntropic agroforestry system: row versus inter-row]." ''Revista Brasileira de Geografia Física'' 17.2 (2024): 838-844.</ref> increases to productivity on marginal land<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Thampy |first1=Sarin |last2=Valogianni |first2=Konstantina |date=2023-01-01 |title=The Impact of Innovation on Sustainability in Agriculture: A Literature Review and Opportunities for Future Research |url=https://aisel.aisnet.org/mcis2023/12/ |journal=MCIS 2023 Proceedings}}</ref> and soil temperature moderation.<ref>Damant, G. "[https://www.repository.utl.pt/bitstream/10400.5/18618/1/EURAFIVConf_Damant_G_et_all_page_161_164.pdf Can agroforestry improve soil water and temperature dynamics in agriculture]? A case study with syntropic farming in Bahia, Brazil." ''European Agroforestry Conference-Agroforestry as Sustainable Land Use, 4th''. EURAF, 2018.
</ref>

== Temperate ==

[[File:Alley cropping corn walnuts.jpg|thumb|Alley cropping corn fields between rows of walnut trees]]

Although originally a concept in tropical agronomy,<ref name="USDA"/> agroforestry's multiple benefits, for instance in nutrient cycles and potential for mitigating droughts, have led to its adoption in the US and Europe.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Iqbal |first1=Nausheen |title=A Food Forest Grows in Atlanta |url=https://www.usda.gov/about-usda/news/blog/food-forest-grows-atlanta |website=USDA.gov blog |access-date=17 June 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Coble |first1=Adam P. |last2= Contosta |first2=Alexandra R. |last3=Smith |first3=Richard G. |last4=Siegert |first4=Nathan W. |last5=Vadeboncoeur |first5=Matthew |last6=Jennings |first6=Katie A. |last7=Stewart |first7=Anthony J. |last8=Asbjornsen |first8=Heidi |date=2020-06-15 |title=Influence of forest-to-silvopasture conversion and drought on components of evapotranspiration |journal=Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment |volume=295 |article-number=106916 |doi=10.1016/j.agee.2020.106916 |s2cid=216426779 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2020AgEE..29506916C}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Schoeneberger |first1=Michele M. |editor1-first=Toral |editor1-last=Patel-Weynand |editor2-first=Gary |editor2-last=Bentrup |editor3-first=Michele M. |editor3-last=Schoeneberger |title=Agroforestry: Enhancing resiliency in U.S. agricultural landscapes under changing conditions |publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]] Forest Service |id=Gen. Tech. Report WO-96 |year=2017 |doi=10.2737/WO-GTR-96 |url=https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/55775 |access-date=17 June 2018}}</ref>

The [[United States Department of Agriculture]] distinguishes five applications of agroforestry for [[temperate climates]], namely alley cropping, forest farming, riparian forest buffers, silvopasture, and windbreaks.<ref name="USDA"/>

=== Alley cropping ===<!--USDA application #1 -->

Alley cropping can also be used in temperate climates. Strip cropping is similar to alley cropping in that trees alternate with crops. The difference is that, with alley cropping, the trees are in single rows. With strip cropping, the trees or shrubs are planted in wide strips. The purpose can be, as with alley cropping, to provide nutrients, in leaf form, to the crop. With strip cropping, the trees can have a purely productive role, providing fruits, nuts, etc. while, at the same time, protecting nearby crops from soil erosion and harmful winds.<ref name="USDA"/>

=== Forest farming ===<!--USDA application #2 -->

In forest farming, high-value crops are grown under a suitably-managed tree canopy. This is sometimes called multi-story cropping, or in tropical villages as home gardening. It can be practised at varying levels of intensity but always involves some degree of management; this distinguishes it from simple harvesting of wild plants from the forest.<ref name="USDA"/><!--https://www.fs.usda.gov/nac/practices/forest-farming.php -->

=== Riparian forest buffers ===<!--USDA application #3 -->

[[File:Riparian buffer on Bear Creek in Story County, Iowa.JPG|thumb |upright |A [[riparian buffer]] bordering a river in Iowa]]

[[Riparian buffer]]s are strips of permanent vegetation located along or near active watercourses or in ditches where [[surface runoff|water runoff]] concentrates. The purpose is to keep nutrients and soil from contaminating the water.<ref name="USDA"/>

=== Silvopasture ===<!--USDA application #4 -->

[[File:Agrosylviculture australie Clive Wawn.jpg|thumb|Silvopasture over the years (Australia)]]

Trees can benefit fauna in a [[silvopasture]] system, where cattle, goats, or sheep browse on grasses grown under trees.<ref name="USDA"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.agroforestry.co.uk/about-agroforestry/silvopasture/ |title=Silvopasture |publisher=Agroforestry Research Trust [in England] |access-date=19 August 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150420215242/http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/silvop.html |archive-date=20 April 2015}}</ref>

The ''[[dehesa]]'' or ''montado'' system of [[silviculture]] are an example of pigs and bulls being held [[extensive farming|extensively]] in Spain and [[Portugal]].<ref>Fra. Paleo, Urbano. (2010). "The dehesa/montado landscape". pp. 149–151 in Sustainable Use of Biological Diversity in Socio-ecological Production Landscapes, eds. Bélair, C., Ichikawa, K., Wong, B.Y.L. and Mulongoy, K.J. Montreal: Secretariat of the [[Convention on Biological Diversity]]. Technical Series no. 52.</ref>

=== Windbreaks ===<!--USDA application #5 -->

[[Windbreaks]] reduce wind velocity over and around crops. This increases yields through reduced drying of the crop and/or by preventing the crop from toppling in strong wind gusts.<ref name="USDA"/>

== Urban ==

'''Urban agroforestry''' is the application of agroforestry principles in urban and suburban environments, where reduced ecological functioning is common. It involves the deliberate integration of trees with shrubs and crops, which together ultimately produce an agricultural product, into managed landscapes such as residential backyards, public parks, and streetscapes.<ref name="pi">{{Cite journal |last=Lovell |first=Sarah |date=2020-05-19 |title=Urban agroforestry and its potential integration into city planning efforts |journal=Urban Agriculture & Regional Food Systems |language=en |volume=5 |issue=1 |article-number=e20000 |doi=10.1002/uar2.20000 |issn=2575-1220|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Benefits ===
The [[United Nations|UN]] state that the implementation of urban agroforestry systems offer a range of ecosystem services that can improve the health and resilience of urban areas. These benefits include improving [[Climate resilience|environmental resilience]], biodiversity, and social and cultural wellbeing.<ref name="wm">{{Cite web |title=The Edible City: Why Food Trees Matter |url=https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/2422244_E_PDF_WEB_0.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250219135632/https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/2422244_E_PDF_WEB_0.pdf |archive-date=2025-02-19 |website=unece.org |access-date=2026-03-04}}</ref>

==== Environmental resilience ====
The integration of agroforestry systems into rooftop gardens improves insulation of buildings reducing the demand of energy for cooling by up to 20%.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ASHRAE European Policy Update – May 15, 2025 – ASHRAE |url=https://ashrae-ireland.org/2025/05/15/ashrae-european-policy-update-may-15-2025/ |access-date=2026-01-29 |language=en-US}}</ref> Moreover, agroforestry systems increase permeable surfaces that alleviate urban drainage systems and enhance [[stormwater]] management.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Do Trees Improve Air Quality? – The Institute for Environmental Research and Education |date=4 June 2025 |url=https://iere.org/how-do-trees-improve-air-quality/ |access-date=2026-01-29 |language=en-US}}</ref> Finally, agroforestry systems improve air quality by absorbing pollutants like [[nitrogen dioxide]], [[ozone]] and [[particulate matter]], as well as releasing [[oxygen]] as quantified by several studies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alam |first1=Mahbubul |last2=Olivier |first2=Alain |last3=Paquette |first3=Alain |last4=Dupras |first4=Jérôme |last5=Revéret |first5=Jean-Pierre |last6=Messier |first6=Christian |date=2014-08-01 |title=A general framework for the quantification and valuation of ecosystem services of tree-based intercropping systems |journal=Agroforestry Systems |language=en |volume=88 |issue=4 |pages=679–691 |doi=10.1007/s10457-014-9681-x |bibcode=2014AgrSy..88..679A |issn=1572-9680}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stewart |first1=Stephen |last2=O'Grady |first2=Anthony |last3=Mendham |first3=Daniel |last4=Smith |first4=Greg |last5=Smethurst |first5=Philip |date=2022-09-27 |title=Digital Tools for Quantifying the Natural Capital Benefits of Agroforestry: A Review |journal=Land |language=en |volume=11 |issue=10 |page=1668 |doi=10.3390/land11101668 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2022Land...11.1668S |issn=2073-445X}}</ref><ref name=":10" />

==== Biodiversity ====
The incorporation of a vast variety of trees, shrubs, and crops creates heterogeneous habitats for various species such as pollinators, birds and small mammals leading to an increase in biodiversity. In addition, through an enhanced connectivity between habitats the persistent problem of [[habitat fragmentation]] in urban areas is alleviated.<ref name="wm"/> However, the current evidence base remains limited, with studies focusing mostly on the improvement of avian diversity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Exantus |first1=Jean-Marry |last2=Beaune |first2=David |last3=Cézilly |first3=Frank |date=2021-08-01 |title=The relevance of urban agroforestry and urban remnant forest for avian diversity in a densely-populated developing country: The case of Port-au-Prince, Haiti |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |volume=63 |article-number=127217 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2021.127217 |issn=1618-8667|doi-access=free |bibcode=2021UFUG...6327217E }}</ref> Overall, the literature supports a context-dependent benefit of agroforestry systems for biodiversity, while indicating the need for further research across a broader range of taxonomic groups, focussing more on urban and suburban areas.

==== Social and cultural wellbeing ====
Integrating food-producing trees and plants into urban landscapes enhances local self-sufficiency by increasing access to fresh, locally grown products. Still, as reported by the UN the actual and potential capacity for food production of urban agroforestry systems is often underestimated.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Oncini |first1=Filippo |last2=Hirth |first2=Steffen |last3=Mylan |first3=Josephine |last4=Robinson |first4=Clare H. |last5=Johnson |first5=David |date=2024-03-01 |title=Where the wild things are: How urban foraging and food forests can contribute to sustainable cities in the Global North |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |volume=93 |article-number=128216 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2024.128216 |bibcode=2024UFUG...9328216O |issn=1618-8667|doi-access=free}}</ref> Beyond the provision of food, these systems create green recreational spaces that support mental health, lower stress and improve community well-being.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wolf |first1=Kathleen L. |last2=Lam |first2=Sharon T. |last3=McKeen |first3=Jennifer K. |last4=Richardson |first4=Gregory R.A. |last5=van den Bosch |first5=Matilda |last6=Bardekjian |first6=Adrina C. |date=2020-06-18 |title=Urban Trees and Human Health: A Scoping Review |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |language=en |volume=17 |issue=12 |page=4371 |doi=10.3390/ijerph17124371 |doi-access=free |issn=1660-4601 |pmc=7345658 |pmid=32570770 |bibcode=2020IJERP..17.4371W}}</ref>

=== Implementation barriers and trade-offs ===
The implementation of urban agroforestry comes with a set of challenges unique to the urban setting. These barriers are often closely associated with economic (opportunity) costs and biophysical challenges.

==== Financial costs ====
Costs include expenditures for constructing and maintaining urban agroforestry spaces. These costs cover plants, equipment, and soil preparation, as well as administrative personnel and labor for pruning, weeding, pest control, and harvesting.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fox-Kämper |first1=Runrid |last2=Wesener |first2=Andreas |last3=Münderlein |first3=Daniel |last4=Sondermann |first4=Martin |last5=McWilliam |first5=Wendy |last6=Kirk |first6=Nick |date=2018-02-01 |title=Urban community gardens: An evaluation of governance approaches and related enablers and barriers at different development stages |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169204617301615 |journal=Landscape and Urban Planning |volume=170 |pages=59–68 |doi=10.1016/j.landurbplan.2017.06.023 |bibcode=2018LUrbP.170...59F |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite journal |last1=Roman |first1=Lara A. |last2=Conway |first2=Tenley M. |last3=Eisenman |first3=Theodore S. |last4=Koeser |first4=Andrew K. |last5=Ordóñez Barona |first5=Camilo |last6=Locke |first6=Dexter H. |last7=Jenerette |first7=G. Darrel |last8=Östberg |first8=Johan |last9=Vogt |first9=Jess |date=2021-03-01 |title=Beyond 'trees are good': Disservices, management costs, and tradeoffs in urban forestry |journal=Ambio |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=615–630 |doi=10.1007/s13280-020-01396-8 |issn=1654-7209 |pmc=7882647 |pmid=33011917 |bibcode=2021Ambio..50..615R }}</ref><ref name="qr">{{Cite journal |last1=Roy |first1=Sudipto |last2=Byrne |first2=Jason |last3=Pickering |first3=Catherine |date=2012-01-01 |title=A systematic quantitative review of urban tree benefits, costs, and assessment methods across cities in different climatic zones |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1618866712000829 |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=351–363 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2012.06.006 |bibcode=2012UFUG...11..351R |hdl=10072/48528 |hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hosseinpour |first1=Nazanin |last2=Kazemi |first2=Fatemeh |last3=Mahdizadeh |first3=Hassan |date=2022-01-01 |title=A cost-benefit analysis of applying urban agriculture in sustainable park design |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264837721005573 |journal=Land Use Policy |volume=112 |article-number=105834 |doi=10.1016/j.landusepol.2021.105834 |bibcode=2022LUPol.11205834H |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lafontaine-Messier |first1=Mariève |last2=Gélinas |first2=Nancy |last3=Olivier |first3=Alain |date=2016-01-01 |title=Profitability of food trees planted in urban public green areas |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1618866716000352 |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |volume=16 |pages=197–207 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2016.02.013 |bibcode=2016UFUG...16..197L |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Maintenance also includes [[irrigation]] and access to electricity, which may require permits or connection costs.<ref name="kf">{{Cite web |last1=Favor |first1=Katherine |last2=Hemmelgarn |first2=Hannah |last3=Stubblefield |first3=Kelsi |title=Urban Agroforestry |url=https://www.ncat.org/publication/urban-agroforestry/ |access-date=26 June 2026 |website=NCAT}}</ref> These upfront investments are often substantial, while the resulting ecological and social benefits only emerge after three to ten years, depending on the species.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Urban Trees: Strategies for Reducing Urban Heat Island in Cities |url=https://www.asla.org/news-insights/the-field/urban-trees-strategies-for-reducing-urban-heat-island-in-cities |website=ASLA |access-date=2026-01-29|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Selecting urban trees for ecosystem service provision |url=https://cdn.forestresearch.gov.uk/2021/05/frib001.pdf|website=cdn.forestresearch.gov.uk |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220930005805/https://cdn.forestresearch.gov.uk/2021/05/frib001.pdf|archive-date=2022-09-30 |access-date=2026-03-04}}</ref>

Besides direct financial costs, urban agroforestry can indirectly cause damages.<ref name="qr"/> Trees can negatively affect nearby gray infrastructure, as they can lift pavement and obstruct drainage systems, ultimately resulting in additional financial costs.<ref name="ReferenceA"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sousa-Silva |first1=Rita |last2=Feurer |first2=Mélanie |last3=Morhart |first3=Christopher |last4=Sheppard |first4=Jonathan P. |last5=Albrecht |first5=Stefanie |last6=Anys |first6=Markus |last7=Beyer |first7=Friderike |last8=Blumenstein |first8=Kathrin |last9=Reinecke |first9=Sabine |last10=Seifert |first10=Thomas |last11=Whitehead |first11=Ian |last12=Pauleit |first12=Stephan |last13=Bauhus |first13=Jürgen |date=2024-08-01 |title=Seeing the Trees Without the Forest: What and How can Agroforestry and Urban Forestry Learn from Each Other? |journal=Current Forestry Reports |language=en |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=239–254 |doi=10.1007/s40725-024-00221-9 |bibcode=2024CForR..10..239S |issn=2198-6436|hdl=1887/4195960 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> Even after successful implementation, challenges such as vandalism and damage from urban pests create additional barriers for urban agroforestry practices.<ref name="dm"/>

==== Biophysical challenges ====
Urban environments pose biophysical challenges, including higher temperatures, which can increase heat and drought stress on trees. Urban soils are frequently compacted and can be contaminated, limiting root development and tree health.<ref name="dm">{{Cite journal|title=Designing multifunctional urban agroforestry with people in mind|journal=Urban Agriculture & Regional Food Systems|date=2021-08-06|issn=2575-1220|volume=6|issue=1|doi=10.1002/uar2.20016|language=en|first1=John R.|last1=Taylor|first2=Sarah Taylor|last2=Lovell|article-number=e20016 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The resulting contamination can raise food safety concerns and limit the recognition of urban agriculture as a food-producing practice.<ref name="pi"/><ref>{{Citation|chapter=Raising the Ambition of Urban Agriculture in Public Space: Nurturing Urban Agroecology and More-than-Human Health|publisher=Springer International Publishing|title=Urban Agriculture in Public Space: Planning and Designing for Human Flourishing in Northern European Cities and Beyond|date=2024|place=Cham|isbn=978-3-031-41550-0|pages=285–309|doi=10.1007/978-3-031-41550-0_13|language=en|first=Chiara|last=Tornaghi|editor-first=Beata|editor-last=Sirowy|series=GeoJournal Library |volume=132 |editor2-first=Deni|editor2-last=Ruggeri}}</ref> Additionally, pollen can cause allergic reactions and thus negatively impact health.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cariñanos |first1=Paloma |last2=Casares-Porcel |first2=Manuel |last3=Quesada-Rubio |first3=Jose-Manuel |date=2014-03-01 |title=Estimating the allergenic potential of urban green spaces: A case-study in Granada, Spain |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169204613002405 |journal=Landscape and Urban Planning |volume=123 |pages=134–144 |doi=10.1016/j.landurbplan.2013.12.009 |bibcode=2014LUrbP.123..134C |issn=0169-2046|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==== Opportunity costs ====
As urban land is valuable, opportunity costs resulting from competition among different land uses can put significant constraint on the implementation due to limited land access.<ref name="pi"/><ref>{{Cite journal|title=Multifunctional Urban Agriculture for Sustainable Land Use Planning in the United States|journal=Sustainability|date=2010-08-04|issn=2071-1050|volume=2|issue=8|doi=10.3390/su2082499|language=en|first=Lovell, Sarah|last=Taylor |pages=2499–2522 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2010Sust....2.2499L}}</ref>

=== Examples/Projects ===

[[File:CapitaSpring2.jpg|thumb|upright|The food forest atop CapitaSpring in Singapore]]

Urban [[Food Forest|food forests]] are a form of urban agroforestry that mimic the natural forest ecosystem. The practice combines trees with food production and can be implemented within cities and on rooftops.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Favor |first=K. |date=September 2023 |title=Urban Agroforestry Tipsheet: food forests and beyond |url=https://attra.ncat.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/urban-agroforestry-tipsheet2-1.pdf |website=attra.ncat.org |publisher=ATTRA}}</ref> Some examples of this practice can be found in [[Singapore]] where [[roof garden]]s are utilised for urban agroforestry.<ref>{{Cite web |title=From Rooftops to Plates: Singapore's Urban Farming for a Sustainable Future {{!}} Southeast Asia |url=https://th.boell.org/en/2025/08/25/rooftops-plates-singapores-urban-farming |access-date=2026-02-02 |publisher=Heinrich Böll Foundation}}</ref>

[[File:Pear orchard - geograph.org.uk - 239741.jpg|thumb|A pear orchard near Faversham]]

[[Community orchard]]s (a prominent form of [[Community gardening|community gardens]]) represent further examples of urban agroforestry, as fruit and/or nut trees are planted (often in linear patterns) and managed by a community.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lovell |first1=Sarah |last2=Hayman |first2=Jann |last3=Hemmelgarn |first3=Hannah |last4=Hunter |first4=Andrea |last5=Taylor |first5=John |date=2021-11-07 |title=Community Orchards for Food Sovereignty, Human Health, and Climate Resilience: Indigenous Roots and Contemporary Applications |journal=Forests |volume=12 |issue=11 |page=1533 |doi=10.3390/f12111533 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021Fore...12.1533L |issn=1999-4907}}</ref>

A city farm becomes a form of urban agroforestry when it intentionally integrates trees and perennial crops with other agricultural components in the urban landscape, thus creating a multifunctional system that produces food while also supporting ecological and community benefits.<ref name="kf"/>

== Forest gardening ==

[[File:Forestgarden2.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Robert Hart (horticulturist)|Robert Hart]]'s forest garden in [[Shropshire]]. ]]

Forest gardening is a low-maintenance, [[Sustainable gardening|sustainable]],<ref>{{cite book |title=Sustaining Forest Ecosystems |author=Klaus von Gadow |author2=Juan Gabriel Álvarez González |author3=Chunyu Zhang |author4=Timo Pukkala |author5=Xiuhai Zhao |page=13 |publisher=Springer Nature |year=2021 |isbn=978-3-030-58714-7 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eyc9EAAAQBAJ&dq=%22sustainable+forest+management+system%22+%22forest+gardening%22&pg=PA13}}</ref> plant-based food production and agroforestry system based on [[woodland]] [[ecosystem]]s, incorporating [[fruit]] and [[Nut (fruit)|nut]] [[tree]]s, [[shrubs]], [[herb]]s, [[vine]]s and [[perennial vegetable]]s which have [[ecological yield|yields]] directly useful to humans. Making use of [[companion planting]], these can be [[Intercropping|intermixed]] to grow in a succession of layers to build a woodland habitat.

Forest [[gardening]] is a [[prehistory|prehistoric]] method of securing food in [[tropical climate|tropical areas]]. In the 1980s, [[Robert Hart (horticulturist)|Robert Hart]] coined the term "forest gardening" after adapting the principles and applying them to [[Temperateness|temperate climates]].<ref name="Crawford 2010 18">{{Cite book |last=Crawford |first=Martin |title=Creating a Forest Garden: Working with Nature to Grow Edible Crops |publisher=Green Books |year=2010 |page=18 |isbn=978-1-900322-62-1 |ol=24327991M}}</ref> Forest gardens, or home gardens, are common in the tropics, using [[intercropping]] to cultivate [[tree]]s, [[agriculture|crops]], and [[livestock]] on the same land. In [[Kerala]] in [[south India]] as well as in [[northeastern India]], the home garden is the most common form of land use and is also found in [[Indonesia]]. One example combines [[coconut]], [[black pepper]], [[Cocoa bean|cocoa]] and [[pineapple]]. These gardens exemplify [[polyculture]], and conserve much crop [[genetic diversity]] and [[heirloom plant]]s that are not found in [[monocultures]]. Forest gardens have been loosely compared to the religious concept of the [[Garden of Eden]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Bell |first=Graham |title=The permaculture garden |date=2004 |publisher=Permanent Publications |others=Sarah Bunker |isbn=1-85623-027-9 |location=East Meon, Hampshire, U.K. |oclc=60454349}}</ref>

=== History ===

Forest [[garden]]s are probably the world's oldest form of land use and most resilient [[agroecosystem]].<ref name="Hart-1996a">{{Cite book |last=Hart |first=Robert |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N01940btQAQC |title=Forest Gardening: Cultivating an Edible Landscape |publisher=Chelsea Green |year=1996 |isbn=978-1-60358-050-2 |edition=2nd |location=White River Junction, VT}}</ref>{{RP|124}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=McConnell |first=Douglas John |title=The forest farms of Kandy: and other gardens of complete design |date=2 March 2017 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-1-351-88963-6 |oclc=976441721 |quote=Forest gardens are probably the world's oldest form of land use and most resilient agroecosystem. They originated in prehistoric times along jungle-clad river banks and in the wet foothills of monsoon regions. ... Robert Hart adapted forest gardening for the United Kingdom's temperate climate during the 1980s.}}</ref> First Nation villages in [[Alaska]] with forest gardens filled with nuts, stone fruit, berries, and herbs, were noted by an archeologist from [[Smithsonian Institution|the Smithsonian]] in the 1930s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Coan |first=K.E.D. |date=2021-05-18 |title=Indigenous forest gardens remain productive and diverse for over a century |url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2021/05/indigenous-forest-gardens-remain-productive-and-diverse-for-over-a-century/ |access-date=2021-05-19 |website=Ars Technica}}</ref>

Forest gardens are still common in the [[tropics]] and known as Kandyan forest gardens in [[Sri Lanka]];<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jacob |first1=V. J. |last2=Alles |first2=W. S. |year=1987 |title=Kandyan gardens of Sri Lanka |journal=Agroforestry Systems |volume=5 |issue=2 |page=123 |doi=10.1007/BF00047517 |bibcode=1987AgrSy...5..123J |s2cid=40793796}}</ref> {{Lang|es|huertos familiares}}, family orchards in [[Mexico]];<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 2, 2004 |title=Inspector Gadget's green fingers and politics |first=Richard |last=Boyle |url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/books/inspector-gadgets-green-fingers-and-politics/182058.article |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120119041135/http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/story.asp?storyCode=182058&sectioncode=34 |archive-date=January 19, 2012 |website=Times Higher Education}}</ref> agroforests; or shrub gardens. They have been shown to be a significant source of income and food security for local populations.<ref>{{cite book |last=McConnell |first=Douglas John |title=The economic structure of Kandyan forest-garden farms |year=1973 |pages= }}</ref>

Robert Hart adapted forest gardening for the [[United Kingdom]]'s temperate climate during the 1980s.<ref name="Crawford 2010 18"/>

=== In temperate climates ===

[[File:Robert Hart (horticulturist).jpg|thumb|left|Robert Hart, forest gardening pioneer]]

Hart began farming at [[Wenlock Edge]] in [[Shropshire]] to provide a healthy and therapeutic environment for himself and his brother Lacon. Starting as relatively conventional [[Smallholding|smallholders]], Hart soon discovered that maintaining large annual vegetable beds, rearing livestock and taking care of an [[orchard]] were tasks beyond their strength. However, a small bed of perennial vegetables and herbs he planted was looking after itself with little intervention.<ref>{{cite web |last=Burnett |first=Graham |title=Seven Storeys of Abundance; A visit to Robert Hart's Forest Garden |url=http://www.spiralseed.co.uk/forestgarden/page2.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111117034606/http://www.spiralseed.co.uk/forestgarden/page2.html |archive-date=2011-11-17}}</ref>

Following Hart's adoption of a [[raw veganism|raw vegan diet]] for health and personal reasons, he replaced his farm animals with plants. The three main products from a forest garden are fruit, nuts and [[Leaf vegetable|green leafy vegetables]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Whitefield |first=Patrick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3rd3e69BnC8C |title=How to Make a Forest Garden |year=2002 |isbn=978-1-85623-008-7 |page=5|publisher=Permanent Publications}}</ref> He created a model forest garden from a 0.12 acre (500&nbsp;m<sup>2</sup>) orchard on his farm and intended naming his gardening method ''ecological horticulture'' or ''ecocultivation''.<ref name="Hart-1996a"/>{{RP|45}} Hart later dropped these terms once he became aware that ''agroforestry'' and ''forest gardens'' were already being used to describe similar systems in other parts of the world.<ref name="Hart-1996a"/>{{RP|28, 43}} He was inspired by the [[forest farming]] methods of [[Toyohiko Kagawa]] and James Sholto Douglas, and the productivity of the Keralan home gardens; as Hart explained, "From the agroforestry point of view, perhaps the world's most advanced country is the Indian state of Kerala, which boasts no fewer than three and a half million forest gardens ... As an example of the extraordinary intensity of cultivation of some forest gardens, one plot of only {{convert|0.12|ha|acre|abbr=off}} was found by a study group to have twenty-three young coconut palms, twelve cloves, fifty-six bananas, and forty-nine pineapples, with thirty pepper vines trained up its trees. In addition, the smallholder grew fodder for his [[house-cow]]."<ref name="Hart-1996a"/>{{RP|4-5}}
{{Clear}}

==== Seven-layer system ====

[[File:Forest garden 7 layers.gif|thumb|upright=1.5|The seven layers of the forest garden<ref name="Hemenway 2009">{{cite web |last1=Hemenway |first1=Toby |title=Designing A Food Forest: The Seven-Layer Forest Garden |url=https://www.chelseagreen.com/2024/designing-a-forest-garden-the-seven-story-garden/?srsltid=AfmBOoogC2ifI_TqGbVorPg3KvMxRr4w3v9J1YQyhGUN7m1Hz0fyqqdq |publisher=Chelsea Green Publishing |access-date=17 November 2025 |year=2009}}</ref>]]

==== Further development ====

The [[Agroforestry Research Trust]], managed by [[Martin Crawford]], runs experimental forest gardening projects on a number of plots in [[Devon]], United Kingdom.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Agroforestry Research Trust |url=http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/trustinf.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111108011007/http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/trustinf.html |archive-date=2011-11-08}}</ref> Crawford describes a forest garden as a low-maintenance way of [[Sustainable agriculture|sustainably producing food]] and other household products.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Forest gardening |url=http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/forgndg.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130211233059/http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/forgndg.html |archive-date=2013-02-11 |access-date=13 Feb 2013 |publisher=Agroforestry Research Trust}}</ref>

Ken Fern had the idea that for a successful temperate forest garden a wider range of edible shade tolerant plants would need to be used. To this end, Fern created the organisation [[Plants for a Future]] which compiled a plant database suitable for such a system. Fern used the term ''woodland gardening'', rather than forest gardening, in his book ''Plants for a Future''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Woodland Gardening |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/PlantUses.aspx?id=19 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111128033102/http://pfaf.org/user/PlantUses.aspx?id=19 |archive-date=2011-11-28}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Plants for a Future - The book |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/cmspage.aspx?pageid=32 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111128105319/http://pfaf.org/user/cmspage.aspx?pageid=32 |archive-date=2011-11-28}}</ref>

=== Projects ===

[[El Pilar]] on the [[Belize]]–[[Guatemala]] border features a forest garden to demonstrate [[Agriculture in Mesoamerica|traditional Maya agricultural]] practices.<ref name="Ford">{{Cite journal |last=Ford |first=Anabel |date=May 2, 2009 |title=El Pilar Archaeological Reserve for Maya Flora and Fauna |url=http://www.guatemala-times.com/archeology/others/1081-el-pilar-archaeological-reserve-for-maya-flora-and-fauna-.html |url-status=live |journal=The Guatemala Times |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090505115733/http://www.guatemala-times.com/archeology/others/1081-el-pilar-archaeological-reserve-for-maya-flora-and-fauna-.html |archive-date=May 5, 2009 |access-date=2009-07-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ford |first=Anabel |date=December 15, 2010 |title=Legacy of the Ancient Maya: The Maya Forest Garden |url=http://popular-archaeology.com/issue/january-2011/article/the-legacy-of-el-pilar-the-maya-forest-garden |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120115154220/http://popular-archaeology.com/issue/january-2011/article/the-legacy-of-el-pilar-the-maya-forest-garden |archive-date=January 15, 2012 |publisher=Popular Archaeology}}</ref> A further one acre model forest garden, called Känan K'aax (meaning 'well-tended garden' in Mayan), is funded by the [[National Geographic Society]] and developed at Santa Familia Primary School in [[Cayo District|Cayo]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=National Geographic Society Funds Mayan Garden |url=http://www.ambergristoday.com/content/stories/2011/may/27/national-geographic-society-funds-mayan-garden |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111223101847/http://www.ambergristoday.com/content/stories/2011/may/27/national-geographic-society-funds-mayan-garden |archive-date=2011-12-23}}</ref>

In the United States, the largest known food forest on public land is believed to be the seven acre [[Beacon Food Forest]] in Seattle, Washington.<ref name="Crosscut">{{Cite news |last=Mellinger |first= Robert |date=16 February 2012 |title=Nation's Largest Food Forest takes root on Beacon Hill |work=Crosscut |url=http://crosscut.com/2012/02/16/agriculture/21892/Nation-s-largest-public-Food-Forest-takes-root-on-Beacon-Hill |access-date=14 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120330165843/http://crosscut.com/2012/02/16/agriculture/21892/Nation-s-largest-public-Food-Forest-takes-root-on-Beacon-Hill/ |archive-date=30 March 2012}}</ref> The Boston Food Forest Coalition promotes local forest gardens.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bukowski |first1=Catherine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=44ViDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA83 |title=The Community Food Forest Handbook: How to Plan, Organize, & Nurture Edible Gathering Places |last2=Munsell |first2=John |year=2018 |isbn=978-1-60358-644-3 |pages=83–86 |publisher=Chelsea Green |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081024110544/http://www.montviewfarm.org/ |archive-date=2008-10-24 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=An Urban Food Forest: The Gift of Harvest|first = Cara |last = Brostrom |url=http://tellnewengland.com/foodforest |website=tell New England}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=He's on a mission to turn Boston into a collection of food forests |url=https://www.dotnews.com/2018/he-s-mission-turn-boston-collection-food-forests |website=Dorchester Reporter |date=16 August 2018 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=May 10, 2018 |title=Community engagement sprouts fresh ideas and nonprofit leadership |url= https://www.gmafoundations.com/nonprofit-leadership-development/ |website=GMA Foundations}}</ref>

In Canada, Richard Walker has been developing and maintaining food forests in [[British Columbia]] for over 30 years. He developed a three-acre food forest that at maturity provided raw materials for a plant nursery and herbal business as well as food for his family.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Richard Walker |url=http://www.permaculturebc.com/Permaculture-Instructor-British-Columbia-Richard-Walker |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110910135747/http://www.permaculturebc.com/Permaculture-Instructor-British-Columbia-Richard-Walker |archive-date=2011-09-10}}</ref> The Living Centre has developed various forest garden projects in [[Ontario]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Forest Gardening |url=http://www.thelivingcentre.com/cms/forest-gardening-home-page |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130526003055/http://www.thelivingcentre.com/cms/forest-gardening-home-page |archive-date=2013-05-26}}</ref>

In the United Kingdom, other than those run by the Agroforestry Research Trust (ART), projects include the Bangor Forest Garden in [[Gwynedd]], northwest Wales.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bangor Forest Garden |url=https://sites.google.com/site/bangorforestgarden/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130801112013/https://sites.google.com/site/bangorforestgarden/ |archive-date=2013-08-01}}</ref> Martin Crawford from ART administers the Forest Garden Network, an informal network of people and organisations who are cultivating forest gardens.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Agroforestry and Forest Garden Network |url=http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/fgnetwork.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120818011124/http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/fgnetwork.html |archive-date=2012-08-18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Crawford |first=Martin |year=2014 |title=List of visitable forest garden and agroforestry projects in the UK, Europe and North America |url=https://docs.google.com/file/d/0BxX6k4pU4Gt1MHpEeHh2NzNJYXc/edit |publisher=Agroforestry Research Trust}}</ref>

Since 2014, Gisela Mir and Mark Biffen have been developing a small-scale edible forest garden in [[Cardedeu]] near [[Barcelona]], Spain, for experimentation and demonstration.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-01-22 |title=El verger de Phoenicurus, un bosc comestible mediterrani |url=https://phoenicurus-permacultura.org/2016/01/22/el-verger-de-phoenicurus-un-bosc-comestible-mediterrani/ |access-date=2021-04-22 |website=phoenicurus |language=ca}}</ref>

== Forest farming ==

Forest farming is the cultivation of high-value specialty [[crops]] under a [[forest canopy]] that is intentionally modified or maintained to provide shade levels and habitat that favor growth and enhance production levels. Forest farming encompasses a range of cultivated systems from introducing plants into the [[understory]] of a timber stand to modifying forest stands to enhance the [[marketability]] and sustainable production of existing plants.<ref>{{cite web |title=Forest Farming |url=https://woodpelletmakingmachine.com/forest-farming/ |access-date=2016-01-20 |website=Forest Farming}}</ref>

[[Non-timber forest product]]s are plants, parts of plants, fungi, and other biological materials harvested from within and on the edges of natural, manipulated, or disturbed forests.<ref>Chamberlain 2009</ref> Examples include ginseng, shiitake mushrooms, decorative ferns, and pine straw.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Vaughan |first=R. C. |author2=J. F. Munsell |author3=J. L. Chamberlain |title=Opportunities for Enhancing Nontimber Forest Products Management in the United States. |journal=Journal of Forestry |year=2013 |volume=111 |issue=1 |pages=26–33 |doi=10.5849/jof.10-106 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== History ===

[[File:KAGAWA Toyohiko young.JPG |thumb |right |[[Toyohiko Kagawa]], forest farming pioneer]]

Forest farming has long been practiced around the world, as people have relied on fruits, nuts, seeds, and foliage from trees and shrubs to feed themselves and their livestock.<ref name=":11">{{cite book |last=Douglas |first=J.S. |title=Forest farming: towards a solution to problems of world hunger and conservation |year=1984 |publisher=Intermediate Technology Publications |location=London |author2=R. A. de J. Hart}}</ref>

In 1929, J. Russell Smith, emeritus Professor of Economic Geography at Columbia University, published "Tree Crops – A Permanent Agriculture," which stated that crop-yielding trees could provide useful substitutes for cereals in animal feeding programs, as well as conserve environmental health.<ref name="Douglas 1984">Douglas 1984</ref> [[Toyohiko Kagawa]] read and was heavily influenced by Smith's publication and began experimental cultivation under trees in Japan during the 1930s.

Through forest farming, or three-dimensional forestry, Kagawa addressed problems of soil erosion by persuading many of Japan's upland farmers to plant fodder trees to conserve soil, supply food and feed animals. He combined extensive plantings of walnut trees, harvested the nuts and fed them to the pigs, then sold the pigs as a source of income. When the walnut trees matured, they were sold for timber and more trees were planted so that there was a continuous cycle of economic cropping that provided both short-term and long-term income to the small landowner.<ref name=":11" /> The success of these trials prompted similar research in other countries. World War II disrupted communication and slowed advances in forest farming.<ref name="Douglas 1984" /> In the mid-1950s research resumed in places such as southern Africa. Kagawa was also an inspiration to [[Robert Hart (horticulturist)|Robert Hart]], who pioneered forest gardening in temperate climates in the sixties in Shropshire, England.<ref name="Hart-1996a" />

Livestock was formerly often considered part of the forest farming system. Now animals are typically excluded and agroforestry systems that integrate trees, forages and livestock are referred to as [[silvopasture]]s.<ref name=":12">{{cite book |last=Garrett |first=H.E. |title=North American agroforestry: an integrated science and practice |year=2009 |publisher=American Society of Agronomy |location=Madison, Wisconsin |edition=2nd |pages=}}</ref> Because forest farming combines the [[ecological stability]] of natural forests with productive agriculture systems, it is considered to have great potential for regenerating soils, restoring ground water supplies, controlling floods and droughts, and cultivating marginal lands.<ref name=":12" />

===Methods===

Forest farming methods may include thinning of overstocked tree stands; integrated entries to accomplish thinning so that systemic shock is minimized; and interactive management to maintain a cross-section of healthy trees and shrubs of all ages and species. Physical [[ecological disturbance|disturbance]] to the surrounding area should be minimized.<ref>{{cite book |title=Training manual for applied agroforestry practices |year=2006 |publisher=University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry |location=[[Columbia, Missouri]] |pages=}}</ref>

=== Food Forest ===
Food forest is a permaculture practice where it prioritizes the growth of perennial species and various layers of plants to create an edible landscape. It is characterized as a perennial polyculture.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last1=Frey |first1=Darrell |title=The food forest handbook: design and manage a home-scale perennial polyculture garden |last2=Czolba |first2=Michelle |date=2017 |publisher=new society publishers |isbn=978-1-55092-622-4 |location=Canada}}</ref> The seven layers of a food forest are as follows: Canopy trees, understory trees, shrub layer, herbaceous plants, ground cover plants, vines and root zone (rhizosphere).<ref name=":4"/> Food Garden or Food Forest are not confined to a specific geographical region or continent and can be established in various environments.<ref name=":4"/>  Food Forest are adaptable in various scale but require access to land where plants can be rooted and integrated into the soil, a key process of regenerative agriculture.<ref name=":4"/> Food Forests are composed primarily of native perennials crops and require careful design and planning before established in the soil, as they represent long-term agriculture systems, along with a foundational understanding of ecological principles.<ref name=":4"/>

==== Indigenous history ====
Indigenous peoples have managed their land for millennia, by applying various agroecology techniques and principles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Armstrong |first1=Chelsey Geralda |last2=Miller |first2=Jesse |last3=McAlvay |first3=Alex |last4=Ritchie |first4=Patrick Morgan |last5=Lepofsky |first5=Dana |date=2021-04-22 |title=Ecology and Society: Historical Indigenous Land-Use Explains Plant Functional Trait Diversity |url=https://ecologyandsociety.org/vol26/iss2/art6/ |journal=Ecology and Society |language=en |volume=26 |issue=2 |doi=10.5751/ES-12322-260206 |issn=1708-3087}}</ref> The ''Milpa'' system, is a sustainable horticulture technic used by the Maya, who are the Indigenous people of what is now known as Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.<ref name=":4"/> This ancient agroecological practice involves intercropping crops such as maize, beans, squash, and chilis.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Benrey |first1=Betty |last2=Bustos-Segura |first2=Carlos |last3=Grof-Tisza |first3=Patrick |date=2024-11-01 |title=The mesoamerican milpa system: Traditional practices, sustainability, biodiversity, and pest control |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1049964424002020 |journal=Biological Control |volume=198 |article-number=105637 |doi=10.1016/j.biocontrol.2024.105637 |bibcode=2024BiolC.19805637B |issn=1049-9644|doi-access=free }}</ref> Similarly, The Haudenosaunee, the Indigenous inhabitant that is now known as United States and Canada, used a technic, referred to as the three sisters, which requires three crops: corn, bean and squash.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Communications |title=Food And Hunting |url=https://www.haudenosauneeconfederacy.com/historical-life-as-a-haudenosaunee/food-and-hunting/ |access-date=2026-05-01 |website=Haudenosaunee Confederacy |language=en-US}}</ref> Both of these techniques requires that the crops help each other by providing nutrients to the soil, ground cover, pest control, and stability.<ref name=":5" /> For millennia, Indigenous communities, The Chumash, Yurok, Karuk, Hupa and Miwok tribes, in what is now known as California have practiced traditional agroecological methods, including controlled burning, to support ecosystem health and maintain soil fertility.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Cagle |first=Susie |date=2019-11-21 |title='Fire is medicine': the tribes burning California forests to save them |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2019/nov/21/wildfire-prescribed-burns-california-native-americans |access-date=2026-05-01 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

==== Contemporary context ====
In the 21st century, food forests have made a resurgence to address issues that current industrial agriculture practices possess.<ref name=":4" /> Agriculture contributes to nearly 30% of greenhouse gases.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |date=2016-04-13 |title=Greenhouse gas reduction |url=http://www.iaea.org/topics/greenhouse-gas-reduction |access-date=2026-05-01 |website=www.iaea.org |language=en}}</ref> Much of the emission is caused by monoculture techniques, where one single crop is grown in a field.<ref name=":6" /> With modern concern of food system, climate change and sustainable living, many experts have addressed permaculture as a mitigation tool.<ref name="Hathaway 239–250">{{Cite journal |last=Hathaway |first=Mark D. |date=2016-06-01 |title=Agroecology and permaculture: addressing key ecological problems by rethinking and redesigning agricultural systems |journal=Journal of Environmental Studies and Sciences |language=en |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=239–250 |doi=10.1007/s13412-015-0254-8 |bibcode=2016JEnSS...6..239H |issn=2190-6491}}</ref> Today, many Indigenous communities are reclaiming control over their food systems as a way of decolonization and resilience.<ref name="Lakhani">{{Cite news |last=Lakhani |first=Nina |date=2022-06-17 |title=The farmers restoring Hawaii's ancient food forests that once fed an island |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/jun/17/hawaii-traditional-farming-methods-ancient-food-forests |access-date=2026-05-01 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> In Hawaiʻi, traditional farmers are working to restore lands damaged by agrochemical corporations across the archipelago by revitalizing ancestral food forest systems that sustained their communities for millennia.<ref name="Lakhani"/>
