=== The Democratic Republic of the Congo ===
{{Main|Deforestation in Democratic Republic of the Congo}}

Deforestation in the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]] has been caused partly by unregulated logging and mining, but mostly by the demands made by the subsistence activities of a poor population. In the east of the country, for example, more than 3 million people live less than a day's walk from [[Virunga National Park]]. Wood from the park's forests is used by many of those people as firewood, lumber for construction, and for the production of charcoal. Deforestation caused by subsistence farming is an acute threat to the park in general, and the habitat of the critically endangered [[mountain gorilla]] in particular.<ref>These deforesting activities have been amply documented by numerous authors (Accion contra el Hambre, 1999; Biswas & Tortajada-Quiroz, 1996; Fuelwood Crisis Consortium, 1994; Henquin & Blondel, 1996; Lodhi et al., 1998; Blondel, 1997; Leusch, 1995; and Languy, 1995).</ref> From 2014 to 2018, the rate of tree-felling in the Democratic Republic of Congo doubled.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-49679883|title=World 'losing battle against deforestation'|last=Kinver|first=Mark|date=2019-09-12|work=BBC News|access-date=2019-09-15|archive-date=2021-06-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210618175810/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-49679883|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Harvey |first=Fiona |author-link=Fiona Harvey |date=2019-09-12 |title=Deforestation damage goes far beyond the Amazon |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2019/sep/12/deforestation-damage-goes-beyond-amazon |work=The Guardian |access-date=2019-09-15 |archive-date=2021-05-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210531070133/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2019/sep/12/deforestation-damage-goes-beyond-amazon |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Ethiopia ===
{{Main|Deforestation in Ethiopia}}

The main cause of deforestation in the [[East Africa]]n country of [[Ethiopia]] is a [[population growth|growing population]] and subsequent higher demand for agriculture, livestock production, and [[biofuel]].<ref name="Sucoff">Sucoff, E. (2003). "Deforestation". ''Environmental Encyclopedia''. pp. 358–359. Detroit: Gale.</ref> Other reasons include low education and inactivity from the government,<ref>{{cite book|last=McCann|first= J.C. |date=1999|title= Green Land, Brown Land, Black Land: An environmental history of Africa 1800–1990|location= Portsmouth, NH|publisher= Heinemann|isbn=9780852557747}}</ref> although the current government has taken some steps to tackle deforestation.<ref>{{cite book|last=Maddox|first= G.H.|date=2006|title= Sub-Saharan Africa: An environmental history|location= Santa Barbara, CA|publisher= ABC-CLIO|series=Nature and Human Societies|url=https://archive.org/details/subsaharanafrica0000madd/page/n5/mode/2up}}</ref> Organizations such as Farm Africa are working with the federal and local governments to create a system of forest management.<ref name="Parry">Parry, J. (2003). {{Full citation needed|date=June 2025}}</ref> Ethiopia, the [[List of African countries by population|second largest country in Africa]] by population, has been hit by [[famine]] many times because of shortages of rain and depletion of natural resources. Deforestation has lowered the chance of getting rain, which is already low, and increased erosion. Berkeley Bayisa, an Ethiopian farmer, offers one example of why deforestation occurs. He reported that his district was once forested and full of wildlife, but that overpopulation caused people to come and clear it to plant crops, cutting all trees to sell as firewood.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Haileselassie |first1=Ayenew |last2=Panos Features Staff |date=April 2004 |title=Ethiopia's Struggle over Land Reform |url=https://www.worldpress.org/africa/1839.cfm |journal=World Press Review |volume=51 |issue=4}}</ref>

Ethiopia has lost 98% of its forested regions in the last 50 years.<ref name="Parry"/> At the beginning of the 20th century, around {{cvt|420,000|km2}} or 35% of Ethiopia's land was covered with forests. Recent reports indicate that forests now cover less than 14.2%<ref name="Parry"/> or even only 11.9% {{as of|2005|lc=on}}.<ref name="mongabay2">{{cite web | publisher = Rhett A. Butler, mongabay.com | url = http://rainforests.mongabay.com/deforestation/2000/Ethiopia.htm | title = Statistics: Ethiopia | date = n.d. | access-date = June 4, 2007 | archive-date = November 14, 2006 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20061114000626/http://rainforests.mongabay.com/deforestation/2000/Ethiopia.htm | url-status = live }}</ref> Between 1990 and 2005, the country lost 14% of its forests or {{cvt|21,000|km2}}.

=== Kenya ===
{{Main|Deforestation in Kenya}}

In 1963, Kenya had a forest cover of some 10 percent; by 2006, it had only 1.7 percent.<ref name= Transparency2011>{{cite web | url=http://files.transparency.org/content/download/103/415/file/2011_GCRclimatechange_EN.pdf | work=Global Corruption Report 2011: Climate Change | title=The plunder of Kenya's forests: Resettling the settlers and holding the loggers accountable | author=Sheila Masinde and Lisa Karanja | publisher=Transparency International | pages=280–282 | access-date=2019-05-07 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191016140652/http://files.transparency.org/content/download/103/415/file/2011_GCRclimatechange_EN.pdf | archive-date=2019-10-16 | url-status=dead }}</ref> Between 2000 and 2020 Kenya experienced a 6% net loss in tree cover, dropping by -285kha (2850000000 m<sup>2</sup>).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kenya |url=https://www.globalforestwatch.org/dashboards/country/KEN/?category=forest-change&%3D%3D&location=WyJjb3VudHJ5IiwiS0VOIl0%3D&%3D%3D&showMap=true |access-date=27 March 2023 |website=Global Forest Watch |archive-date=27 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230327175420/https://www.globalforestwatch.org/dashboards/country/KEN/?category=forest-change&&location=WyJjb3VudHJ5IiwiS0VOIl0=&&showMap=true |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Madagascar ===
{{Main|Deforestation in Madagascar}}

Deforestation,<ref>{{cite news

|title=Saving the Wildlife of Madagascar
|newspaper= Time
|date= September 25, 2008

|url=http://www.time.com/time/health/article/0,8599,1844474,00.html
|last1=Walsh
|first1=Bryan}}</ref> with resulting [[desertification]], [[Water scarcity|water resource degradation]], and [[soil degradation|soil loss]] has affected approximately 94% of Madagascar's previously biologically productive lands. Since the arrival of humans 2000 years ago, [[Madagascar]] has lost more than 90% of its original forest.<ref>{{NatGeo ecoregion|id=at0118|name=Madagascar subhumid forests}}</ref> Most of this loss has occurred since independence from the French and is the result of local people using [[slash-and-burn]] agricultural practices as they try to subsist.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.mongabay.com/2007/0307-madagascar.html |title=Deforestation causes species extinction in Madagascar |publisher=News.mongabay.com |access-date=2010-09-10 |archive-date=2015-06-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150601234736/http://news.mongabay.com/2007/0307-madagascar.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Nigeria ===
{{Main|Deforestation in Nigeria}}

According to the FAO, Nigeria has the world's highest deforestation rate of primary forests. It has lost more than half of its primary forest in the last five years. The causes cited are logging, [[slash-and-burn|subsistence agriculture]], and the collection of fuelwood. Almost 90% of [[West Africa]]'s rainforest has been destroyed.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.csupomona.edu/~admckettrick/projects/ag101_project/html/size.html |title=Rainforests & Agriculture |publisher=Csupomona.edu |access-date=2010-09-10 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120930064512/http://www.csupomona.edu/~admckettrick/projects/ag101_project/html/size.html |archive-date=2012-09-30 }}</ref>

== Asia ==
=== East Asia ===
==== Japan ====
[[Yoichi Kuroda]] sketches a history and current outline of 'large scale land and landscape destruction' due to industrial timber and paper demands.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kuroda |first=Yoichi |title=The Development and Resource Politics Between Japan and Indonesia in the Post-War Period |url=http://wrm.org.uy/deforestation/Asia/Japan.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726121234/http://wrm.org.uy/deforestation/Asia/Japan.html |archive-date=26 July 2011 |website=World Rainforest Movement}}</ref>

=== North Asia ===
==== Russia ====
{{See also|Environmental issues in Russia#Deforestation and logging}}

Russia has the largest area of forests of any country on Earth, with around 12 million km<sup>2</sup> of [[boreal forest]], larger than the [[Amazon rainforest]]. Russia's forests contain 55% of the world's conifers and represent 11% of [[biomass]] on Earth. It is estimated that {{cvt|20,000|km2}} are deforested each year.<ref>{{Citation |title=Russia's Boreal Forests |date=November 2007 |url=http://assets.panda.org/downloads/russia_forest_cc_final_13nov07.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110917221054/http://assets.panda.org/downloads/russia_forest_cc_final_13nov07.pdf |archive-date=17 September 2011 |url-status=usurped |publisher=WWF}}</ref> Areas nearer to China are most affected, as it is the main source for timber.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://wrm.org.uy/articles-from-the-wrm-bulletin/section1/china-exporting-deforestation-and-promoting-tree-monocultures/ | title=China: Exporting deforestation and promoting tree monocultures | publisher=World Rainforest Movement | date=2001-04-13 | access-date=2019-05-07 | archive-date=2019-05-07 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190507091009/https://wrm.org.uy/articles-from-the-wrm-bulletin/section1/china-exporting-deforestation-and-promoting-tree-monocultures/ | url-status=live }}</ref> Deforestation in Russia is particularly damaging as the forests have a short growing season due to extremely cold winters and therefore take longer to recover.

=== Southeast Asia ===

Forest loss is acute in [[Southeast Asia]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=AsiaNews.it |title=China is black hole of Asia's deforestation |url=https://www.asianews.it/index.php?l=en&art=5728 |access-date=2024-10-20 |website=www.asianews.it |language=en |archive-date=2024-05-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518033542/https://www.asianews.it/index.php?l=en&art=5728 |url-status=live }}</ref> the second of the world's great biodiversity hot spots.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2003-07-23 |title=SE Asia faces 'catastrophic' extinction rate |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/3090071.stm |access-date=2024-10-20 |work=BBC News |language=en-GB |archive-date=2017-12-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201161903/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/3090071.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> According to a 2005 report conducted by the FAO, [[Vietnam]] has the second highest rate of deforestation of primary forests in the world, second to only [[Nigeria]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.mongabay.com/2005/1117-forests.html |title=Nigeria has worst deforestation rate, FAO revises figures |publisher=News.mongabay.com |date=2005-11-17 |access-date=2010-09-10 |archive-date=2009-06-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090618101657/http://news.mongabay.com/2005/1117-forests.html |url-status=live }}</ref> More than 90% of the old-growth rainforests of the [[Philippine Archipelago]] have been cut.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fieldmuseum.org/Vanishing_Treasures/Deforestation_1.htm |title=The Lost Forest |publisher=Fieldmuseum.org |access-date=2010-09-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101231111807/http://www.fieldmuseum.org/vanishing_treasures/Deforestation_1.htm |archive-date=2010-12-31 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Other Southeast Asian countries where major deforestation is ongoing are [[Cambodia]] and [[Laos]]. According to a documentary by TelePool, deforestation is being directed by [[Political corruption|corrupt]] military personnel and the government (forestry services).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ckK-tN7JtOM  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211220/ckK-tN7JtOM |archive-date=2021-12-20 |url-status=live|title=Die Tropenholz-Mafia – Kriminelle Geschäfte mit dem Regenwald – Telepool, 2008 |publisher=Youtube.com |date=2008-11-08 |access-date=2010-09-10}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

==== Indonesia ====
{{Main|Deforestation in Indonesia}}
{{See also|Deforestation of Borneo}}

{{As of|2008}}, at present rates, rainforests in [[Indonesia]] would be logged out in 10 years, [[Papua New Guinea]] in 13 to 16 years.<ref>{{Cite web |last=AsiaNews.it |title=China is black hole of Asia's deforestation |url=https://www.asianews.it/index.php?l=en&art=5728 |access-date=2024-10-20 |website=www.asianews.it |language=en |archive-date=2024-05-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518033542/https://www.asianews.it/index.php?l=en&art=5728 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Indonesia]] had lost over 72% of intact forests and 40% of all forests completely in 2005.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.greenpeace.org/usa/wp-content/uploads/legacy/Global/usa/report/2010/2/indonesian-deforestation-facts.pdf| author=Greenpeace Southeast Asia| title=Indonesian deforestation factsheet: Indonesia, a great country?| date=March 30, 2009| access-date=May 7, 2019| archive-date=May 7, 2019| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190507081656/https://www.greenpeace.org/usa/wp-content/uploads/legacy/Global/usa/report/2010/2/indonesian-deforestation-facts.pdf| url-status=live}}</ref> Illegal logging took place in 37 out of 41 national parks. Illegal logging costs up to US$4 billion a year. The lowland forests of [[Sumatra]] and [[Borneo]] were at risk of being wiped out by 2022. According to [[Transparency International]], numerous controversial court decisions in this area have raised concerns about the integrity of the judiciary.<ref name=GCR2009>{{cite web| url=https://www.transparency.org/whatwedo/publication/global_corruption_report_2009| title=Global Corruption Report 2009: Corruption and the Private Sector| author=Transparency International| page=264| date=September 14, 2009| access-date=May 7, 2019| website=transparency.org| archive-date=May 7, 2019| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190507081655/https://www.transparency.org/whatwedo/publication/global_corruption_report_2009| url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Image:Deforestation central Europe - Rodungen Mitteleuropa.jpg|thumb|350px|right|Deforestation in Europe, 2020]]

Europe has lost more than half of its forests in the past 6,000 years. This has primarily been due to [[agricultural expansion]] and demand for wood fuel.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.mongabay.com/2018/01/more-than-half-of-europes-forests-lost-over-6000-years/|title=More than half of Europe's forests lost over 6,000 years|date=2018-01-24|website=Mongabay Environmental News|language=en-US|access-date=2020-02-03|archive-date=2021-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304064319/https://news.mongabay.com/2018/01/more-than-half-of-europes-forests-lost-over-6000-years/|url-status=live}}</ref> According to satellite data, the loss of biomass in EU's forests increased by 69% in the period from 2016 to 2018, compared with the period from 2011 to 2015.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Harvey |first=Fiona |author-link=Fiona Harvey |date=2020-07-01 |title=Europe losing forest to harvesting at alarming rate, data suggests |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/jul/01/europe-losing-forest-to-harvesting-at-alarming-rate-data-suggests |access-date=2020-07-07 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077 |archive-date=2021-06-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210622062319/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/jul/01/europe-losing-forest-to-harvesting-at-alarming-rate-data-suggests |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ceccherini |first1=Guido |last2=Duveiller |first2=Gregory |last3=Grassi |first3=Giacomo |last4=Lemoine |first4=Guido |last5=Avitabile |first5=Valerio |last6=Pilli |first6=Roberto |last7=Cescatti |first7=Alessandro |date=2020-07-02 |title=Abrupt increase in harvested forest area over Europe after 2015 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2438-y |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=583 |issue=7814 |pages=72–77 |doi=10.1038/s41586-020-2438-y |pmid=32612223 |bibcode=2020Natur.583...72C |issn=0028-0836|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Iceland===
Prior to the [[Settlement of Iceland#Environmental effects|deforestation of Iceland in the Middle Ages]], some 40% of the land was forested.<ref>{{cite web |last=Beach |first=Greg |date=6 April 2018 |title=Iceland is replanting its forests 1,000 years after vikings razed them |url=https://inhabitat.com/iceland-is-regrowing-its-forests-1000-years-after-vikings-razed-them/ |access-date=17 December 2023 |website=INHABITAT |publisher=MH Sub I, LLC dba Inhabitat |archive-date=29 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230129220105/https://inhabitat.com/iceland-is-regrowing-its-forests-1000-years-after-vikings-razed-them/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Today, the country is about 2% forested, with the [[Icelandic Forest Service]] aiming to increase that share to 10% through [[Reforestation#Iceland|reforestation]] and natural regrowth.<ref>{{cite web |last=Rossi |first=Marcello |date=29 December 2017 |title=Spades, saplings and sheep: Iceland battles to restore long-lost forests |url=https://www.skogur.is/en/moya/news/spades-saplings-and-sheep-iceland-battles-to-restore-long-lost-forests |website=SKÓGRÆKTIN Icelandic Forest Service |access-date=6 July 2023 |archive-date=7 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230707161500/https://www.skogur.is/en/moya/news/spades-saplings-and-sheep-iceland-battles-to-restore-long-lost-forests |url-status=live }}</ref>

Iceland has undergone extensive deforestation since Scandinavians settled in the ninth century. At the time of human settlement about 1,150 years ago, birch forest and woodland covered 'at least 25%' of Iceland's land area. The settlers began by cutting down the forests and burning shrubland to create fields and grazing land. Deforestation did not end in Iceland until the middle of the 20th century. Afforestation and revegetation have restored small areas of land.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://landbunadur.is/landbunadur/wgrala.nsf/key2/hhjn7etf6x.html |title=LandUse: Why Iceland |publisher=Landbunadur.is |date=2008-05-09 |access-date=2010-09-10 |archive-date=2009-05-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090513053757/http://landbunadur.is/landbunadur/wgrala.nsf/key2/hhjn7etf6x.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> However, agriculture was the main reason birch forests and woodland did not grow back.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}}

===Ireland===
Ireland was historically a [[temperate rainforest]] with 80% of the island under tree cover. Deforestation by humans began taking place already in the Bronze Age but reached its peak under British colonial rule, particularly the 16th and 17th century [[Plantations of Ireland|Plantations]], that saw mass scale deforestation to create agricultural lands, and to supplement the need for timber for shipbuilding for Britain's early phase of empire building.<ref>{{cite web |last=Northern |first=Black |title=The Plantation of Ulster and Its Effect on Native Woodlands |url=https://meonjournal.com/read/the-plantation-of-ulster-and-its-effect-on-native-woodlands |website=Meon Journal |access-date=2024-09-12 |archive-date=2024-09-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240912094059/https://meonjournal.com/read/the-plantation-of-ulster-and-its-effect-on-native-woodlands |url-status=live }}</ref> Tree cover reached its lowest point of 1.5% at the beginning of the twentieth century, prior to Irish independence, due to more industrialised sawmills used in late nineteenth century. The Irish state promoted reforestation during the 20th century, reversing the trend (albeit primarily via plantations of non-native conifers intended for felling), with an increase to 12% tree cover today, which still however remains one of the lowest percentages in Europe, where the average is 39%.<ref>{{cite web |title=Forests, forestry and logging |url=https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Forests,_forestry_and_logging |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240927150708/https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Forests%2C_forestry_and_logging |archive-date=2024-09-27 |access-date=2024-09-12 |website=eurostat Statistics Explained}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=History of Forestry in Ireland |url=https://www.teagasc.ie/crops/forestry/advice/general-topics/history-of-forestry-in-ireland/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130053644/https://www.teagasc.ie/crops/forestry/advice/general-topics/history-of-forestry-in-ireland/ |archive-date=2019-01-30 |access-date=2024-09-12 |website=Teagasc &#124; Agriculture and Food Development Authority}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Baraniuk |first=Chris |date=12 February 2021 |title=What would a truly wild Ireland look like? |url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20210211-rewilding-can-ireland-regrow-its-wilderness |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210217105438/https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20210211-rewilding-can-ireland-regrow-its-wilderness |archive-date=2021-02-17 |access-date=2024-09-12 |website=BBC News}}</ref>

===Italy===
[[File:Veduta-Vallone-Caltanissetta.jpg|thumb|Countryside of central Sicily]] [[Sicily]] is an oft-cited example of man-made deforestation, practiced since Roman times when the island was made into an agricultural region,<ref name=frommers>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vZDLw0nOnfsC&pg=PA26 |title=Frommer's Sicily |author=Darwin Porter |author2=Danforth Prince |publisher=Frommer's |year=2009 |page=268|isbn=9780470398999 }}</ref> and continued to this day. Deforestation gradually modified the climate, leading to a decline in rainfall and the drying of rivers. Today, the entire central and southwest provinces are practically without any forests.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bestofsicily.com/mag/art51.htm |title=A Sicilian Desert? |first=Carlo |last=Trabia |publisher=Best of Sicily Magazine |year=2002 |access-date=2011-07-13 |archive-date=2002-06-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020602183405/http://www.bestofsicily.com/mag/art51.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> This has also affected Sicily's wild fauna, of which little is left in the island's pastures and crop fields.<ref name=frommers/>

===Netherlands===
[[File:NL-Nationaleparken.svg|thumb|Map of national parks in the Netherlands.]]
The Netherlands, once home to [[forest]]s and [[marsh]]es, has also experienced deforestation. The remaining forests and marshes are strictly regulated by [[staatsbosbeheer]] (or in English: state forest management) and crisscrossed by service roads and cycling paths. But they are also protected by the Dutch government with the government taking action with many national parks and protected regions.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}}

=== Central America ===
{{Main|Deforestation in Central America}}

The history of most Central American countries involves cycles of [[deforestation]] and reforestation. By the 15th century, intensive Mayan agriculture had significantly thinned the forests. Before Europeans arrived, forests covered 500,000 square km– approximately 90% of the region. Eventually, the forcing of "Europe's money economy on Latin America" created the demand for the exportation of primary products, which introduced the need for large amounts of cleared agricultural land to produce those products.<ref name="Myers, Norman 1987">{{Cite journal |last1=Myers |first1=Norman |last2=Tucker |first2=Richard |date=1987 |title=Deforestation in Central America: Spanish Legacy and North American Consumers |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3984219 |journal=Environmental Review |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=55–71 |doi=10.2307/3984219 |jstor=3984219 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Since the 1960s, cattle ranching has become the primary reason for land clearing. The lean grass-fed cattle produced by Central American ranches (as opposed to grain-fed cattle raised elsewhere) was perfectly suited for American [[fast-food]] restaurants and this seemingly bottomless market has created the so-called "hamburger connection" which links "consumer lifestyles in North America with deforestation in Central America".<ref name="Myers, Norman 1987"/>

=== Northern America ===
==== Canada ====
{{Update section|date=December 2019}}

[[File:A "Working Forest".jpg|thumb|Though replanted in 1987, this forest near Clayoquot Sound, British Columbia lost much topsoil and resembled a desert by 1993]]

In 2005, an estimated 56,000 hectares were deforested in Canada. Deforestation affected less than 0.02% of Canada's forests in 2005. The agricultural sector accounted for just over half of the deforestation in 2005, the result of forests having been cleared for pasture or crops. The remainder was caused by urban development, transportation corridors, and recreation (19%); hydroelectric development (10%); the forest sector (10%); and other natural resource extraction industries (8%). About two thirds of this deforestation occurred in [[Canada's boreal forest]], mainly in Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba where the forest borders the Prairies.<ref>{{cite web |date=May 2008 |title=Deforestation in Canada – What Are the Facts? |url=http://cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/pubwarehouse/pdfs/28159.pdf |access-date=2018-04-17 |publisher=Natural Resources Canada |archive-date=2018-05-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180516184451/http://cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/pubwarehouse/pdfs/28159.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

In Canada, prior to 2000, less than 8% of the boreal forest was protected from development and more than 50% has been allocated to logging companies for cutting.<ref>{{Citation |title=Canada's Forests at a Crossroads: An Assessment in the Year 2000 |date=2000 |url=https://files.wri.org/d8/s3fs-public/pdf/gfw_canada.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240629163234/https://files.wri.org/d8/s3fs-public/pdf/gfw_canada.pdf |archive-date=29 June 2024 |url-status=live |place=Washington, DC |publisher=Global Forest Watch, World Resources Institute}}</ref>

===== British Columbia =====
{{Excerpt|Deforestation in British Columbia}}

==== United States ====
{{Main|Deforestation in the United States}}

[[File:Lewis and Clark River 2148s.JPG|thumb|Clearcutting in [[Clatsop County, Oregon]]]]

In 1600, prior to the arrival of European-Americans, roughly half of the land area of the present-day United States was forest{{snd}}about {{convert|4000000|km2|acre}}. For the next 300 years land was cleared, mostly for agriculture, at a rate that matched the rate of population growth. For every person added to the population, one to two hectares of land was cultivated. This trend continued until the 1920s when the amount of crop land stabilized in spite of continued population growth. As abandoned farmland reverted to forest, the amount of forestland increased from 1952, reaching a peak in 1963 of {{convert|3,080,000|km2|acre|abbr=on}}. Since 1963 there has been a steady decrease of forest area with the exception of some gains from 1997.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}}

==Oceania==
===Australia===
{{Main|Land clearing in Australia}}

Due to relatively recent colonisation, Australia has had high rates of deforestation, primarily due to clearing for agricultural purposes.<ref name=":1">{{Citation |last=Australian Greenhouse Office |title=Land Clearing: A Social History |date=September 2000 |url=http://www.climatechange.gov.au/ncas/reports/pubs/tr04final.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080720125539/http://www.climatechange.gov.au/ncas/reports/pubs/tr04final.pdf |url-status=dead |series=National Carbon Accounting System Technical Report no. 4 |archive-date=20 July 2008}}</ref> Since colonisation approximately 50% of rainforests have been cleared and overall forest cover has reduced by over a third.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Land clearing |url=https://www.bushheritage.org.au/what-we-do/our-challenge/land-clearing |access-date=2023-12-17 |website=BushHeritageMVC |language=en |archive-date=2024-01-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240119162715/https://www.bushheritage.org.au/what-we-do/our-challenge/land-clearing |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2007, rates were expected to decrease with the implementation of new legislation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fpa.tas.gov.au/fileadmin/user_upload/PDFs/Botany/Land_Clearing_Information_Sheet_feb_08.pdf| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090519024800/http://www.fpa.tas.gov.au/fileadmin/user_upload/PDFs/Botany/Land_Clearing_Information_Sheet_feb_08.pdf|archive-date=2009-05-19|website= Forest Practices Authority|date= 2007|title=Information on Land Clearing Controls in Tasmania }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wwf.org.au/articles/feature08/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090623054809/http://www.wwf.org.au/articles/feature08/|archive-date=2009-06-23|website= WWF-Australia|title=World class legislation – new land clearing policy for Queensland|date=29 April 2004 }}</ref>

In 1998, deforestation was thought to be responsible for around 12% of Australia's total carbon emissions.<ref name=":1" /> Between 2000 and 2015 emissions from land clearing decreased by 64%.<ref>{{Citation |title=Tracking to 2020 An interim update of Australia's greenhouse gas emissions projections |date=December 2015 |url=http://www.environment.gov.au/system/files/resources/d46b4104-0a04-4efb-9e83-df97e58eb2ff/files/tracking-to-2020-interim-update-emissions-projections.pdf |pages=18–19 |access-date=17 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160418202901/http://www.environment.gov.au/system/files/resources/d46b4104-0a04-4efb-9e83-df97e58eb2ff/files/tracking-to-2020-interim-update-emissions-projections.pdf |url-status=dead |publisher=Australia Department of the Environment |archive-date=18 April 2016 }}</ref>

An additional factor currently causing the loss of forest cover is the expansion of [[urban area]]s. [[Littoral]] rainforest growing along coastal areas of eastern Australia is now rare due to [[ribbon development]] to accommodate the demand for [[seachange (demography)|seachange]] lifestyles.<ref>{{cite web |title=Littoral Rainforest – Why is it threatened? |url=http://www.pittwater.nsw.gov.au/environment/plants__and__animals/threatened_species/endangered_ecological_communities/littoral_rainforest |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090621043641/http://www.pittwater.nsw.gov.au/environment/plants__and__animals/threatened_species/endangered_ecological_communities/littoral_rainforest |archive-date=2009-06-21 |access-date=2010-09-10 |publisher=Pittwater Council}}</ref>

===New Zealand===
{{Main|Deforestation in New Zealand}}

In the 800 years of human occupation of New Zealand, 75% of the forests have been lost. Initially, it was by wholesale burning by the British. Remaining forests were logged for lumber for the burgeoning population. By 2000, all logging of native trees on public land was stopped. Logging on private land is controlled with a permit system and with the [[Resource Management Act 1991|Resource Management Act]].{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}}

===Papua New Guinea===
{{Main|Deforestation in Papua New Guinea}}

[[Papua New Guinea]] has one of the world's largest [[rainforests]]. Illegal logging was among highest in the world in 2007, estimated as ca 70–90% of all timber export.<ref name="GCR2011">{{Citation |last=Alley |first=Patrick |title=Global Corruption Report |date=2011 |pages=299–314 |url=https://images.transparencycdn.org/images/2011_GCRclimatechange_EN.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210825140608/https://images.transparencycdn.org/images/2011_GCRclimatechange_EN.pdf |archive-date=25 August 2021 |url-status=live |chapter=6.1 Corruption: a root cause of deforestation and forest degradation |publisher=Earthscan}}</ref>

There is no agreement on what drives deforestation in Brazil, though a broad consensus exists that expansion of croplands and pastures is important. Increases in [[commodity]] prices may increase the rate of deforestation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.mongabay.com/2007/0516-ethanol_amazon.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120713153639/http://news.mongabay.com/2007/0516-ethanol_amazon.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-07-13 |title=U.S. ethanol may drive Amazon deforestation displacement of beef ranches and farms of other crops, which, in turn, move farther into the forest.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mongabay.com/external/soybeans2003.htm |title=Booming Soybean Business Means Continued Deforestation in the Amazon |publisher=Mongabay.com |access-date=2010-09-10 |archive-date=2009-06-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090614002744/http://www.mongabay.com/external/soybeans2003.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Certain areas such as the [[Atlantic Rainforest]] have been diminished to just 7% of their original size.<ref>{{cite web| url= http://www.panda.org/about_wwf/where_we_work/ecoregions/atlantic_forests.cfm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080503205418/http://www.panda.org/about_wwf/where_we_work/ecoregions/atlantic_forests.cfm| url-status=dead | title=Atlantic Forests – A Global Ecoregion| author=World Wildlife Fund| archive-date=2008-05-03| date=2007-01-22 }}</ref> Although much conservation work has been done, few national parks or reserves are efficiently enforced.<ref>{{cite news | [[Amazon Rainforest|Amazon]] is [[Illegal logging|illegal]].<ref>{{cite web | author=Paul Toyne, Cliona O'Brien and Rod Nelson | publisher=WWF International | year=2002 | In 2008, Brazil's government announced a record rate of deforestation in the Amazon.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.irishtimes.com/newspaper/breaking/2008/0124/breaking22.html |title=Record Amazon deforestation in Brazil |publisher=Irishtimes.com |date=2008-01-24 |access-date=2010-09-10 |archive-date=2013-01-27 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130127060835/http://www.irishtimes.com/newspaper/breaking/2008/0124/breaking22.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/7206165.stm|title=Brazil Amazon deforestation soars|date=2008-01-24|work=BBC News|access-date=2019-05-07|archive-date=2009-02-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090214210113/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/7206165.stm|url-status=live}}</ref> Deforestation jumped by 69% in 2008 compared to 2007's twelve

===Chile===
Despite modern views of [[Atacama Desert]] as fully devoid of vegetation in pre-Hispanic and Colonial times a large flatland area known as [[Pampa del Tamarugal]] was forested, with demand of firewood associated silver and [[Nitratine|saltpeter]] mining causing widespread deforestation. While [[Department of Tarapacá (Peru)|Tarapacá]] was still part of Peru demand of firewood by salpeter processing using the [[paradas method]] led to widespread deforestation around [[La Tirana]] and [[Canchones]] plus some areas to the south of these localities.<ref name=Castro2020>{{Cite journal|title=El bosque de la Pampa del Tamarugal y la industria salitrera: El problema de la deforestación, los proyectos para su manejo sustentable y el debate político (Tarapacá, Peru-Chile 1829–1941)|journal=Scripta Nova|url=https://revistes.ub.edu/index.php/ScriptaNova/article/viewFile/26507/31629|last=Castro Castro|first=Luis|date=2020-07-01|volume=XXIV|publisher=[[Universitat de Barcelona]]|issue=641|language=Spanish|trans-title=The Forest of Pampa del Tamarugal and the Saltpeter Industry: The Deforestation Problem, the Projects for their Sustainable Management and the Political Debate (Tarapacá, Perú-Chile 1829–1941)|access-date=2021-01-26|archive-date=2021-01-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210130161008/https://revistes.ub.edu/index.php/ScriptaNova/article/viewFile/26507/31629|url-status=live}}</ref> Reforestation efforts in Pampa del Tamarugal begun in 1963 and since 1987 reforestated areas are protected in the [[Pampa del Tamarugal National Reserve]].<ref name=Castro2020/>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Ecosystem collapse
======================================================================

{{Short description|Ecological communities abruptly losing biodiversity, often irreversibly}}
[[File:Aral Sea 1964 vs. August 25, 2026.png|thumb|300x300px|Image of the [[Aral Sea]] in August 22, 1964 (left) and August 25, 2026. The Aral Sea is an example of a collapsed ecosystem.<ref name="Keith2013"/> (image source: [[NASA]])]]
An [[ecosystem]], short for ecological [[systems theory|system]], is defined as a collection of interacting [[organism]]s within a [[biophysical environment]].<ref name="Chapinglossary">{{Cite book|last=Chapin|first=F. Stuart III|title=Principles of terrestrial ecosystem ecology|date=2011|publisher=Springer|others=P. A. Matson, Peter Morrison Vitousek, Melissa C. Chapin|isbn=978-1-4419-9504-9|edition=2nd|location=New York|chapter=Glossary|oclc=755081405}}</ref>{{rp|458}} Ecosystems are never static, and are continually subject to both stabilizing and destabilizing processes.<ref name="Allesina2012">{{Cite journal |last1=Allesina |first1=Stefano |last2=Tang |first2=Si |title=Stability criteria for complex ecosystems |date=19 February 2012 |journal=Nature |volume=483 |issue=7388 |pages=205–208 |doi=10.1038/nature10832 |pmid=22343894 |arxiv=1105.2071 }}</ref> Stabilizing processes allow ecosystems to adequately respond to destabilizing changes, or perturbations, in ecological conditions, or to recover from degradation induced by them. Yet, if destabilizing processes become strong enough or fast enough to cross a critical threshold within that ecosystem, often described as an ecological 'tipping point', then an '''ecosystem collapse''' (sometimes also termed '''ecological collapse''')<ref name="GTCFEcological">{{Cite web|title=Ecological collapse|url=https://globalchallenges.org/global-risks/ecological-collapse/|access-date=2021-12-03|website=The Global Challenges Foundation|language=en-US}}</ref> occurs.<ref name="Canadell2021">{{Cite book |last1=Canadell |first1=Josep G. |last2=Jackson |first2=Robert B. |chapter=Ecosystem Collapse and Climate Change: An Introduction|date=2021|title=Ecosystem Collapse and Climate Change|pages=1–9|place=Cham|publisher=Springer International Publishing|series=Ecological Studies |volume=241 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-71330-0_1 |isbn=978-3-030-71329-4 |s2cid=237994459 }}</ref>

Ecosystem collapse does not mean total disappearance of life from the area, but it does result in the loss of the original ecosystem's defining characteristics, typically including the [[ecosystem services]] it may have provided. Collapse of an ecosystem is effectively irreversible more often than not, and even if the reversal is possible, it tends to be slow and difficult.<ref name="Bergstrom-Wienecke2021" /><ref name="Keith2013" /> Ecosystems with low resilience may collapse even during a comparatively stable time, which then typically leads to their replacement with a more resilient system in the [[biosphere]]. However, even resilient ecosystems may disappear during the times of rapid environmental change,<ref name="Canadell2021" /> and study of the [[fossil record]] was able to identify how certain ecosystems went through a collapse, such as with the [[Carboniferous rainforest collapse]] or the collapse of [[Lake Baikal]] and [[Lake Hovsgol]] ecosystems during the [[Last Glacial Maximum]].<ref name="Karabanov2004" /><ref name="Sahney2010" />

Today, the ongoing [[Holocene extinction]] is caused primarily by [[human impact on the environment]], and the greatest [[biodiversity loss]] so far had been due to [[habitat degradation]] and [[habitat fragmentation|fragmentation]], which eventually destroys entire ecosystems if left unchecked.<ref>{{cite web| title=Living Planet Report|publisher=World Wildlife Fund|url=http://wwf.panda.org/about_our_earth/all_publications/living_planet_report/}}</ref> There have been multiple notable examples of such an ecosystem collapse in the recent past, such as the [[collapse of the Atlantic northwest cod fishery]].<ref name="Hamilton2001" /> More are likely to occur without a change in course, since estimates show that 87% of oceans and 77% of the land surface have been altered by humanity, with 30% of global land area is degraded and a global decline in ecosystem resilience.<ref name="Bergstrom-Wienecke2021">{{Cite journal |last1=Bergstrom |first1=Dana M. |last2=Wienecke |first2=Barbara C. |last3=van den Hoff |first3=John |last4=Hughes |first4=Lesley |last5=Lindenmayer |first5=David B. |last6=Ainsworth |first6=Tracy D. |last7=Baker |first7=Christopher M. |last8=Bland |first8=Lucie |last9=Bowman |first9=David M. J. S. |last10=Brooks |first10=Shaun T. |last11=Canadell |first11=Josep G. |last12=Constable |first12=Andrew J. |last13=Dafforn |first13=Katherine A. |last14=Depledge |first14=Michael H. |last15=Dickson |first15=Catherine R. |last16=Duke |first16=Norman C. |last17=Helmstedt |first17=Kate J. |last18=Holz |first18=Andrés |last19=Johnson |first19=Craig R. |last20=McGeoch |first20=Melodie A. |last21=Melbourne-Thomas |first21=Jessica |last22=Morgain |first22=Rachel |last23=Nicholson |first23=Emily |last24=Prober |first24=Suzanne M. |last25=Raymond |first25=Ben |last26=Ritchie |first26=Euan G. |last27=Robinson |first27=Sharon A. |last28=Ruthrof |first28=Katinka X. |last29=Setterfield |first29=Samantha A. |last30=Sgrò |first30=Carla M. |last31=Stark |first31=Jonathan S. |last32=Travers |first32=Toby |last33=Trebilco |first33=Rowan |last34=Ward |first34=Delphi F. L. |last35=Wardle |first35=Glenda M. |last36=Williams |first36=Kristen J. |last37=Zylstra |first37=Phillip J. |last38=Shaw |first38=Justine D. |date=25 February 2021 |title=Combating ecosystem collapse from the tropics to the Antarctic |journal=Global Change Biology |volume=27 |issue=9 |pages=1692–1703 |doi=10.1111/gcb.15539 |pmid=33629799 |doi-access=free |hdl=10536/DRO/DU:30148368 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> [[Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest]] is the most dramatic example of a massive, continuous ecosystem and a [[biodiversity]] hotspot being under the immediate threat from [[habitat destruction]] through logging, and the less-visible, yet ever-growing and persistent threat from [[climate change]].<ref name="Boulton2022" /><ref name="Carrington2022" />

[[Biological conservation]] can help to preserve threatened species and threatened ecosystems alike. However, time is of the essence. Just as interventions to preserve a species have to occur before it falls below viable population limits, at which point an [[extinction debt]] occurs regardless of what comes after, efforts to protect ecosystems must occur in response to early warning signals, before the tipping point to a [[regime shift]] is crossed. Further, there is a substantial gap between the extent of scientific knowledge how extinctions occur, and the knowledge about how ecosystems collapse. While there have been efforts to create objective criteria used to determine when an ecosystem is at risk of collapsing, they are comparatively recent, and are not yet as comprehensive. While the [[IUCN Red List]] of threatened species has existed for decades, the [[IUCN Red List of Ecosystems]] has only been in development since 2008.<ref name="Keith2013" /><ref name="Bergstrom-Wienecke2021" />

== Definition ==
Ecosystem collapse has been defined as a "transformation of identity, loss of defining features, and replacement by a novel ecosystem", and involves the loss of "defining biotic or abiotic features", including the ability to sustain the species which used to be associated with that ecosystem.<ref name="Keith2013" /> According to another definition, it is "a change from a baseline state beyond the point where an ecosystem has lost key defining features and functions, and is characterised by declining spatial extent, increased environmental degradation, decreases in, or loss of, key [[species]], disruption of biotic processes, and ultimately loss of [[ecosystem services]] and functions".<ref name="Bergstrom-Wienecke2021" /> Ecosystem collapse has also been described as "an analogue of [[species extinction]]", and in many cases, it is irreversible, with a new ecosystem appearing instead, which may retain some characteristics of the previous ecosystem, yet has a greatly altered structure and function.<ref name="Keith2013" /> There are exceptions where an ecosystem can be recovered past the point of a collapse,<ref name="Boitani2014">{{cite journal|last1=Boitani|first1=Luigi|last2=Mace|first2=Georgina M. |last3=Rondinini|first3=Carlo |title=Challenging the Scientific Foundations for an IUCN Red List of Ecosystems|journal=Conservation Letters|doi=10.1111/conl.12111 |volume=8|issue=2|date=2014|pages=125–131|hdl=11573/624610 |url=http://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/1443166/1/conl12111.pdf |doi-access=free}}</ref> but by definition, will always be far more difficult to reverse than allowing a disturbed yet functioning ecosystem to recover, requiring active intervention and/or a prolonged period of time even if it can be reversed.<ref name="Bergstrom-Wienecke2021" /><ref name="Keith2013">{{cite journal|last1=Keith|first1=DA|last2=Rodríguez|first2=J.P.|last3=Rodríguez-Clark|first3=K.M.|last4=Aapala|first4=K.|last5=Alonso|first5=A.|last6=Asmussen|first6=M.|last7=Bachman|first7=S.|last8=Bassett|first8=A.|last9=Barrow|first9=E.G.|last10=Benson|first10=J.S.|last11=Bishop|first11=M.J.|last12=Bonifacio|first12=R.|last13=Brooks|first13=T.M.|last14=Burgman|first14=M.A.|last15=Comer|first15=P.|last16=Comín|first16=F.A.|last17=Essl|first17=F.|last18=Faber-Langendoen|first18=D.|last19=Fairweather|first19=P.G.|last20=Holdaway|first20=R.J.|last21=Jennings|first21=M.|last22=Kingsford|first22=R.T.|last23=Lester|first23=R.E.|last24=Mac Nally|first24=R.|last25=McCarthy|first25=M.A.|last26=Moat|first26=J.|last27=Nicholson|first27=E.|last28=Oliveira-Miranda|first28=M.A.|last29=Pisanu|first29=P.|last30=Poulin|first30=B.|last31=Riecken|first31=U.|last32=Spalding|first32=M.D.|last33=Zambrano-Martínez|first33=S.|title=Scientific Foundations for an IUCN Red List of Ecosystems|journal=PLOS ONE|date=2013|volume=8|issue=5|article-number=e62111|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0062111|pmid=23667454|pmc=3648534|bibcode=2013PLoSO...862111K|url=https://iucnrle.org/resources/key-documents/|access-date=8 September 2018|doi-access=free|archive-date=28 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028130727/https://iucnrle.org/resources/key-documents/}}</ref>

== Drivers ==
[[File:Keith2013_process_circle.png|thumb|A diagram of the typical drivers of ecosystem collapse.<ref name="Keith2013" />]]
While collapse events can occur naturally with disturbances to an ecosystem—through fires, landslides, flooding, severe weather events, disease, or [[species invasion]]—there has been a noticeable increase in human-caused disturbances over the past fifty years.<ref name="GTCFEcological"/><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=MacDougall|first1=A. S.|last2=McCann|first2=K. S.|last3=Gellner|first3=G.|last4=Turkington|first4=R.|date=2013-02-06|title=Diversity loss with persistent human disturbance increases vulnerability to ecosystem collapse|journal=Nature|volume=494|issue=7435|pages=86–89|doi=10.1038/nature11869|pmid=23389543 |bibcode=2013Natur.494...86M |s2cid=4320064 |issn=0028-0836}}</ref> The combination of environmental change and the presence of human activity is increasingly detrimental to ecosystems of all types, as our unrestricted actions often increase the risk of abrupt (and potentially irreversible) changes post-disturbance; when a system would otherwise have been able to recover.<ref name=":1" />

Some behaviors that induce transformation are: human intervention in the balance of local diversity (through introduction of new species or [[overexploitation]]), alterations in the chemical balance of environments through pollution, modifications of local climate or weather with [[Anthropogenic climate change|anthropogenic]] climate change, and habitat destruction or [[Habitat fragmentation|fragmentation]] in terrestrial/marine systems.<ref name="GTCFEcological"/> For instance, [[overgrazing]] was found to cause [[land degradation]], specifically in [[Southern Europe]], which is another driver of ecological collapse and natural landscape loss. Proper management of pastoral landscapes can mitigate risk of [[desertification]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Exploring the Impact of Overgrazing on Soil Erosion and Land Degradation in a Dry Mediterranean Agro-Forest Landscape (Crete, Greece)|journal = Arid Land Research and Management|date = 2015-07-03|issn = 1532-4982|pages = 360–374|volume = 29|issue = 3|doi = 10.1080/15324982.2014.968691|first1 = Orestis|last1 = Kairis|first2 = Christos|last2 = Karavitis|first3 = Luca|last3 = Salvati|first4 = Aikaterini|last4 = Kounalaki|first5 = Kostas|last5 = Kosmas|s2cid = 128464303}}</ref>

Despite the strong empirical evidence and highly visible collapse-inducing disturbances, anticipating collapse is a complex problem. The collapse can happen when the ecosystem's distribution decreases below a minimal sustainable size, or when key biotic processes and features disappear due to [[environmental degradation]] or disruption of biotic interactions. These different pathways to collapse can be used as criteria for estimating the risk of ecosystem collapse.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gigante|first1=Daniela|last2=Foggi|first2=Bruno|last3=Venanzoni|first3=Roberto|last4=Viciani|first4=Daniele|last5=Buffa|first5=Gabriella|date=2016|title=Habitats on the grid: The spatial dimension does matter for red-listing|url=https://iris.unive.it/bitstream/10278/3671359/2/2016_Gigante_etal_Habitats%20on%20the%20grid.pdf|journal=Journal for Nature Conservation|volume=32|pages=1–9|doi=10.1016/j.jnc.2016.03.007|bibcode=2016JNatC..32....1G |hdl-access=free|hdl=10278/3671359}}</ref><ref name="BlandMAR">{{cite journal|last1=Bland|first1=L.|last2=Regan|first2=T.|last3=Ngoc Dinh|first3=M.|last4=Ferrari|first4=R.|last5=Keith|first5=D.|last6=Lester|first6=R.|last7=Mouillot|first7=D.|last8=Murray|first8=N.|last9=Anh Nguyen|first9=H.|last10=Nicholson|first10=E.|date=2017|title=Meso-American Reef: Using multiple lines of evidence to assess the risk of ecosystem collapse|url=https://iucnrle.org/resources/published-assessments/|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B|volume=284|issue=1863|article-number=20170660|doi=10.1098/rspb.2017.0660|pmc=5627190|pmid=28931744|access-date=9 September 2018|archive-date=28 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028162615/https://iucnrle.org/resources/published-assessments/}}</ref> Although states of ecosystem collapse are often defined quantitatively, few studies adequately describe transitions from pristine or original state towards collapse.<ref name="Bland2018">{{cite journal|last1=Bland|first1=L.|last2=Rowland|first2=J.|last3=Regan|first3=T.|last4=Keith|first4=D.|last5=Murray|first5=N.|last6=Lester|first6=R.|last7=Linn|first7=M.|last8=Rodríguez|first8=J.P.|last9=Nicholson|first9=E.|date=2018|title=Developing a standardized definition of ecosystem collapse for risk assessment|journal=Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment|volume=16|issue=1|pages=29–36|doi=10.1002/fee.1747|doi-access=free|hdl=11343/283474|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Sato2017" />

== Geological record ==
{{See also|Regime shift}}
In another example, 2004 research demonstrated how during the [[Last Glacial Maximum]] (LGM), alternations in the environment and climate led to a collapse of [[Lake Baikal]] and [[Lake Hovsgol]] ecosystems, which then drove species evolution.<ref name="Karabanov2004">{{Cite journal|title = Ecological collapse of Lake Baikal and Lake Hovsgol ecosystems during the Last Glacial and consequences for aquatic species diversity|journal = Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology|date = 2004-07-06|pages = 227–243|volume = 209|series = High Latitude Eurasian Palaeoenvironments|issue = 1–4|doi = 10.1016/j.palaeo.2004.02.017|first1 = Eugene|last1 = Karabanov|first2 = Douglas|last2 = Williams|first3 = Mikhail|last3 = Kuzmin|first4 = Valentina|last4 = Sideleva|first5 = Galina|last5 = Khursevich|first6 = Alexander|last6 = Prokopenko|first7 = Emilia|last7 = Solotchina|first8 = Lilia|last8 = Tkachenko|first9 = Svetlana|last9 = Fedenya|bibcode = 2004PPP...209..227K}}</ref> The collapse of Hovsgol's ecosystem during the LGM brought forth a new ecosystem, with limited biodiversity in species and low levels of [[endemism]] during the Holocene. That research also shows how ecosystem collapse during LGM in Lake Hovsgol led to higher levels of diversity and higher levels of endemism as a byproduct of subsequent evolution.

In the [[Carboniferous]] period, [[coal forest]]s, great tropical [[wetland]]s, extended over much of Euramerica (Europe and America). This land supported towering [[lycopsid]]s which fragmented and collapsed abruptly.<ref name="Sahney2010">{{ cite journal | url=http://geology.geoscienceworld.org/cgi/content/abstract/38/12/1079 |last1=Sahney |first1=S. |last2=Benton |first2=M.J. |last3=Falcon-Lang |first3=H.J. | year=2010 | title= Rainforest collapse triggered Pennsylvanian tetrapod diversification in Euramerica | journal=Geology | volume = 38 | pages = 1079–1082 | format=PDF | doi=10.1130/G31182.1 | issue=12 | bibcode=2010Geo....38.1079S| url-access=subscription }}</ref> The collapse of the rainforests during the [[Carboniferous]] has been attributed to [[Carboniferous rainforest collapse#Possible causes|multiple causes]], including [[Climate change (general concept)|climate change]] and [[volcanism]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fielding |first1=C.R. |last2=Frank |first2=T.D. |last3=Birgenheier |first3=L.P. |author-link3=Lauren Birgenheier |last4=Rygel |first4=M.C. |last5=Jones |first5=A.T. |last6=Roberts |first6=J. |year=2008 |title=Stratigraphic imprint of the Late Palaeozoic Ice Age in eastern Australia: A record of alternating glacial and nonglacial climate regime |journal=Journal of the Geological Society |volume=165 |issue=1 |pages=129–140 |bibcode=2008JGSoc.165..129F |doi=10.1144/0016-76492007-036 |s2cid=31953303}}</ref> Specifically, at this time climate became cooler and drier, conditions that are not favourable to the growth of rainforests and much of the biodiversity within them. The sudden collapse in the terrestrial environment made many large [[vascular plants]], giant [[arthropods]], and diverse [[amphibians]] to go extinct, allowing [[seed plants|seed-bearing plants]] and [[amniotes]] to take over (but smaller relatives of the affected ones survived also).<ref name="Sahney2010"/>

== Historic examples ==
[[File:Hangaroa Moais.jpg|thumb|300px|Subtropical broadleaf forests disappeared from [[Easter Island]]. The island is currently mostly covered in [[grassland]] with [[totora (plant)|''nga'atu'' or bulrush]] (''Schoenoplectus californicus tatora'') in the crater lakes of [[Rano Raraku]] and [[Rano Kau]].]]
The [[Rapa Nui]] [[tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests|subtropical broadleaf forests]] in [[Easter Island]], formerly dominated by an [[Paschalococos|endemic palm]], are considered collapsed due to the combined effects of overexploitation, climate change and introduced exotic rats.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/j.jas.2009.10.006| title = Humans, climate or introduced rats – which is to blame for the woodland destruction on prehistoric Rapa Nui (Easter Island)?| journal = Journal of Archaeological Science| volume = 37| issue = 2| page = 417| year = 2010| last1 = Mieth | first1 = A. | last2 = Bork | first2 = H. R. | bibcode = 2010JArSc..37..417M}}</ref>

The [[Aral Sea]] is an [[endorheic basin|endorheic lake]] between [[Kazakhstan]] and [[Uzbekistan]]. It was once considered one of the [[largest lakes]] in the world but has been shrinking since the 1960s after the rivers that fed it were diverted for large scale irrigation. By 1997, it had declined to 10% of its original size, splitting into much smaller [[hypersaline]] lakes, while dried areas have transformed into desert steppes.<ref name="Keith2013" /><ref name="sciam">{{cite news|author1=Philip Micklin |author2=Nikolay V. Aladin |title=Reclaiming the Aral Sea|url=http://www.sciam.com/article.cfm?id=reclaiming-the-aral-sea&sc=rss|work=Scientific American|date=March 2008| access-date=17 May 2008}}</ref>

The regime shift in the northern [[Benguela Current#Upwelling and primary production|Benguela]] [[upwelling]] ecosystem is considered an example of ecosystem collapse in [[Pelagic zone|open marine]] environments.<ref name="BlandWatermeyer2018">{{cite journal|last1=Bland|first1=Lucie M.|last2=Watermeyer|first2=Kate E.|last3=Keith|first3=David A.|last4=Nicholson|first4=Emily|last5=Regan|first5=Tracey J.|last6=Shannon|first6=Lynne J.|title=Assessing risks to marine ecosystems with indicators, ecosystem models and experts|journal=Biological Conservation|volume=227|year=2018|pages=19–28|issn=0006-3207|doi=10.1016/j.biocon.2018.08.019|s2cid=92093006 }}</ref> Prior to the 1970s [[sardines]] were the dominant vertebrate consumers, but overfishing and two adverse climatic events ([[Benguela Current#Benguela Niño|Benguela Niño]] in 1974 and 1984)  lead to an impoverished ecosystem state with high biomass of [[jellyfish]] and [[pelagic goby]].<ref name="HeymansTomczak2016">{{cite journal|last1=Heymans|first1=Johanna J.|last2=Tomczak|first2=Maciej T.|title=Regime shifts in the Northern Benguela ecosystem: Challenges for management|journal=Ecological Modelling|volume=331|year=2016|pages=151–159|issn=0304-3800|doi=10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2015.10.027}}</ref>

Another notable example is the [[collapse of the Atlantic northwest cod fishery|collapse of the Grand Banks cod]] in the early 1990s, when [[overfishing]] reduced fish populations to 1% of their historical levels.<ref name="Hamilton2001">{{cite journal |last1=Hamilton |first1=Lawrence C. |last2=Butler |first2=M. J. |title=Outport adaptations: Social indicators through Newfoundland's Cod crisis |journal=Human Ecology Review |date=January 2001 |volume=8 |issue=2|pages=1–11 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/247089244}}</ref>

== Currently collapsing ==
Some environments are not currently considered collapsed, but they are well on the way to collapse without intervention.

[[Kimberley (Western Australia)|The Kimberley]] in Western Australia and the [[Cape York Peninsula]], both in Australia's northern savannas, are considered some of the largest intact ecosystems, with the Kimberley containing 2,000 native plants and the Cape York Peninsula containing roughly 3,000. Both are home to hundreds of birds, mammals, reptiles, and insects. Because of fire-promoting weeds, the landscape has changed from woodlands to grasslands over the years. Additional pressures from climate change, [[overgrazing]], and [[forestry]] have begun to cause a significant decline.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Murphy |first1=Brett |last2=Ritchie |first2=Euan |date=2016-08-26 |title=EcoCheck: Australia's vast, majestic northern savannas need more care |url=https://theconversation.com/ecocheck-australias-vast-majestic-northern-savannas-need-more-care-59897 |access-date=2025-04-25 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

The [[mangrove]]s of northern Australia continue to lose nutrients and landmass. Approximately 7,400 [[hectare]]s (18,286 acres) of mangroves were lost in the largest recorded dieback event between 2015 and 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Duke |first1=Norman |last2=Oosterzee |first2=Penny van |date=2017-03-13 |title=Extreme weather likely behind worst recorded mangrove dieback in northern Australia |url=https://theconversation.com/extreme-weather-likely-behind-worst-recorded-mangrove-dieback-in-northern-australia-71880 |access-date=2025-04-25 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

The [[Great Barrier Reef]] recorded its first [[Coral bleaching|bleaching]] event in 1998, and the largest spread of bleaching occurred in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Pratchett |first1=Morgan |last2=Hughes |first2=Terry |date=2020-04-06 |title=We just spent two weeks surveying the Great Barrier Reef. What we saw was an utter tragedy |url=https://theconversation.com/we-just-spent-two-weeks-surveying-the-great-barrier-reef-what-we-saw-was-an-utter-tragedy-135197 |access-date=2025-04-25 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref> Roughly 50% of the coral had been lost as of 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Team |first=Enviroliteracy |date=2025-04-25 |title=What is the status of the Great Barrier Reef in 2023? |url=https://enviroliteracy.org/what-is-the-status-of-the-great-barrier-reef-in-2023/ |access-date=2025-04-25 |website=The Environmental Literacy Council |language=en-US}}</ref> As the coral bleaches, it dies, and the organisms that rely on it for survival are also affected. The Great Barrier Reef is estimated to support over 9,000 organisms.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bellwood |first=David |last2=Mallela |first2=Jennie |date=2016-06-27 |title=Biodiversity of the Great Barrier Reef |url=https://www.science.org.au/curious/great-barrier-reef |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171109230353/https://www.science.org.au/curious/great-barrier-reef |archive-date=2017-11-09 |access-date=2026-10-07 |work=Curious |language=en}}</ref> The continued decline of the Great Barrier Reef is caused by many factors, the largest being [[climate change]] and [[pollution]].{{Citation needed|date=October 2026}}

According to the Climate Change Vulnerability Index, [[Shark Bay]] is considered the most vulnerable ecosystem. The ecosystem supports the local community, but declines caused by global warming and climate change have heavily affected it. [[Seagrass|Seagrass]], the main source of habitat for fish and marine life, is not sustainable under changing climate conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Sequeira |first1=Ana M. M. |last2=Burns |first2=Brendan Paul |last3=Walker |first3=Diana |last4=Day |first4=Jon C. |last5=Fraser |first5=Matthew |last6=Heron |first6=Scott F. |date=2019-02-07 |title=Shark Bay: A World Heritage Site at catastrophic risk |url=https://theconversation.com/shark-bay-a-world-heritage-site-at-catastrophic-risk-111194 |access-date=2025-04-25 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

The [[Great Salt Lake]] in [[Utah]] is considered a keystone ecosystem and a key economic factor for the state. It has lost over 73% of its water and 60% of its surface area since 1850.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Emergency measures needed to rescue Great Salt Lake from ongoing collapse |url=https://pws.byu.edu/great-salt-lake |access-date=2025-04-25 |website=Plant & Wildlife Sciences |language=en}}</ref> Unless drastic measures are taken, the lake is expected to dry up completely, causing irreparable damage that will harm wildlife and public health while leading to environmental and economic decline.

== Contemporary risk ==
[[File:Empirical relationship between system area and regime shift duration.webp|thumb|[[Ecological collapse#Scientific research|Log–log linear relationship between the spatial area and the temporal duration]] of 42 observed Earth system regime shifts<ref name="Cooper2020">{{cite journal |last1=Cooper |first1=Gregory S. |last2=Willcock |first2=Simon |last3=Dearing |first3=John A. |title=Regime shifts occur disproportionately faster in larger ecosystems |journal=Nature Communications |date=10 March 2020 |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=1175 |doi=10.1038/s41467-020-15029-x  |doi-access=free|pmid=32157098 |pmc=7064493 |bibcode=2020NatCo..11.1175C |language=en |issn=2041-1723}}</ref>]]
There are two tools commonly used together to assess risks to ecosystems and biodiversity: generic risk assessment protocols and stochastic simulation models. The most notable of the two tactics is risk assessment protocol, particularly because of the [[IUCN Red List of Ecosystems]] (RLE), which is widely applicable to many ecosystems even in data-poor circumstances. However, because using this tool is essentially comparing systems to a list of criteria, it is often limited in its ability to look at ecosystem decline holistically; and is thus often used in conjunction with simulation models that consider more aspects of decline such as eco[[system dynamics]], future threats, and social-ecological relationships.<ref name="BlandMAR" />

The IUCN RLE is a global standard that was developed to assess threats to various ecosystems on local, regional, national, and global scales, as well as to prompt conservation efforts in the face of the unparalleled decline of natural systems in the last decade.<ref name="Sato2017" /><ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-12-08|title=Red List of Ecosystems|url=https://www.iucn.org/theme/ecosystem-management/our-work/red-list-ecosystems|access-date=2021-12-07|website=IUCN|language=en}}</ref> And though this effort is still in the earlier stages of implementation, the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] has a goal to assess the risk of collapse for all of the world's ecosystems by 2025.<ref name="Sato2017" /> The concept of '''''ecosystem collapse''''' is used in the framework to establish categories of risk for ecosystems, with the category ''Collapsed'' used as the end-point of risk assessment. Other categories of threat (Vulnerable, Endangered and Critically Endangered) are defined in terms of the probability or risk of collapse.<ref name="Keith2013" /> A paper by Bland et al. suggests four aspects for defining ecosystem collapse in risk assessments:<ref name="Bland2018" /> 
# qualitatively defining initial and collapsed states 
# describing collapse and recovery transitions 
# identifying and selecting indicators of collapse 
# setting quantitative collapse thresholds.

=== Early detection and monitoring ===
{{Further|Regime shift#Early-warning signals and critical slowing down}}
[[File:Emerging signals of declining forest resilience under climate change.webp|thumb|100px|Emerging signals of declining forest resilience under climate change.<ref name="Forzieri2022" />]]
Scientists can predict tipping points for ecosystem collapse. The most frequently used model for predicting [[food web]] collapse is called R50, which is a reliable measurement model for food web robustness.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = The reliability of R50 as a measure of vulnerability of food webs to sequential species deletions|journal = Oikos|date = 2015-04-01|issn = 1600-0706|pages = 446–457|volume = 124|issue = 4|doi = 10.1111/oik.01588|first1 = Tomas|last1 = Jonsson|first2 = Sofia|last2 = Berg|first3 = Alexander|last3 = Pimenov|first4 = Catherine|last4 = Palmer|first5 = Mark|last5 = Emmerson}}</ref> However, there are others: i.e. [[marine ecosystem]] assessments can use RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database. In one example, 154 different marine fish species were studied to establish the relationship between pressures on fish populations such as [[overfishing]] and [[climate change]], these populations; traits like growth rate, and the risk of ecosystem collapse.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Fishing, fast growth and climate variability increase the risk of collapse|journal = Proc. R. Soc. B|date = 2015-08-22|issn = 0962-8452|pmid = 26246548|article-number = 20151053|volume = 282|issue = 1813|doi = 10.1098/rspb.2015.1053|first1 = Malin L.|last1 = Pinsky|first2 = David|last2 = Byler|pmc=4632620}}</ref>

The measurement of "critical slowing down" (CSD) is one approach for developing early warning signals for a potential or likely onset of approaching collapse. It refers to increasingly slow recovery from perturbations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dakos |first1=Vasilis |last2=Bascompte |first2=Jordi |title=Critical slowing down as early warning for the onset of collapse in mutualistic communities |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=9 December 2014 |volume=111 |issue=49 |pages=17546–17551 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1406326111 |pmid=25422412 |pmc=4267327 |bibcode=2014PNAS..11117546D |issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=van Nes |first1=Egbert H. |last2=Scheffer |first2=Marten |title=Slow recovery from perturbations as a generic indicator of a nearby catastrophic shift |journal=The American Naturalist |date=June 2007 |volume=169 |issue=6 |pages=738–747 |doi=10.1086/516845 |pmid=17479460 |s2cid=6916712 |issn=1537-5323}}</ref>

In 2020, one paper suggested that once a 'point of no return' is reached, breakdowns do not occur gradually but rapidly and that the [[Amazon rainforest]] could shift to a [[savannah]]-type mixture of trees and grass within 50 years and the Caribbean coral reefs could collapse within 15 years once a state of collapse has been reached.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/mar/10/ecosystems-size-of-amazon-rainforest-can-collapse-within-decades|title=Ecosystems the size of Amazon 'can collapse within decades'|date=10 March 2020|access-date=10 March 2020|work=The Guardian}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2020-03/bu-arc030920.php|title=Amazon rainforest could be gone within a lifetime|date=10 March 2020|access-date=10 March 2020|work=EurekAlert!|archive-date=11 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200311155150/https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2020-03/bu-arc030920.php}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Ecosystems the size of Amazon 'can collapse within decades' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/mar/10/ecosystems-size-of-amazon-rainforest-can-collapse-within-decades |website=The Guardian |access-date=13 April 2020 |language=en |date=10 March 2020}}</ref><ref name="Cooper2020" /> Another indicated that large ecosystem disruptions will occur earlier under more intense climate change: under the high-emissions [[Representative Concentration Pathway|RCP8.5]] scenario, ecosystems in the tropical oceans would be the first to experience abrupt disruption before 2030, with tropical forests and polar environments following by 2050. In total, 15% of ecological assemblages would have over 20% of their species abruptly disrupted if as warming eventually reaches {{convert|4|C-change|F-change}}; in contrast, this would happen to fewer than 2% if the warming were to stay below {{convert|2|C-change|F-change}}.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Trisos |first1=Christopher H. |last2=Merow |first2=Cory |last3=Pigot |first3=Alex L. |title=The projected timing of abrupt ecological disruption from climate change |journal=Nature |date=8 April 2020 |volume=580 |issue=7804 |pages=496–501 |doi=10.1038/s41586-020-2189-9 |pmid=32322063 |bibcode=2020Natur.580..496T |s2cid=256822113 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Rainforest collapse ===
[[File:Deforestation in Borneo.jpg|thumb|Trees being felled in [[Kalimantan]], the [[Indonesia]]n part of Borneo, in 2013, to make way for a new coal mining project]]
[[File:Sugarcane Deforestation, Bolivia, 2016-06-15 by Planet Labs.jpg|thumb|250px|[[Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest]] in [[Bolivia]] in 2016]]
Rainforest collapse refers to the actual past and theoretical future ecological collapse of [[rainforest]]s. It may involve [[habitat fragmentation]] to the point where little rainforest [[biome]] is left, and rainforest species only survive in isolated refugia. Habitat fragmentation can be caused by roads. When humans start to cut down the trees for logging, secondary roads are created that will go unused after its primary use. Once abandoned, the plants of the rainforest will find it difficult to grow back in that area.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Legacy of logging roads in the Congo Basin: How persistent are the scars in forest cover?|journal = Ecosphere|date = 2015-04-01|issn = 2150-8925|pages = art64|volume = 6|issue = 4|doi = 10.1890/ES14-00488.1|first1 = Fritz|last1 = Kleinschroth|first2 = Sylvie|last2 = Gourlet-Fleury|first3 = Plinio|last3 = Sist|first4 = Fréderic|last4 = Mortier|first5 = John R.|last5 = Healey|doi-access = free}}</ref> Forest fragmentation also opens the path for illegal hunting. Species have a hard time finding a new place to settle in these fragments causing ecological collapse. This leads to extinction of many animals in the rainforest.

A classic pattern of [[forest fragmentation]] is occurring in many [[rainforest]]s including those of the [[Amazon basin|Amazon]], specifically a 'fishbone' pattern formed by the development of roads into the forest. This is of great concern, not only because of the loss of a [[biome]] with many untapped resources and wholesale death of living organisms, but also because plant and animal species extinction is known to correlate with habitat fragmentation.<ref name = Rosenzweig>{{cite book | last = Rosenzweig | first = Michael L. | author-link = Michael Rosenzweig | title = Species diversity in space & time | year = 1995 | publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]] | location = Cambridge, United Kingdom}}</ref>

In 2022, research found that more than three-quarters of [[Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest|the Amazon rainforest has been losing resilience due to deforestation and climate change]] since the early 2000s as measured by recovery-time from short-term perturbations (the critical slowing down), reinforcing the theory that it is approaching a [[critical transition]].<ref name="Carrington2022">{{cite news |last=Carrington |first=Damian |title=Climate crisis: Amazon rainforest tipping point is looming, data shows |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/mar/07/climate-crisis-amazon-rainforest-tipping-point |access-date=18 April 2022 |work=The Guardian |date=7 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Boulton2022">{{cite journal |last1=Boulton |first1=Chris A. |last2=Lenton |first2=Timothy M. |last3=Boers |first3=Niklas |title=Pronounced loss of Amazon rainforest resilience since the early 2000s |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=March 2022 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=271–278 |doi=10.1038/s41558-022-01287-8 |bibcode=2022NatCC..12..271B |s2cid=234889502 |language=en |issn=1758-6798|doi-access=free }}</ref> Another study from 2022 found that tropical, arid and temperate forests are substantially losing resilience.<ref name="Forzieri2022">{{cite journal |last1=Forzieri |first1=Giovanni |last2=Dakos |first2=Vasilis |last3=McDowell |first3=Nate G. |last4=Ramdane |first4=Alkama |last5=Cescatti |first5=Alessandro |title=Emerging signals of declining forest resilience under climate change |journal=Nature |date=August 2022 |volume=608 |issue=7923 |pages=534–539 |doi=10.1038/s41586-022-04959-9 |pmid=35831499 |pmc=9385496 |language=en |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Forests are becoming less resilient because of climate change |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2328268-forests-are-becoming-less-resilient-because-of-climate-change/ |access-date=21 August 2022 |work=New Scientist}}</ref>

=== Coral reefs ===
{{See also|Environmental issues with coral reefs}}
[[File:How Global Warming is Affecting Coral Reefs.jpg|thumb|Human activities release large amounts of carbon dioxide, which then lead to ocean warming, harming marine life and coral reefs.]]
A major concern for [[marine biologist]]s is the collapse of coral reef ecosystems.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|title = The future of coral reefs|journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date = 2001-05-08|issn = 0027-8424|pmc = 33228|pmid = 11344288|pages = 5419–5425|volume = 98|issue = 10|doi = 10.1073/pnas.091092998|first = Nancy|last = Knowlton|bibcode = 2001PNAS...98.5419K|doi-access = free}}</ref> An effect of global climate change is the rising sea levels which can lead to reef drowning or [[coral bleaching]].<ref name=":0" /> Human activity, such as fishing, mining, deforestation, ..., serves as a threat for coral reefs by affecting the niche of the coral reefs. For example, there is a demonstrated correlation between a loss in diversity of coral reefs by 30-60% and human activity such as sewage and/or industrial pollution.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Reef degradation and coral biodiversity in Indonesia: Effects of land-based pollution, destructive fishing practices and changes over time|journal = Marine Pollution Bulletin|date = 1998-08-01|pages = 617–630|volume = 36|issue = 8|doi = 10.1016/S0025-326X(98)00047-2|first1 = Evan N|last1 = Edinger|first2 = Jamaluddin|last2 = Jompa|first3 = Gino V|last3 = Limmon|first4 = Wisnu|last4 = Widjatmoko|first5 = Michael J|last5 = Risk}}</ref>

{{Excerpt|Extinction risk from climate change#Corals}}

== Conservation and reversal ==
{{See also|Restoration ecology|Conservation biology}}
As of now, there is not much information on effective conservation or reversal methods for ecosystem collapse. Rather, there has been increased focus on the predictability of ecosystem collapse, whether it is possible, and whether it is productive to explore.<ref name="Sato2017">{{Cite journal|last1=Sato|first1=Chloe F.|last2=Lindenmayer|first2=David B.|date=27 February 2017 |title=Meeting the Global Ecosystem Collapse Challenge|journal=Conservation Letters|volume=11|issue=1|article-number=e12348 |doi=10.1111/conl.12348|s2cid=90179066 |issn=1755-263X|hdl=10536/DRO/DU:30144542|hdl-access=free}}</ref> This is likely because thorough studies of at-risk ecosystems are a more recent development and trend in ecological fields, so collapse dynamics are either too recent to observe or still emerging. Since studies are not yet long term, conclusions about reversibility or transformation potential are often hard to draw from newer, more focused studies.<ref name="Canadell2021" />
