Heavy metal contamination impacts the quality of nectar and thus the growth, reproduction and survival of plants and their pollinators.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Musah |first=Baba Imoro |date=2024-12-03 |title=Effects of heavy metals and metalloids on plant-animal interaction and biodiversity of terrestrial ecosystems—an overview |journal=Environmental Monitoring and Assessment |language=en |volume=197 |issue=1 |article-number=12 |doi=10.1007/s10661-024-13490-5 |pmid=39623084 |bibcode=2024EMnAs.197...12M |issn=1573-2959}}</ref> Over time the hostile environmental conditions may lead to a plant population with more stress tolerant traits, but abiotic stressors could also decrease the functional diversity of plants, disrupting the ecosystems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fazlioglu |first1=Fatih |last2=Keskin |first2=Gulaycan P. |last3=Akcin |first3=Oznur E. |last4=Ozbucak |first4=Tugba |date=2021-08-01 |title=Mining and quarrying activities tend to favor stress-tolerant plants |journal=Ecological Indicators |volume=127 |article-number=107759 |doi=10.1016/j.ecolind.2021.107759 |bibcode=2021EcInd.12707759F |issn=1470-160X|doi-access=free }}</ref> Microbial soil and tree biodiversity loss from mining has been remedied by liming and phytoremediation technology; which has a significant improvement to soil microbial biomass.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nkongolo |first1=K. K. |last2=Michael |first2=P. |last3=Theriault |first3=G. |last4=Narendrula |first4=R. |last5=Castilloux |first5=P. |last6=Kalubi |first6=K. N. |last7=Beckett |first7=P. |last8=Spiers |first8=G. |date=2016-03-10 |title=Assessing Biological Impacts of Land Reclamation in a Mining Region in Canada: Effects of Dolomitic Lime Applications on Forest Ecosystems and Microbial Phospholipid Fatty Acid Signatures |journal=Water, Air, & Soil Pollution |language=en |volume=227 |issue=4 |page=104 |doi=10.1007/s11270-016-2803-5 |bibcode=2016WASP..227..104N}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rezania |first1=Shahabaldin |last2=Taib |first2=Shazwin Mat |last3=Md Din |first3=Mohd Fadhil |last4=Dahalan |first4=Farrah Aini |last5=Kamyab |first5=Hesam |date=2016-11-15 |title=Comprehensive review on phytotechnology: Heavy metals removal by diverse aquatic plants species from wastewater |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304389416306860 |journal=Journal of Hazardous Materials |volume=318 |pages=587–599 |doi=10.1016/j.jhazmat.2016.07.053 |pmid=27474848 |bibcode=2016JHzM..318..587R|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Organic matter also plays a significant role in alleviating negative metal contamination effects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stefanowicz |first1=Anna M. |last2=Kapusta |first2=Paweł |last3=Zubek |first3=Szymon |last4=Stanek |first4=Małgorzata |last5=Woch |first5=Marcin W. |date=2020-02-01 |title=Soil organic matter prevails over heavy metal pollution and vegetation as a factor shaping soil microbial communities at historical Zn–Pb mining sites |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045653519321617 |journal=Chemosphere |volume=240 |article-number=124922 |doi=10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.124922 |pmid=31563718 |bibcode=2020Chmsp.24024922S}}</ref>

=== Urbanization and agriculture ===
Urbanization fragments habitats into roads, cities, and infrastructure development.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Faulkner |first=Stephen |date=2004-06-01 |title=Urbanization impacts on the structure and function of forested wetlands |journal=Urban Ecosystems |language=en |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=89–106 |doi=10.1023/B:UECO.0000036269.56249.66 |bibcode=2004UrbEc...7...89F |issn=1573-1642}}</ref> This displaces wildlife and exposes forests to human disturbances. Likewise, agricultural activities transform forests into farmland and monocultures,<ref name=":6" /> introducing chemicals like fertilizers and pesticides that harm the soil.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Addison |first1=S. L. |last2=Smaill |first2=S. J. |last3=Garrett |first3=L. G. |last4=Wakelin |first4=S. A. |date=2021-07-01 |title=Fertiliser use has multi-decadal effects on microbial diversity and functionality of forest soils |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0929139321000858 |journal=Applied Soil Ecology |volume=163 |article-number=103964 |doi=10.1016/j.apsoil.2021.103964 |bibcode=2021AppSE.16303964A |issn=0929-1393|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This impacts forest ecology by altering nutrient cycles<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Guo |first1=Dali |last2=Mou |first2=Pu |last3=Jones |first3=Robert H. |last4=Mitchell |first4=Robert J. |date=2004-03-01 |title=Spatio-temporal patterns of soil available nutrients following experimental disturbance in a pine forest |journal=Oecologia |volume=138 |issue=4 |pages=613–621 |doi=10.1007/s00442-003-1473-3 |pmid=14689301 |issn=1432-1939}}</ref> degrading ecosystem health.

=== Approaches ===

[[File: Redwood M D Vaden.jpg|thumb|right|[[Sequoia sempervirens|Redwood]] tree in northern California forest, where many trees are managed for preservation and longevity]]

Forests are studied at a number of organizational levels, from the individual [[organism]] to the ecosystem. However, as the term [[forest]] connotes an area inhabited by more than one [[organism]], forest ecology most often concentrates on the level of the [[Population (biology)|population]], [[community]] or ecosystem. Logically, [[tree]]s are an important component of forest research, but the wide variety of other life forms and [[abiotic components]] in most forests means that other elements, such as [[wildlife]] or [[soil]] [[nutrients]], are also crucial components.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dunson |first1=William A. |last2=Travis |first2=Joseph |date=1991 |title=The Role of Abiotic Factors in Community Organization |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=138 |issue=5 |pages=1067–1091 |doi=10.1086/285270 |jstor=2462508 |bibcode=1991ANat..138.1067D}}</ref>

Forest ecology shares characteristics and methodological approaches with other areas of [[terrestrial plant]] ecology, however, the presence of trees makes forest ecosystems and their study unique in numerous ways due to the potential for a wide variety of forest structures created by the uniquely large size and height of trees compared with other terrestrial plants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ehbrecht |first1=Martin |last2=Seidel |first2=Dominik |last3=Annighöfer |first3=Peter |last4=Kreft |first4=Holger |last5=Köhler |first5=Michael |last6=Zemp |first6=Delphine Clara |last7=Puettmann |first7=Klaus |last8=Nilus |first8=Reuben |last9=Babweteera |first9=Fred |last10=Willim |first10=Katharina |last11=Stiers |first11=Melissa |last12=Soto |first12=Daniel |last13=Boehmer |first13=Hans Juergen |last14=Fisichelli |first14=Nicholas |last15=Burnett |first15=Michael |display-authors=5 |date=2021-01-22 |title=Global patterns and climatic controls of forest structural complexity |journal=Nature Communications |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=519 |doi=10.1038/s41467-020-20767-z  |doi-access=free|pmid=33483481 |pmc=7822964 |bibcode=2021NatCo..12..519E}}</ref>

The emergence of [[machine learning]](ML) has allowed for new methods of approaching forest ecology, as it can process larger and more complex data. Since the 1990s, machine learning is increasingly used to improve the accuracy of [[Species distribution modelling|species distribution models]], predict [[Carbon cycle|carbon flux]], and in hazard assessment procedures.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Zelin |last2=Peng |first2=Changhui |last3=Work |first3=Timothy |last4=Candau |first4=Jean-Noel |last5=DesRochers |first5=Annie |last6=Kneeshaw |first6=Daniel |date=2018 |title=Application of machine-learning methods in forest ecology: recent progress and future challenges |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/er-2018-0034 |journal=Environmental Reviews |language=en |volume=26 |issue=4 |pages=339–350 |doi=10.1139/er-2018-0034 |bibcode=2018EnvRv..26..339L |hdl=1807/92561 |issn=1181-8700|hdl-access=free }}</ref> Drones are also heavily used in forest ecology research.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bygjymi |first1=Xhulia |last2=Begu |first2=Enkela |last3=Lloci |first3=Dritan |last4=Sinjari |first4=Sonila |last5=Hanxhari |first5=Romeo |date=2025 |title=The Use of Drone/Uav Technology in Precision Forestry. Case Study: National Park Divjake Karavasta |url=https://ijees.net/images/pdf/XhuliaBygjymi1EnkelaBegu1DritanLloci1SonilaSinjari1RomeoHanxhari1THEUSEOFDRONEUAVTECHNOLOGYINPRECISIONFORESTRYCASESTUDY:NATIONALPARKDIVJAKEKARAVASTApage103-108;-ab083755a2.pdf |journal=International Journal of Ecosystems and Ecology Sciences |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=103–108 |doi=10.31407/ijees15.413 }}</ref>  The use of drones allows for easier mapping of forest landscapes, and surveying large sections of land. Using drones, information such as [[Tree height measurement|tree height]], diameter, species, and plant stress can be acquired with fewer expensive, labour intensive methods. They also aid in the identification of wildfires, especially when [[Drones in wildfire management|drones]] are equipped with [[Thermography|thermal cameras]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Buchelt |first1=Alexander |last2=Adrowitzer |first2=Alexander |last3=Kieseberg |first3=Peter |last4=Gollob |first4=Christoph |last5=Nothdurft |first5=Arne |last6=Eresheim |first6=Sebastian |last7=Tschiatschek |first7=Sebastian |last8=Stampfer |first8=Karl |last9=Holzinger |first9=Andreas |date=2024 |title=Exploring artificial intelligence for applications of drones in forest ecology and management |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |language=en |volume=551 |article-number=121530 |doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2023.121530 |bibcode=2024ForEM.55121530B |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Climate Change and Carbon Cycling ===

Climate change has an effect on forests from wildfires, droughts, soil erosion, and heat stress effects on vegetation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chapter 4: Land Degradation — Special Report on Climate Change and Land|url=https://www.ipcc.ch/srccl/chapter/chapter-4/|access-date=2026-04-05}}</ref> The world resource institute summarizes the IPCC AR6 report and anthropogenic effects on global warming.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boehm|first1=Sophie|last2=Schumer|first2=Clea|date=2023-03-20|title=10 Big Findings from the 2023 IPCC Report on Climate Change|url=https://www.wri.org/insights/2023-ipcc-ar6-synthesis-report-climate-change-findings|language=en}}</ref> The [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|IPCC]] covers carbon removal and reforestation; loss of vegetation impacts carbon cycling, and these effects can vary among canopy structures .<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nave|first1=Lucas E.|last2=Gough |first2=Christopher M.|last3=Clay |first3=Cameron|last4=Santos |first4=Fernanda |last5=Atkins|first5=Jeff W. |last6=Benjamins-Carey|first6=Sonja E. |last7=Bohrer |first7=Gil|last8=Castillo |first8=Buck T.|last9=Fahey |first9=Robert T. |last10=Hardiman|first10=Brady S.|last11=Hofmeister |first11=Kathryn L.|last12=Ivanov |first12=Valeriy Y.|last13=Kalejs |first13=Jennifer |last14=Matheny |first14=Ashley M.|last15=Menna|first15=Angela C. |display-authors=5|date=January 2025|title=Carbon cycling across ecosystem succession in a north temperate forest: Controls and management implications |url=https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eap.70001|journal=[[Ecological Applications]] |volume=35 |issue=1 |article-number=e70001 |doi=10.1002/eap.70001 |pmid=39989402 |bibcode=2025EcoAp..3570001N |osti=2538457 |issn=1051-0761 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250513002026/https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eap.70001|archive-date=2025-05-13|hdl=2027.42/196623 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Community diversity and complexity ==
[[File:Overall decline in a forest-specialist index for 268 forest vertebrate species (455 populations), 1970–2014.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Overall decline in a forest-specialist index for 268 forest vertebrate species (455 populations), 1970–2014, from the [[Food and Agriculture Organization]] publication The State of the World's Forests 2020. Forests, biodiversity and people – In brief<ref>{{Cite book|title=The State of the World's Forests 2020. Forests, biodiversity and people – In brief|publisher=FAO & UNEP|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132707-4|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/ca8985en|s2cid=241416114}}</ref>]]
Since trees can grow larger than other plant life-forms, there is the potential for a wide variety of forest structures (or physiognomies). The infinite number of possible spatial arrangements of trees of varying size and species makes for a highly intricate and diverse micro-environment in which environmental variables such as [[solar radiation]], temperature, [[relative humidity]], and [[wind speed]] can vary considerably over large and small distances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schnabel |first1=Florian |last2=Beugnon |first2=Rémy |last3=Yang |first3=Bo |last4=Richter |first4=Ronny |last5=Eisenhauer |first5=Nico |last6=Huang |first6=Yuanyuan |last7=Liu |first7=Xiaojuan |last8=Wirth |first8=Christian |last9=Cesarz |first9=Simone |last10=Fichtner |first10=Andreas |last11=Perles-Garcia |first11=Maria D. |last12=Hähn |first12=Georg J. A. |last13=Härdtle |first13=Werner |last14=Kunz |first14=Matthias |last15=Castro Izaguirre |first15=Nadia C. |display-authors=5 |date=March 2025 |title=Tree Diversity Increases Forest Temperature Buffering via Enhancing Canopy Density and Structural Diversity |journal=Ecology Letters |volume=28 |issue=3 |article-number=e70096 |doi=10.1111/ele.70096 |issn=1461-0248 |pmc=11928777 |pmid=40119529 |bibcode=2025EcolL..28E0096S }}</ref> In addition, an important proportion of a forest ecosystem's [[biomass (ecology)|biomass]] is often underground, where soil structure, [[water quality]] and quantity, and levels of various soil nutrients can vary greatly.<ref>James P. Kimmins. 2004</ref> Thus, forests are often highly [[heterogeneous]] environments compared to other [[terrestrial plant]] communities. This heterogeneity in turn can enable great biodiversity of species of both plants and animals. Some structures, such as tree ferns may be keystone species for a diverse range of other species.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fountain-Jones | first1=Nicholas M. | last2=McQuillan | first2=Peter B. | last3=Grove | first3=Simon | title=Beetle communities associated with the tree fern ''Dicksonia antarctica'' Labill. In Tasmania | journal=Australian Journal of Entomology | date=2012 | volume=51 | issue=3 | pages=154–165 | doi=10.1111/j.1440-6055.2011.00855.x }}</ref>

A number of factors within the forest affect biodiversity; primary factors enhancing wildlife abundance and biodiversity was the presence of diverse tree species within the forest and the absence of [[even aged timber management]].<ref>Philip Joseph Burton. 2003</ref> For example, the [[wild turkey]] thrives when uneven heights and [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] variations exist and its numbers are diminished by even aged timber management.

Forest management techniques that mimic natural disturbance events<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Putz |first1=Francis E |last2=Romero |first2=Claudia |last3=Sist |first3=Plinio |last4=Schwartz |first4=Gustavo |last5=Thompson |first5=Ian |last6=Roopsind |first6=Anand |last7=Ruslandi |last8=Medjibe |first8=Vincent |last9=Ellis |first9=Peter |date=2022-07-01 |editor-last=Bayer |editor-first=Edward |title=Sustained timber yield claims, considerations, and tradeoffs for selectively logged forests |journal=PNAS Nexus |language=en |volume=1 |issue=3 |article-number=pgac102 |doi=10.1093/pnasnexus/pgac102 |doi-access=free |issn=2752-6542 |pmc=10468026 |pmid=37654970}}</ref> (variable retention forestry<ref>Franklin et al 1997</ref>) can allow community diversity to recover rapidly for a variety of groups, including beetles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kuuluvainen |first1=Timo |last2=Angelstam |first2=Per |last3=Frelich |first3=Lee |last4=Jõgiste |first4=Kalev |last5=Koivula |first5=Matti |last6=Kubota |first6=Yasuhiro |last7=Lafleur |first7=Benoit |last8=Macdonald |first8=Ellen |date=2021-04-09 |title=Natural Disturbance-Based Forest Management: Moving Beyond Retention and Continuous-Cover Forestry |journal=Frontiers in Forests and Global Change |volume=4 |article-number=629020 |doi=10.3389/ffgc.2021.629020 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021FrFGC...4.9020K |issn=2624-893X|hdl=10138/330240 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fountain-Jones | first1=Nicholas M. | last2=Baker | first2=Susan C. | last3=Jordan | first3=Gregory J. | title=Moving beyond the guild concept: Developing a practical functional trait framework for terrestrial beetles | journal=Ecological Entomology | date=2015 | volume=40 | issue=1 | pages=1–13 | doi=10.1111/een.12158 | bibcode=2015EcoEn..40....1F | url=https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/22921565 }}</ref>

== Types of forest ecosystems ==

=== Boreal forests ===
The [[boreal forest]], also referred to as the [[taiga]] is found at high polar latitudes around the globe.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Gauthier |first1=S. |last2=Bernier |first2=P. |last3=Kuuluvainen |first3=T. |last4=Shvidenko |first4=A. Z. |last5=Schepaschenko |first5=D. G. |date=2015-08-21 |title=Boreal forest health and global change |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaa9092 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=349 |issue=6250 |pages=819–822 |doi=10.1126/science.aaa9092 |pmid=26293953 |bibcode=2015Sci...349..819G |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> As one of the largest biomes, the taiga provides an exceptional amount of value to human populations including [[lumber]] and [[paper]] production.<ref name=":4" /> The biome is largely dominated by [[conifer]]ous tree species that are able to handle the challenges of plant life in a [[subarctic climate]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Esseen |first1=Per-Anders |last2=Ehnström |first2=Bengt |last3=Ericson |first3=Lars |last4=Sjöberg |first4=Kjell |date=1997 |title=Boreal Forests |journal=Ecological Bulletins |issue=46 |pages=16–47 |jstor=20113207 |issn=0346-6868}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chang |first1=Christine Yao-Yun |last2=Bräutigam |first2=Katharina |last3=Hüner |first3=Norman P. A. |last4=Ensminger |first4=Ingo |date=2020-09-27 |title=Champions of winter survival: cold acclimation and molecular regulation of cold hardiness in evergreen conifers |journal=New Phytologist |volume=229 |issue=2 |pages=675–691 |doi=10.1111/nph.16904 |pmid=32869329}}</ref> Dominant tree species is influenced by lumbering activities within plots of the boreal forest however, the most significant factor in forest composition is [[wildfire]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Reich |first1=Peter B. |last2=Bakken |first2=Peter |last3=Carlson |first3=Daren |last4=Frelich |first4=Lee E. |last5=Friedman |first5=Steve K. |last6=Grigal |first6=David F. |date=2001 |title=Influence of Logging, Fire, and Forest Type on Biodiversity and Productivity in Southern Boreal Forests |journal=Ecology |volume=82 |issue=10 |page=2731 |doi=10.2307/2679957 |jstor=2679957 |hdl=11299/174931 |issn=0012-9658|hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hart |first1=Stephen A. |last2=Chen |first2=Han Y. H. |date=2008 |title=Fire, Logging, and Overstory Affect Understory Abundance, Diversity, and Composition in Boreal Forest |journal=Ecological Monographs |volume=78 |issue=1 |pages=123–140 |doi=10.1890/06-2140.1 |bibcode=2008EcoM...78..123H |issn=0012-9615}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Byrne |first1=Brendan |last2=Liu |first2=Junjie |last3=Bowman |first3=Kevin W. |last4=Pascolini-Campbell |first4=Madeleine |last5=Chatterjee |first5=Abhishek |last6=Pandey |first6=Sudhanshu |last7=Miyazaki |first7=Kazuyuki |last8=Van Der Werf |first8=Guido R. |last9=Wunch |first9=Debra |last10=Wennberg |first10=Paul O. |last11=Roehl |first11=Coleen M. |display-authors=5 |last12=Sinha |first12=Saptarshi |date=28 August 2024 |title=Carbon emissions from the 2023 Canadian wildfires |journal=Nature |volume=633 |issue=8031 |pages=835–839 |doi=10.1038/s41586-024-07878-z |pmid=39198654 |pmc=11424480 |bibcode=2024Natur.633..835B }}</ref> Dominant boreal conifers include [[fir]], [[pine]]s and [[spruce]] dependent on the time elapsed since the last wildfire.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Jianguo |last2=Tardif |first2=Jacques C. |last3=Bergeron |first3=Yves |last4=Denneler |first4=Bernhard |last5=Berninger |first5=Frank |last6=Girardin |first6=Martin P. |date=2010-01-04 |title=Radial growth response of four dominant boreal tree species to climate along a latitudinal gradient in the eastern Canadian boreal forest |journal=Global Change Biology |volume=16 |issue=2 |pages=711–731 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2486.2009.01990.x |bibcode=2010GCBio..16..711H |issn=1354-1013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bergeron |first=Yves |date=2000 |title=Species and Stand Dynamics in the Mixed Woods of Quebec's Southern Boreal Forest |journal=Ecology |volume=81 |issue=6 |pages=1500–1516 |doi=10.2307/177302 |jstor=177302}}</ref> [[Deciduous]] trees play an important role in boreal forests, mainly as [[Ecological succession|successional]] species.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bergeron |first1=Yves |last2=Fenton |first2=Nicole J. |date=2012 |title=Boreal forests of eastern Canada revisited: old growth, nonfire disturbances, forest succession, and biodiversity |journal=Botany |volume=90 |issue=6 |pages=509–523 |doi=10.1139/b2012-034 |bibcode=2012Botan..90..509B |issn=1916-2790}}</ref> Parts of the boreal forest are of mixed wood composition or entirely deciduous however these plots are only frequent at the southern border of the [[taiga]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Goldblum |first1=David |last2=Rigg |first2=Lesley S. |date=2010 |title=The Deciduous Forest – Boreal Forest Ecotone |url=https://compass.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1749-8198.2010.00342.x |journal=Geography Compass |language=en |volume=4 |issue=7 |pages=701–717 |doi=10.1111/j.1749-8198.2010.00342.x |bibcode=2010GComp...4..701G |issn=1749-8198|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Common Deciduous species include [[birch]], [[aspen]], [[alder]] and [[willow]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Owens |first1=John N. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=htqpCwAAQBAJ&dq=common+deciduous+trees+in+boreal+forest&pg=PA152 |title=Forests And Forest Plants - Volume I |last2=Lund |first2=H. Gyde |date=2009 |publisher=EOLSS Publications |isbn=978-1-905839-38-4}}</ref> These species can sometimes be found in [[Old-growth forest|old growth]] coniferous forests as [[Snag (ecology)|snags]] or stunted specimens of a transitional stage.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Esseen |first1=Per-Anders |last2=Ehnström |first2=Bengt |last3=Ericson |first3=Lars |last4=Sjöberg |first4=Kjell |date=1997 |title=Boreal Forests |journal=Ecological Bulletins |issue=46 |pages=16–47 |jstor=20113207}}</ref>

=== Temperate forests ===
[[Temperate forest]]s account for nearly 25% of forest habitats.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Temperate Zone |url=http://globalforestatlas.yale.edu/ecoregions/temperate-zone |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160423152950/http://globalforestatlas.yale.edu/ecoregions/temperate-zone |archive-date=2016-04-23 |access-date=2026-02-13 |website=globalforestatlas.yale.edu |language=en}}</ref> The temperate zone is generally attributed to latitudes between [[Tropics|tropical]] and [[Polar regions of Earth|polar]] regions however, forests in these zones can have significant differences in weather.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Platnick |first=Norman I. |date=1991 |title=Patterns of biodiversity: tropical vs temperate |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00222939100770701 |journal=Journal of Natural History |language=en |volume=25 |issue=5 |pages=1083–1088 |doi=10.1080/00222939100770701 |bibcode=1991JNatH..25.1083P |issn=0022-2933|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Temperate forests vary depending on the climate of the region, they can be [[conifer]]ous, [[deciduous]] or mixed in composition.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bohn |first1=Friedrich J. |last2=May |first2=Felix |last3=Huth |first3=Andreas |date=2018-03-26 |title=Species composition and forest structure explain the temperature sensitivity patterns of productivity in temperate forests |url=https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/15/1795/2018/bg-15-1795-2018.html |journal=Biogeosciences |language=English |volume=15 |issue=6 |pages=1795–1813 |doi=10.5194/bg-15-1795-2018  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2018BGeo...15.1795B |issn=1726-4170}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Reichle |first=D. E. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Y3XpCAAAQBAJ&dq=temperate+forest&pg=PA1 |title=Analysis of Temperate Forest Ecosystems |date=2013-11-11 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-642-85587-0 |language=en}}</ref> Regardless of composition, plant species have adapted to the constraints of the temperate zone, most notably [[drought]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bréda |first1=Nathalie |last2=Huc |first2=Roland |last3=Granier |first3=André |last4=Dreyer |first4=Erwin |date=2006-09-01 |title=Temperate forest trees and stands under severe drought: a review of ecophysiological responses, adaptation processes and long-term consequences |journal=Annals of Forest Science |language=en |volume=63 |issue=6 |pages=625–644 |doi=10.1051/forest:2006042 |bibcode=2006AnFSc..63..625B |issn=1286-4560}}</ref> Unlike tropical environments, water is not consistently available in temperate forests and is dependent on annual weather trends.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rubio-Cuadrado |first1=Álvaro |last2=Camarero |first2=J. Julio |last3=del Río |first3=Miren |last4=Sánchez-González |first4=Mariola |last5=Ruiz-Peinado |first5=Ricardo |last6=Bravo-Oviedo |first6=Andrés |last7=Gil |first7=Luis |last8=Montes |first8=Fernando |date=2018-09-15 |title=Long-term impacts of drought on growth and forest dynamics in a temperate beech-oak-birch forest |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0168192318301370 |journal=Agricultural and Forest Meteorology |volume=259 |pages=48–59 |doi=10.1016/j.agrformet.2018.04.015 |bibcode=2018AgFM..259...48R |issn=0168-1923|hdl=20.500.12792/746 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> A common adaptation involves highly responsive [[stoma]]ta that are able to rapidly respond to dry conditions, preventing water loss.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Congcong |last2=He |first2=Nianpeng |last3=Zhang |first3=Jiahui |last4=Li |first4=Ying |last5=Wang |first5=Qiufeng |last6=Sack |first6=Lawren |last7=Yu |first7=Guirui |date=2017-09-25 |title=Variation of stomatal traits from cold temperate to tropical forests and association with water use efficiency |journal=Functional Ecology |language=en |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=20–28 |doi=10.1111/1365-2435.12973 |doi-access=free |issn=0269-8463 }}</ref> Variable leaf budding in deciduous species is another common trait that allows plants to avoid freezing conditions based on yearly weather opposed to an average climate.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lechowicz |first=Martin J. |date=December 1984 |title=Why Do Temperate Deciduous Trees Leaf Out at Different Times? Adaptation and Ecology of Forest Communities |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=124 |issue=6 |pages=821–842 |doi=10.1086/284319 |bibcode=1984ANat..124..821L |issn=0003-0147}}</ref> Water scarcity is not a factor in [[temperate rainforest]]s, a biome that typically occurs along the west coast of the Americas,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Alaback |first=Paul B. |date=1991 |title=Comparative ecology of temperate rainforests of the Americas along analogous climatic gradients |url=https://rchn.biologiachile.cl/pdfs/1991/3/Alaback_1991.pdf |journal=Revista Chilena de Historia Natural |volume=64 |pages=399–412}}</ref> and Australasia,<ref>{{Citation |last1=Kirkpatrick |first1=James B. |chapter=Temperate Rainforests of Australasia |date=2011 |title=Temperate and Boreal Rainforests of the World: Ecology and Conservation |pages=195–212 |editor-last=DellaSala |editor-first=Dominick A.  |place=Washington, DC |publisher=Island Press/Center for Resource Economics |language=en |doi=10.5822/978-1-61091-008-8_8 |isbn=978-1-61091-008-8 |last2=DellaSala |first2=Dominick A. |chapter-url=https://figshare.com/articles/chapter/Temperate_rainforests_of_Australasia/23054558 }}</ref> though other instances exist. This biome is characterized by cool and wet conditions, where precipitation may be rain snow or sleet.<ref>{{Citation |last1=DellaSala |first1=Dominick A. |chapter=Just What Are Temperate and Boreal Rainforests? |date=2011 |title=Temperate and Boreal Rainforests of the World: Ecology and Conservation |pages=1–41 |editor-last=DellaSala |editor-first=Dominick A.  |place=Washington, DC |publisher=Island Press/Center for Resource Economics |language=en |doi=10.5822/978-1-61091-008-8_1 |isbn=978-1-61091-008-8 |last2=Alaback |first2=Paul |last3=Spribille |first3=Toby |last4=von Wehrden |first4=Henrik |last5=Nauman |first5=Richard S.}}</ref> They have lower evaporation rates compared to tropical rainforests. Temperate rainforests in the northern hemisphere are generally dominated by conifers as opposed to broad-leafed species, and support many lichens.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Strother |first1=Ivy Evergreen |last2=Coxson |first2=Darwyn |last3=Goward |first3=Trevor |date=2022 |title=Why is the rainforest lichen Methuselah's beard ( Usnea longissima ) so rare in British Columbia's inland temperate rainforest? |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/cjb-2021-0057 |journal=Botany |language=en |volume=100 |issue=3 |pages=283–299 |doi=10.1139/cjb-2021-0057 |hdl=1807/109849|hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Tropical forests ===

[[File:Cuniculus_paca.jpg|thumb|Paca the South American rodent species that has shared features with the African chevrotain due to convergent evolution.]]

[[File:Indian_spotted_chevrotain_Moschiola_indica_Mouse_deer_from_the_Anaimalai_hills_DSC9927_03.jpg|thumb|The African chevrotain an ungulate that shares convergently evolved features with the South American paca.]]

[[Tropical forest]]s are some of the most [[Biodiversity|diverse]] ecosystems in the world.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Paul R. |title=The science of ecology |last2=Roughgarden |first2=Joan |date=1987 |publisher=Macmillan ; Collier Macmillan |isbn=978-0-02-331700-2 |location=New York : London}}</ref> Although there are many different tree species present per acre of forest, many share similar appearances due to the similar environmental pressures.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |title=The International book of the forest |date=1981 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=978-0-671-41004-9 |location=New York}}</ref> Some of these shared traits, possessed by many tropical trees, include thick and leathery leaves that are elongated and ovular with [[Midrib|mid-ribs]] and [[drip-tip]]s.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> These adaptations help to quickly drain water from the leaves, likely to help prevent [[algae]] or [[lichen]] growth<ref name=":3" /> and prevent water reflecting the sunlight or restricting [[transpiration]].<ref name=":2" /> Commonly, tropical trees have large [[buttress root]]s on larger trees, and [[stilt roots]] on mid-sized trees which help support their tall and vertical structures in the shallow and moist soil.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> Tropical forests grow very densely due to the heavy rainfall and year-round growing season. This creates competition for light which causes many trees to grow very tall, blocking out most or all of the light from reaching the [[forest floor]].<ref name=":3" /> Because of this, the [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] exhibits distinct stratified layers from the tallest trees to the tightly packed midstory trees below.<ref name=":3" /> Due to low light on the forest floor, there is a diverse population of [[epiphyte]]s, a type of plant that grows on the canopy trees, rather than soil, to access better light. Many [[vine]]s use a similar tactic, however they root in the ground, growing up the trees to reach light.<ref name=":3" /> The [[fauna]] in tropical forests also show many unique adaptations to fill various [[Ecological niche|niches]]. These adaptations are possessed by different species depending on where they are located.<ref name=":3" /> For example, there are similar looking animals in the rainforests of South America and Africa that share ecological niches, however the mammals from South America are [[rodent]]s while the African ones are [[ungulate]]s. This clearly demonstrates the [[convergent evolution]] between species found in tropical forest environments.<ref name=":3" />

=== Coniferous forests ===

[[Conifer]]s have unique traits that make them especially adapted to harsh conditions, including cold, drought, wind, and snow.<ref name=":2" /> Their leaves have a [[wax]] coating and are filled with [[resin]] to help prevent moisture loss, this makes them unpalatable to animals and slow to [[Decomposition|decompose]]. This [[leaf litter]] creates an acidic forest floor that is distinct to coniferous forests.<ref name=":2" /> Because of the types of leaves possessed by conifers, they face the problem of soil nutrient loss; this problem is solved through [[Mycorrhizal network|mycorrhizal symbiosis]] with [[Fungus|fungi]] that help transport the limited nutrients to the trees in exchange for [[Glucose|sugars]].<ref name=":2" /> Some conifers are incapable of surviving without mycorrhizal fungi.<ref name=":2" /> The majority of conifers are also [[evergreen]], allowing them to take advantage of the short growing seasons of their respective environments.<ref name=":2" /> Their thin tapered structure helps them to withstand strong winds without being blown over.<ref name=":2" /> The stereotypically cone shape of conifers helps prevent large quantities of snow from building up on their branches and breaking them.<ref name=":3" /> Due to the harsh environments that coniferous forests are commonly found, the diversity is limited in both plant and animal species. The colder climates limit the number of [[Reptile|reptilian]] and [[amphibian]] species that can survive.<ref name=":2" /> The species more commonly found in coniferous forests are [[mammal]]s, including large [[herbivore]]s such as [[moose]] and [[elk]], [[Predation|predators]] like [[bear]]s and [[Wolf|wolves]], along with a few smaller species like [[rabbit]]s, [[fox]]es, and [[mink]]. There are also a variety of [[migratory bird]] species and some [[Bird of prey|birds of prey]] such as [[owl]]s and [[hawk]]s.<ref name=":2" /> Coniferous forests contain a variety of valuable [[Pulp (paper)|pulp]] and [[lumber]] trees making them some of the most [[economically]] important ecosystems.<ref name=":2" /> They have also been historically sought for the [[fur trade]] due to the animals species that inhabit them.<ref name=":2" />

== Ecological interactions ==

=== Plant-plant interactions ===

In forests, trees and shrubs often serve as [[nurse plants]] that facilitate the establishment and seedling growth of understory plants. The forest canopy protects young understory plants from extremes of temperature and dry conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lemenih |first1=Mulugeta |last2=Gidyelew |first2=Taye |last3=Teketay |first3=Demel |date=June 2004 |title=Effects of canopy cover and understory environment of tree plantations on richness, density and size of colonizing woody species in southern Ethiopia |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0378112704001124 |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |language=en |volume=194 |issue=1–3 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2004.01.050 |bibcode=2004ForEM.194....1L |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Martinkova |first1=Zdenka |last2=Honek |first2=Alois |last3=Pekar |first3=Stano |title=The Role of Nurse Plants in Facilitating the Germination of Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) Seeds |journal=Weed Science |date=2014 |volume=62 |issue=3|pages=474–482 |doi=10.1614/WS-D-13-00162.1 |bibcode=2014WeedS..62..474M |s2cid=85658841 }}</ref>

=== Mycorrhizal symbiosis ===

[[File:Positive_effects_of_arbuscular_mycorrhizal_(AM)_colonization.png|thumb|The benefits of mycorrhizal fungi interacting with plant roots to improve nutrient absorption among other benefits compared to a plant without this symbiotic relationship.]]

{{main|Mycorrhizal network}}

An important interaction in forest ecosystems is the mycorrhizal network, which consists of fungi and plants that share [[Symbiosis|symbiotic]] relationships.<ref name="10.1111_nph.13288">{{Cite journal |last1=van der Heijden |first1=Marcel G. A. |last2=Martin |first2=Francis M. |last3=Selosse |first3=Marc-André |last4=Sanders |first4=Ian R. |date=March 2015 |title=Mycorrhizal ecology and evolution: the past, the present, and the future |url=https://nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/nph.13288 |journal=New Phytologist |language=en |volume=205 |issue=4 |pages=1406–1423 |doi=10.1111/nph.13288 |pmid=25639293 |bibcode=2015NewPh.205.1406V |hdl=1874/329560 |issn=0028-646X|hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":02">{{cite journal |last1=Van der Heijden |first1=Marcel G. A. |last2=Horton |first2=Thomas R. |date=2009 |title=Socialism in Soil? the Importance of Mycorrhizal Fungal Networks for Facilitation in Natural Ecosystems |journal=Journal of Ecology |volume=97 |issue=6}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Agathokleous |first1=E. |last2=Feng |first2=Z. |last3=Oksanen |first3=E. |last4=Sicard |first4=P. |last5=Wang |first5=Q. |last6=Saitanis |first6=C. J. |last7=Araminiene |first7=V. |last8=Blande |first8=J. D. |last9=Hayes |first9=F. |last10=Calatayud |first10=V. |last11=Domingos |first11=M. |last12=Veresoglou |first12=S. D. |last13=Peñuelas |first13=J. |last14=Wardle |first14=D. A. |last15=De Marco |first15=A. |last16=Li |first16=Z. |last17=Harmens |first17=H. |last18=Yuan |first18=X. |last19=Vitale |first19=M. |last20=Paoletti |first20=E. |display-authors=5 |date=12 August 2020 |title=Ozone affects plant, insect, and soil microbial communities: A threat to terrestrial ecosystems and biodiversity |journal=Science Advances |volume=6 |issue=33 |article-number=eabc1176 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.abc1176 |pmid=32851188 |pmc=7423369 |bibcode=2020SciA....6.1176A }}</ref> Mycorrhizal networks have been shown to increase the uptake of important nutrients, especially ones which disperse slowly into the soil like [[Phosphorus cycle|phosphorus]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |title=Environmental restoration: science and strategies for restoring the Earth |date=1990 |publisher=Island Press |isbn=978-0-933280-94-6 |editor-last=Berger |editor-first=John J. |location=Washington, D.C. |editor-last2=Restoring the Earth (Organization) |editor-last3=University of California, Berkeley |editor-last4=University of California, Berkeley |editor-last5=San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission}}</ref> The fine [[hypha]] of the [[mycelium]] is able to reach farther into the soil than the roots of the plant, allowing it to better access phosphorus and water.<ref name=":1" /> The mycorrhizal network can also transport water and nutrients between plants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rosling |first1=Anna |last2=Midgley |first2=Meghan G. |last3=Cheeke |first3=Tanya |last4=Urbina |first4=Hector |last5=Fransson |first5=Petra |last6=Phillips |first6=Richard P. |date=February 2016 |title=Phosphorus cycling in deciduous forest soil differs between stands dominated by ecto- and arbuscular mycorrhizal trees |url=https://nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/nph.13720 |journal=New Phytologist |language=en |volume=209 |issue=3 |pages=1184–1195 |doi=10.1111/nph.13720 |pmid=26510093 |bibcode=2016NewPh.209.1184R |issn=0028-646X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="10.1111_nph.13288"/><ref name="Binghman20112">{{cite journal |last1=Bingham |first1=Marcus A. |last2=Simard |first2=Suzanne W. |year=2011 |title=Do mycorrhizal network benefits to survival and growth of interior Douglas-fir seedlings increase with soil moisture stress? |journal=Ecology and Evolution |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=306–316 |doi=10.1002/ece3.24 |doi-access=free |pmc=3287316 |pmid=22393502|bibcode=2011EcoEv...1..306B }}</ref> These interactions can help provide [[drought resistance]] to their symbiotic plants, helping protect them through the progression of [[climate change]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=van der Heijden |first1=Marcel G. A. |last2=Martin |first2=Francis M. |last3=Selosse |first3=Marc-André |last4=Sanders |first4=Ian R. |date=March 2015 |title=Mycorrhizal ecology and evolution: the past, the present, and the future |url=https://nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/nph.13288 |journal=New Phytologist |language=en |volume=205 |issue=4 |pages=1406–1423 |doi=10.1111/nph.13288 |pmid=25639293 |bibcode=2015NewPh.205.1406V |hdl=1874/329560 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":1" /> However, it's been shown that the benefit of mycorrhizal networks vary greatly depending on the species of plant and nutrient availability. The plants' benefit from mycorrhizal [[fungus]] decreases as nutrient density increases, because the plants' loss of [[Glucose|sugars]] costs more than the benefit they receive.<ref name=":02" /> While many plants rely on mycorrhizal symbiosis, not all possess this ability, and those without are shown to be negatively affected by the presence of mycorrhizal fungi.<ref name=":02" />

=== Ecological potential of forest species ===

The ecological potential of a particular species is a measure of its capacity to effectively compete in a given geographical area, ahead of other species, as they all try to occupy a natural space. For some areas it has been quantified, as for instance by Hans-Jürgen Otto, for central Europe.<ref>{{cite book|last=Otto|first=Hans-Jürgen|title=Écologie Forestière|year=1998|publisher=Institut pour le Développement Forestier|location=Paris|isbn=978-2-904740-65-7|language=fr}}</ref> He takes three groups of parameters:

# Related to site requirements: Tolerance to low temperatures, tolerance to dry climate, frugality.
# Specific qualities: [[Shade tolerance]], height growth, stability, longevity, regeneration capacity.
# Specific risks: Resistance to late freezing, resistance to wind/ice storm, resistance to fire, resistance to biotic agents.

Every parameter is scored between 0 and 5 for each considered species, and then a global mean value calculated. A value above 3.5 is considered high, below 3.0 low, and intermediate for those in between. In this study ''[[Fagus sylvatica]]'' has a score of 3.82, ''[[Fraxinus excelsior]]'' 3.08 and ''[[Juglans regia]]'' 2.92; and are examples of the three categories.

=== Competition ===

Forest ecosystem interactions consist of not only symbiotic relationships, but also competition. Competition can either be in forms of [[Intraspecific competition|intraspecific]] or [[Interspecific competition|interspecific]] competition.<ref name="sciencedirect.com">{{Cite book |title=Interspecific Competition - an overview {{!}} ScienceDirect Topics|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/interspecific-competition|access-date=2026-04-05|isbn=978-0-12-813252-4 }}</ref>{{better source needed|date=May 2026}} Intraspecific competition can occur between members of the same species for resources, whereas interspecific competition occurs between different species in a population.<ref name="sciencedirect.com"/>{{better source needed|date=May 2026}} For example, in order to fulfil nutritional needs decomposing organic matter in soils is a sought after resource by plants, microbes and fungi.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fontaine|first1=Sébastien|last2=Mariotti|first2=André|last3=Abbadie|first3=Luc|date=2003-06-01|title=The priming effect of organic matter: a question of microbial competition?|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0038071703001238|journal=Soil Biology and Biochemistry|volume=35|issue=6|pages=837–843|doi=10.1016/S0038-0717(03)00123-8|bibcode=2003SBiBi..35..837F |issn=0038-0717|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Invasive species in forest ecosystems also play a role in interspecific competition.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Invasive Species - an overview {{!}} ScienceDirect Topics|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/invasive-species|access-date=2026-04-05 |website=www.sciencedirect.com}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=May 2026}} They often compete with native species for resources and may conquer these resources successfully due to low intraspecific competition.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Woo|first1=Sohyun|last2=Kim|first2=Tae-Min|last3=Kim|first3=Yousuk |last4=Jeong|first4=Seorin |last5=Kim|first5=Eunsuk |date=October 2024 |title=Inter- and Intraspecific Competition in Invasive Lactuca serriola and Co-Occurring Weedy Plant Species |journal=Ecology and Evolution |volume=14|issue=10 |article-number=e70496|doi=10.1002/ece3.70496 |doi-access=free |pmc=11522139|pmid=39478980 |bibcode=2024EcoEv..1470496W }}</ref> The [[hemlock woolly adelgid]] and the [[emerald ash borer]] are examples of well known invasive species that colonize an area and create disturbances in forest ecology by killing host trees and reducing forest vegetation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Environmental and Ecological Impacts {{!}} National Invasive Species Information Center|url=https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/subject/environmental-and-ecological-impacts|access-date=2026-04-05|website=www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada|first=Natural Resources|date=2013-10-24|title=Emerald ash borer (factsheet)|url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/forests-forestry/insects-disturbances/emerald-ash-borer-factsheet|access-date=2026-04-05|website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref>

== Matter and energy flows ==

=== Energy flux ===
[[File:RockyPointTrailAsFirebreak.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Forest ecologists are interested in the effects of large disturbances, such as [[wildfire]]s. [[Montana]], United States.]]
Forests accumulate large amounts of standing biomass, and many are capable of accumulating it at high rates, i.e. they are highly productive. Such high levels of biomass and tall vertical structures represent large stores of [[potential energy]] that can be converted to [[kinetic energy]] under the right circumstances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Running |first1=Steven W. |title=Ecosystem Disturbance, Carbon, and Climate |journal=Science |date=2008 |volume=321 |issue=5889 |pages=652–653 |doi=10.1126/science.1159607 |pmid=18669853 }}</ref>

The world's forests contain about 606 [[Metric ton|gigatonnes]] of living biomass (above- and below-ground) and 59 gigatonnes of dead wood.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 – Key findings|publisher=FAO|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132581-0|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/ca8753en|s2cid=130116768}}</ref>

Two such conversions of great importance are [[wildfires|fires]] and [[windthrow|treefall]]s, both of which radically alter forest structure and ecosystem processes and the physical environment where they occur.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bowd |first1=Elle |last2=Lindenmayer |first2=David |date=January 2026 |title=Setting the benchmark: Patterns of forest structure after wildfire in temperate, montane forests across a multi-century chronosequence |url=https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2745.70227 |journal=Journal of Ecology |language=en |volume=114 |issue=1 |article-number=e70227 |doi=10.1111/1365-2745.70227 |bibcode=2026JEcol.11470227B |issn=0022-0477|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Seidl |first1=Rupert |last2=Rammer |first2=Werner |last3=Spies |first3=Thomas A. |date=2014-12-01 |title=Disturbance legacies increase the resilience of forest ecosystem structure, composition, and functioning |journal=Ecological Applications |volume=24 |issue=8 |pages=2063–2077 |doi=10.1890/14-0255.1 |issn=1051-0761 |pmc=4820056 |pmid=27053913 |bibcode=2014EcoAp..24.2063S }}</ref> Also, in forests of high productivity, the rapid growth of the trees themselves induces biome and environmental changes, although at a slower rate and lower intensity than relatively instantaneous [[disturbance (ecology)|disturbances]] such as fires.

=== Water ===
Forest trees store large amounts of water because of their large size and anatomical/physiological characteristics.  They are therefore important regulators of hydrological processes, especially those involving groundwater [[hydrology]] and local evaporation and [[Precipitation (meteorology)|rainfall/snowfall]] patterns.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hadiwijaya |first1=Bram |last2=Isabelle |first2=Pierre-Erik |last3=Nadeau |first3=Daniel F. |last4=Pepin |first4=Steeve |date=February 2021 |title=Observations of canopy storage capacity and wet canopy evaporation in a humid boreal forest |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.14021 |journal=Hydrological Processes |volume=35 |issue=2 |article-number=e14021 |doi=10.1002/hyp.14021 |bibcode=2021HyPr...35E4021H |issn=0885-6087|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Smerdon |first=Brian D. |display-authors=etal|year=2009 |title=An overview of the effects of forest management on ground water hydrology|url=http://forrex.org/sites/default/files/publications/jem_archive/ISS50/vol10_no1_art4.pdf |journal=BC Journal of Ecosystems and Management|volume=10|issue=1|pages=22–44|access-date=2016-11-21|archive-date=2016-11-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161122153621/http://forrex.org/sites/default/files/publications/jem_archive/ISS50/vol10_no1_art4.pdf}}</ref>

An estimated 399 million ha of forest is designated primarily for the protection of soil and water, an increase of 119 million ha since 1990.<ref name=":0" />

Thus, forest ecological studies are sometimes closely aligned with [[meteorology|meteorological]] and hydrological studies in regional ecosystem or resource planning studies. Perhaps more importantly the duff or [[leaf litter]] can form a major repository of water storage. When this litter is removed or compacted (through grazing or human overuse), erosion and flooding are exacerbated as well as deprivation of dry season water for forest organisms.

=== Death and regeneration ===

[[File:Cascades Regrowth after forest fire.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Forest regrowth after a forest fire, [[Cascade Range]], United States]]

Woody material, often referred to as [[coarse woody debris]], [[decomposition|decay]]s relatively slowly in many forests in comparison to most other [[organic matter|organic]] materials, due to a combination of environmental factors and wood chemistry (see [[lignin]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Vamosi |first1=Jana C. |last2=Wilson |first2=John R. U. |date=October 2008 |title=Nonrandom extinction leads to elevated loss of angiosperm evolutionary history |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2008.01215.x |journal=Ecology Letters |language=en |volume=11 |issue=10 |pages=1047–1053 |doi=10.1111/j.1461-0248.2008.01215.x |pmid=18616544 |bibcode=2008EcolL..11.1047V |hdl=10019.1/112326 |issn=1461-023X|hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ganjegunte |first1=Girisha K |last2=Condron |first2=Leo M |last3=Clinton |first3=Peter W |last4=Davis |first4=Murray R |last5=Mahieu |first5=Nathalie |date=2004-01-23 |title=Decomposition and nutrient release from radiata pine (Pinus radiata) coarse woody debris |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378112703003323 |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |language=en |volume=187 |issue=2 |pages=197–211 |doi=10.1016/S0378-1127(03)00332-3 |bibcode=2004ForEM.187..197G |issn=0378-1127|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Trees growing in [[arid]] and/or cold environments do so especially slowly. Thus, tree trunks and branches can remain on the [[forest floor]] for long periods, affecting such things as wildlife [[habitat]], fire behaviour, and tree [[regeneration (biology)|regeneration]] processes.

Some trees leave behind eerie skeletons after death. In reality these deaths are actually very few compared to the amount of tree deaths that go unnoticed. Thousands of seedlings can be produced from a single tree but only a few can actually grow to maturity.<ref name="Tree Death: Cause and Consequence">{{Cite journal|date=1987|title=Competition and Tree Death|journal=BioScience |volume=37|pages=586–595|jstor=1310669|last1=Peet|first1=Robert K.|last2=Christensen|first2=Norman L.|issue=8|doi=10.2307/1310669}}</ref> Most of those deaths are caused from competition for light, water, or soil nutrients, this is called natural thinning. Singular deaths caused by natural thinning go unnoticed, but many deaths can help form forest ecosystems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Swanson |first1=Mark E |last2=Franklin |first2=Jerry F |last3=Beschta |first3=Robert L |last4=Crisafulli |first4=Charles M |last5=DellaSala |first5=Dominick A |last6=Hutto |first6=Richard L |last7=Lindenmayer |first7=David B |last8=Swanson |first8=Frederick J |date=2011 |title=The forgotten stage of forest succession: early-successional ecosystems on forest sites |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/090157 |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment |language=en |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=117–125 |doi=10.1890/090157 |bibcode=2011FrEE....9..117S |hdl=1885/60278 |issn=1540-9309|hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Luu |first1=Hoang |last2=Ris Lambers |first2=Janneke Hille |last3=Lutz |first3=James A. |last4=Metz |first4=Margaret |last5=Snell |first5=Rebecca S. |date=2024-04-08 |title=The importance of regeneration processes on forest biodiversity in old-growth forests in the Pacific Northwest |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |volume=379 |issue=1902 |article-number=20230016 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2023.0016 |pmid=38583471 |pmc=10999264 |bibcode=2024PTRSB.37930016L}}</ref><ref name="Tree Death: Cause and Consequence"/> There are four stages to forest regrowth after a disturbance, the establishment phase which is rapid increase in seedlings, the thinning phase which happens after a canopy is formed and the seedlings covered by it die, the transition phase which occurs when one tree from the canopy dies and creates a pocket of light giving new seedlings opportunity to grow, and lastly the steady-state phase which happens when the forest has different sizes and ages of trees.<ref name="Tree Death: Cause and Consequence"/>

{{Short description|Branch of forestry}}
[[File:Great outdoors 06.jpg|thumb|Sustainable forest management balances local socioeconomic, cultural, and ecological needs and constraints.]]
'''Forest management''' is a [[Topic outline of forestry#Branches of forestry|branch]] of [[forestry]] concerned with overall administrative, legal, economic, and social aspects, as well as scientific and technical aspects, such as [[#Silviculture|silviculture]], [[#Forest protection|forest protection]], and regulation. This includes management for timber, [[aesthetics]], [[outdoor recreation|recreation]], urban values, [[watershed management|water]], [[wildlife]], inland and nearshore fisheries, [[forest product|wood products]], [[plant genetic resources]], and other [[Nontimber forest products|forest resource values]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Glossary of Forestry Terms in British Columbia | publisher = Ministry of Forests and Range (Canada) | date = March 2008| url = http://www.for.gov.bc.ca/hfd/library/documents/glossary/Glossary.pdf | access-date = 2009-04-06}}</ref> Management objectives can be for conservation, utilisation, or a mixture of the two. Techniques include [[Lumber|timber]] extraction, [[#Afforestation|planting]] and [[#Reforestation|replanting]] of different [[Tree|species]], building and maintenance of roads and pathways through forests, and preventing [[#Wildfires|fire]]. Forest Management plays an important part in maintaining ecosystem health and supporting biodiversity.<ref>Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. https://www.fao.org/</ref>

==Role of forests==
{{Main|Forest}}

The forest is a natural system that can supply different products and services. Forests supply water, [[Climate change mitigation|mitigate climate change]], provide habitats for wildlife including many pollinators which are essential for sustainable food production, provide timber and fuelwood, serve as a source of non-wood forest products including food and medicine, and contribute to rural livelihoods.<ref name=":3"/> The working of a forest is influenced by the natural environment: climate, topography, soil, etc., and also by human activity. The actions of humans in forests constitute forest management.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Natural Forest Management |url=https://www.fao.org/forestry/sfm/85084/en/ |access-date=2022-10-24 |website=www.fao.org |archive-date=2022-12-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221226123935/https://www.fao.org/forestry/sfm/85084/en/ }}</ref>

== Aims ==
Some forests have been and are managed to obtain traditional forest products such as firewood, fiber for paper, and timber, with little thinking for other products and services. Nevertheless, as a result of the progression of environmental awareness, management of forests for multiple use is becoming more common.<ref name="Young">{{cite book |last1=Young |first1=Raymond |title=Introduction to Forest Science |date=1982 |publisher=John Wiley & sons |isbn=978-0-471-06438-1|page=207}}</ref>

Forests provide a variety of [[ecosystem service]]s: cleaning the air, accumulating carbon, filtering water, and reducing flooding and erosion.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ecosystem Services |url=https://research.fs.usda.gov/centers/ccrc |access-date=21 April 2021 |website=Climate Change Resource Center |publisher=USDA and US Forest Service}}</ref> Forests are the most biodiverse land-based ecosystem, and provide habitat for a vast array of animals, birds, plants and other life. They can provide food and material and also opportunities for recreation and education. Research has found that forest plantations "may result in reduced diversity and abundance of pollinators compared with natural forests that have greater structural and plant species diversity."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brockerhoff |first1=Eckehard |last2=et |first2=al |date=4 November 2017 |title=Forest biodiversity, ecosystem functioning and the provision of ecosystem services |journal=Biodiversity and Conservation |volume=26 |issue=13 |pages=3005–3035 |bibcode=2017BiCon..26.3005B |doi=10.1007/s10531-017-1453-2 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Coverage ==
Globally in 2025, 1.20 billion ha of forest (29% of the total forest area) is managed primarily to produce wood and non-wood forest products. In addition, about 616 million ha of forest is designated for multiple use, which often includes production. The largest forest area designated for production is in Europe, at 548 million ha, which is more than half the region’s total forest area and almost half the total forest area designated for production globally. The area of forest designated primarily for production and multiple use worldwide decreased by 29.8 million ha and 97.5 million ha, respectively, between 1990 and 2025.<ref name=":7" />

== Monitoring and planning ==
[[File:Proportion of total forest area designated for various primary management objectives, 2025.svg|thumb|Proportion of total forest area worldwide designated for various primary management objectives, 2025.]]
[[File:Proportion of forest area with long-term management plans, by region, 2025.svg|thumb|Proportion of forest area with long-term management plans, by region, 2025.]]
Foresters develop and implement forest management plans relying on mapped resources, [[Forest inventory|inventories]] showing an area's [[Topography|topographical]] features as well as its distribution of trees (by species) and other plant covers. Plans also include landowner objectives, roads, [[culvert]]s, proximity to human habitation, water features and hydrological conditions, and soil information. Forest management plans typically include recommended [[Silviculture|silvicultural]] treatments and a timetable for their implementation. Application of digital maps in Geographic Information systems (GIS) that extracts and integrates different information about forest terrains, [[soil type]] and tree covers, etc. using, e.g. laser scanning enhances forest management plans in modern systems.<ref>{{Cite web |last=eugene |date=2022-09-20 |title=What is Geographic Information System Analysis In Forestry? |url=https://tallpinesforestmanagement.com/2022/09/20/what-is-gis-analysis-and-whats-its-role-in-forest-management/ |access-date=2023-01-23 |website=Tall Pines Forest Management |language=en-US}}</ref>

Forest management plans include recommendations to achieve the landowner's objectives and desired future conditions for the property subject to ecological, financial, logistical (e.g. access to resources), and other constraints. On some properties, plans focus on producing quality wood products for processing or sale. Hence, tree species, quantity, and form, all central to the value of harvested products quality and quantity, tend to be important components of silvicultural plans.

Good management plans include consideration of future conditions of the stand after any recommended harvest treatments, including future treatments (particularly in intermediate stand treatments), and plans for natural or artificial regeneration after final harvests.

The objectives of [[landowner]]s and [[Leasehold estate|leaseholders]] influence plans for harvest and subsequent site treatment. In Britain, plans featuring "good forestry practice" must always consider the needs of other stakeholders such as nearby communities or rural residents living within or adjacent to woodland areas. Foresters consider tree felling and environmental legislation when developing plans. Plans instruct the sustainable harvesting and replacement of trees.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Garcia-Grant |first=Ian |date=Dec 20, 2021 |title=Planning For Long Term Forest Management |url=https://tallpinesforestmanagement.com/2021/12/20/planning-for-long-term-forest-management/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221202232002/https://tallpinesforestmanagement.com/2021/12/20/planning-for-long-term-forest-management/ |archive-date=Dec 2, 2022 |access-date=Jan 23, 2023 |website=Tall Pines Forest Management}}</ref> They indicate whether road building or other forest engineering operations are required.

[[Agriculture]] and forest leaders are also trying to understand how the [[Politics of climate change|climate change legislation]] will affect what they do. The information gathered will provide the data that will determine the role of agriculture and forestry in a new climate change regulatory system.<ref name="galegroup1">{{cite web |url=http://find.galegroup.com/gps/start.do?prodId=IPS |title=PowerSearch Logout |publisher=Find.galegroup.com |access-date=2014-03-15 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130510172355/http://find.galegroup.com/gps/start.do?prodId=IPS |archive-date=2013-05-10 }}</ref>

In Sweden, where forest management is based on liberal governance principles, forest management plans primarily function as information tools that support decision-making by forest owners rather than as regulatory instruments. Studies have identified limitations in current planning systems, including outdated planning templates, a lack of harmonised data, and limited consideration of forest owners' objectives and broader ecological and social values.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Karlsson |first=Anna |last2=Brukas |first2=Vilis |date=2026-06-23 |title=“The production forest is, after all, quite boring for a planner” - Integrating landscape perspective in forest planning under laissez-faire governance |url=https://forestsmonitor.com/index.php/fm/article/view/forest-planning-landscape-perspective |journal=Forests Monitor |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=1–43 |doi=10.62320/fm.v3i1.29 |issn=3071-8465}}</ref>

=== Forest inventory ===

{{main|Forest inventory}}

Forest inventory is the systematic collection of data and forest information for assessment or analysis. An estimate of the value and possible uses of [[timber]] is an important part of the broader information required to [[sustainability|sustain ecosystems]].<ref name="Moores_et_al">{{Citation |journal=Environmental Monitoring and Assessment |year=1996 |volume=39 |issue=1–3 |pages=571–577 |title=Forest ecological classification and mapping: their application for ecosystem management in Newfoundland |author1=L. J. Moores |author2=B. Pittman |author3=G. Kitchen |doi=10.1007/bf00396169|pmid=24198030 |bibcode=1996EMnAs..39..571M |s2cid=206779166 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-06-14 |title=An Introduction To The Business Of Small-scale Forestry. Private Forestry Guidance Materials Report 2023 |url=https://fwpa.com.au/report/an-introduction-to-the-business-of-small-scale-forestry/ |access-date=2025-02-06 |website=FWPA}}</ref>

===Wildlife considerations===

The abundance and diversity of birds, mammals, amphibians and other wildlife are affected by strategies and types of forest management.<ref>*Philip Joseph Burton. 2003. ''Towards sustainable management of the boreal forest'' 1039 pages</ref> Forests are important because they provide these species with food, space and water.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home {{!}} Ohio Woodland Stewards Program |url=https://woodlandstewards.osu.edu/ |access-date=2022-10-24 |website=woodlandstewards.osu.edu}}</ref> Forest management is also important as it helps in conservation and utilization of the forest resources. Forest clearing to aid specific species of wildlife has been criticized because it can fragment forests leading to deleterious effects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kellett |first1=Michael J. |last2=Maloof |first2=Joan E. |last3=Masino |first3=Susan A. |last4=Frelich |first4=Lee E. |last5=Faison |first5=Edward K. |last6=Brosi |first6=Sunshine L. |last7=Foster |first7=David R. |date=2023-01-09 |title=Forest-clearing to create early-successional habitats: Questionable benefits, significant costs |journal=Frontiers in Forests and Global Change |language=English |volume=5 |article-number=1073677 |doi=10.3389/ffgc.2022.1073677 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2023FrFGC...573677K |issn=2624-893X}}</ref>{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

Approximately 50 million hectares (or 24%) of European forest land is protected for biodiversity and landscape protection. Forests allocated for soil, water, and other ecosystem services encompass around 72 million hectares (32% of European forest area).<ref name=":107">{{Cite book |last=Bank |first=European Investment |url=https://www.eib.org/en/publications/20220173-forests-at-the-heart-of-sustainable-development |title=Forests at the heart of sustainable development: Investing in forests to meet biodiversity and climate goals |date=2022-12-08 |publisher=European Investment Bank |isbn=978-92-861-5403-4 |language=EN}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Forests - Environment - European Commission |url=https://ec.europa.eu/environment/forests/policy_en.htm |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=ec.europa.eu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://foresteurope.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/08/protected-forests-in-europe.pdf|title=Protected Forests in Europe}}</ref> Over 90% of the world's forests regenerate organically, and more than half are covered by forest management plans or equivalents.<ref name=":107"/><ref name=":6" />

===Management intensity===
[[File:Proportion of forest area with long-term management plans, by region, 2020.svg|thumb|Proportion of forest area with long-term management plans, by region, 2020<ref name="auto1">{{Cite book|title=Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 – Key findings|publisher=FAO|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132581-0|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/ca8753en|s2cid=130116768 }}</ref>]]

Forest management varies in intensity from a leave alone, natural situation to a highly intensive regime with silvicultural interventions. Forest Management is generally increased in intensity to achieve either economic criteria (increased timber yields, [[non-timber forest product]]s, [[ecosystem services]]) or ecological criteria (species recovery, fostering of rare species, carbon sequestration).<ref>{{Cite journal | title=Classification of Forest Management Approaches: A New Conceptual Framework and Its Applicability to European Forestry | author1=Philipp S. Duncker | author2=Susana M. Barreiro | author3=Geerten M. Hengeveld | author4=Torgny Lind | author5=William L. Mason  | author6=Slawomir Ambrozy | author7=Heinrich Spiecker | url=http://www.ecologyandsociety.org/vol17/iss4/art51/ | journal=Ecology and Society | date=2012 | volume=17 | issue=4 | article-number=art51 | doi=10.5751/ES-05262-170451 }}</ref>

Most of the forests in Europe have management plans; on the other hand, management plans exist for less than 25 percent of forests in Africa and less than 20 percent in South America. The area of forest under management plans is increasing in all regions – globally, it has increased by 233 million ha since 2000, reaching 2.05 billion ha in 2020.<ref name="auto1"/>

=== Monitoring ===
Long-term monitoring studies are conducted to track forest dynamics over extended periods.<ref name="Prevedello Winck Weber et al 2019"/><ref name="Benedek & Fertő 2013"/> These studies involve monitoring factors such as tree growth, mortality rates, and species composition. By observing forest changes over time, scientists can assess the health of forests and their responses to environmental shifts. Long-term monitoring is invaluable for informing sustainable forest management practices.<ref name="Zhang & Wei 2021"/><ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022"/> Yet such monitoring is usually of the type that provide "early warning" only, while a more valuable approach would be to combine long-term monitoring and long-term experiments, thereby revealing causality <ref>Nichols, J.D & Williams, B.K. (2006). Monitoring for conservation. Trends in Ecology 21: 668-673.</ref>     

Scientific research employs [[Remote sensing|remote sensing technologies]] and [[geographic information system]]s (GIS) to monitor changes in forest cover, deforestation rates, and forest health over time.<ref name="Zhang & Wei 2021"/><ref name="AbdulBaqi2022"/> These tools provide valuable data for forest assessments and support evidence-based decision making in forest management and conservation. By remotely monitoring forest changes, scientists can respond more effectively to threats and challenges facing forests.<ref name="Zhang & Wei 2021" /><ref name="AbdulBaqi2022" />

Researchers conduct [[biodiversity]] assessments to gain insights into the diversity and distribution of plant and animal species in various forest ecosystems.<ref name="Prevedello Winck Weber et al 2019"/><ref name="Zhang & Wei 2021"/> These studies are essential for identifying areas of high conservation value and understanding the ecological importance of different habitats. By studying biodiversity patterns, scientists can recommend targeted approaches to forest management that protect and promote the richness of forest life.<ref name="Windisch Davin Seneviratne 2021"/><ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022"/><ref name="Prevedello Winck Weber et al 2019" /><ref name="Portmann Beyerle Davin et al 2022"/>

=== Effects of climate change on forests ===
{{Further|Effects of climate change on biomes}}
Research explores the specific [[Effects of climate change on biomes|impacts of climate change on forest ecosystems]], including extreme heat and drought events.<ref name="Prevedello Winck Weber et al 2019"/><ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022"/> Understanding these effects is vital for developing [[Climate change adaptation|adaptive strategies]] to mitigate climate change impacts on forests. By recognizing the vulnerabilities of forests to changing climatic conditions, scientists can implement conservation methods that enhance their resilience.<ref name="Portmann Beyerle Davin et al 2022"/><ref name="Windisch Davin Seneviratne 2021"/><ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022" />

Scientific research plays a crucial role in forest management by utilizing [[climate model]]ing to project future [[Climate change scenario|climate scenarios]].<ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022"/><ref name="Benedek & Fertő 2013"/><ref name="Windisch Davin Seneviratne 2021"/> These models help scientists understand potential changes in temperature, precipitation patterns, and extreme weather events, enabling them to assess the impact of these changes on forest ecosystems. By predicting climate trends, researchers can develop more effective strategies for forest management and conservation.<ref name="Zhang & Wei 2021"/><ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022" /><ref name="Windisch Davin Seneviratne 2021" />

== Methods for creating or recreating forests ==
The term ''forestation'' is sometimes used as an umbrella term to include [[afforestation]] and [[reforestation]]. Both of those are processes for establishing and nurturing [[forest]]s on lands that either previously had forest cover or were subjected to [[deforestation]] or degradation.<ref name="Prevedello Winck Weber et al 2019"/>

=== Hardwood timber production ===
Hardwood timber production is the process of managing stands of [[deciduous]] trees to maximize woody output. The production process is not linear because other factors must be considered, including marketable and non-marketable goods, financial benefits, management practices, and the environmental implications, of those management practices.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Nyland |first=Ralph D. |title=Silviculture: concepts and applications |date=2002 |publisher=McGraw-Hill |isbn=978-0-07-366190-2 |edition=2nd |series=McGraw-Hill series in forest resources |location=Boston}}</ref>

The more biodiverse the hardwood-forest ecosystem, the more challenges and opportunities its managers face. Managers aim for sustainable forest management to keep their cash crop renewing itself, using [[silvicultural]] practices that include growing, selling, controlling insects and most diseases, providing manure, applying herbicide treatments, and thinning.<ref name=":1" />

But management can also harm the ecosystem; for example, machinery used in a timber harvest can compact the soil, stress the root system, reduce tree growth, lengthen the time needed for a stand to mature to harvestability. Machinery can also damage the [[understory]], disturbing wildlife habitat and prevent regeneration.<ref name=":1" />
