== Sustainable forest management ==
Sustainable forest management (SFM) is the management of forests according to the principles of [[sustainable development]]. Sustainable forest management must keep a balance between the three main pillars: [[Natural environment|ecological]], [[economic]] and [[Sociocultural evolution|sociocultural]]. The goal of sustainable forestry is to allow for a balance to be found between making use of trees while maintaining natural patterns of disturbance and regeneration.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-07-28 |title=What is Sustainable Forestry? |url=https://www.rainforest-alliance.org/insights/what-is-sustainable-forestry/ |access-date=2022-03-31 |website=Rainforest Alliance |language=en-US}}</ref> The forestry industry [[Climate change mitigation|mitigates climate change]] by boosting [[Carbon capture and storage|carbon storage]] in growing trees and soils and improving the sustainable supply of [[Renewable resource|renewable raw materials]] via sustainable forest management.<ref>{{Cite web |last=MÜLLER |first=Ulrike |title=REPORT on a new EU Forest Strategy for 2030 – Sustainable Forest Management in Europe {{!}} A9-0225/2022 {{!}} European Parliament |url=https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/A-9-2022-0225_EN.html |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=www.europarl.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref>

Successfully achieving sustainable forest management provides benefits ranging from safeguarding local livelihoods to protecting biodiversity and ecosystems provided by forests, reducing [[rural poverty]] and mitigating some of the [[effects of climate change]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ledsgp.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/CDKN_LEDS_Forestry_WG_factsheet.pdf|title=LEDS GP Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use Working Group factsheet|publisher=[[Low Emission Development Strategies Global Partnership (LEDS GP)]]|access-date=23 March 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Law |first1=Beverly |last2=Moomaw |first2=William |title=Keeping Trees in the Ground: An Effective Low-Tech Way to Slow Climate Change |url=https://www.ecowatch.com/forest-conservation-climate-change-2650741678.html |access-date=28 February 2021 |agency=Ecowatch |date=24 February 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Dennehymarch |first1=Kevin |title=Using more wood for construction can slash global reliance on fossil fuels |url=https://news.yale.edu/2014/03/31/using-more-wood-construction-can-slash-global-reliance-fossil-fuels |website=Yale News |date=31 March 2014 |publisher=Yale School of Forestry & Environmental Studies (F&ES), University of Washington's College of the Environment |access-date=15 August 2021}}</ref>

Sustainable forest management also helps with [[climate change adaptation]] by increasing forest ecosystems' resistance to future climatic hazards and lowering the danger of additional [[land degradation]] by repairing and stabilizing soils and boosting their water-retention capacity.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate Challenge |url=https://forests.org/climate/ |access-date=2024-04-06 |website=forests.org |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Martin |title=Forests, desertification and biodiversity |url=https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/biodiversity/ |access-date=2024-04-06 |website=United Nations Sustainable Development |language=en-US}}</ref> It contributes to the provision of a wide range of vital [[ecosystem service]]s and biodiversity conservation, such as [[Habitat|wildlife habitats]], recreational amenity values, and a variety of [[non-timber forest product]]s.<ref name=":107" /><ref name=":109">{{Cite web |date=17 December 2021 |title=FOREST EUROPE {{!}} Sustainable Forest Management |url=https://foresteurope.org/workstreams/sustainable-forest-management/ |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=foresteurope.org}}</ref> Conservation of biodiversity is the major management aim in around 13% of the world's forests, while preservation of soil and water resources is the primary management goal in more than 30%.<ref name=":107" /><ref name=":108">{{Cite web |last=Martin |title=Forests, desertification and biodiversity |url=https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/biodiversity/ |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=United Nations Sustainable Development |language=en-US}}</ref>

Feeding humanity and conserving and sustainably using ecosystems are complementary and closely interdependent goals. Forests supply water, mitigate climate change and provide habitats for many pollinators, which are essential for sustainable food production. It is estimated that 75 percent of the world's leading food crops, representing 35 percent of global food production, benefit from animal pollination for fruit, vegetable or seed production.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=The State of the World's Forests 2020. Forests, biodiversity and people – In brief|chapter=The State of the World's Forests 2020. In brief |publisher=FAO & UNEP|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132707-4|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/ca8985en|s2cid=241416114}}</ref>

The "[[Forest Principles]]" adopted at the [[Earth Summit]] (United Nations Conference on Environment and Development) in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 captured the general international understanding of [[sustainability|sustainable]] forest management at that time. A number of sets of [[Criteria & Indicators of Sustainable Forest Management|criteria and indicators]] have since been developed to evaluate the achievement of SFM at the global, regional, country and management unit level. These were all attempts to codify and provide for assessment of the degree to which the broader objectives of sustainable forest management are being achieved in practice. In 2007, the [[United Nations General Assembly]] adopted the [[United Nations Forum on Forests#Non-Legally Binding Instrument on All Types of Forests|Non-Legally Binding Instrument on All Types of Forests]]. The instrument was the first of its kind that reflected the strong international commitment to promote implementation of sustainable forest management through a new approach bringing all stakeholders together.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Forestry Principles And Applications|last=Antony, J R., Lal, S.B.|year=2013|page=166}}</ref>

The [[Sustainable Development Goal 15]] is also a global initiative aimed at promoting the implementation of sustainable forest management.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Goal 15 targets|url=https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/sustainable-development-goals/goal-15-life-on-land/targets.html|access-date=2020-09-24|website=UNDP|language=en|archive-date=4 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170904001634/https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/sustainable-development-goals/goal-15-life-on-land/targets.html}}</ref>

The area of forest under management plans has increased in all regions since 1990; globally, it has grown by 365 million ha, reaching 2.13 billion ha, 55% of the total forest area in 2025 up from 50% in 2020 in 2025. Of the six regions, Europe has the highest percentage of forests under management plans, at 94%.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=FAO |url=https://openknowledge.fao.org/handle/20.500.14283/cd6709en |title=Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025 |date=2025 |publisher=FAO |isbn=978-92-5-140082-1 |language=English |doi=10.4060/cd6709en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Global Forest Resource Assessment 2020 |url=https://www.fao.org/interactive/forest-resources-assessment/2020/en/ |access-date=2026-03-02 |website=www.fao.org |language=en}}</ref>

=== Definition ===
A definition of SFM was developed by the [[Ministerial Conference on the Protection of Forests in Europe]] (FOREST EUROPE) and has since been adopted by the [[Food and Agriculture Organization]] (FAO).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mcpfe.org |title=Ministerial Conference on the Protection of Forests in Europe |publisher=Mcpfe.org |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref> It defines sustainable forest management as:

<blockquote>The stewardship and use of [[forest]]s and forest lands in a way, and at a rate, that maintains their biodiversity, productivity, regeneration capacity, vitality and their potential to fulfill, now and in the future, relevant ecological, economic and social functions, at local, national, and global levels, and that does not cause damage to other ecosystems.</blockquote>

In simpler terms, the concept can be described as the attainment of balance: balance between society's increasing demands for forest products and benefits, and the preservation of forest health and diversity. This balance is critical to the survival of forests, and to the prosperity of forest-dependent communities.<ref name=":107" /><ref name=":109" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=sustainable forest management — European Environment Agency |url=https://www.eea.europa.eu/help/glossary/eea-glossary/sustainable-forest-management |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=www.eea.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref>

For forest managers, sustainably managing a particular forest tract means determining, in a tangible way, how to use it today to ensure similar benefits, health and productivity in the future. Forest managers must assess and integrate a wide array of sometimes conflicting factors: commercial and non-commercial values, environmental considerations, community needs,<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://sapiens.revues.org/index209.html |last1=Evans |first1=K. |last2=De Jong |first2=W. |last3=Cronkleton |first3=P.  |title=Future Scenarios as a Tool for Collaboration in Forest Communities |journal=S.A.P.I.EN.S |date=1 October 2008 |volume=1 |issue=2 |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref> even global impact to produce sound forest plans. In most cases, forest managers develop their forest plans in consultation with citizens, businesses, organizations and other interested parties in and around the forest tract being managed. The tools and visualization have been recently evolving for better management practices.<ref name=":5">{{cite journal|url=http://sapiens.revues.org/index734.html |last=Mozgeris |first=G.  |title=The continuous field view of representing forest geographically: from cartographic representation towards improved management planning |journal=S.A.P.I.EN.S |date=30 May 2009 |volume=2 |issue=2 |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref>

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, at the request of Member States, developed and launched the [http://www.fao.org/sustainable-forest-management/toolbox/sfm-home/en/ Sustainable Forest Management Toolbox] in 2014, an online collection of tools''',''' best practices and examples of their application to support countries implementing sustainable forest management.<ref>{{cite web|title=Sustainable Forest Management Toolbox|url=http://www.fao.org/3/a-mk154e.pdf|publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations|access-date=24 June 2014}}</ref>

Because forests and societies are in constant flux, the desired outcome of sustainable forest management is not a fixed one. What constitutes a sustainably managed forest will change over time as values held by the public change.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rametsteiner |first1=Ewald |last2=Simula |first2=Markku |title=Forest certification—an instrument to promote sustainable forest management? |journal=Journal of Environmental Management |year=2003 |volume=67 |issue=1 |pages=87–98 |doi=10.1016/S0301-4797(02)00191-3 |pmid=12659807 |bibcode=2003JEnvM..67...87R |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0301479702001913 |access-date=20 April 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Criteria and indicators ===
[[File:Deforestation central Europe - Rodungen Mitteleuropa.jpg|thumb|[[Deforestation]] in [[Europe]], 2020. France is the most deforested country in Europe, with only 15% of the native vegetation remaining.]]
[[File:Sugarcane Deforestation, Bolivia, 2016-06-15 by Planet Labs.jpg|thumb|[[Deforestation]] in [[Bolivia]].]]

{{Main|Criteria and indicators of sustainable forest management}}

Criteria and indicators are tools which can be used to conceptualise, evaluate and implement sustainable forest management.<ref>[http://www.cifor.cgiar.org/acm/methods/toolbox1.html Guidelines for Developing, Testing and Selecting Criteria and Indicators for Sustainable Forest Management] Ravi Prabhu, Carol J. P. Colfer and Richard G. Dudley. 1999. CIFOR. The Criteria & Indicators Toolbox Series.</ref> Criteria define and characterize the essential elements, as well as a set of conditions or processes, by which sustainable forest management may be assessed. Periodically measured indicators reveal the direction of change with respect to each criterion.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

Criteria and indicators of sustainable forest management are widely used and many countries produce national reports that assess their progress toward sustainable forest management. There are nine international and regional criteria and indicators initiatives, which collectively involve more than 150 countries.<ref>[http://www.fao.org/DOCREP/004/AC135E/AC135E00.HTM Criteria and Indicators for Sustainable Forest Management: A Compendium]. Paper compiled by Froylán Castañeda, Christel Palmberg-Lerche and Petteri Vuorinen, May 2001. Forest Management Working Papers, Working Paper 5. Forest Resources Development Service, Forest Resources Division. FAO, Rome (unpublished).</ref> Three of the more advanced initiatives are those of the Working Group on Criteria and Indicators for the Conservation and Sustainable Management of Temperate and Boreal Forests (also called the [[Montréal Process]]),<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.rinya.maff.go.jp/mpci/2009p_1.pdf|title=Montréal Process Indicators|access-date=3 March 2024|archive-date=20 April 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120420075341/http://www.rinya.maff.go.jp/mpci/2009p_1.pdf}}</ref> [[Ministerial Conference on the Protection of Forests in Europe|Forest Europe]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.foresteurope.org/filestore/foresteurope/Publications/pdf/improved_indicators.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100614035658/http://www.foresteurope.org/filestore/foresteurope/Publications/pdf/improved_indicators.pdf|title=MCPFE indicators|archive-date=14 June 2010}}</ref> and the [[International Tropical Timber Organization]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.itto.int/direct/topics/topics_pdf_download/topics_id=9630000&no=1&disp=inline|title=ITTO}}</ref> Countries who are members of the same initiative usually agree to produce reports at the same time and using the same indicators. Within countries, at the management unit level, efforts have also been directed at developing local level criteria and indicators of sustainable forest management. The [[Center for International Forestry Research]], the [[International Model Forest Network]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.imfn.net |title=International Model Forest Network |publisher=Imfn.net |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref> and researchers at the [[University of British Columbia]] have developed a number of tools and techniques to help forest-dependent communities develop their own local level criteria and indicators.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cifor.cgiar.org/acm/pub/toolbox.html |title=CIFOR Criteria and Indicators Toolbox Series |publisher=Cifor.cgiar.org |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.idrc.ca/en/ev-54246-201-1-DO_TOPIC.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061023185421/http://www.idrc.ca/en/ev-54246-201-1-DO_TOPIC.html|title=International Model Forest Network Criteria and Indicators|archive-date=23 October 2006}}</ref> Criteria and Indicators also form the basis of third-party forest certification programs such as the [[Canadian Standards Association]]'s<ref name=":4">{{cite web |url=http://www.csa-international.org/product_areas/forest_products_marking/Default.asp?language=english |title=Canadian Standards Association |publisher=Csa-international.org |access-date=30 November 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111118085104/http://www.csa-international.org/product_areas/forest_products_marking/default.asp?language=english |archive-date=18 November 2011}}</ref> [[Sustainable Forest Management Standards]] and the [[Sustainable Forestry Initiative]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.sfiprogram.org/files/pdf/Section1_sfi_requirements_2010-2014.pdf |title=Sustainable Forestry Initiative Introduction Page 1 |access-date=30 November 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120125143402/http://www.sfiprogram.org/files/pdf/Section1_sfi_requirements_2010-2014.pdf |archive-date=25 January 2012}}</ref>

There appears to be growing international consensus on the key elements of sustainable forest management. Seven common thematic areas of sustainable forest management have emerged based on the criteria of the nine ongoing regional and international criteria and indicators initiatives. The seven thematic areas are:
* Extent of forest resources
* [[Biological diversity]]
* [[Forest health]] and vitality
* Productive functions of forest resources
* Protective functions of forest resources
* Socio-economic functions
* Legal, policy and institutional framework.

This consensus on common thematic areas (or criteria) effectively provides a common and implicit definition of sustainable forest management. The seven thematic areas were acknowledged by the international forest community at the fourth session of the [[United Nations Forum on Forests]] and the 16th session of the Committee on Forestry.<ref>{{Cite web|title=United Nations Forum on Forests|url=https://www.un.org/esa/forests/|access-date=2023-03-16|website=www.un.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=FAO PROGRAMMES IN FORESTRY|url=https://www.fao.org/3/Y9203e/y9203e09.htm|access-date=2023-03-16|website=www.fao.org}}</ref> These thematic areas have since been enshrined in the [[United Nations Forum on Forests#Non-Legally Binding Instrument on All Types of Forests|Non-Legally Binding Instrument on All Types of Forests]] as a reference framework for sustainable forest management to help achieve the purpose of the instrument.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

In 2012, the Montréal Process, Forest Europe, the International Tropical Timber Organization, and the [[Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations]], acknowledging the seven thematic areas, endorsed a joint statement of collaboration to improve global forest-related data collection and reporting and avoiding the proliferation of monitoring requirements and associated reporting burdens.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ostr-backend-prod.azurewebsites.net/server/api/core/bitstreams/b0fc270d-cab5-47d5-a115-b4e59f5a5810/content|title=Joint statement}}</ref>

Sustainable forestry operations must also adhere to the [[International Labour Organization]]'s 18 criteria on human and social rights. [[Gender equality]], health and well-being and community consultation are examples of such rights.<ref name=":107" /><ref name="auto2">{{Cite web |title=What is sustainable forest management? |url=https://www.pefc.org/what-we-do/our-approach/what-is-sustainable-forest-management |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=www.pefc.org |language=en}}</ref>

===Ecosystem approach===
The [[ecosystem approach]] has been prominent on the agenda of the [[Convention on Biological Diversity]] (CBD) since 1995. The [[Convention on Biological Diversity|CBD]] definition of the Ecosystem Approach and a set of principles for its application were developed at an expert meeting in [[Malawi]] in 1995, known as the Malawi Principles.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.fao.org/documents/show_cdr.asp?url_file=/DOCREP/006/Y4773E/y4773e0e.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071223012737/http://www.fao.org/documents/show_cdr.asp?url_file=%2FDOCREP%2F006%2FY4773E%2Fy4773e0e.htm|title=Malawi Principles|archive-date=23 December 2007|access-date=3 March 2024}}</ref> The definition, 12 principles and 5 points of "operational guidance" were adopted by the fifth Conference of Parties (COP5) in 2000. The CBD definition is as follows:

<blockquote>The ecosystem approach is a strategy for the integrated management of land, water and living resources that promotes conservation and sustainable use in an equitable way. Application of the ecosystem approach will help to reach a balance of the three objectives of the Convention. An ecosystem approach is based on the application of appropriate scientific methodologies focused on levels of biological organization, which encompasses the essential structures, processes, functions and interactions among organisms and their environment. It recognizes that humans, with their [[cultural diversity]], are an integral component of many ecosystems.</blockquote>

Sustainable forest management was recognized by parties to the [[Convention on Biological Diversity]] in 2004 (Decision VII/11 of COP7) to be a concrete means of applying the Ecosystem Approach to forest ecosystems. The two concepts, sustainable forest management and the ecosystem approach, aim at promoting conservation and management practices which are environmentally, socially and economically sustainable, and which generate and maintain benefits for both present and future generations. In Europe, the MCPFE and the Council for the Pan-European Biological and Landscape Diversity Strategy (PEBLDS) jointly recognized sustainable forest management to be consistent with the Ecosystem Approach in 2006.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mcpfe.org/ |title=MCPFE |publisher=MCPFE |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.strategyguide.org/stracont.html |title=Council |publisher=Strategyguide.org |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.strategyguide.org/straabou.html |title=Pan-European Biological and Landscape Diversity Strategy |publisher=Strategyguide.org |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.strategyguide.org/200602/Documents/STRA-CO%202006%202%20_EA%20SFM%20JT%20STMT__E_final.pdf |title=PEBLD Strategy |publisher=Strategyguide.org |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref>

==== Alternative harvesting methods ====
Reduced impact logging (RIL) is a sustainable forestry method as it decreases the forest and canopy damages by approximately 75% compared to the conventional logging methods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pereira |first1=Rodrigo |last2=Zweede |first2=Johan |last3=Asner |first3=Gregory P. |last4=Keller |first4=Michael |date=2001 |title=Forest canopy damage and recovery in reduced-impact and conventional selective logging in eastern Para, Brazil |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |volume=168 |issue=1–3 |pages=77–89 |doi=10.1016/s0378-1127(01)00732-0 |issn=0378-1127 |s2cid=85014787}}</ref> Additionally, a 120-year regression model found that RIL would have a significantly higher [[reforestation]] in 30 years ("18.3 m<sup>3</sup> ha<sup>−1</sup>") in relation to conventional logging ("14.0 m<sup>3</sup> ha<sup>−1</sup>").<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Macpherson |first1=Alexander J. |last2=Schulze |first2=Mark D. |last3=Carter |first3=Douglas R. |last4=Vidal |first4=Edson |date=November 2010 |title=A Model for comparing reduced impact logging with conventional logging for an Eastern Amazonian Forest |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |volume=260 |issue=11 |page=2010 |doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2010.08.050 |bibcode=2010ForEM.260.2002M |issn=0378-1127}}</ref> Furthermore, it is essential that RIL should be practiced as soon as possible to improve reforestation in the future. For instance, a study concluded that logging would have to reduce by 40% in Brazil if the current logging measures stay of "''6 trees/hectare'' with a 30-year cutting cycle" stay in place. This would be to ensure that future ground biomass to have regeneration of the original ground biomass prior to harvesting.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mazzei |first1=Lucas |last2=Sist |first2=Plinio |last3=Ruschel |first3=Ademir |last4=Putz |first4=Francis E. |last5=Marco |first5=Phidias |last6=Pena |first6=Wagner |last7=Ferreira |first7=Josué Evandro Ribeiro |date=2010 |title=Above-ground biomass dynamics after reduced-impact logging in the Eastern Amazon |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |volume=259 |issue=3 |pages=367–373 |doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2009.10.031 |bibcode=2010ForEM.259..367M |issn=0378-1127}}</ref>

==== Preserving forest genetic resources ====
{{See also|Deforestation and climate change}}
Appropriate use and long-term conservation of [[forest genetic resources]] (FGR) is a part of sustainable forest management.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations ([[FAO]])|title=The State of the World's Forest Genetic Resources|journal=[[Commission on Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture]]|year=2014|url=http://www.fao.org/3/a-i3825e.pdf}}</ref> In particular when it comes to the adaptation of [[forests]] and forest management to [[climate change]].<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Koskela, J. | author2= Buck, A. | author3=Teissier du Cros, E. |title=Climate change and forest genetic diversity: Implications for sustainable forest management in Europe|journal=European Forest Genetic Resources Programme|year=2007|volume=[[Bioversity International]], Rome, Italy.|url=http://www.euforgen.org/fileadmin/bioversity/publications/pdfs/1216.pdf}}</ref> [[Genetic diversity]] ensures that forest trees can survive, adapt and evolve under changing environmental conditions. Genetic diversity in forests also contributes to tree vitality and to the [[climate resilience|resilience]] towards pests and diseases. Furthermore, FGR has a crucial role in maintaining forest biological diversity at both species and [[Forest ecosystem|ecosystem]] levels.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=de Vries, S.M.G., Alan, M., Bozzano, M., Burianek, V., Collin, E., Cottrell, J., Ivankovic, M., Kelleher, C.T., Koskela, J., Rotach, P., Vietto, L. and Yrjänä, L|title=Pan-European strategy for genetic conservation of forest trees and establishment of a core network of dynamic conservation units|journal=European Forest Genetic Resources Programme, Bioversity International|year=2015|volume=Rome, Italy|url=http://www.euforgen.org/fileadmin/templates/euforgen.org/upload/Publications/Thematic_publications/EUFORGEN_FGR_conservation_strategy.pdf}}</ref>

Selecting carefully the [[forest reproductive material]] with emphasis on getting a high genetic diversity rather than aiming at producing a uniform stand of trees, is essential for sustainable use of FGR. Considering the [[provenance]] is crucial as well. For example, in relation to climate change, local material may not have the genetic diversity or [[phenotypic plasticity]] to guarantee good performance under changed conditions. A different [[Population (biology)|population]] from further away, which may have experienced [[Selection (biology)|selection]] under conditions more like those forecast for the site to be [[reforestation|reforested]], might represent a more suitable seed source.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Konnert, M., Fady, B., Gömöry, D., A'Hara, S., Wolter, F., Ducci, F., Koskela, J., Bozzano, M., Maaten, T. and Kowalczyk, J.|title=Use and transfer of forest reproductive material in Europe in the context of climate change|journal=European Forest Genetic Resources Programme, Bioversity International, Rome, Italy.|year=2015|page=xvi and 75 p|url=http://www.euforgen.org/fileadmin/templates/euforgen.org/upload/Publications/Thematic_publications/EUFORGEN_FRM_use_transfer.pdf}}</ref>

=== Checkerboarding ===
{{excerpt|Checkerboarding (land)}}

[[File:Checkerboard forest in Idaho.jpg|thumb|250px|Checkerboard pattern alongside the Priest River in northern Idaho]]
Checkerboarding can create problems for access and ecological management. It is one of the major causes of [[inholding]]s within the boundaries of [[National forest (United States)|national forests]]. As is the case in northwestern [[California]], checkerboarding has resulted in issues with managing national forest land.<ref name="poli">{{cite journal |jstor=3159757 |title=Ownership and Use of Forest Land in Northwestern California |last=Poli |first=Adon |journal=Land Economics |year=1956 |publisher=University of Wisconsin Press |pages=144–151 |volume=32|issue=2 |doi=10.2307/3159757 |bibcode=1956LandE..32..144P }}</ref> Checkerboarding was previously applied to these areas during the period of western expansion, and they are now commercial forest land. Conflicting policies establishing the rights of the private owners of this land have caused some difficulties in the local hardwood timber production economy.

While relieving this land from its checkerboard ownership structure could benefit the timber production economy of the region, checkerboards can allow government to extend good forestry practices over intermingled private lands, by demonstration or applying pressure via economy of scale or the right of access.<ref name="ballaine">{{cite journal |jstor=3144830 |title=The Revested Oregon and California Railroad Grand Lands: A Problem in Land Management |last=Ballaine |first=Wesley C. |journal=Land Economics |year=1953 |publisher=University of Wisconsin Press |pages=219–232 |volume=29|issue=3 |doi=10.2307/3144830 |bibcode=1953LandE..29..219B }}</ref>

== Certification systems ==
{{Main|Certified wood}}

[[Certified wood|Forest certification]] is a globally recognized system for encouraging sustainable forest management and assuring that forest-based goods are derived from sustainably managed forests.<ref name=":107"/><ref name=":110">{{Cite web |title=What is certification? |url=https://pefc.org/what-we-do/our-approach/what-is-certification |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=pefc.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=An Introduction to Forest Certification {{!}} NC State Extension Publications |url=https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/an-introduction-to-forest-certification |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=content.ces.ncsu.edu |language=en-US |archive-date=2023-01-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230129115609/https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/an-introduction-to-forest-certification |url-status=dead }}</ref> This is a voluntary procedure in which an impartial third-party organization evaluates the quality of forest management and output against a set of criteria established by a governmental or commercial certification agency.<ref name=":107"/><ref name=":110"/>

Growing [[environmental awareness]] and [[consumer demand]] for more socially responsible businesses helped third-party forest [[certification]] emerge in the 1990s as a credible tool for communicating the environmental and social performance of forest operations.

There are many potential users of certification, including: forest managers, scientists, policy makers, investors, environmental advocates, business consumers of wood and paper, and individuals.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

With third-party [[Certified wood|forest certification]], an independent [[Standards organization|standards setting organization (SSO)]] develops [[technical standard|standards]] of good forest management, and independent auditors issue certificates to forest operations that comply with those standards. Forest certification verifies that forests are well-managed – as defined by a particular standard – and chain-of-custody certification tracks wood and paper products from the certified forest through processing to the point of sale.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

This rise of certification led to the emergence of several different systems throughout the world. As a result, there is no single accepted forest management [[international standard]] worldwide. [[ISO]] members<ref>{{cite web |date=20 October 2022 |title=Members |url=https://www.iso.org/members.html |website=so.org |publisher=International Organization for Standardization}}</ref> rejected a proposal for a forestry management system as requirements standard, with a consensus that a management system for certification would not be effective. Instead ISO members voted for a chain of custody of wood and wood-based products with ISO 38200 published in 2018. Without an international standard each system takes a somewhat different approach with scheme owners defining [[technical standard|private standards]] for sustainable forest management.

In its 2009–2010 Forest Products Annual Market Review United Nations Economic Commission for Europe/Food and Agriculture Organization stated: "Over the years, many of the issues that previously divided the (certification) systems have become much less distinct. The largest certification systems now generally have the same structural programmatic requirements."<ref>{{cite web |title=2009–2010 Forest Products Annual Market Review Page 121 |url=http://timber.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/publications/sp-25.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100820151542/http://timber.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/publications/sp-25.pdf |archive-date=20 August 2010 |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref>

Third-party forest certification is an important tool for those seeking to ensure that the paper and wood products they purchase and use come from forests that are well-managed and legally harvested. Incorporating third-party certification into forest product procurement practices can be a centerpiece for comprehensive wood and paper policies that include factors such as the protection of sensitive forest values, thoughtful material selection and efficient use of products.<ref>{{cite web |author=Erin Malec |date=5 October 2011 |title=Forest Certification Resource Center |url=http://www.metafore.org/?s=147 |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=Metafore.org |archive-date=22 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110122190944/http://www.metafore.org/?s=147 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
[[File:Forest Stewardship Council Logo.svg|thumb|203x203px|The [[Forest Stewardship Council]] is one of many [[forest certification]] programs.]]
Without a single [[international standard]], there are a proliferation of [[technical standard|private standards]],<ref>{{cite book |url=https://docplayer.net/23885374-International-standards-and-private-standards.html |title=International standards and private standards |date=2010 |publisher=International Organization for Standardization |isbn=978-92-67-10518-5}}</ref> with more than fifty scheme owners offering certification worldwide, addressing the diversity of forest types and tenures. Globally, the two largest umbrella certification programs are:
* [[Programme for the Endorsement of Forest Certification]] (PEFC)
* [[Forest Stewardship Council]] (FSC)
The Forest Stewardship Council's Policy on Conversion states that land areas converted from natural forests to round [[wood production]] after November 1994 are ineligible for Forest Stewardship Council certification.<ref name=":107" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=FSC Policy on Conversion |url=https://fsc.org/sites/default/files/2020-03/FSC-POL-01-007%20Policy%20on%20Conversion%20V1-0%20D1-0_EN.pdf |website=FSC}}</ref>

The area of forest certified worldwide is growing slowly. PEFC is the world's largest forest certification system, with more than two-thirds of the total global certified area certified to its Sustainability Benchmarks.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sorry, We didn't find what you were looking for &#124; UNECE |url=https://unece.org/page404/timber%20docs%20fpama%202008%20FPAMR2008%20pdf |access-date=3 March 2024 |website=unece.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=PEFC |url=http://www.pefc.org/about-pefc/who-we-are/facts-a-figures |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=PEFC}}</ref> In 2021, PEFC issued a position statement<ref>{{cite web |date=11 March 2021 |title=PEFC response to the Greenpeace report, "Destruction: Certified" |url=https://pefc.org/news/pefc-response-to-greenpeace-report-destruction-certified |website=pefc.org |publisher=PEFC}}</ref> defending their use of [[technical standard|private standards]] in response to the Destruction: Certified report from [[Greenpeace]].<ref>{{cite web |date=10 March 2021 |title=Destruction: Certified |url=https://www.greenpeace.org/international/publication/46812/destruction-certified/ |website=greenpeace.org |publisher=Greenpeace International}}</ref>

In North America, there are three certification standards endorsed by PEFC – the Sustainable Forestry Initiative,<ref>{{cite web |title=Sustainable Forest Initiative |url=http://www.sfiprogram.org |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=Sfiprogram.org}}</ref> the Canadian Standards Association's Sustainable Forest Management Standard,<ref name=":4" /> and the American Tree Farm System.<ref>{{cite web |date=22 November 2011 |title=American Tree Farm System |url=http://www.treefarmsystem.org/ |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=Treefarmsystem.org}}</ref> SFI is the world's largest single forest certification standard by area.<ref>"SFI Inc. Launches New Standard, Leads Forest Certification Forward" (PDF). Archived from the original (PDF) on 2012-10-18. Retrieved 2013-02-19</ref> FSC has five standards in North America – one in the United States<ref>{{cite web |title=Forest Stewardship Council (US) |url=http://www.fscus.org/ |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=Fscus.org}}</ref> and four in Canada.<ref>{{cite web |title=Forest Stewardship Council (Canada) |url=http://www.fsccanada.org |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=Fsccanada.org}}</ref>

While certification is intended as a tool to enhance forest management practices throughout the world, to date most certified forestry operations are located in Europe and North America. A significant barrier for many forest managers in [[developing countries]] is that they lack the capacity to undergo a certification audit and maintain operations to a certification standard.<ref>Auer, M. (2012). 'Group forest certification for smallholders in Vietnam: An early test and future prospects'. ''Human ecology'' 40(1): 5–14.</ref>

== Forest governance ==
[[File:Richea_pandanifolia.jpg|thumb|Pandani ([[Richea pandanifolia]]) near Lake Dobson, [[Mount Field National Park]], Tasmania, Australia]]
[[File:Proportion of publicly owned forest area, by holder of management rights and region, 2020.svg|thumb|Proportion of publicly owned forest area, by holder of management rights and region, 2020.]]
Although a majority of forests continue to be owned formally by government, the effectiveness of forest governance is increasingly independent of formal ownership.<ref name="agrawal2008">Agrawal, A., Chhatre, A, and Hardin, R. (2008). 'Changing Governance of the World's Forest'. ''Science'' 320: 1460–1462</ref> Since neo-liberal ideology in the 1980s and the emanation of the [[climate change]] challenges, evidence that the state is failing to effectively manage environmental resources has emerged.<ref>Lutz, E, and Caldecott, J. (1996). Decentralization and biodiversity: a world bank symposium. Washington: The World Bank.</ref> Under [[neo-liberal]] regimes in the developing countries, the role of the state has diminished and the [[market forces]] have increasingly taken over the dominant socio-economic role.<ref>Hague, M. (1999). 'The Fate of sustainable development under neo-liberal regime in developing countries', ''International political review'' 20(2): 197–218.</ref>

The shifting of natural resource management responsibilities from central to state and local governments, where this is occurring, is usually a part of broader decentralization process.<ref>Margulis, S. {{date?}}. 'Decentralized environmental management', Annual World Bank Report.</ref>

The development of National Forest Funds is one way to address the issue of financing sustainable forest management.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://www.un.org/esa/forests/pdf/AGF_Study_July_2012.pdf |title=2012 STUDY ON FOREST FINANCING |date=June 2012 |publisher=Advisory Group on Finance Collaborative Partnership on Forests}}</ref> National forest funds (NFFs) are dedicated financing mechanisms managed by public institutions designed to support the conservation and sustainable use of forest resources.<ref name="auto">{{cite book |last1=Matta |first1=Rao |url=http://www.fao.org/3/a-i4359e.pdf |title=Towards effective national forest funds, FAO Forestry Paper 174 |publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations |year=2015 |isbn=978-92-5-108706-0 |location=Rome, Italy}}</ref> As of 2014, there are 70 NFFs operating globally.<ref name="auto" />

=== Community forestry ===
Community-based forest management (CBFM) is a scheme that links governmental forest agencies and the local community in efforts to regenerate degraded forests, reforest deforested areas, and decrease carbon emissions that contribute to climate change. This partnership is done with the intent of not only repairing damage to the environment but also providing economic and social benefits to the affected area.<ref name=":06">{{Cite journal |last=Singh |first=P |date=August 2008 |title=Exploring biodiversity and climate change benefits of community-based forest management |journal=Global Environmental Change |language=en |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=468–478 |bibcode=2008GEC....18..468S |doi=10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2008.04.006}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mahanty |first1=Sango |last2=Gronow |first2=Jane |last3=Nurse |first3=Mike |last4=Malla |first4=Yam |date=2009-06-24 |title=Reducing Poverty through Community Based Forest Management in Asia |url=https://www.nepjol.info/index.php/JFL/article/view/1983 |journal=Journal of Forest and Livelihood |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=78–89 |doi=10.3126/jfl.v5i1.1983 |issn=1684-0186 |hdl-access=free |hdl=10535/8464}}</ref>

In principle, the benefits for the local community involvement in the management and protection of their forests would be to provide employment and to supplement income from both the wage labor and additional agriculture which would then strength the entire local economy while improving environmental conditions and mitigating climate change. Therefore, implementing a CBFM system can provide rural development while mitigating climate change and sustaining biodiversity within the region. It is important to engage the local community members, many of which are indigenous since presumably, they would have a deeper knowledge of the local ecosystems as well as the life cycles of those ecosystems over time. Their involvement also helps to ensure that their cultural practices remain intact.<ref name=":06" />

== Mitigation of deforestation and climate change ==
[[File:UNREDDandFCPFcountries.svg|400px|thumb|right| Countries participating in the [[United Nations REDD Programme|UNREDD program]] and/or [[Forest Carbon Partnership Facility]].
{{Legend|#A6D785|UN-REDD participants}}

]]{{See also|Deforestation and climate change}}Scientific studies investigate the ability of forests to absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere ([[carbon sequestration]]). Through such analysis, researchers can quantify the carbon stocks present in different types of forests and assess their effectiveness as [[carbon sink]]s. Understanding the capacity of forests to sequester carbon is crucial for [[climate change mitigation]] efforts.<ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022"/><ref name="Windisch Davin Seneviratne 2021"/><ref name="Portmann Beyerle Davin et al 2022"/>

=== Proforestation ===
Proforestation is the practice of protecting existing natural [[forests]] to foster continuous growth, carbon accumulation, and structural complexity.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite journal |doi=10.3389/ffgc.2019.00027 |title=Intact Forests in the United States: Proforestation Mitigates Climate Change and Serves the Greatest Good |journal=Frontiers in Forests and Global Change|volume=2|year=2019|last1=Moomaw|first1=William R. |last2=Masino|first2=Susan A. |last3=Faison|first3=Edward K.|article-number=27 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2019FrFGC...2...27M }}</ref><ref name="10 rules">{{cite journal |last1=Di Sacco |first1=Alice |last2=Hardwick |first2=Kate A. |last3=Blakesley |first3=David |last4=Brancalion |first4=Pedro H. S. |last5=Breman |first5=Elinor |last6=Cecilio Rebola |first6=Loic |last7=Chomba |first7=Susan |last8=Dixon |first8=Kingsley |last9=Elliott |first9=Stephen |last10=Ruyonga |first10=Godfrey |last11=Shaw |first11=Kirsty |last12=Smith |first12=Paul |last13=Smith |first13=Rhian J. |last14=Antonelli |first14=Alexandre |title=Ten golden rules for reforestation to optimize carbon sequestration, biodiversity recovery and livelihood benefits |journal=Global Change Biology |date=25 January 2021 |volume=27 |issue=7 |pages=1328–1348 |doi=10.1111/gcb.15498 |pmid=33494123 |s2cid=225324365 |issn=1354-1013|doi-access=free |bibcode=2021GCBio..27.1328D |hdl=20.500.11937/88524 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> It is recognized as an important forest based strategy for addressing the global crises in [[climate]] and [[biodiversity]].<ref name="10 rules" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mackey |first1=Brendan |last2=Kormos |first2=Cyril F. |last3=Keith |first3=Heather |last4=Moomaw |first4=William R. |last5=Houghton |first5=Richard A. |last6=Mittermeier |first6=Russell A. |last7=Hole |first7=David |last8=Hugh |first8=Sonia |title=Understanding the importance of primary tropical forest protection as a mitigation strategy |journal=Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change |date=1 May 2020 |volume=25 |issue=5 |pages=763–787 |doi=10.1007/s11027-019-09891-4 |s2cid=212681305 |language=en |issn=1573-1596|doi-access=free |bibcode=2020MASGC..25..763M |hdl=10072/394944 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> [[Forest restoration]] can be a strategy for [[climate change mitigation]].<ref name="AR6 WGIII Ch 13">IPCC (2022) [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_SPM.pdf Summary for policy makers] in [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/ Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change. Contribution of Working Group III to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change], Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA</ref>{{rp|37}} Proforestation complements other forest-based solutions like [[afforestation]], [[reforestation]] and improved forest management.

Allowing proforestation in some secondary forests will increase their accumulated carbon and biodiversity over time. Strategies for proforestation include [[Rewilding (conservation biology)|rewilding]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Protecting 50% of our Lands and Oceans |url=https://www.oneearth.org/protecting-50-of-our-lands-and-oceans/ |website=One Earth|date=23 May 2024 }}</ref> such as reintroducing [[apex predator]]s and [[keystone species]] as, for example, predators keep the population of herbivores in check (which reduce the [[Biosequestration|biomass of vegetation]]). Another strategy is establishing [[wildlife corridor]]s connecting isolated protected areas.<ref name="ReferenceA2">{{Cite web |date=3 April 2019 |title=The natural world can help save us from climate catastrophe &#124; George Monbiot |url=http://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2019/apr/03/natural-world-climate-catastrophe-rewilding |website=The Guardian}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wilmers |first1=Christopher C. |last2=Schmitz |first2=Oswald J. |date=October 19, 2016 |title=Effects of gray wolf-induced trophic cascades on ecosystem carbon cycling |journal=Ecosphere |volume=7 |issue=10 |article-number=e01501 |doi=10.1002/ecs2.1501|doi-access=free |bibcode=2016Ecosp...7E1501W }}</ref>

Proforestation refers specifically to enabling continuous forest growth uninterrupted by active management or timber harvesting, a term coined by scientists [[William Moomaw]], Susan Masino, and Edward Faison.<ref name="e360.yale.edu">Fen Montaigne, [https://e360.yale.edu/features/why-keeping-mature-forests-intact-is-key-to-the-climate-fight Why Keeping Mature Forests Intact Is Key to the Climate Fight], ''Yale Environment 360'', 15 October 2019.</ref><ref name="ReferenceA" />

Proforestation differs from [[agroforestry]] or the cultivation of forest [[plantations]], the latter consisting of similarly aged trees of just one or two species. Plantations can be an efficient source of wood but often come at the expense of natural forests and cultivate little habitat for biodiversity, such as dead and fallen trees or understory plants. Further, once factoring in emissions from clearing the land and the decay of plantation waste and products at the end of their often brief lifecycles (e.g. paper products), plantations sequester 40 times less carbon than natural forests.<ref name="nature.com">{{cite journal |last1=Lewis |first1=Simon |last2=Wheeler |first2=Charlotte |last3=Mitchard |first3=Edward |last4=Koch |first4=Alexander |title=Restoring natural forests is the best way to remove atmospheric carbon |journal=Nature |date=4 April 2019 |volume=568 |issue=7750 |pages=25–28 |doi=10.1038/d41586-019-01026-8 |pmid=30940972 |s2cid=91190309 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019Natur.568...25L }}</ref>

Proforestation is specifically recommended in "World Scientists' Warning of a Climate Emergency, as a means to "quickly curtail [[habitat loss|habitat]] and [[biodiversity loss]]" and protect "high carbon stores" and areas "with the capacity to rapidly sequester carbon."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ripple |first1=William |last2=Wolf |first2=Christopher |last3=Newsome |first3=Thomas |last4=Barnard |first4=Phoebe |last5=Moomaw |first5=William |title=World Scientists' Warning of a Climate Emergency |journal=BioScience |date=January 2020 |volume=70 |issue=1 |pages=8–12 |doi=10.1093/biosci/biz088 |url=https://academic.oup.com/bioscience/article/70/1/8/5610806 |access-date=12 November 2020|doi-access=free |hdl=2445/151800 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==== Increasing Forest and Community Resilience ====
1.6 billion people worldwide depend on forests for their livelihoods, including 300–350 million (half of whom are Indigenous peoples) who live near or within "dense forests" and depend almost entirely on these ecosystems for their survival.<ref name="auto3">{{cite book |last1=Jenkins |first1=Michael |last2=Schaap |first2=Brian |title=Background Analytical Study 1: Forest Ecosystem Services |date=April 2018 |publisher=United Nations Forum on Forests |url=https://www.un.org/esa/forests/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/UNFF13_BkgdStudy_ForestsEcoServices.pdf |access-date=21 April 2021}}</ref> Rural households in Asia, Africa, and Latin America also depend on forests for about a quarter of their total incomes, with about half of this in the form of food, fodder, energy, building materials and medicine.<ref name="auto3"/> Proforestation can protect full native biodiversity and support the forests and other land types that provide resources we need. For example, research has found that old growth and complex forests are more resistant to the effects of climate change. One study found that taller trees had increased drought resistance, being able to capture and retain water better, due to their deeper root system and larger biomass. This means that even in dry conditions, these trees continued to photosynthesize at a higher rate than smaller trees.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Giardina |first1=Francesco |last2=et |first2=al |title=Tall Amazonian forests are less sensitive to precipitation variability |journal=Nature Geoscience |date=28 May 2018 |volume=11 |issue=6 |pages=405–409 |doi=10.1038/s41561-018-0133-5 |bibcode=2018NatGe..11..405G |s2cid=47004415 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-018-0133-5 |access-date=21 April 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Further, old-growth forests have been shown to be more resistant to fires compared to young forests with trees that have thinner bark and with more fuel available for increasing temperatures and fire damage.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Binkley |first1=Daniel |last2=Sisk |first2=Tom |last3=Chambers |first3=Carol |last4=Springer |first4=Judy |last5=Block |first5=William |title=The Role of Old-growth Forests in Frequent-fire Landscapes |journal=Ecology and Society |date=2007 |volume=12 |issue=2 |page=18 |doi=10.5751/ES-02170-120218 |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs_other/rmrs_2007_binkley_d001.pdf|doi-access=free }}</ref> Proforestation can help to reduce fire risks to forests and the surrounding communities. They can also help absorb water and prevent flooding to surrounding communities.<ref name="auto3"/> Considering the variety of ecosystem services complex forests provide, sustaining healthy forests means adjacent communities will be better off as well.

== Workers ==

==History==
The [[Pre-industrial society|preindustrial age]] has been dubbed by [[Werner Sombart]] and others as the 'wooden age', as timber and firewood were the basic resources for energy, construction and housing. The development of modern forestry is closely connected with the rise of [[capitalism]], the economy as a science and varying notions of land use and property.<ref>compare Joachim Radkau Wood: A History, 2011</ref> Roman [[Latifundium|Latifundiae]], large agricultural estates, were quite successful in maintaining the large supply of wood that was necessary for the Roman Empire.<ref name="yale">The Nature of Mediterranean Europe: An Ecological History, by [[Alfred Thomas Grove]], [[Oliver Rackham]], Yale University Press, 2003, [http://yalepress.yale.edu/book.asp?isbn=9780300100556 review at Yale university press] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006140735/http://yalepress.yale.edu/book.asp?isbn=9780300100556|date=2014-10-06}} [https://muse.jhu.edu/login?auth=0&type=summary&url=/journals/journal_of_interdisciplinary_history/v032/32.3fagan.pdfThe Nature of Mediterranean Europe: An Ecological History (review) ][[Brian M. Fagan]]<span>, Journal of Interdisciplinary History, Volume 32, Number 3, Winter 2002, pp. 454-455 |</span> {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006073018/https://muse.jhu.edu/login?auth=0&type=summary&url=%2Fjournals%2Fjournal_of_interdisciplinary_history%2Fv032%2F32.3fagan.pdfThe|date=2014-10-06}}</ref> Large [[deforestation]]s came with the decline of the Romans.<ref name="yale" /> However already in the 5th century, [[monk]]s in the then Byzantine [[Romagna]] on the [[Adriatic]] coast, were able to establish [[stone pine]] plantations to provide [[Firewood|fuelwood]] and [[Pine nut|food]].<ref name="Pines">{{cite book |last1=T. Mirov |first1=Nicholas |title=The story of pines |last2=Hasbrouck |first2=Jean |publisher=Indiana University Press |year=1976 |isbn=978-0-253-35462-4 |location=Bloomington and London |page=[https://archive.org/details/storyofpines00ntmi/page/111 111] |chapter=6 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/storyofpines00ntmi/page/111 |chapter-url-access=registration}}</ref> This was the beginning of the massive forest mentioned by [[Dante Alighieri]] in his 1308 poem [[Divine Comedy]].<ref name="Pines" />

Similar sustainable formal forestry practices were developed by the [[Visigoths]] in the 7th century when, faced with the ever-increasing shortage of wood, they instituted a code concerned with the preservation of [[oak]] and [[pine]] forests.<ref name="Pines" /> The use and management of many forest resources has a long history in China as well, dating back to the [[Han dynasty]] and taking place under the landowning [[gentry]]. A similar approach was used in Japan. It was also later written about by the [[Ming dynasty]] Chinese scholar [[Xu Guangqi]] (1562–1633).

In Europe, land usage rights in medieval and early modern times allowed different users to access forests and pastures. [[Plant litter]] and [[resin extraction]] were important, as [[pitch (resin)]] was essential for the [[caulking]] of ships, falking and hunting rights, firewood and building, timber gathering in [[wood pastures]], and grazing animals in forests. The notion of "[[commons]]" (German "Allmende") refers to the underlying traditional legal term of [[common land]]. The idea of enclosed private property came about during modern times. However, most hunting rights were retained by members of the nobility which preserved the right of the nobility to access and use common land for recreation, like [[fox hunting]].

=== 13th to 16th century ===
[[File:Forstarbeiten_in_Österreich.JPG|thumb|Forestry work in Austria]]
[[File:Gewinnung_von_Schnittreisig.jpg|thumb|Exploitation of brushwood at the [[:de:Goldner Steinrück|Golden Steinrueck]], [[Vogelsberg Mountains|Vogelsberg]]]]
[[File:Hans_Carl_von_Carlowitz.jpg|thumb|[[Hans Carl von Carlowitz]], German miner]]
Systematic management of forests for a [[sustainable yield]] of timber began in [[Portugal]] in the 13th century when [[Afonso III of Portugal|King Afonso III]] planted the Pinhal do Rei (King's Pine Forest) near [[Leiria]] to prevent coastal erosion and [[soil degradation]], and as a sustainable source for timber used in naval construction.<ref name="Livermore2004">{{cite book |author=H. V. Livermore |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7Cd0bKhByz8C&pg=PA15 |title=Portugal: A Traveller's History |publisher=Boydell Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-1-84383-063-4 |page=15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171211144023/https://books.google.com/books?id=7Cd0bKhByz8C&pg=PA15&lpg=PA15 |archive-date=2017-12-11 |url-status=live}}</ref> His successor [[Denis, King of Portugal|King Denis of Portugal]] continued the practice and the forest exists still today.<ref>{{cite web |title=PGF - Mata Nacional de Leiria — ICNF |url=http://www.icnf.pt/portal/florestas/gf/pgf/publicitacoes/drf-centro/2011/pgf-mn-leiria |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191210135748/http://www2.icnf.pt/portal/florestas/gf/pgf/publicitacoes/encerradas/dcnf-centr/pgf-mn-leiria |archive-date=2019-12-10 |access-date=2017-10-17 |website=www.icnf.pt}}</ref>

Forest management also flourished in the [[History of the forest in Central Europe|German]] states in the 14th century, e.g. in [[Nuremberg]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Buttinger |first=Sabine |year=2013 |title=Idee der Nachhaltigkeit |trans-title=The Idea of Sustainability |journal=[[Damals]] |language=de |volume=45 |issue=4 |page=8}}</ref> and in 16th-century [[Japan]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Forestry in Yashino |url=http://www.pref.nara.jp/nara/kaido/eg/syugen/d5_trad/trad1.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110628224026/http://www.pref.nara.jp/nara/kaido/eg/syugen/d5_trad/trad1.htm |archive-date=2011-06-28 |access-date=2010-10-12 |publisher=City of [[Nara, Nara]]}}</ref> Typically, a forest was divided into specific sections and mapped; the harvest of timber was planned with an eye to regeneration. As [[timber rafting]] allowed for connecting large continental forests, as in south western Germany, via Main, Neckar, Danube and Rhine with the coastal cities and states, early modern forestry and remote trading were closely connected. Large firs in the black forest were called "Holländer," as they were [[Timber trade|traded]] to the Dutch ship yards. Large timber rafts on the Rhine were 200 to 400m in length, 40m in width and consisted of several thousand logs. The crew consisted of 400 to 500 men, including shelter, bakeries, ovens and livestock stables.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dilibri.de/rlb/content/pageview/607408/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129034645/http://www.dilibri.de/rlb/content/pageview/607408/|title=Abbildungen der verschiedenen Gattungen von Fahrzeugen, wie man sie auf dem Rheine sieht / von H. Herman|date=October 3, 1820|archive-date=November 29, 2014|website=www.dilibri.de}}</ref> Timber rafting infrastructure allowed for large interconnected networks all over continental Europe and is still of importance in Finland.

Starting with the 16th century, enhanced world [[maritime trade]], a boom in housing construction in Europe, and the success and further [[Berggeschrey]] (rushes) of the mining industry increased timber consumption sharply. The notion of 'Nachhaltigkeit', [[sustainability]] in forestry, is closely connected to the work of [[Hans Carl von Carlowitz]] (1645–1714), a mining administrator in [[Saxony]]. His book ''Sylvicultura oeconomica, oder haußwirthliche Nachricht und Naturmäßige Anweisung zur wilden Baum-Zucht'' (1713) was the first comprehensive treatise about sustainable yield forestry.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dangel |first=Ulrich |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dP-xDQAAQBAJ&q=first+comprehensive+treatise+about+forestry&pg=PA30 |title=Turning Point in Timber Construction: A New Economy |date=2016-12-05 |publisher=Birkhäuser |isbn=978-3-0356-0863-2 |language=en}}</ref> In the UK, and, to an extent, in continental Europe, the [[enclosure]] movement and the [[Highland Clearances|Clearances]] favored strictly enclosed private property.<ref name="Rad">Radkau, Joachim. Nature and Power. A Global History of the Environment. Cambridge University Press. 2008.</ref> The Agrarian reformers, early economic writers and scientists tried to get rid of the traditional commons.<ref name="rad1">Nature and Power, A Global History of the Environment, by Joachim Radkau, 2008, p. 72</ref> At the time, an alleged [[tragedy of the commons]] together with fears of a [[Holznot]], an imminent wood shortage played a watershed role in the controversies about cooperative land use patterns.<ref name="ws">The end of the commons as a watershed' ''The Age of Ecology'', Joachim Radkau, John Wiley & Sons, 03.04.2014,{{Clarify|reason=ambiguous date format|date=September 2017}} p. 15 ff</ref>

The practice of establishing tree plantations in the [[British Isles]] was promoted by [[John Evelyn]], though it had already acquired some popularity. [[Louis XIV]]'s minister [[Jean-Baptiste Colbert]]'s oak [[Forest of Tronçais]], planted for the future use of the [[French Navy]], matured as expected in the mid-19th century: "Colbert had thought of everything except the steamship," [[Fernand Braudel]] observed.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Braudel |first=Fernand |title=The Wheels of Commerce: Civilization and Capitalism: 15th-18th Century (Volume II) |publisher=University of California Press |year=1979 |isbn=978-0-520-08115-4 |page=240}}</ref> Colbert's vision of forestry management was encoded in the [[French forestry ordinance of 1669|French forestry Ordinance of 1669]], which proved to be an influential management system throughout Europe.<ref>Kohler, Yann & Tissot, Wilfried. (2013). Integration of Nature Protection in Forest Policy in France - INTEGRATE Country Report.</ref> In parallel, schools of forestry were established beginning in the late 18th century in [[Hesse]], [[Russia]], [[Austria-Hungary]], [[Sweden]], [[France]] and elsewhere in Europe.

=== Mechanization in 19th century ===
Forestry mechanization was always in close connection to metal working and the development of mechanical tools to cut and transport timber to its destination.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Sundberg |first1=B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PiRffqqUcIQC&dq=Forestry+mechanization+was+always+in+close+connection+to+metal+working+and+the+development+of+mechanical+tools+to+cut+and+transport+timber+to+its+destination.&pg=PA1 |title=Operational Efficiency in Forestry: Vol. 1: Analysis |last2=Silversides |first2=C. R. |date=1988-04-30 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-90-247-3683-6 |language=en}}</ref> Rafting belongs to the earliest means of transport. Steel saws came up in the 15th century. The 19th century widely increased the availability of steel for [[whipsaw]]s and introduced [[forest railway]]s and railways in general for transport and as forestry customer. Further human induced changes, however, came since World War II, respectively in line with the "1950s syndrome."<ref>Christian Pfister (Hrsg.), Das 1950er Syndrom: Der Weg in die Konsumgesellschaft, Bern 1995</ref> The first portable chainsaw was invented in [[Chainsaw#History|1918 in Canada]], but large impact of mechanization in forestry started after World War II.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Silversides |first=C. R. |date=1984-08-01 |title=Mechanized Forestry, World War II to the Present |journal=The Forestry Chronicle |language=en |volume=60 |issue=4 |pages=231–235 |doi=10.5558/tfc60231-4 |issn=0015-7546 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Forestry [[Harvester (forestry)|harvesters]] are among the most recent developments. Although drones, [[Aerial Forest Protection Service (Russia)|planes]], [[Forest inventory#Tools used in inventory|laser scanning]], [[Landsat 5#Mission history|satellites]] and robots also play a part in forestry.

=== Forest conservation and early globalization ===
{{further|forest conservation}}

Starting from the 1750s modern [[scientific forestry]] was developed in France and the German speaking countries in the context of [[natural history]] scholarship and state administration inspired by [[physiocracy]] and [[cameralism]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Oosthoek |first1=K. Jan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6UItDwAAQBAJ&dq=Starting+from+the+1750s+modern+scientific+forestry+was+developed+in+France+and+the+German+speaking+countries+in+the+context+of+natural+history+scholarship+and+state+administration+inspired+by+physiocracy+and+cameralism.&pg=PA15 |title=Managing Northern Europe's Forests: Histories from the Age of Improvement to the Age of Ecology |last2=Hölzl |first2=Richard |date=2018-02-19 |publisher=Berghahn Books |isbn=978-1-78533-601-0 |language=en}}</ref> Its main traits were centralized management by professional foresters, the adherence to [[sustainable yield]] concepts with a bias towards fuelwood and timber production, artificial afforestation, and a critical view of pastoral and agricultural uses of forests.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hölzl |first=Richard |date=2010-12-01 |title=Historicizing Sustainability: German Scientific Forestry in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries |journal=Science as Culture |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=431–460 |doi=10.1080/09505431.2010.519866 |issn=0950-5431 |s2cid=143441568}}</ref>

During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, forest preservation programs were established in [[British India]], the [[United States]], and Europe. Many foresters were either from continental Europe (like [[Dietrich Brandis|Sir Dietrich Brandis]]), or educated there (like [[Gifford Pinchot]]). Sir Dietrich Brandis is considered the father of tropical forestry, European concepts and practices had to be adapted in tropical and semi-arid climate zones. The development of [[plantation]] forestry was one of the (controversial) answers to the specific challenges in the tropical colonies. The enactment and evolution of [[Forestry law|forest laws]] and binding regulations occurred in most Western nations in the 20th century in response to growing conservation concerns and the increasing technological capacity of [[logging]] companies. [[Tropical forestry]] is a separate branch of forestry which deals mainly with equatorial forests that yield woods such as [[teak]] and [[mahogany]].

=== 21st century ===
A strong body of [[research]] exists regarding the management of [[Forest ecology|forest ecosystems]] and the genetic improvement of [[Tree breeding|tree species and varieties]]. Forestry studies also include the development of better methods for the planting, protecting, [[thinning]], [[controlled burn]]ing, [[felling]], extracting, and processing of [[timber]]. One of the applications of modern forestry is [[reforestation]], in which trees are planted and tended in a given area.<gallery mode="packed">
File:A_deciduous_beech_forest_in_Slovenia.jpg|A deciduous [[beech]] forest in [[Slovenia]]
File:Laser_guided_cutting_of_wood_inside_modern_woodmill.jpg|A modern [[sawmill]]
File:Employment_In_Agriculture,_Forestry_And_Fishing_By_Region.svg|A comparison of employment In agriculture, forestry and fishing by region
</gallery>Trees provide numerous environmental, social and economic benefits for people.<ref>{{cite web |title=Department of environmental conservation |url=http://www.dec.ny.gov/lands/4957.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150221114633/http://www.dec.ny.gov/lands/4957.html |archive-date=2015-02-21 |access-date=2014-11-29 |publisher=New York State Department}}</ref> In many regions, the [[forest industry]] is of major ecological, economic, and social importance, with the United States producing more [[timber]] than any other country in the world.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Casanova |first1=Vanessa |last2=Hamilton |first2=James |date=2019-04-03 |title=Non-Timber Forest Products in the Southeastern United States: Implications for Worker Safety and Health |journal=Journal of Agromedicine |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=121–124 |doi=10.1080/1059924X.2019.1578141 |issn=1059-924X |pmid=30712502 |s2cid=73422895}}</ref> Third-party [[certification]] systems that provide independent verification of sound forest [[stewardship]] and [[Sustainable forest management|sustainable forestry]] have become commonplace in many areas since the 1990s. These certification systems developed as a response to criticism of some forestry practices, particularly deforestation in less-developed regions along with concerns over resource management in the [[developed world]]. Sustainable forestry operations must also adhere to the [[International Labour Organization]]'s 18 criteria on [[Human rights|human]] and social rights. [[Gender equality]], health and well-being and community consultation are examples of mentioned rights.<ref name="auto2"/><ref name=":107"/>

In topographically severe forested terrain, proper forestry is important for the prevention or minimization of serious soil [[erosion]] or even [[landslide]]s. In areas with a high potential for landslides, forests can [[Erosion control|stabilize soils]] and prevent property damage or loss, human injury, or loss of life.

Global production of roundwood rose from 3.5 billion m''³'' in 2000 to 4 billion m''³'' in 2021. In 2021, wood fuel was the main product with a 49 percent share of the total (2 billion m''³''), followed by coniferous industrial roundwood with 30 percent (1.2 billion m''³'') and non-coniferous industrial roundwood with 21 percent (0.9 billion m''³''). Asia and the Americas are the two main producing regions, accounting for 29 and 28 percent of the total roundwood production, respectively; Africa and Europe have similar shares of 20–21 percent, while Oceania produces the remaining 2 percent.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |url=http://www.fao.org/documents/card/en/c/cc8166en |title=World Food and Agriculture – Statistical Yearbook 2023 |date=2023-11-29 |publisher=FAO |isbn=978-92-5-138262-2 |language=en |doi=10.4060/cc8166en}}</ref>

Many lower- and middle-income countries rely on wood for energy purposes (notably cooking). The largest producers are all in these income groups and have large populations with a high reliance on wood for energy: in 2021, India ranked first with 300 million m''³'' (15 percent of total production), followed by China with 156 million m3 and Brazil with 129 million m''³'' (8 percent and 7 percent of global production).<ref name=":2" />

=== Journals ===
