======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Mangrove forest
======================================================================

{{Short description|Productive wetlands that occur in coastal intertidal zones}}
[[File:Mangroves at sunset.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|{{center|[[Mangrove]]s in an [[ebb tide]]}}]]
{{Ocean habitat topics}}
{{AI-generated|date=October 2026|reason=2026 the three-example bulleted list in the section "Biogeochemical implications of conservation" is almost certainly AI-generated; the lists in "exploitation and conservation" and biodiversity/birds are also suspect; the title "biogeochemical implications of conservation" itself sounds AI-generated; there may be other issues}}

'''Mangrove forests''', also called '''mangrove swamps''', '''mangrove thickets''' or '''mangals''', are productive [[wetland]]s located in tropical and subtropical [[intertidal zone]]s.<ref name=":4">{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.ibiod.2016.04.023|title=Nutrient limitation status in a subtropical mangrove ecosystem revealed by analysis of enzymatic stoichiometry and microbial abundance for sediment carbon cycling|year=2018|last1=Luo|first1=L. |last2=Gu|first2=J.-D. |journal=International Biodeterioration & Biodegradation |volume=128 |pages=3–10|bibcode=2018IBiBi.128....3L}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.seares.2011.10.006|title=A cross-system analysis of sedimentary organic carbon in the mangrove ecosystems of Xuan Thuy National Park, Vietnam |year=2012|last1=Tue|first1=N. T. |last2=Ngoc|first2=N. T. |last3=Quy|first3=T. D. |last4=Hamaoka|first4=H. |last5=Nhuan |first5=M. T. |last6=Omori|first6=K. |journal=Journal of Sea Research|volume=67|issue =1|pages=69–76|bibcode=2012JSR....67...69T}}</ref> Approximately 80 [[mangrove]] species exist, all adapted to areas where slow-moving water allows for the deposition of fine sediment and low-oxygen soil conditions. These trees cannot endure freezing temperatures, which restricts their distribution to warmer climates.<ref name="NOAA2021">{{Cite web |last=National Ocean Service |work=National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration |title=What is a mangrove forest? |url=https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/mangroves.html |access-date=2025-10-10}}</ref>

Their distinct, stilt-like roots allow the trees to slow the movement of tidal waters, causing the settlement of suspended sediments and acting as a protective barrier to reduce coastal erosion. These roots also provide an important habitat for many species.<ref name=NOAA2021 />

Mangrove forests live at the interface between the land, the ocean, and the atmosphere, and are centres for the flow of energy and matter between these systems. They have attracted much research interest because of the various ecological functions of the mangrove ecosystems, including runoff and flood prevention, storage and recycling of nutrients and wastes, cultivation and energy conversion.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rqiZAAAAIAAJ |title=Functions of Nature: Evaluation of Nature in Environmental Planning, Management and Decision Making |isbn=978-90-01-35594-4 |last1=De Groot|first1=R.S.|year=1992 |publisher=Wolters-Noordhoff }}</ref> The forests are major [[blue carbon]] systems, storing considerable amounts of carbon in [[marine sediment]]s, thus becoming important regulators of [[climate change]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s11273-015-9446-y |title=Indonesia's blue carbon: A globally significant and vulnerable sink for seagrass and mangrove carbon|year=2016 |last1=Alongi |first1=D. M.|last2=Murdiyarso |first2=D.|last3=Fourqurean|first3=J. W.|last4=Kauffman|first4=J. B.|last5=Hutahaean|first5=A.|last6=Crooks|first6 = S. |last7=Lovelock|first7=C. E.|last8=Howard|first8=J.|last9=Herr|first9=D.|last10=Fortes|first10=M.|last11=Pidgeon|first11=E.|last12=Wagey|first12=T. |journal=Wetlands Ecology and Management |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=3–13 |bibcode=2016WetEM..24....3A |s2cid=4983675}}</ref> [[Marine microorganisms]] are key parts of these mangrove ecosystems. However, much remains to be discovered about how [[mangrove microbiome]]s contribute to high ecosystem productivity and efficient cycling of elements.<ref name=Lin2018>{{cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=X. |last2=Hetharua |first2=B. |last3=Lin |first3=L. |last4=Xu |first4=H. |last5=Zheng |first5=T. |last6=He |first6=Z. |last7=Tian |first7=Y. |title=Mangrove Sediment Microbiome: Adaptive Microbial Assemblages and Their Routed Biogeochemical Processes in Yunxiao Mangrove National Nature Reserve, China |journal=Microbial Ecology |volume=78 |issue=1 |date=2018 |doi=10.1007/s00248-018-1261-6 |pages=57–69 |pmid=30284602 |s2cid=52917236}}</ref>

In 2025, the area of mangroves globally was estimated at 15.9 million hectares. Asia has the largest area, at 6.10 million ha, and Europe reported no mangrove area. Among countries and areas, Indonesia has the world's largest extent of mangroves, at 3.40 million ha, followed by Brazil (1.39 million ha), Australia (1.11 million ha), Nigeria (976 000 ha) and Mexico (947 000 ha). Collectively, these five countries host almost half (49%) of the global mangrove area.<ref>{{Cite book |last=FAO |url=https://openknowledge.fao.org/handle/20.500.14283/cd6709en |title=Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025 |date=2025 |publisher=FAO |isbn=978-92-5-140082-1 |language=English |doi=10.4060/cd6709en}}</ref>

==Overview==
{{ external media
| float  = right
| width  = 269px
| video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DGrKIDUtYjo&ab_channel=MangroveActionProject Mangrove Photography Awards 2020] {{align|right|– ''Mangrove Action Project''}}
}}

Mangrove forests, are productive wetlands located in tropical and subtropical intertidal zones.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /> Approximately 80 mangrove species exist, all adapted to areas where slow-moving water allows for the deposition of fine sediment and low-oxygen soil conditions. These trees cannot endure freezing temperatures, which restricts their distribution to warmer climates.<ref name="NOAA2021" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Komiyama |first1=Akira |last2=Ong |first2=Jin Eong |last3=Poungparn |first3=Sasitorn |date=2008-08-01 |title=Allometry, biomass, and productivity of mangrove forests: A review |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304377007001829 |journal=Aquatic Botany |series=Mangrove Ecology – Applications in Forestry and Costal Zone Management |language=en |volume=89 |issue=2 |pages=128–137 |bibcode=2008AqBot..89..128K |doi=10.1016/j.aquabot.2007.12.006 |issn=0304-3770 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> 

Their distinct, [[Buttress root|stilt-like roots]] allow the trees to slow the movement of tidal waters, causing the settlement of suspended sediments and acting as a protective barrier to reduce coastal erosion from storm surge and waves. These roots also provide a habitat for many species and act as nurseries for [[juvenile fish]], including species that are recreationally and commercially important.<ref name="NOAA2021" /><ref name="NOAA-Mangroves">{{Cite web |title=Mangrove Forest {{!}} Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary |url=https://floridakeys.noaa.gov/plants/mangroves.html |access-date=2025-10-10 |website=floridakeys.noaa.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Malmquist |first=David |date=2019-03-26 |title=Study confirms and ranks nursery value of coastal habitats |url=https://www.vims.edu/newsandevents/topstories/2019/nursery_value.php#:~:text=A%20comprehensive%20analysis%20of%20more,managers%20of%20threatened%20marine%20resources. |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250524183920/https://www.vims.edu/newsandevents/topstories/2019/nursery_value.php |archive-date=2025-05-24 |access-date=2025-10-10 |website=Virginia Institute of Marine Science |language=en}}</ref>

The main contribution of mangroves to the larger ecosystem comes from [[Plant litter|litter fall]] from the trees, which is then decomposed by [[Herbivore|primary consumers]]. Bacteria and protozoans colonise the plant litter and break it down chemically into [[organic compound]]s, minerals, carbon dioxide, and [[Metabolic waste|nitrogenous wastes]].<ref name=NOAA-Mangroves /> The [[Intertidal zone|intertidal]] existence to which these trees are adapted represents the major limitation to the number of species able to thrive in their habitat. High tide brings in salt water, and when the tide recedes, solar evaporation of the seawater in the soil leads to further increases in salinity. The return of tide can flush out these soils, bringing them back to salinity levels comparable to that of seawater.<ref name="Friess" /><ref name="Zimmer">{{cite journal |last1=Zimmer |first1=Katarina |title=Many mangrove restorations fail. Is there a better way? |journal=Knowable Magazine |date=22 July 2021 |doi=10.1146/knowable-072221-1 |url=https://knowablemagazine.org/article/food-environment/2021/many-mangrove-restorations-fail |access-date=11 August 2021 |doi-access=free|url-access=subscription }}</ref> At low tide, organisms are exposed to increases in temperature and reduced moisture before being then cooled and flooded by the tide. Thus, for a plant to survive in this environment, it must tolerate broad ranges of salinity, temperature, and moisture, as well as several other key environmental factors—thus only a select few species make up the mangrove tree community.<ref name="Zimmer" /><ref name="Friess">{{cite journal |last1=Friess |first1=D. A. |last2=Rogers |first2=K. |last3=Lovelock |first3=C. E. |last4=Krauss |first4=K. W. |last5=Hamilton |first5=S. E. |last6=Lee |first6=S. Y. |last7=Lucas |first7=R. |last8=Primavera |first8=J. |last9=Rajkaran |first9=A. |last10=Shi |first10=S. |title=The State of the World's Mangrove Forests: Past, Present, and Future |journal=Annual Review of Environment and Resources |date=2019 |volume=44 |issue=1 |pages=89–115 |doi=10.1146/annurev-environ-101718-033302 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2019ARER...44...16F |hdl=10072/394397 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

A mangrove swamp typically features only a small number of tree species. It is not uncommon for a mangrove forest in the Caribbean to feature only three or four tree species. For comparison, a [[tropical rainforest]] biome may contain thousands of tree species, but this is not to say mangrove forests lack diversity. Though the trees are few in species, the ecosystem that these trees create provides a [[habitat]] for a great variety of other species, including as many as 174 species of marine [[megafauna]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sievers|first1=Michael|last2=Brown|first2=Christopher J.|last3=Tulloch|first3=Vivitskaia J.D.|last4=Pearson|first4=Ryan M.|last5=Haig|first5=Jodie A.|last6=Turschwell|first6=Mischa P.|last7=Connolly|first7=Rod M.|date=2019|title=The Role of Vegetated Coastal Wetlands for Marine Megafauna Conservation|url=https://www.cell.com/trends/ecology-evolution/abstract/S0169-5347(19)30109-0|journal=Trends in Ecology & Evolution|volume=34|language=en|issue=9|pages=807–817|doi=10.1016/j.tree.2019.04.004|pmid=31126633|bibcode=2019TEcoE..34..807S |issn=0169-5347|hdl=10072/391960|s2cid=164219103|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

[[File:Mangrove ecosystem in the coastal intertidal zone.png|thumb|upright=2| {{center|Mangrove ecosystem in the coastal intertidal zone{{hsp}}<ref name= Giraldes2020>{{cite journal | last1=Giraldes | first1=Bruno Welter | last2=Goodwin | first2=Claire | last3=Al-Fardi | first3=Noora A. A. | last4=Engmann | first4=Amanda | last5=Leitão | first5=Alexandra | last6=Ahmed | first6=Asma A. | last7=Ahmed | first7=Kamelia O. | last8=Abdulkader | first8=Hadil A. | last9=Al-Korbi | first9=Halah A. | last10=Al Easa | first10=Hala Sultan Saif | last11=Ahmed Eltai | first11=Nahla O. | last12=Hanifi-Moghaddam | first12=Pejman | editor-last=Bianchi | editor-first=Carlo Nike | title=Two new sponge species (Demospongiae: Chalinidae and Suberitidae) isolated from hyperarid mangroves of Qatar with notes on their potential antibacterial bioactivity | journal=PLOS ONE | publisher=Public Library of Science (PLoS) | volume=15 | issue=5 | date=13 May 2020 | issn=1932-6203 | doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0232205 | article-number=e0232205| pmid=32401792 | pmc=7219822 | bibcode=2020PLoSO..1532205G | doi-access=free }} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Material was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License].</ref><br />[[Seagrass]] and [[oyster bed]]s can inhabit the shallow subtidal zone}}]]

Mangrove plants require a number of physiological adaptations to overcome the problems of [[Hypoxia (environmental)|low environmental oxygen]] levels, high [[salinity]], and frequent [[tidal flooding]]. Each species has its own solutions to these problems; this may be the primary reason why, on some shorelines, mangrove tree species show distinct zonation. Small environmental variations within a mangal may lead to greatly differing methods for coping with the environment. Therefore, the mix of species is partly determined by the tolerances of individual species to physical conditions, such as tidal flooding and salinity, but may also be influenced by other factors, such as crabs preying on plant seedlings.<ref name="Cannicci">{{cite journal |last1=Cannicci |first1=Stefano |last2=Fusi |first2=Marco |last3=Cimó |first3=Filippo |last4=Dahdouh-Guebas |first4=Farid |last5=Fratini |first5=Sara |title=Interference competition as a key determinant for spatial distribution of mangrove crabs |journal=BMC Ecology |date=December 2018 |volume=18 |issue=1 |page=8 |doi=10.1186/s12898-018-0164-1 |pmid=29448932 |pmc=5815208 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2018BMCE...18....8C }}</ref>

Once established, mangrove roots provide an [[oyster]] habitat and slow water flow, thereby enhancing sediment deposition in areas where it is already occurring. The fine, [[Anoxic waters|anoxic]] sediments under mangroves act as sinks for a variety of [[Heavy metals|heavy (trace) metals]] which [[colloidal particle]]s in the sediments have concentrated from the water. Mangrove removal disturbs these underlying sediments, often creating problems of trace metal contamination of seawater and organisms of the area.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Saenger |first1=P. |last2=McConchie |first2=D. |title=Heavy metals in mangroves: methodology, monitoring and management |journal=Envis Forest Bulletin |date=2004 |volume=4 |pages=52–62 |citeseerx=10.1.1.961.9649 }}</ref>

Mangrove swamps protect coastal areas from [[erosion]], [[storm surge]] (especially during [[tropical cyclone]]s), and [[tsunami]]s.<ref name="Mazda-2">{{cite journal|last1= Mazda |first1=Y. |last2=Kobashi |first2=D. |last3=Okada |first3=S.|year=2005|title=Tidal-Scale Hydrodynamics within Mangrove Swamps |journal=Wetlands Ecology and Management |volume = 13 | issue = 6| pages = 647–655 |doi=10.1007/s11273-005-0613-4 |bibcode=2005WetEM..13..647M |s2cid=35322400 }}</ref><ref name="Danielsen">{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.1118387 |pmid=16254180 |title=The Asian Tsunami: A Protective Role for Coastal Vegetation |journal=Science |volume=310 |issue=5748 |page=643 |year=2005 |last1=Danielsen |first1=F. |last2=Sørensen |first2=M. K. |last3=Olwig |first3=M. F |last4=Selvam |first4=V |last5=Parish |first5=F |last6=Burgess |first6=N. D |last7=Hiraishi |first7=T. |last8=Karunagaran |first8=V. M. |last9=Rasmussen |first9=M. S. |last10=Hansen |first10=L. B. |last11=Quarto |first11=A. |last12=Suryadiputra |first12=N.|s2cid=31945341 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Mangrove forest against dyke-break-induced tsunami on rapidly subsiding coasts |journal=Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences |volume=16 |issue=7 |pages=1629–1638 |date=2016 |doi=10.5194/nhess-16-1629-2016 |last1=Takagi |first1=H. |last2=Mikami |first2=T. |last3=Fujii |first3=D. |last4=Esteban |first4=M. |last5=Kurobe |first5=S.|bibcode=2016NHESS..16.1629T |doi-access=free }}</ref> They limit high-energy wave erosion mainly during events such as storm surges and tsunamis.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2005.06.008 |pmid=15964259 |title=How effective were mangroves as a defence against the recent tsunami? |journal=Current Biology |volume=15 |issue=12 |pages=R443–447 |year=2005 |last1=Dahdouh-Guebas |first1=F. |last2=Jayatissa |first2=L. P. |last3=Di Nitto |first3=D. |last4=Bosire |first4=J. O. |last5=Lo Seen |first5=D. |last6=Koedam |first6=N.|s2cid=8772526 |url=http://agritrop.cirad.fr/529549/ |doi-access=free |hdl=2013/ULB-DIPOT:oai:dipot.ulb.ac.be:2013/46641 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The mangroves' massive root systems are efficient at dissipating wave energy.<ref name="Massel">{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/s0169-5983(98)00024-0 |title=Surface wave propagation in mangrove forests |journal=Fluid Dynamics Research |volume=24 |issue=4 |page=219 |year=1999 |last1=Massel |first1=S. R. |last2=Furukawa |first2=K. |last3=Brinkman |first3=R. M. |bibcode=1999FlDyR..24..219M|s2cid=122572658 }}</ref> Likewise, they slow down tidal water enough so that its sediment is deposited as the tide comes in, leaving all except fine particles when the tide ebbs.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1023/A:1009949411068 |year=1997 |last1=Mazda |first1=Y. |journal=Mangroves and Salt Marshes |title=Drag force due to vegetation in mangrove swamps|volume=1 |issue=3 |page=193 |last2=Wolanski |first2=E. |last3=King |first3=B. |last4=Sase |first4=A. |last5=Ohtsuka |first5=D. |last6=Magi |first6=M.|s2cid=126945589 }}</ref> In this way, mangroves build their  environments.<ref name="Mazda-2" /> Because of the uniqueness of mangrove ecosystems and the protection against erosion they provide, they are often the object of conservation programs,<ref name="Zimmer"/> including national [[biodiversity action plan]]s.<ref name="Danielsen" />

==Distribution==
[[File:Map of global mangrove distribution.png|thumb|upright=2| {{center|Global distribution of mangrove forests, 2011{{hsp}}<ref name="Giri2010" />{{legend|#3e9c07|Mangrove forest <small> (click to enlarge)</small>}}}}]]
[[File:Distribution of mangroves and carbonate sediments around South-East Asia.png|thumb|upright=2|right|{{center|'''Diversity of mangroves is greatest in [[Southeast Asia]]'''<br />Distribution of delta, estuary, lagoon and open coast mangrove types<br />in (i) South Asia, (ii) Southeast Asia and (iii) East Asia{{hsp}}<ref name=Worthington2020>{{cite journal | last1=Worthington | first1=Thomas A. | last2=zu Ermgassen | first2=Philine S. E. | last3=Friess | first3=Daniel A. | last4=Krauss | first4=Ken W. | last5=Lovelock | first5=Catherine E. | last6=Thorley | first6=Julia | last7=Tingey | first7=Rick | last8=Woodroffe | first8=Colin D. | last9=Bunting | first9=Pete | last10=Cormier | first10=Nicole | last11=Lagomasino | first11=David | last12=Lucas | first12=Richard | last13=Murray | first13=Nicholas J. | last14=Sutherland | first14=William J. | last15=Spalding | first15=Mark | title=A global biophysical typology of mangroves and its relevance for ecosystem structure and deforestation | journal=Scientific Reports | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=10 | issue=1 | date=4 September 2020 | page=14652 | issn=2045-2322 | doi=10.1038/s41598-020-71194-5 | doi-access=free| pmid=32887898 | pmc=7473852 | bibcode=2020NatSR..1014652W }} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Material was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License].</ref><br /><small>Bar charts show percentage change in area between 1996 and 2016</small>}}]]
{{Main|Mangrove tree distribution}}
{{Further|List of mangrove ecoregions}}

Worldwide there are about 80 described species of mangroves that live along marine coasts. About 60 of these species are true mangroves which live only in the intertidal zone between high and low tides.<ref name=AMNH2 /> "Mangroves once covered three-quarters of the world's tropical coastlines, with Southeast Asia hosting the greatest diversity. Only 12 species live in the Americas. Mangroves range in size from small bushes to the 60-meter giants found in Ecuador. Within a given mangrove forest, different species occupy distinct niches. Those that can handle tidal soakings grow in the open sea, in sheltered bays, and on fringe islands. Trees adapted to drier, less salty soil can be found farther from the shoreline. Some mangroves flourish along riverbanks far inland, as long as the freshwater current is met by ocean tides."<ref name=AMNH2>[https://www.amnh.org/explore/videos/biodiversity/mangroves-the-roots-of-the-sea/what-is-a-mangrove What's a Mangrove? And How Does It Work?] ''American Museum of Natural History''. Accessed 8 November 2021.</ref>

[[File:Map Halophytes.png|thumb|upright=2|Mangroves dominate in tropical regions and salt marshes in temperate regions
{{legend|#ff8000|mangroves dominate}}
{{legend|#008000|salt marshes dominate}}]]

Mangroves can be found in 118 countries and territories in the tropical and subtropical regions of the world.<ref name="Giri2010" /> 
The largest percentage of mangroves is found between the 5° N and 5° S latitudes. Approximately 75% of world's mangroves are found in just 15 countries.<ref name="Giri2010">{{cite journal |last1=Giri |first1=C. |last2=Ochieng |first2=E. |last3=Tieszen |first3=L. L. |last4=Zhu |first4=Z. |last5=Singh |first5=A. |last6=Loveland |first6=T. |last7=Masek |first7=J. |last8=Duke |first8=N. |title=Status and distribution of mangrove forests of the world using earth observation satellite data: Status and distributions of global mangroves |journal=Global Ecology and Biogeography |date=January 2011 |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=154–159 |doi=10.1111/j.1466-8238.2010.00584.x |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1466-8238.2010.00584.x |access-date=12 August 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Estimates of mangrove area based on remote sensing and global data tend to be lower than estimates based on literature and surveys for comparable periods.<ref name="Friess" />

In 2018, the Global Mangrove Watch Initiative released a global baseline based on remote sensing and global data for 2010.<ref name="Giri2010" /> They estimated the total mangrove forest area of the world as of 2010 at {{convert|137600|km2|mi2|abbr=unit}}, spanning 118 countries and territories.<ref name="Friess" /><ref name="Bunting">{{cite journal |last1=Bunting |first1=Pete |last2=Rosenqvist |first2=Ake |last3=Lucas |first3=Richard |last4=Rebelo |first4=Lisa-Maria |last5=Hilarides |first5=Lammert |last6=Thomas |first6=Nathan |last7=Hardy |first7=Andy |last8=Itoh |first8=Takuya |last9=Shimada |first9=Masanobu |last10=Finlayson |first10=C. |title=The Global Mangrove Watch—A New 2010 Global Baseline of Mangrove Extent |journal=Remote Sensing |date=22 October 2018 |volume=10 |issue=10 |page=1669 |doi=10.3390/rs10101669 |bibcode=2018RemS...10.1669B |doi-access=free |hdl=10568/101185 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Following the conventions for identifying geographic regions from the [[Ramsar Convention]] on Wetlands, researchers reported that Asia has the largest share (38.7%) of the world's mangroves, followed by Latin America and the Caribbean (20.3%), Africa (20.0%), [[Oceania]] (11.9%), and Northern America (8.4%).<ref name="Bunting" />

=== Sundarbans ===
The largest mangrove forest in the world is in the [[Sundarbans]]. The Sundarban forest lies in the vast delta on the [[Bay of Bengal]] formed by the super confluence of the [[Brahmaputra River|Brahmaputra]] and [[Meghna River|Meghna]] rivers with distributaries of the [[Ganges]]. The seasonally flooded [[Sundarbans freshwater swamp forests]] lie inland from the mangrove forests on the coastal fringe. The forest covers {{convert|10000|km2|mi2|abbr=on}} of which about {{convert|6000|km2|mi2|abbr=on}} are in [[Bangladesh]].<ref name="Pani_al2013">{{cite journal |last1=Pani |first1=D. R. |last2=Sarangi |first2=S. K. |last3=Subudhi |first3=H. N. |last4=Misra |first4=R. C. |last5=Bhandari |first5=D. C. |year=2013 |title=Exploration, evaluation and conservation of salt tolerant rice genetic resources from Sundarbans region of West Bengal |journal=Journal of the Indian Society of Coastal Agricultural Research |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=45–53 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Dilip_Kundu2/post/What_are_the_rice_varieties_that_show_salt_tolerance_naturally/attachment/59d6397779197b8077996ae6/AS%3A401904459894785%401472832898899/download/Art+9+Pani+et+al..pdf}}</ref>

The Sundarbans is intersected by a complex network of tidal waterways, [[mudflat]]s and small islands of salt-tolerant mangrove forests. The interconnected network of waterways makes almost every portion of the forest accessible by boat. The area is known as an important habitat for the endangered [[Bengal tiger]], as well as numerous fauna including species of birds, [[chital|spotted deer]], [[crocodile]]s and snakes. The fertile soils of the delta have been subject to intensive human use for centuries, and the ecoregion has been mostly converted to intensive agriculture, with few enclaves of forest remaining.<ref name="Iftekhar2004">{{cite journal |last1=Iftekhar |first1=M. S. |last2=Islam |first2=M. R. |year=2004 |title=Managing mangroves in Bangladesh: A strategy analysis |journal=Journal of Coastal Conservation |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=139–146 |url=http://balticeucc.databases.eucc-d.de/files/documents/00000613_C10.139-146.pdf |doi=10.1652/1400-0350(2004)010[0139:MMIBAS]2.0.CO;2|s2cid=130056584 }}</ref> Additionally, the Sundarbans serves a crucial function as a protective barrier for millions of inhabitants against floods that result from [[cyclone]]s.

Four protected areas in the Sundarbans are listed as UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Giri |first1=C. |last2=Pengra |first2=B. |last3=Zhu |first3=Z. |last4=Singh |first4=A. |last5=Tieszen |first5=L. L. |year=2007 |title=Monitoring mangrove forest dynamics of the Sundarbans in Bangladesh and India using multi-temporal satellite data from 1973 to 2000 |journal=Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science |volume=73 |issue=1–2 |pages=91–100 |doi=10.1016/j.ecss.2006.12.019 |bibcode=2007ECSS...73...91G}}</ref> Despite these protections, the Indian Sundarbans were assessed as endangered in 2020 under the [[IUCN Red List of Ecosystems]] framework.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sievers |first1=M. |last2=Chowdhury |first2=M. R. |last3=Adame |first3=M. F. |last4=Bhadury |first4=P. |last5=Bhargava |first5=R. |last6=Buelow |first6=C. |last7=Friess |first7=D. A. |last8=Ghosh |first8=A. |last9=Hayes |first9=M. A. |last10=McClure |first10=E. C. |last11=Pearson |first11=R. M. |year=2020 |title=Indian Sundarbans mangrove forest considered endangered under Red List of Ecosystems, but there is cause for optimism |journal=Biological Conservation |volume=251 |article-number=108751 |doi=10.1016/j.biocon.2020.108751 |bibcode=2020BCons.25108751S |hdl=10072/400371 |s2cid=222206165 |url=https://iucnrle.org/static/media/uploads/references/published-assessments/sievers_etal_2020_indian_sundarbans_mangrove_forest_assessment.pdf |access-date=2021-11-07 |archive-date=2021-10-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211015191835/https://iucnrle.org/static/media/uploads/references/published-assessments/sievers_etal_2020_indian_sundarbans_mangrove_forest_assessment.pdf }}</ref> There is a consistent pattern of depleted biodiversity or loss of species and the ecological quality of the forest is declining.<ref>{{Cite journal |year=2010 |last1=Manna|first1 = S. |title=Dynamics of Sundarban estuarine ecosystem: Eutrophication induced threat to mangroves |journal=Saline Systems |volume=6 |article-number=8 |last2=Chaudhuri|first2=K. |last3=Bhattacharyya |first3=S. |last4=Bhattacharyya |first4=M. |pmid=20699005 |pmc=2928246 |doi=10.1186/1746-1448-6-8 |doi-access=free }}</ref><gallery mode="packed" heights="150" style="float:center">

==Ecosystem==
The unique ecosystem found in the intricate mesh of mangrove roots offers a quiet [[marine habitat]] for young organisms.<ref name=BOS>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s00227-010-1588-0 |pmid=24391259 |pmc=3873073 |title=Ontogenetic habitat shift, population growth, and burrowing behavior of the Indo-Pacific beach star, Archaster typicus (Echinodermata; Asteroidea) |journal=Marine Biology |volume=158 |issue=3 |pages=639–648 |year=2010 |last1=Bos |first1=AR |last2=Gumanao |first2=GS |last3=Van Katwijk |first3=MM |last4=Mueller |first4=B |last5=Saceda |first5=MM |last6=Tejada |first6=RL}}</ref> In areas where roots are permanently submerged, the organisms they host include [[algae]], [[barnacle]]s, [[oyster]]s, [[sponge]]s, and [[bryozoa]], which all require a hard surface for anchoring while they filter-feed. [[Shrimp]] and [[Thalassinidea|mud lobsters]] use the muddy bottoms as their home.<ref>''[[Encarta]] Encyclopedia 2005''. "Seashore", by [[Heidi Nepf]].</ref> [[Mangrove crab]]s eat the mangrove leaves, adding nutrients to the mangal mud for other bottom feeders.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s00442-001-0847-7 |pmid=28547499 |bibcode=2002Oecol.131....1S |title=Paradoxical selective feeding on a low-nutrient diet: Why do mangrove crabs eat leaves? |journal=Oecologia |volume=131 |issue=1 |pages=1–7 |year=2002 |last1=Skov |first1=M. W. |last2=Hartnoll |first2=R. G.|s2cid=23407273 }}</ref> In at least some cases, the export of carbon fixed in mangroves is important in coastal food webs.<ref>{{Cite journal|vauthors=Abrantes KG, Johnston R, Connolly RM, Sheaves M|date=2015-01-01|title=Importance of Mangrove Carbon for Aquatic Food Webs in Wet–Dry Tropical Estuaries|journal=Estuaries and Coasts|language=en|volume=38|issue=1|pages=383–99|doi=10.1007/s12237-014-9817-2|bibcode=2015EstCo..38..383A |hdl=10072/141734|s2cid=3957868|issn=1559-2731|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Mangrove plantations host several commercially important species of fish and crustaceans.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Gupta|first1=S. K.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KuneDwAAQBAJ&q=Mangrove+plantations+in+Vietnam%2C+Thailand%2C+Philippines%2C+and+India+host+several+commercially+important+species+of+fish+and+crustaceans&pg=PA34|title=Soil Salinity Management in Agriculture: Technological Advances and Applications|last2=Goyal|first2=Megh R.|date=2017-03-16|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-1-315-34177-4|language=en}}</ref>

In [[Puerto Rico]], the [[Rhizophora mangle|red]], [[Laguncularia racemosa|white]], and [[Avicennia germinans|black]] mangroves occupy different ecological niches and have slightly different chemical compositions, so the carbon content varies between the species, as well between the different tissues of the plant (e.g., leaf matter versus roots).<ref name="Vane" /> There is a clear succession of these three trees from the lower elevations, which are dominated by red mangroves, to farther inland with a higher concentration of white mangroves.<ref name="Vane" />

[[File:Acrostichum aureum? 00811.JPG|thumb| The mangrove fern (''[[Acrostichum aureum]]'') can grow vigorously in disturbed areas of mangrove forest.<ref>{{cite iucn |author=Ellison, J. |author2=Koedam, N.E. |author3=Wang, Y. |author4=Primavera, J. |author5=Jin Eong, O. |author6=Wan-Hong Yong, J. |author7=Ngoc Nam, V. |date=2010 |title=''Acrostichum aureum'' |volume=2010 |article-number=e.T177110A7366131 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2010-2.RLTS.T177110A7366131.en |access-date=19 November 2021}}</ref>]]

Mangrove forests are an important part of the cycling and storage of carbon in tropical coastal ecosystems.<ref name="Vane" /> Knowing this, scientists seek to reconstruct the environment and investigate changes to the coastal ecosystem over thousands of years using sediment cores.<ref name="versteegh">{{cite journal |last1=Versteegh |first1=GJ |display-authors=et al. |year=2004 |title=Taraxerol and Rhizophora pollen as proxies for tracking past mangrove ecosystems |journal=Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta |volume=68 |issue=3 |pages=411–22 |doi= 10.1016/S0016-7037(03)00456-3|bibcode=2004GeCoA..68..411V}}</ref> However, an additional complication is the imported marine organic matter that also gets deposited in the sediment through the tidal flushing of mangrove forests.<ref name="Vane" />

Mangrove forests can decay into [[peat]] deposits because of fungal and bacterial processes as well as by the action of [[termite]]s.<ref name="Vane" /> It becomes peat in good [[Geochemistry|geochemical]], sedimentary, and [[Tectonics|tectonic]] conditions.<ref name="Vane">{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/ggge.20194 |title=Degradation of mangrove tissues by arboreal termites (Nasutitermes acajutlae) and their role in the mangrove C cycle (Puerto Rico): Chemical characterization and organic matter provenance using bulk δ13C, C/N, alkaline CuO oxidation-GC/MS, and solid-state |journal=Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems |volume=14 |issue=8 |page=3176 |year=2013 |last1=Vane |first1=CH |last2=Kim |first2=AW |last3=Moss-Hayes |first3=V |last4=Snape |first4=CE |last5=Diaz |first5=MC |last6=Khan |first6=NS |last7=Engelhart |first7=SE |last8=Horton |first8=BP |bibcode=2013GGG....14.3176V|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/id/eprint/503347/1/ggge20194.pdf |doi-access=free }}</ref> The nature of these deposits depends on the environment and the types of mangroves involved. Termites process fallen [[leaf litter]], root systems and wood from mangroves into peat to build their nests.<ref name="Vane" /> Termites stabilise the chemistry of this peat and represent approximately 2% of above ground carbon storage in mangroves.<ref name="Vane" /> As the nests are buried over time this carbon is stored in the sediment, and the [[carbon cycle]] continues.<ref name="Vane" />

Mangroves are an important source of [[blue carbon]]. Globally, mangroves stored {{Convert|4.19|Gt|lb|abbr=unit}} of carbon in 2012.<ref name="auto">{{Cite journal|last1=Hamilton |first1=SE |last2=Friess |first2=DA |date=2018 |title=Global carbon stocks and potential emissions due to mangrove deforestation from 2000 to 2012 |journal=Nature Climate Change |volume=8 |issue=3|pages=240–244 |doi=10.1038/s41558-018-0090-4 |bibcode=2018NatCC...8..240H|arxiv=1611.00307 |s2cid=89785740 }}</ref> Two percent of global mangrove carbon was lost between 2000 and 2012, equivalent to a maximum potential of {{Convert|0.316996250|Gt|lbs|abbr=unit}} of [[Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|CO<sub>2</sub> emissions]].<ref name="auto" /> Globally, mangroves have been shown to provide measurable economic protections to coastal communities affected by tropical storms.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hochard|first1=Jacob P.|last2=Hamilton|first2=S|last3=Barbier|first3=EB|date=2019-06-03|title=Mangroves shelter coastal economic activity from cyclones|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=116|issue=25|pages=12232–37|doi=10.1073/pnas.1820067116|pmid=31160457|pmc=6589649|bibcode=2019PNAS..11612232H |issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Biodiversity==

===Birds===
[[Homogeneity and heterogeneity|Heterogeneity]] in [[landscape ecology]] is a measure of how different parts of a landscape are from one another. It can manifest in an ecosystem from the abiotic or biotic characteristics of the environment. For example, coastal mangrove forests are located at the land-sea interface, so their functioning is influenced by [[Abiotic component|abiotic factors]] such as tides, as well as biotic factors such as the extent and configuration of adjacent vegetation.<ref name=Buelow2018 /> For forest birds, tidal inundation means that the availability of many mangrove resources fluctuates daily, suggesting foraging flexibility is likely to be important. Mangroves also offer estuarine prey items, such as mudskippers and crabs, that are not found in terrestrial forest types. Further, mangroves are often situated in a complex mosaic of adjacent vegetation types such as grasslands, saltmarshes, and woodlands, and this can mean that flexibility in foraging strategy and choice of foraging habitat may be advantageous for highly mobile forest birds.<ref name=Buelow2018>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0206145|doi-access = free|title = Stable isotopes reveal opportunistic foraging in a spatiotemporally heterogeneous environment: Bird assemblages in mangrove forests|year = 2018|last1 = Buelow|first1 = Christina A.|last2 = Reside|first2 = April E.|last3 = Baker|first3 = Ronald|last4 = Sheaves|first4 = Marcus|journal = PLOS ONE|volume = 13|issue = 11|article-number = e0206145|pmid = 30439959|pmc = 6237324|bibcode = 2018PLoSO..1306145B}} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Material was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License].</ref> Relative to other forest types, mangroves support few bird species that are obligate habitat (mangrove) specialists and instead host many species with generalised foraging niches.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0206145|doi-access = free|title = Stable isotopes reveal opportunistic foraging in a spatiotemporally heterogeneous environment: Bird assemblages in mangrove forests|year = 2018|last1 = Buelow|first1 = Christina A.|last2 = Reside|first2 = April E.|last3 = Baker|first3 = Ronald|last4 = Sheaves|first4 = Marcus|journal = PLOS ONE|volume = 13|issue = 11|article-number = e0206145|pmid = 30439959|pmc = 6237324|bibcode = 2018PLoSO..1306145B}}</ref><ref name=Buelow2018 />

===Fish===
The intricate root system of mangrove forests makes them attractive to adult fish seeking food and juvenile fish seeking shelter.<ref name=NOAA2021 />

===Mangrove crabs and holobionts===
Mangrove forests are among the more productive and diverse ecosystems on the planet, despite limited [[nitrogen]] availability. Under such conditions, animal-microbe associations ([[holobiont]]s) are often key to ecosystem functioning. An example is the role of [[fiddler crab]]s and their [[carapace]]-associated microbial [[biofilm]] as hotspots of microbial nitrogen transformations and sources of nitrogen within the mangrove ecosystem.<ref name=Zilius2020 />

Among coastal ecosystems, mangrove forests are of great importance as they account for three quarters of the tropical coastline and provide different ecosystem services.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1111/geb.12155|title = Ecological role and services of tropical mangrove ecosystems: A reassessment|year = 2014|last1 = Lee|first1 = Shing Yip|last2 = Primavera|first2 = Jurgene H.|last3 = Dahdouh-Guebas|first3 = Farid|last4 = McKee|first4 = Karen|last5 = Bosire|first5 = Jared O.|last6 = Cannicci|first6 = Stefano|last7 = Diele|first7 = Karen|last8 = Fromard|first8 = Francois|last9 = Koedam|first9 = Nico|last10 = Marchand|first10 = Cyril|last11 = Mendelssohn|first11 = Irving|last12 = Mukherjee|first12 = Nibedita|last13 = Record|first13 = Sydne|journal = Global Ecology and Biogeography|volume = 23|issue = 7|pages = 726–743|hdl = 10862/2247| s2cid=52904699 |doi-access = free| bibcode=2014GloEB..23..726L }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi = 10.1016/S0065-2881(01)40003-4|title = Biology of mangroves and mangrove Ecosystems|series = Advances in Marine Biology|year = 2001|last1 = Kathiresan|first1 = K.|last2 = Bingham|first2 = B.L.|volume = 40|pages = 81–251|isbn = 978-0-12-026140-6}}</ref> Mangrove ecosystems generally act as a net sink of carbon, although they release organic matter to the sea in the form of dissolved refractory macromolecules, leaves, branches and other debris.<ref name=Dittmar2006>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1029/2005GB002570|title = Mangroves, a major source of dissolved organic carbon to the oceans|year = 2006|last1 = Dittmar|first1 = Thorsten|last2 = Hertkorn|first2 = Norbert|last3 = Kattner|first3 = Gerhard|last4 = Lara|first4 = Rubén J.|journal = Global Biogeochemical Cycles|volume = 20|issue = 1| article-number=2005GB002570 |pages = n/a|bibcode = 2006GBioC..20.1012D| s2cid=128922131 |doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1016/j.aquabot.2007.12.005|title = Organic carbon dynamics in mangrove ecosystems: A review|year = 2008|last1 = Kristensen|first1 = Erik|last2 = Bouillon|first2 = Steven|last3 = Dittmar|first3 = Thorsten|last4 = Marchand|first4 = Cyril|journal = Aquatic Botany|volume = 89|issue = 2|pages = 201–219| bibcode=2008AqBot..89..201K |url = https://lirias.kuleuven.be/handle/123456789/203718|url-access = subscription}}</ref> In pristine environments, mangroves are among the most productive ecosystems on the planet, despite growing in tropical waters that are often nutrient depleted.<ref name="Nutrition of mangroves">{{cite journal |doi = 10.1093/treephys/tpq048|title = Nutrition of mangroves|year = 2010|last1 = Reef|first1 = R.|last2 = Feller|first2 = I. C.|last3 = Lovelock|first3 = C. E.|journal = Tree Physiology|volume = 30|issue = 9|pages = 1148–1160|pmid = 20566581|doi-access = free}}</ref> The refractory nature of the organic matter produced and retained in mangroves can slow the recycling of nutrients, particularly of nitrogen.<ref name=Dittmar2006 /><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1007/BF01204455|title = Sedimentary C/S relationships in a large tropical estuary: Evidence for refractory carbon inputs from mangroves|year = 1995|last1 = Woolfe|first1 = Ken J.|last2 = Dale|first2 = Paul J.|last3 = Brunskill|first3 = Gregg J.|journal = Geo-Marine Letters|volume = 15|issue = 3–4|pages = 140–144|bibcode = 1995GML....15..140W|s2cid = 128709551}}</ref> Nitrogen limitation in such systems may be overcome by microbial [[nitrogen fixation]] when combined with high rates of [[bioturbation]] by [[macrofauna]], such as crabs and lobsters.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1023/A:1005850032254 | title=Nitrogen enrichment during decomposition of mangrove leaf litter in an east African coastal lagoon (Kenya): Relative importance of biological nitrogen fixation |year = 1997|last1 = Woitchik|first1 = A.F.|last2 = Ohowa|first2 = B.|last3 = Kazungu|first3 = J.M.|last4 = Rao|first4 = R.G.|last5 = Goeyens|first5 = L.|last6 = Dehairs|first6 = F.|journal = Biogeochemistry|volume = 39| issue=1 |pages = 15–35| bibcode=1997Biogc..39...15W |s2cid = 91314553}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1128/aem.35.3.567-575.1978|title = Biological Dinitrogen Fixation (Acetylene Reduction) Associated with Florida Mangroves|year = 1978|last1 = Zuberer|first1 = D. A.|last2 = Silver|first2 = W. S.|journal = Applied and Environmental Microbiology|volume = 35|issue = 3|pages = 567–575|pmid = 637550|pmc = 242881|bibcode = 1978ApEnM..35..567Z}}</ref><ref name= Zilius2020 />

Bioturbation by macrofauna affect nitrogen availability and multiple nitrogen related microbial processes through sediment reworking, burrow construction and [[bioirrigation]], feeding and excretion.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.3354/meps09506 |title = What is bioturbation? The need for a precise definition for fauna in aquatic sciences |year = 2012 |last1 = Kristensen |first1 = E. |last2 = Penha-Lopes |first2 = G. |last3 = Delefosse |first3 = M. |last4 = Valdemarsen |first4 = T. |last5 = Quintana |first5 = CO |last6 = Banta |first6 = GT |journal = Marine Ecology Progress Series |volume = 446 |pages = 285–302 |bibcode = 2012MEPS..446..285K |doi-access = free }}</ref> Macrofauna mix old and fresh organic matter, extend [[Anoxic waters|oxic–anoxic]] sediment interfaces, increase the availability of energy-yielding [[electron acceptor]]s and increase nitrogen turnover via direct excretion.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1080/0275754031000155474|title = It's a dirty job but someone has to do it: The role of marine benthic macrofauna in organic matter turnover and nutrient recycling to the water column|year = 2003|last1 = Welsh|first1 = David T.|journal = Chemistry and Ecology|volume = 19|issue = 5|pages = 321–342| bibcode=2003ChEco..19..321W |s2cid = 94773926}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.5194/bg-10-7829-2013 |title = Stimulation of microbial nitrogen cycling in aquatic ecosystems by benthic macrofauna: Mechanisms and environmental implications |year = 2013 |last1 = Stief |first1 = P. |journal = Biogeosciences |volume = 10 |issue = 12 |pages = 7829–7846 |bibcode = 2013BGeo...10.7829S |doi-access = free |hdl = 21.11116/0000-0001-C75E-6 |hdl-access = free }}</ref> Thus, macrofauna may alleviate nitrogen limitation by priming the [[remineralisation]] of refractory nitrogen (that is, the nitrogen that can't be biologically decomposed), reducing plant-microbe competition.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1111/j.1574-6941.2012.01400.x|title = Differential effects of microorganism-invertebrate interactions on benthic nitrogen cycling|year = 2012|last1 = Gilbertson|first1 = William W.|last2 = Solan|first2 = Martin|last3 = Prosser|first3 = James I.|journal = FEMS Microbiology Ecology|volume = 82|issue = 1|pages = 11–22|pmid = 22533682|doi-access = free| bibcode=2012FEMME..82...11G }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1042/BST0390315|title = Bioturbation: Impact on the marine nitrogen cycle|year = 2011|last1 = Laverock|first1 = Bonnie|last2 = Gilbert|first2 = Jack A.|last3 = Tait|first3 = Karen|last4 = Osborn|first4 = A. Mark|last5 = Widdicombe|first5 = Steve|journal = Biochemical Society Transactions|volume = 39|issue = 1|pages = 315–320|pmid = 21265795 | url=https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/24403453 }}</ref> Such activity ultimately promotes nitrogen recycling, plant assimilation and high nitrogen retention, as well as favours its loss by stimulating coupled [[nitrification]] and [[denitrification]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1002/lno.10724|title = Benthic N pathways in illuminated and bioturbated sediments studied with network analysis|year = 2018|last1 = Magri|first1 = M.|last2 = Benelli|first2 = S.|last3 = Bondavalli|first3 = C.|last4 = Bartoli|first4 = M.|last5 = Christian|first5 = R. R.|last6 = Bodini|first6 = A.|journal = Limnology and Oceanography|volume = 63|issue = S1|pages = S68–S84|bibcode = 2018LimOc..63S..68M| s2cid=89783098 |doi-access = free}}</ref><ref name= Zilius2020 />

[[File:Nitrogen cycling in a mangrove fiddler crab holobiont.webp|thumb|upright=1.7|left|{{center|'''Nitrogen cycling in a mangrove fiddler crab holobiont'''{{hsp}}<ref name= Zilius2020>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1038/s41598-020-70834-0 |doi-access = free|title = N2 fixation dominates nitrogen cycling in a mangrove fiddler crab holobiont|year = 2020|last1 = Zilius|first1 = Mindaugas|last2 = Bonaglia|first2 = Stefano|last3 = Broman|first3 = Elias|last4 = Chiozzini|first4 = Vitor Gonsalez|last5 = Samuiloviene|first5 = Aurelija|last6 = Nascimento|first6 = Francisco J. Mangrove sediments are highly bioturbated by [[Decapoda|decapod]]s such as crabs.<ref name=Kristensen2008>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1016/j.seares.2007.05.004|title = Mangrove crabs as ecosystem engineers; with emphasis on sediment processes|year = 2008|last1 = Kristensen|first1 = Erik|journal = Journal of Sea Research|volume = 59|issue = 1–2|pages = 30–43|bibcode = 2008JSR....59...30K}}</ref> Crab populations continuously rework sediment by constructing burrows, creating new niches, transporting or selectively grazing on sediment microbial communities.<ref name=Kristensen2008 /><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1038/s41598-019-40315-0 |doi-access = free|title = Fiddler crab bioturbation determines consistent changes in bacterial communities across contrasting environmental conditions|year = 2019|last1 = Booth|first1 = Jenny Marie|last2 = Fusi|first2 = Marco|last3 = Marasco|first3 = Ramona|last4 = Mbobo|first4 = Tumeka|last5 = Daffonchio|first5 Leibold|first2 = Mathew A.|author-link1=Catalina Cuellar-Gempeler|journal = The ISME Journal|volume = 12|issue = 3|pages = 825–837|pmid = 29362507|pmc = 5864236|bibcode=2018ISMEJ..12..825C }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite journal |doi = 10.1016/j.jembe.2004.06.003|title = Impact of fiddler crab foraging and tidal inundation on an intertidal sandflat: Season-dependent effects in one tidal cycle|year = 2004|last1 = Reinsel|first1 = K.A.|journal = Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology|volume = 313| issue=1 |pages = 1–17| bibcode=2004JEMBE.313....1R }}</ref> In addition, crabs can affect organic matter turnover by assimilating leaves and producing finely fragmented faeces, or by carrying them into their burrows.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1016/j.jembe.2009.04.002|title = Activity patterns, feeding and burrowing behaviour of the crab Ucides cordatus (Ucididae) in a high intertidal mangrove forest in North Brazil|year = 2009|last1 = Nordhaus|first1 = Inga|last2 = Diele|first2 = Karen|last3 = Wolff|first3 = Matthias |journal=Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology|volume = 374|issue = 2|pages = 104–112| bibcode=2009JEMBE.374..104N }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1007/s00227-006-0597-5|title = Feeding ecology of the mangrove crab Ucides cordatus (Ocypodidae): Food choice, food quality and 10.1016/j.ecss.2011.03.002|title = Impact of crab bioturbation on benthic flux and nitrogen dynamics of Southwest Atlantic intertidal marshes and mudflats|year = 2011|last1 = Fanjul|first1 = Brazilian sediments|year = 2015|last1 = Quintana|first1 = Cintia O.|last2 = Shimabukuro|first2 = Maurício|last3 = Pereira|first3 = Camila O.|last4 = Alves|first4 = Betina G. G.|journal = Scientific Reports|volume = 5|article-number = 16122|pmid = 26525137|pmc = 4630785|bibcode = 2015NatSR...516122Q}}</ref> In contrast to burrowing polychaetes or amphipods, the abundant Ocipodid crabs, mainly represented by fiddler crabs, do not permanently ventilate their burrows. These crabs may temporarily leave their burrows for surface activities,<ref name=":0" /> or otherwise plug their burrow entrance during tidal inundation in order to trap air.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1016/0031-9384(94)90079-5|title = Burrow plugging in the crab Uca uruguayensis and its synchronization with photoperiod and tides|year = 1994|last1 = de la Iglesia|first1 = Horacio O.|last2 = Rodríguez|first2 = Enrique M.|last3 = Dezi|first3 = Rubén E.|journal = Physiology & Behavior|volume = 55|issue = 5|pages = 913–919|pmid = 8022913|s2cid = 7366251}}</ref> A recent study showed that these crabs can be associated with a diverse microbial community, either on their carapace or in their gut.<ref name="Booth2019" /><ref name= Zilius2020 />

The exoskeleton of living animals, such as shells or carapaces, offers a habitat for microbial biofilms which are actively involved in different N-cycling pathways such as nitrification, denitrification and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA).<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0185071|doi-access = free|title = Denitrification potential of the eastern oyster ==Biogeochemistry==
{{further|Marine biogeochemistry}}

===Carbon cycle===
[[File:Fate of mangrove primary production.jpg|thumb|upright=1.7| {{center|'''Fate of mangrove primary production'''{{hsp}}<ref name=Walton2021>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.142677|title = Faunal mediated carbon export from mangroves in an arid area|year = 2021|last1 = Walton|first1 = M.E.M.|last2 = Al-Maslamani|first2 = I.|last3 = Chatting|first3 = M.|last4 = Smyth|first4 = D.|last5 = Castillo|first5 = A.|last6 = Skov|first6 = M.W.|last7 = Le Vay|first7 = L.|journal = Science of the Total Environment|volume = 755|issue = Pt 1|article-number = 142677|pmid = 33077211|bibcode = 2021ScTEn.75542677W|s2cid = 224810608|doi-access = free|hdl = 10576/16945|hdl-access = free}} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Material was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License].</ref>}} A.) Fate of mangrove [[primary production]] and importance of each component, as a percentage of net mangrove primary productivity.<ref name="Bouillon2008a"/><ref name="Alongi2014"/><br />B.) Isotopic profile of sediments across the transition from mangrove to intertidal [[mudflat]]s and [[seagrass bed]]s, illustrating the retention of mangrove productivity within the forest.]]

Mangrove forests are amongst the world's most productive marine ecosystems,<ref name=Alongi2014>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1146/annurev-marine-010213-135020|title = Carbon Cycling and Storage in Mangrove Forests|year = 2014|last1 = Alongi|first1 = Daniel M.|journal = Annual Review of Marine Science|volume = 6|pages = 195–219|pmid = 24405426|bibcode = 2014ARMS....6..195A|doi-access = free}}</ref> with net primary productivity (NPP) in the order of 208 Tg C yr<sup>−1</sup>.<ref name=Bouillon2008a>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1029/2007gb003052|title = Mangrove production and carbon sinks: A revision of global budget estimates|year = 2008|last1 = Bouillon|first1 = Steven|last2 = Borges|first2 = Alberto V.|last3 = Castañeda-Moya|first3 = Edward|last4 = Diele|first4 = Karen|last5 = Dittmar|first5 = Thorsten|last6 = Duke|first6 = Norman C.|last7 = Kristensen|first7 = Erik|last8 = Lee|first8 = Shing Y.|last9 = Marchand|first9 = Cyril|last10 = Middelburg|first10 = Jack J.|last11 = Rivera-Monroy|first11 = Victor H.|last12 = Smith|first12 = Thomas J.|last13 = Twilley|first13 = Robert R.|journal = Global Biogeochemical Cycles|volume = 22|issue = 2| article-number=2007GB003052 |pages = n/a|bibcode = 2008GBioC..22.2013B| s2cid=42641476 |doi-access = free|hdl = 10072/20205|hdl-access = free}}</ref> Mangrove forests achieve a steady state once the forest reaches maximum biomass at around 20–30 years through a constant process of mortality and renewal{{hsp}}<ref name=Lugo1980>{{cite journal |doi = 10.2307/2388158|jstor = 2388158|title = Mangrove Ecosystems: Successional or Steady State?|last1 = Lugo|first1 = Ariel E.|journal = Biotropica|year = 1980|volume = 12|issue = 2|pages = 65–72| bibcode=1980Biotr..12...65L }}</ref> so, assuming the living biomass is not becoming more carbon dense, then carbon has to be lost at a rate equal to the amount of carbon fixed as NPP. Hence this productivity is either retained within the mangrove forest, as a standing stock of live material such as wood, buried in [[Marine sediment|sediments]], or exported to neighbouring habitats as litter, [[particulate organic carbon|particulate]] and [[dissolved organic carbon]] (POC and DOC) and [[dissolved inorganic carbon]] (DIC), or lost to the atmosphere.<ref name=Bouillon2008a /><ref name=Maher2013>{{cite journal |doi = 10.4319/lo.2013.58.2.0475|title = Groundwater-derived dissolved inorganic and organic carbon exports from a mangrove tidal creek: The missing mangrove carbon sink?|year = 2013|last1 = Maher|first1 = D. T.|last2 = Santos|first2 = I. R.|last3 = Golsby-Smith|first3 = L.|last4 = Gleeson|first4 = J.|last5 = Eyre|first5 = B. D.|journal = Limnology and Oceanography|volume = 58|issue = 2|pages = 475–488|bibcode = 2013LimOc..58..475M| s2cid=86841519 |doi-access = free}}</ref><ref name=Alongi2014 /><ref name=Walton2021 />

The outwelling hypothesis argues that export of locally derived POC and DOC is an important ecosystem function of mangroves, which drives detrital based [[food web]]s in adjacent coastal habitats.<ref>Odum, E.P. (1968) "A research challenge: evaluating the productivity of coastal and estuarine water". In: ''Proceedings of the second sea grant conference'', pages 63-64. University of Rhode Island.</ref><ref>Odum, W.E. and Heald, E.J. (1972) ""Trophic analyses of an estuarine mangrove community". ''Bulletin of Marine Science'', '''22'''(3): 671-738.</ref> Export of mangrove carbon has been estimated to make a significant trophic contribution to adjacent ecosystems.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1007/bf00029127|title = Mangrove outwelling: A review|year = 1995|last1 = Lee|first1 = S. Y.|journal = Hydrobiologia|volume = 295|issue = 1–3|pages = 203–212| bibcode=1995HyBio.295..203L |s2cid = 28803158}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1007/s00114-001-0283-x|title = Relevance of mangroves for the production and deposition of organic matter along tropical continental margins|year = 2002|last1 = Jennerjahn|first1 = Tim C.|last2 = Ittekkot|first2 = Venugopalan|journal = Naturwissenschaften|volume = 89|issue = 1|pages = 23–30|pmid = 12008969|bibcode = 2002NW.....89...23J|s2cid = 33556308}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1029/2005gb002570|title = Mangroves, a major source of dissolved organic carbon to the oceans|year = 2006|last1 = Dittmar|first1 = Thorsten|last2 = Hertkorn|first2 = Norbert|last3 = Kattner|first3 = Gerhard|last4 = Lara|first4 = Rubén J.|journal = Global Biogeochemical Cycles|volume = 20|issue = 1| article-number=2005GB002570 |pages = n/a|bibcode = 2006GBioC..20.1012D| s2cid=128922131 |doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1007/s12237-014-9817-2|title = Importance of Mangrove Carbon for Aquatic Food Webs in Wet–Dry Tropical Estuaries|year = 2015|last1 = Abrantes|first1 = Kátya G.|last2 = Johnston|first2 = Ross|last3 = Connolly|first3 = Rod M.|last4 = Sheaves|first4 = Marcus|journal = Estuaries and Coasts|volume = 38| issue=1 |pages = 383–399| bibcode=2015EstCo..38..383A |hdl = 10072/141734|s2cid = 3957868|hdl-access = free}}</ref> The theory of outwelling is supported by mass balance evaluations that show the amount of carbon fixed by mangroves normally greatly exceeds the amount stored within the forest,<ref name=Alongi2014 /><ref>{{cite book |doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-62206-4_5|chapter = Productivity and Carbon Dynamics in Mangrove Wetlands|title = Mangrove Ecosystems: A Global Biogeographic Perspective|year = 2017|last1 = Twilley|first1 = Robert R.|last2 = Castañeda-Moya|first2 = Edward|last3 = Rivera-Monroy|first3 = Victor H.|last4 = Rovai|first4 = Andre|pages = 113–162|isbn = 978-3-319-62204-0}}</ref> although the scale of outwelling varies considerably between forests,<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1007/s10452-004-0442-1|title = Fine-scale movement and assimilation of carbon in saltmarsh and mangrove habitat by resident animals|year = 2004|last1 = Guest|first1 = Michaela A.|last2 = Connolly|first2 = Rod M.|journal = Aquatic Ecology|volume = 38|issue = 4|pages = 599–609| bibcode=2004AqEco..38..599G |s2cid = 3901928}}</ref> due to differences in [[coastal geomorphology]], tidal regimes, freshwater flow and productivity.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1007/s10021-009-9235-7|title = Mangrove-Exported Nutrient Incorporation by Sessile Coral Reef Invertebrates|year = 2009|last1 = Granek|first1 = Elise F.|last2 = Compton|first2 = Jana E.|last3 = Phillips|first3 = Donald L.|journal = Ecosystems|volume = 12|issue = 3|pages = 462–472| bibcode=2009Ecosy..12..462G |s2cid = 587963|url = https://pdxscholar.library.pdx.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1074&context=esm_fac|url-access = subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1016/j.jembe.2012.07.024|title = The relative importance of mangroves and seagrass beds as feeding areas for resident and transient fishes among different mangrove habitats in Florida and Belize: Evidence from dietary and stable-isotope analyses|year = 2012|last1 = Vaslet|first1 = A.|last2 = Phillips|first2 = D.L.|last3 = France|first3 = C.|last4 = Feller|first4 = I.C.|last5 = Baldwin|first5 = C.C.|journal = Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology|volume = 434-435|pages = 81–93| bibcode=2012JEMBE.434...81V }}</ref><ref name=Walton2021 />

[[File:Pathways for the nitrogen cycle in mangrove forests.webp|thumb|upright=1.7|right|{{center|'''Pathways for the [[nitrogen cycle]] in mangrove forests'''{{hsp}}<ref name= Vepraskas2015>{{cite book | last=Vepraskas | first=Michael | title=Wetland soils: genesis, hydrology, landscapes, and classification | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YmbmCgAAQBAJ| publisher=CRC Press | publication-place=Boca Raton, Florida | year=2016 | isbn=978-1-4398-9800-0 | oclc=928883552}}</ref><ref name=Shiau2020>{{cite journal |doi = 10.3390/f11050492|doi-access = free|title = Biogeochemical Processes of C and N in the Soil of Mangrove Forest Ecosystems|year = 2020|last1 = Shiau|first1 = Yo-Jin|last2 = Chiu|first2 = Chih-Yu|journal = Forests|volume = 11|issue = 5|page = 492| bibcode=2020Fore...11..492S }} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Material was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]</ref>}} Black arrows indicate nitrogen pathways. Blue arrows indicate the direction where increased environmental factors (salinity, carbon source, nitrogen source) may affect nitrogen pathways.]]

In the 1990s, global estimates could account for 48% of the total global mangrove [[primary production]] of 218 ± 72 million tons C yr<sup>−1</sup> (see diagram on the right). By incorporating information on carbon burial, {{CO2}} efflux and carbon outwelled as [[leaf litter]], POC and DOC, the remaining 52% was thought outwelled as DIC, though there was insufficient data to confirm this.<ref name=Bouillon2008a /> More recent assessments of DIC export at two sites in Australia{{hsp}}<ref name=Maher2013 /><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1002/lno.11090|title = Carbon outwelling and outgassing vs. Burial in an estuarine tidal creek surrounded by mangrove and saltmarsh wetlands|year = 2019|last1 = Santos|first1 = Isaac R.|last2 = Maher|first2 = Damien T.|last3 = Larkin|first3 = Reece|last4 = Webb|first4 = Jackie R.|last5 = Sanders|first5 = Christian J.|journal = Limnology and Oceanography|volume = 64|issue = 3|pages = 996–1013| doi-access=free |bibcode = 2019LimOc..64..996S| hdl=10536/DRO/DU:30144450 |s2cid = 91613293|hdl-access = free}}</ref> supported the estimates of Bouillon et al. in 2008,<ref name="Bouillon2008a"/> although in 2014 Alongi suggested that only 40% of NPP was exported as DIC.<ref name="Alongi2014"/><ref name=Walton2021 />

===Nitrogen assimilation===
Mangrove forests and coastal marshes are typically considered N-limited ecosystems because of their high primary production.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1023/A:1021166010892 | title=Nitrogen vs. phosphorus limitation across an ecotonal gradient in a mangrove forest |year = 2003|last1 = Feller|first1 = Ilka C.|last2 = McKee|first2 = Karen L.|last3 = Whigham|first3 = Dennis F.|last4 = O'Neill|first4 = John P.|journal = Biogeochemistry|volume = 62|issue = 2|pages = 145–175| bibcode=2003Biogc..62..145F |s2cid = 42854661}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1890/1051-0761(1997)007[0737:HAOTGN]2.0.CO;2|issn = 1051-0761|year = 1997|volume = 7|page = 737|title = Human Alteration of the Global Nitrogen Cycle: Sources and Consequences|last1 = Vitousek|first1 = Peter M.|last2 = Aber|first2 = John D.|last3 = Howarth|first3 = Robert W.|last4 = Likens|first4 = Gene E.|last5 = Matson|first5 = Pamela A.|last6 = Schindler|first6 = David W.|last7 = Schlesinger|first7 = William H.|last8 = Tilman|first8 = David G.|journal = Ecological Applications|issue = 3|hdl = 1813/60830|hdl-access = free}}</ref> Therefore, mangrove plants are highly efficient at utilising soil nitrogen, making them an important sink for excess nitrogen from upstream.<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1016/j.marpolbul.2014.11.040|title = Nutrient removal in a closed silvofishery system using three mangrove species (Avicennia germinans, Laguncularia racemosa, and Rhizophora mangle)|year = 2015|last1 = De-León-Herrera|first1 = R.|last2 = Flores-Verdugo|first2 = F.|last3 = Flores-De-Santiago|first3 = F.|last4 = González-Farías|first4 = F.|journal = Marine Pollution Bulletin|volume = 91|issue = 1|pages = 243–248|pmid = 25499182| bibcode=2015MarPB..91..243D }}</ref><ref name="Nutrition of mangroves"/> However, different mangrove species may still utilise nitrogen at different efficiencies,<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1016/j.ecss.2005.01.004|title = Rapid sediment accumulation and microbial mineralization in forests of the mangrove Kandelia candel in the Jiulongjiang Estuary, China|year = 2005|last1 = Alongi|first1 = D.M.|last2 = Pfitzner|first2 = J.|last3 = Trott|first3 = L.A.|last4 = Tirendi|first4 = F.|last5 = Dixon|first5 = P.|last6 = Klumpp|first6 = D.W.|journal = Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science|volume = 63|issue = 4|pages = 605–618|bibcode = 2005ECSS...63..605A}}</ref> even though they share similar nitrogen pathways (see diagram on right). Reported nitrogen assimilation rates in mangrove plants ranged from 2 to 8 μmol g<sup>−1</sup> h<sup>−1</sup> under ambient nitrogen conditions,<ref>Datta, R.; Datta, B.K. (1999 ) "Desiccation induced nitrate and ammonium uptake in the red alga ''Catenella repens'' (Rhodophyta, Gigartinales)". ''Indian J. Geo Mar. Sci.'', '''28''': 458–460.</ref> and 19 to 251 μmol g<sup>−1</sup> h<sup>−1</sup> when the nitrogen supply was unlimited.<ref name="Assessing N2 fixation in estuarine">{{cite journal |doi = 10.1016/j.ecss.2017.03.005|title = Assessing N2 fixation in estuarine mangrove soils|year = 2017|last1 = Shiau|first1 = Yo-Jin|last2 = Lin|first2 = Ming-Fen|last3 = Tan|first3 = Chen-Chung|last4 = Tian|first4 = Guanglong|last5 = Chiu|first5 = Chih-Yu|journal = Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science|volume = 189|pages = 84–89|bibcode = 2017ECSS..189...84S}}</ref><ref name=Shiau2020 />

In addition to species variation, different environmental conditions can also affect the nitrogen assimilation rates in mangrove plants. Because [[Chloride|Cl<sup>−</sup> ions]] can reduce [[protein synthesis]] and [[nitrogen assimilation]],<ref>{{cite journal |doi = 10.1007/s00468-003-0293-8|title = Effects of salt on growth, ion accumulation, photosynthesis and leaf anatomy of the mangrove, Bruguiera parviflora|year = 2004|last1 = Parida|first1 = Asish Kumar|last2 = Das|first2 = A. B.|last3 = Mittra|first3 = B.|journal = Trees - Structure and Function|volume = 18|issue = 2|pages = 167–174| bibcode=2004Trees..18..167P |s2cid = 20302042}}</ref> soil [[Groundwater|pore water]] salinity appears to be a negative factor that significantly alters the nitrogen uptake rates of mangrove plants.<ref name="Assessing N2 fixation in estuarine"/><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Khan | first1=M. Ajmal | last2=Aziz | first2=Irfan | journal=Wetlands Ecology and Management | title=Salinity tolerance in some mangrove species from Pakistan | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=9 | issue=3 | year=2001 | issn=0923-4861 | doi=10.1023/a:1011112908069 | pages=229–233| bibcode=2001WetEM...9..229K | s2cid=40743147 }}</ref><ref name=Shiau2020 />

== Exploitation and conservation ==
[[File:Arrière-mangrove de Majicavo janvier 2017.jpg|thumb|Mangrove roots act as a net, retaining waste. [[Mayotte]] at low tide]]
[[File:Bali Barat mangroves.jpg|thumb|Mangroves in [[West Bali National Park]], Indonesia]]

Adequate data is only available for about half of the global area of mangroves. However, of those areas for which data has been collected, it appears that 35% of the mangroves have been destroyed.<ref>Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) ''Ecosystems and Human Well-being: Synthesis'' (p.2) Island Press, Washington, DC. World Resources Institute {{ISBN|1-59726-040-1}}</ref> Since the 1980s, around 2% of mangrove area is estimated to be lost each year.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Valiela, I. |author2=Bowen, J.L. |author3=York, J.K. |date=2001 |title=Mangrove Forests: One of the World's Threatened Major Tropical Environments: At least 35% of the area of mangrove forests has been lost in the past two decades, losses that exceed those for tropical rain forests and coral reefs, two other well-known threatened environments |journal=BioScience |volume=51 |issue=10 |pages=807–815 |doi=10.1641/0006-3568(2001)051[0807:MFOOTW]2.0.CO;2|doi-access=free }}</ref> Assessments of global variation in mangrove loss indicates that national regulatory quality mediates how different drivers and pressures influence loss rates.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Turschwell|first1=Mischa P. |last2=Tulloch |first2=Vivitskaia J.D.|last3=Sievers|first3=M. |last4=Pearson|first4=R.M.|last5=Andradi-Brown|first5=D.A.|last6=Ahmadia|first6=G.N.|last7=Connolly|first7=R.M. |last8=Bryan-Brown |first8=D. |last9=Lopez-Marcano|first9=S. |last10=Adame|first10=M.F. |last11=Brown|first11=C.J. |date=2020 |title=Multi-scale estimation of the effects of pressures and drivers on mangrove forest loss globally|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0006320720306959|journal=Biological Conservation |volume=247 |article-number=108637 |doi=10.1016/j.biocon.2020.108637|bibcode=2020BCons.24708637T |s2cid=219750253 |url-access=subscription|hdl=10072/394300|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

[[Shrimp farming]] causes approximately a quarter of the destruction of mangrove forests.<ref>Botkin, D. and E. Keller (2003) ''Environmental Science: Earth as a living planet'' (p.2) John Wiley & Sons. {{ISBN|0-471-38914-5}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.5343/bms.2012.1069 |title=Assessing the Role of Commercial Aquaculture in Displacing Mangrove Forest |journal=Bulletin of Marine Science |volume=89 |issue=2 |pages=585–601 |year=2013 |last1=Hamilton |first1=Stuart |bibcode=2013BuMS...89..585H }}</ref> Likewise, the 2010 update of the World Mangrove Atlas indicated that approximately one fifth of the world's mangrove ecosystems have been lost since 1980,<ref name="nature.org">{{cite web|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100717013054/http://www.nature.org/pressroom/press/press4573.html|archive-date= 2010-07-17|url=http://www.nature.org/pressroom/press/press4573.html |title= 2010a. ""World Atlas of Mangroves" Highlights the Importance of and Threats to Mangroves: Mangroves among World's Most Valuable Ecosystems." Press release. Arlington, Virginia |publisher=The Nature Conservancy|access-date=2014-01-25}}</ref> although this rapid loss rate appears to have decreased since 2000 with global losses estimated at between 0.16% and 0.39% annually between 2000 and 2012.<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/geb.12449 |title=Creation of a high spatio-temporal resolution global database of continuous mangrove forest cover for the 21st century (CGMFC-21) |journal=Global Ecology and Biogeography |volume=25 |issue=6 |pages=729–38 |year=2016 |last1=Hamilton |first1=Stuart E |last2=Casey |first2=Daniel |arxiv=1412.0722 |bibcode=2016GloEB..25..729H |s2cid=55999275 }}</ref> Despite global loss rates decreasing since 2000, Southeast Asia remains an area of concern with loss rates between 3.6% and 8.1% between 2000 and 2012.<ref name=":2" /> By far the most damaging form of shrimp farming is when a closed ponds system (non-[[integrated multi-trophic aquaculture]]) is used, as these require destruction of a large part of the mangrove, and use antibiotics and disinfectants to suppress diseases that occur in this system, and which may also leak into the surrounding environment. Far less damage occurs when [[integrated mangrove-shrimp aquaculture]] is used, as this is connected to the sea and subjected to the tides, and less diseases occur, and as far less mangrove is destroyed for it.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.zed.fr/en/tv/distribution/catalogue/programme/the-secret-life-of-mangroves|title=The Secret Life of Mangroves - Television - Distribution - ZED|website=www.zed.fr}}</ref>

Grassroots efforts to protect mangroves from development and from citizens cutting down the mangroves for [[Charcoal kiln|charcoal production]],<ref>Charcoal is used as a cheap source of energy in developing countries for cooking purposes</ref><ref name="zed.fr">{{Cite web|url=https://www.zed.fr/en/tv/distribution/catalogue/programme/the-secret-life-of-mangroves?media=3808|title=The Secret Life of Mangroves - Television - Distribution - ZED|website=www.zed.fr|access-date=2021-11-09|archive-date=2022-04-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220406194758/https://www.zed.fr/en/tv/distribution/catalogue/programme/the-secret-life-of-mangroves?media=3808}}</ref> cooking, heating and as a building material are becoming more popular. [[Solar cooker]]s are distributed by many non-government organizations as a low-cost alternative to wood and charcoal stoves. These may help in reducing the demand for charcoal.
* In Thailand, community management has been effective in restoring damaged mangroves.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ecotippingpoints.org/our-stories/indepth/thailand-mangrove-restoration-community-management.html |title=Thailand – Trang Province – Taking Back the Mangroves with Community Management &#124; The EcoTipping Points Project |publisher=Ecotippingpoints.org |access-date=2012-02-08}}</ref> Also, production of mangrove [[honey]] is practiced, as a way to generate sustainable income for nearby people, keeping them from destroying the mangrove and generate a short-term revenue.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iucn.org/news/asia/201612/bees-income-generator-and-mangrove-conservation-tool-community-thailand|title=Bees: An income generator and mangrove conservation tool for a community in Thailand|date=December 14, 2016|website=IUCN}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last1=Hub |first1=Knowledge |url=http://www.mangrovealliance.org/harvesting-honey-mangrove-resilience-tsiribihina-delta/|title=Harvesting honey for mangrove resilience in the Tsiribihina delta|date=February 5, 2018|website=The Mangrove Alliance}}</ref>
* In [[Madagascar]], honey is also produced in mangroves as a source of (non-destructive) income generation. In addition, silk pods from endemic silkworm species are also collected in the [[Madagascar mangroves]] for [[wild silk]] production.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.mongabay.com/2019/08/madagascar-whats-good-for-the-forest-is-good-for-the-native-silk-industry/|title=Madagascar: What's good for the forest is good for the native silk industry|date=August 16, 2019|website=Mongabay Environmental News}}</ref><ref name="zed.fr"/>
* In the [[Bahamas]], for example, active efforts to save mangroves are occurring on the islands of [[Bimini]] and [[Great Guana Cay]]. 
* In [[Trinidad and Tobago]] as well, efforts are underway to protect a mangrove threatened by the construction of a steel mill and a port.{{citation needed|date=August 2013}}
* Within northern Ecuador, mangrove regrowth is reported in almost all estuaries and stems primarily from local actors responding to earlier periods of deforestation in the Esmeraldas region.<ref name="mingaonline.uach.cl">Hamilton, S. & S. Collins (2013) [http://mingaonline.uach.cl/scielo.php?script=sci_pdf&pid=S0717-92002013000200003&lng=es&nrm=iso&tlng=en Las respuestas a los medios de subsistencia deforestación de los manglares en las provincias del norte de Ecuador] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160102121228/http://mingaonline.uach.cl/scielo.php?script=sci_pdf&pid=S0717-92002013000200003&lng=es&nrm=iso&tlng=en |date=2016-01-02 }}. Bosque 34:2</ref>

Mangroves have been reported to be able to help buffer against tsunami, cyclones, and other storms, and as such may be considered a flagship system for [[ecosystem-based adaptation]] to the impacts of climate change. One village in [[Tamil Nadu]] was protected from tsunami destruction—the villagers in [[Naluvedapathy]] planted 80,244 saplings to get into the [[Guinness Book of World Records]]. This created a kilometre-wide belt of trees of various varieties. When the [[2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami|2004 tsunami]] struck, much of the land around the village was flooded, but the village suffered minimal damage.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.treecouncil.org.uk |title=Tree News, Spring/Summer 2005, Publisher Felix Press |publisher=Treecouncil.org.uk |access-date=2012-02-08}}</ref>

=== Biogeochemical implications of conservation ===
Mangroves sequester over 25 million tons of carbon annually.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Polidoro |first1=Beth A. |last2=Carpenter |first2=Kent E. |last3=Collins |first3=Lorna |last4=Duke |first4=Norman C. |last5=Ellison |first5=Aaron M. |last6=Ellison |first6=Joanna C. |last7=Farnsworth |first7=Elizabeth J. |last8=Fernando |first8=Edwino S. |last9=Kathiresan |first9=Kandasamy |last10=Koedam |first10=Nico E. |last11=Livingstone |first11=Suzanne R. |last12=Miyagi |first12=Toyohiko |last13=Moore |first13=Gregg E. |last14=Ngoc Nam |first14=Vien |last15=Ong |first15=Jin Eong |date=2010-04-08 |editor-last=Hansen |editor-first=Dennis Marinus |title=The Loss of Species: Mangrove Extinction Risk and Geographic Areas of Global Concern |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=5 |issue=4 |article-number=e10095 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0010095 |doi-access=free |pmid=20386710 |pmc=2851656 |bibcode=2010PLoSO...510095P |issn=1932-6203}}</ref> Mangrove areas have declined globally over recent decades due to the expansion of aquaculture, and oil and timber production.<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Goldberg |first1=Liza |last2=Lagomasino |first2=David |last3=Thomas |first3=Nathan |last4=Fatoyinbo |first4=Temilola |date=October 2020 |title=Global declines in human-driven mangrove loss |journal=Global Change Biology |language=en |volume=26 |issue=10 |pages=5844–5855 |doi=10.1111/gcb.15275 |issn=1354-1013 |pmc=7540710 |pmid=32654309 |bibcode=2020GCBio..26.5844G }}</ref><ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last1=Sunkur |first1=Reshma |last2=Kantamaneni |first2=Komali |last3=Bokhoree |first3=Chandradeo |last4=Ravan |first4=Shirish |date=2023-12-01 |title=Mangroves' role in supporting ecosystem-based techniques to reduce disaster risk and adapt to |bibcode=2023JSR...19602449S |issn=1385-1101}}</ref> Mangrove loss has been associated with reduced carbon storage and altered carbon export dynamics.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":8">{{Cite journal * '''Gazi Bay, Kenya:''' In 2010, residents of Gazi Bay partnered Plan Vivo and Association for Coastal Ecosystem Services (ACES) to implement a mangrove conservation and restoration project. The project generates income for local communities through carbon credits based on emission reductions.<ref name=":10">{{Citation | date=2020 |title=Community-led Mangrove Restoration and Conservation in Gazi Bay, Kenya: Lessons from Early Blue Carbon Projects. |url=https://comsec-web-static.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2022-02/Community-led%20Mangrove%20Restoration%20and%20Conservation%20in%20Gazi%20Bay,%20Kenya-%20Lessons%20From%20Early%20Blue%20Carbon%20Projects%20(on-going).pdf |publisher=The Commonwealth Blue Charter | location = London, UK | series=Ocean and Climate Change}}</ref>
