The project has the primary goal of conserving and protecting coastal natural resources and biodiversity.<ref name=":11">{{Citation |last1=Anthonsen Aamot | first1= Tiril Marie |last2=Sim | first2 = Vichet |last3=Enseñado | first3 = Elena Marie |title=Conservation, Restoration and Ecotourism in Trapeang Sangkae, Cambodia |date=2026 |publisher = Columbia University Libraries | series = Urban Climate Change Research Network Case Study | url=https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/5ka4-wj40 |doi=10.7916/5KA4-WJ40}}</ref>

=== Ocean deoxygenation ===
Compared to [[seagrass meadow]]s and [[coral reef]]s, [[Hypoxia (environmental)|hypoxia]] is more common on a regular basis in mangrove ecosystems, through [[ocean deoxygenation]] is compounding the negative effects by anthropogenic nutrient inputs and land use modification.<ref name=Laffoley2019>Laffoley, D. & Baxter, J.M. (eds.) (2019). [https://portals.iucn.org/library/sites/library/files/documents/08.8%20DEOX.pdf Ocean deoxygenation: Everyone's problem - Causes, impacts, consequences and solutions]. IUCN, Switzerland.</ref>

Like seagrass, mangrove trees transport oxygen to roots of [[rhizome]]s, reduce sulfide concentrations, and alter microbial communities. Dissolved oxygen is more readily consumed in the interior of the mangrove forest. Anthropogenic inputs may push the limits of survival in many mangrove microhabitats. For example, shrimp ponds constructed in mangrove forests are considered the greatest anthropogenic threat to mangrove ecosystems. These shrimp ponds reduce [[estuary]] circulation and water quality which leads to the promotion of [[Diel cycle|diel-cycling]] hypoxia. When the quality of the water degrades, the shrimp ponds are quickly abandoned leaving massive amounts of wastewater. This is a major source of water pollution that promotes ocean deoxygenation in the adjacent habitats.<ref name=Laffoley2019 /><ref name="nature.org2">{{cite web|title=2010a. ""World Atlas of Mangroves" Highlights the Importance of and Threats to Mangroves: Mangroves among World's Most Valuable Ecosystems." Press release. Arlington, Virginia|url=http://www.nature.org/pressroom/press/press4573.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100717013054/http://www.nature.org/pressroom/press/press4573.html|archive-date=2010-07-17|access-date=2014-01-25|publisher=The Nature Conservancy}}</ref>

Due to these frequent hypoxic conditions, the water does not provide habitats to fish. When exposed to extreme hypoxia, ecosystem function can completely collapse. Extreme deoxygenation will affect the local fish populations, which are an essential food source. The environmental costs of shrimp farms in the mangrove forests grossly outweigh the economic benefits of them. Cessation of shrimp production and restoration of these areas reduce eutrophication and anthropogenic hypoxia.<ref name=Laffoley2019 />

{{clear}}

== Reforestation ==
[[File:Mangroves of Bohol.png|thumb|upright=1.2|Mangroves in [[Bohol]], Philippines]]
[[File:Karachi Mangroves.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|Mangroves in [[Karachi]], Pakistan]]
{{Main|Mangrove restoration}}

In some areas, mangrove [[reforestation]] and [[mangrove restoration]] is also underway. Red mangroves are the most common choice for cultivation, used particularly in [[marine aquariums]] in a [[Sump (aquarium)|sump]] to reduce [[nitrates]] and other [[nutrients]] in the water. Mangroves also appear in home [[aquariums]], and as ornamental plants, such as in [[Japan]].{{citation needed|date=May 2019}}

{{external media
| float  = right
| width  = 269px
| video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vh7CoPBLQa8&ab_channel=MangroveActionProject Restoring The Natural Mangrove Forest] {{align|right|– ''Mangrove Action Project''}}
}}

The Manzanar Mangrove Initiative is an ongoing experiment in [[Arkiko]], [[Eritrea]], part of the Manzanar Project founded by [[Gordon H. Sato]], establishing new mangrove plantations on the coastal [[mudflat]]s. Initial plantings failed, but observation of the areas where mangroves did survive by themselves led to the conclusion that nutrients in water flow from inland were important to the health of the mangroves. Trials with the Eritrean Ministry of Fisheries followed, and a planting system was designed to provide the nitrogen, phosphorus, and iron missing from seawater.<ref name="NatGeo2007-02"/><ref name="SocWetlandSci"/>

The propagules are planted inside a reused galvanized steel can with the bottom knocked out; a small piece of iron and a pierced plastic bag with fertilizer containing nitrogen and phosphorus are buried with the propagule. {{As of|2007}}, after six years of planting, 700,000 mangroves are growing; providing stock feed for sheep and habitat for oysters, crabs, other bivalves, and fish.<ref name="NatGeo2007-02">{{cite web | last = Warne | first = Kennedy | others = Tim Laman, photographer | title = Mangroves: Forests of the Tide | work = [[National Geographic]] | publisher = National Geographic Society | date = February 2007 | url = http://ngm.nationalgeographic.com/2007/02/mangroves/warne-text/5 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20081012045111/http://ngm.nationalgeographic.com/2007/02/mangroves/warne-text/5 | archive-date = October 12, 2008 | access-date = 2010-08-08}}</ref><ref name="SocWetlandSci">{{Cite journal | last = Sato | first = Gordon | author-link = Gordon H. Sato | author2 = Abraham Fisseha |author3=Simon Gebrekiros |author4=Hassan Abdul Karim |author5=Samuel Negassi |author6=Martin Fischer |author7=Emanuel Yemane |author8=Johannes Teclemariam  |author9=Robert Riley |name-list-style=amp | title = A novel approach to growing mangroves on the coastal mud flats of Eritrea with the potential for relieving regional poverty and hunger | journal = Wetlands | volume = 25 | issue = 3 | pages = 776–779 | doi = 10.1672/0277-5212(2005)025[0776:ANATGM]2.0.CO;2 | year = 2005| s2cid = 45705546 }}</ref>

Another method of restoring mangroves is by using [[quadcopters]] (which are able to carry and deposit seed pods). According to Irina Fedorenko, an amount of work equivalent to weeks of planting using traditional methods can be done by a drone in days, and at a fraction of the cost.<ref name="Guest">{{cite magazine |last1=Guest |first1=Peter |title=Tropical forests are dying. Seed-slinging drones can save them |url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/feature-biocarbon-drones |access-date=11 August 2021 |magazine=WIRED |date=April 28, 2019}}</ref>

Seventy percent of mangrove forests have been lost in [[Java]], [[Indonesia]]. Mangroves formerly protected the island's coastal land from flooding and erosion.<ref name=3360_Yale_Pearce_20190502/> [[Wetlands International]], an NGC based in the Netherlands, in collaboration with nine villages in [[Demak Regency|Demak]] where lands and homes had been flooded, began reviving mangrove forests in Java. Wetlands International introduced the idea of developing tropical versions of techniques traditionally used by the Dutch to catch sediment in North Sea coastal salt marshes.<ref name=3360_Yale_Pearce_20190502>{{Cite news| title = On Java's Coast, A Natural Approach to Holding Back the Waters| work = Yale E360| access-date = 2019-05-15| url = https://e360.yale.edu/features/on-javas-coast-a-natural-approach-to-holding-back-the-waters |first=Fred |last=Pearce |date=May 2, 2019}}</ref> Originally, the villagers constructed a sea barrier by hammering two rows of vertical bamboo poles into the seabed and filling the gaps with brushwood held in place with netting. Later the bamboo was replaced by PVC pipes filled with concrete. As sediment gets deposited around the brushwood, it serves to catch floating mangrove seeds and provide them with a stable base to germinate, take root and regrow. This creates a green belt of protection around the islands. As the mangroves mature, more sediment is held in the catchment area; the process is repeated until a mangrove forest has been restored. Eventually the protective structures will not be needed.<ref name=3360_Yale_Pearce_20190502/> By late 2018, {{Convert|16|km|mi|abbr=unit}} of brushwood barriers along the coastline had been completed.<ref name=3360_Yale_Pearce_20190502/>

A concern over reforestation is that although it supports increases in mangrove area it may actually result in a decrease in global mangrove functionality and poor restoration processes may result in longer term depletion of the mangrove resource.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=Shing Yip|last2=Hamilton|first2=Stu|last3=Barbier|first3=Edward B.|last4=Primavera|first4=Jurgenne|last5=Lewis|first5=Roy R.|date=June 2019|title=Better restoration policies are needed to conserve mangrove ecosystems|journal=Nature Ecology & Evolution|volume=3|issue=6|pages=870–872|doi=10.1038/s41559-019-0861-y|pmid=31036899|bibcode=2019NatEE...3..870L |s2cid=139106235|issn=2397-334X}}</ref>

== National and international studies ==
In terms of local and national studies of mangrove loss, the case of Belize's mangroves is illustrative in its contrast to the global picture. A recent, satellite-based study<ref name="maps.cathalac.org">{{cite report |url=http://maps.cathalac.org/Downloads/data/bz/bz_mangroves_1980-2010_highres.pdf |vauthors=Cherrington EA, Hernandez BE, Trejos NA, Smith OA, Anderson ER, Flores AI, Garcia BC |date=2010 |title=Identification of Threatened and Resilient Mangroves in the Belize Barrier Reef System |series=Technical report to the World Wildlife Fund |work=Water Center for the Humid Tropics of Latin America and the Caribbean (CATHALAC) / Regional Visualization & Monitoring System (SERVIR) |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130731035556/http://maps.cathalac.org/Downloads/data/bz/bz_mangroves_1980-2010_highres.pdf |archive-date=July 31, 2013 }}</ref>—funded by the World Wildlife Fund and conducted by the Water Center for the Humid Tropics of Latin America and the Caribbean (CATHALAC)—indicates Belize's mangrove cover declined by a mere 2% over a 30-year period. The study was born out of the need to verify the popular conception that mangrove clearing in Belize was rampant.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ambergriscaye.com/pages/town/art/Pelican_Review.pdf |title=Pelican_Cays_Review |access-date=2012-02-08}}</ref>

Instead, the assessment showed, between 1980 and 2010, under {{convert|16|km2|mi2|abbr=unit}} of mangroves had been cleared, although clearing of mangroves near Belize's main coastal settlements (e.g. [[Belize City]] and San Pedro) was relatively high. The rate of loss of Belize's mangroves—at 0.07% per year between 1980 and 2010—was much lower than Belize's overall rate of forest clearing (0.6% per year in the same period).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.servir.net/servir_bz_forest_cover_1980-2010.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130729135101/http://www.servir.net/servir_bz_forest_cover_1980-2010.pdf |title=Cherrington, E.A., Ek, E., Cho, P., Howell, B.F., Hernandez, B.E., Anderson, E.R., Flores, A.I., Garcia, B.C., Sempris, E., and D.E. Irwin. 2010. "Forest Cover and Deforestation in Belize: 1980–2010." Water Center for the Humid Tropics of Latin America and the Caribbean. Panama City, Panama. 42 pp.|archive-date=July 29, 2013}}</ref> These findings can also be interpreted to indicate Belize's mangrove regulations (under the nation's)<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.belizelaw.org/lawadmin/PDF%20files/cap213s.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120313105434/http://www.belizelaw.org/lawadmin/PDF%20files/cap213s.pdf |title=Government of Belize (GOB). 2003. "Forests Act Subsidiary Laws." Chapter 213 in: Substantive Laws of Belize. Revised Edition 2003. Government Printer: Belmopan, Belize. 137 pp.|archive-date=March 13, 2012}}</ref> have largely been effective. Nevertheless, the need to protect Belize's mangroves is imperative, as a 2009 study by the World Resources Institute (WRI) indicates the ecosystems contribute {{Currency|174}} to {{Currency|249|USD}} million per year to Belize's national economy.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://pdf.wri.org/working_papers/coastal_capital_belize_wp.pdf |title=Coastal Capital: Belize. The Economic Contribution of Belize's Coral Reefs and Mangroves |last1=Cooper |first1=E. |last2=Burke |first2=L. |last3=Bood |first3=N. |date=2009 |publisher=World Resources Institute |location=Washington, DC |access-date=2014-06-23}}</ref>

From 1990, in Tanzania, [[Adelaida K. Semesi]] led aresearch programme which resulted in Tanzania being one of the first countries to have an environmental management plan for mangroves.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |date=July 2001 |title=Adelaida Kleti Semesi 1951-2001 |url=http://www.glomis.com/news/newsletter/ISMENews24.pdf |journal=Mangroves |publisher=International Society for Mangrove Ecosystems |issue=24}}</ref> Nicknamed "mama mikoko" ("mama mangroves" in Swahili),<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last=Brock-Utne |first=Birgit |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C1KqEAAAQBAJ&dq=Adelaida+Semesi&pg=PA73 |title=Learning from and Teaching Africans |date=2022-12-08 |publisher=Cambridge Scholars Publishing |isbn=978-1-5275-9157-8 |page=73 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |date=March 2001 |title=A Tribute to Adelaida K. Semesi |url=https://www.wiomsa.org/download/wiomsa_newsbriefs_/2001/WIOMSA-Newsbrief-March-2001.pdf |journal=WIOMSA Newsbrief |volume=6 |issue=1 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211122043928/https://www.wiomsa.org/download/wiomsa_newsbriefs_/2001/WIOMSA-Newsbrief-March-2001.pdf |archive-date=2021-11-22}}</ref> Semesi also was a Council Member for the [[International Society for Mangrove Ecosystems]].<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |date=July 2001 |title=Adelaida Kleti Semesi 1951-2001 |url=http://www.glomis.com/news/newsletter/ISMENews24.pdf |journal=Mangroves |publisher=International Society for Mangrove Ecosystems |issue=24}}</ref>

In May 2019, ORNL DAAC News announced that [[NASA]]'s [[Carbon monitoring#NASA Carbon Monitoring System (CMS)|Carbon Monitoring System]] (CMS), using new satellite-based maps of global mangrove forests across 116 countries, had created a new dataset to characterize the "distribution, biomass, and canopy height of mangrove-forested wetlands".<ref name="ORNL_DAAC_20190506">{{Citation| title = Mapping Global Mangrove Forests| work = ORNL DAAC News| access-date = May 15, 2019| date = May 6, 2019| url = https://daac-news.ornl.gov/content/mapping-global-mangrove-forests}}</ref><ref name="earthobservatory_20190225">{{Citation| title = New Satellite-Based Maps of Mangrove Heights| format = Text.Article| access-date = May 15, 2019| date = February 25, 2019| url = https://earthobservatory.nasa.gov/images/144573/new-satellite-based-maps-of-mangrove-heights?_ga=2.242896961.239110103.1557888044-1148588132.1557888044 |first1=Carol |last1= Rasmussen |first2=Mike |last2=Carlowicz}}</ref> Mangrove forests move carbon dioxide "from the atmosphere into long-term storage" in greater quantities than other forests, making them "among the planet's best [[Carbon dioxide scrubber|carbon scrubbers]]" according to a NASA-led study.<ref name="earthobservatory_20190225"/><ref name="Simard2018">{{cite journal|last1= Simard|first1= M.|last2= Fatoyinbo|first2= L.|author2-link=Lola Fatoyinbo|last3= Smetanka|first3= C.|last4= Rivera-Monroy|first4=V. WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Montane ecosystem
======================================================================

{{Short description|Ecosystems found in mountains}}
{{Redirect|Montane|the surname|Montané}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2022}}
[[File:Lila Lake 26527.JPG|thumb|right|upright=1.35|A subalpine lake in the [[Cascade Range]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]], United States]]
[[File:Coverage by protected areas of important sites for mountain biodiversity, OWID.svg|thumb|Coverage of important mountain [[biodiversity]] sites in [[protected areas]] by country]]
'''Montane ecosystems''' are found on the slopes of [[mountain]]s. The [[alpine climate]] in these regions strongly affects the [[ecosystem]] because temperatures [[lapse rate|fall as elevation increases]], causing the ecosystem to stratify. This stratification is a crucial factor in shaping plant community, biodiversity, metabolic processes and ecosystem dynamics for montane ecosystems.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mayor|first1=Jordan R.|last2=Sanders|first2=Nathan J.|last3=Classen|first3=Aimée T.|last4=Bardgett|first4=Richard D.|last5=Clément|first5=Jean-Christophe|last6=Fajardo|first6=Alex|last7=Lavorel|first7=Sandra|last8=Sundqvist|first8=Maja K.|last9=Bahn|first9=Michael|last10=Chisholm|first10=Chelsea|last11=Cieraad|first11=Ellen |date=February 2017|title=Elevation alters ecosystem properties across temperate tree lines globally|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature21027|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=542|issue=7639|pages=91–95|doi=10.1038/nature21027|pmid=28117440|bibcode=2017Natur.542...91M|hdl=1874/394068|s2cid=4455333|issn=1476-4687|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Dense montane [[forest]]s are common at moderate elevations, due to moderate temperatures and high rainfall. At higher elevations, the climate is harsher, with lower temperatures and higher winds, preventing the growth of trees and causing the plant community to transition to [[montane grasslands and shrublands]] or [[alpine tundra]]. Due to the unique climate conditions of montane ecosystems, they contain increased numbers of endemic species. Montane ecosystems also exhibit variation in [[ecosystem service]]s, which include carbon storage and water supply.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Aparecido|first1=Luiza Maria T.|last2=Teodoro|first2=Gazelle S.|last3=Mosquera|first3=Giovanny|last4=Brum|first4=Mauro|last5=Barros|first5=Fernanda de V.|last6=Pompeu|first6=Patricia Vieira|last7=Rodas|first7=Melissa|last8=Lazo|first8=Patricio|last9=Müller|first9=Caroline S.|last10=Mulligan|first10=Mark|last11=Asbjornsen|first11=Heidi|date=2018|title=Ecohydrological drivers of Neotropical vegetation in montane ecosystems|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/eco.1932|journal=Ecohydrology|language=en|volume=11|issue=3|article-number=e1932|doi=10.1002/eco.1932|bibcode=2018Ecohy..11E1932A |s2cid=134197371 |issn=1936-0592}}</ref>

==Life zones==
[[File:Mountain-birch-Trollheimen.jpg|thumb|A stand of [[Betula pubescens|mountain birch]] at around 750&nbsp;m in [[Trollheimen]], typical of [[Scandinavia]]n subalpine forests]]

As elevation increases, the [[alpine climate|climate becomes cooler]], due to a decrease in [[atmospheric pressure]] and the [[adiabatic cooling]] of airmasses.<ref name=goodywilson>{{cite book |first1=Richard M. |last1=Goody |first2=James C.G. |last2=Walker |title=Atmospheres |chapter=Atmospheric Temperatures |chapter-url=http://lasp.colorado.edu/~bagenal/3720/GoodyWalker/AtmosCh3sm.pdf |publisher=Prentice-Hall |year=1972 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160729075851/http://lasp.colorado.edu/~bagenal/3720/GoodyWalker/AtmosCh3sm.pdf |archive-date=29 July 2016 }}</ref> In [[middle latitudes]], the change in climate by moving up 100&nbsp;meters on a mountain is roughly equivalent to moving 80&nbsp;kilometers (45&nbsp;miles or 0.75° of [[latitude]]) towards the nearest pole.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Blyth |first1=S. |last2=Groombridge |first2=B. |last3=Lysenko |first3=I. |last4=Miles |first4=L. |last5=Newton |first5=A. |url=http://www.unep-wcmc.org/mountains/mountain_watch/pdfs/WholeReport.pdf |archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20080511044709/http://www.unep-wcmc.org/mountains/mountain_watch/pdfs/WholeReport.pdf |archive-date=11 May 2008 |title=Mountain Watch |year=2002 |publisher=UNEP World Conservation Monitoring Centre, Cambridge, UK |page=15}}</ref> The characteristic flora and fauna in the mountains tend to strongly depend on elevation, because of the change in climate. This dependency causes [[life zone]]s to form: bands of similar ecosystems at similar elevations.<ref name=lugo/>

One of the typical life zones on mountains is the montane forest: at moderate elevations, the rainfall and temperate climate encourages dense forests to grow. [[Holdridge life zone|Holdridge]] defines the climate of montane forest as having a biotemperature of between {{convert|6|and|12|C|F}}, where biotemperature is the mean temperature considering temperatures below {{convert|0|C|F}} to be {{convert|0|C|F}}.<ref name=lugo>{{cite journal|last1=Lugo|first1=Ariel E.|first2=Sandra L.|last2=Brown|first3=Rusty|last3=Dodson|first4=Tom S.|last4=Smith|first5=Hank H.|last5=Shugart|year=1999|title=The Holdridge Life Zones of the conterminous United States in relation to ecosystem mapping|journal=Journal of Biogeography|volume=26|pages=1025–1038|url=http://www.fs.fed.us/global/iitf/pubs/ja_iitf_1999_lugo002.pdf|doi=10.1046/j.1365-2699.1999.00329.x|issue=5|bibcode=1999JBiog..26.1025L |s2cid=11733879 }}</ref> Above the elevation of the montane forest, the trees thin out in the subalpine zone, become twisted [[krummholz]], and eventually fail to grow. Therefore, montane forests often contain trees with twisted trunks. This phenomenon is observed due to the increase in the wind strength with the elevation. The elevation where trees fail to grow is called the [[tree line]]. The biotemperature of the subalpine zone is between {{convert|3|and|6|C|F}}.<ref name=lugo/>
[[File:Treeline elevation.gif|thumb|left|Treeline elevation by latitude<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Testolin|first1=Riccardo|last2=Attorre|first2=Fabio|last3=Jiménez-Alfaro|first3=Borja|year=2020|title=Global distribution and bioclimatic characterization of alpine biomes|journal=Ecography|volume=43|issue=6 |pages=779–788 |doi=10.1111/ecog.05012|bibcode=2020Ecogr..43..779T |hdl=11585/896830|hdl-access=free}}</ref>]]

Above the tree line the ecosystem is called the alpine zone or [[alpine tundra]], dominated by grasses and low-growing shrubs. The biotemperature of the alpine zone is between {{convert|1.5|and|3|C|F}}. Many different plant species live in the alpine environment, including [[perennial grass]]es, [[sedges]], [[forb]]s, [[cushion plant]]s, [[moss]]es, and [[lichen]]s.<ref name=functional>{{Cite book
 | first = Christian
 | last = Körner
 | title = Alpine Plant Life: Functional Plant Ecology of High Mountain Ecosystems
 | place = Berlin
 | publisher = Springer
 | isbn = 978-3-642-98018-3
 | year = 2013}}</ref> Alpine plants must adapt to the harsh conditions of the alpine environment, which include low temperatures, dryness, ultraviolet radiation, and a short growing season. Alpine plants display adaptations such as rosette structures, waxy surfaces, and hairy leaves. Because of the common characteristics of these zones, the [[World Wildlife Fund]] groups a set of related [[ecoregions]] into the "[[montane grassland and shrubland]]" biome. A region in the [[Hengduan Mountains]] adjoining Asia's Tibetan Plateau have been identified as the world's oldest continuous alpine ecosystem with a community of 3000 plant species, some of them continuously co-existing for 30 million years.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Stokstad|first=Erik|date=2020-07-30|title=Many beloved garden flowers originated in this mountain hot spot—the oldest of its kind on Earth|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/many-beloved-garden-flowers-originated-mountain-hot-spot-oldest-its-kind-earth|access-date=2020-08-01|website=Science {{!}} AAAS|language=en}}</ref>

Climates with biotemperatures below {{convert|1.5|C|F|0}} tend to consist purely of rock and ice.<ref name=lugo/>
{{clear left}}

==Montane forests==
[[File:Overlooking Waimea Canyon.jpg|thumb|[[Waimea Canyon]], Hawaii, is known for its montane [[vegetation]]]]
Montane forests occur between the [[submontane zone]] and the [[subalpine zone]]. The elevation at which one habitat changes to another varies across the globe, particularly by [[latitude]]. The upper limit of montane forests, the [[tree line]], is often marked by a change to hardier species that occur in less dense stands.<ref name=Price/> For example, in the [[Sierra Nevada]] of [[California]], the montane forest has dense stands of [[lodgepole pine]] and [[red fir]], while the [[Sierra Nevada subalpine zone]] contains sparse stands of [[whitebark pine]].<ref name="Rundel">{{Cite book|last=Rundel|first=P.W.|author2=D. J. Parsons |author3=D. T. Gordon |year=1977|contribution=Montane and subalpine vegetation of the Sierra Nevada and Cascade Ranges|pages=559–599|editor1-first=M.G.|editor1-last=[[Michael G. Barbour|Barbour]]|editor2-first=J.|editor2-last=Major|title=Terrestrial vegetation of California|publisher=Wiley|place=New York, USA}}</ref>

The lower bound of the montane zone may be a "lower timberline" that separates the montane forest from drier [[steppe]] or [[desert]] region.<ref name=Price>{{cite book | last = Price | first = Larry W. | year = 1986 | title = Mountains and Man: A Study of Process and Environment | publisher = University of California Press | page = [https://archive.org/details/mountainsmanstud00pric/page/271 271] | url = https://archive.org/details/mountainsmanstud00pric | url-access = registration | access-date = 2012-03-09 | isbn = 978-0-520-05886-6}}</ref>

Montane forests differ from lowland forests in the same area.<ref name=Nagy>{{cite book|title=The biology of alpine habitats|first1=László|last1=Nagy|first2=Georg|last2=Grabherr|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2009}}</ref> The climate of montane forests is colder than lowland climate at the same latitude, so the montane forests often have species typical of higher-latitude lowland forests.<ref>{{cite book | last = Perry | first = David A. | year = 1994 | title = Forest Ecosystems | publisher = JHU Press | isbn = 0-8018-4987-X | page = [https://archive.org/details/forestecosystems00perr/page/49 49] | url = https://archive.org/details/forestecosystems00perr | url-access = registration | access-date = 2012-03-09}}</ref>  Humans can disturb montane forests through [[forestry]] and [[agriculture]].<ref name=Nagy/> On isolated mountains, montane forests surrounded by treeless dry regions are typical "[[sky island]]" ecosystems.<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Albert | first1 = James S. | last2 = Reis | first2 = Roberto E. | year = 2011 | title = Historical Biogeography of Neotropical Freshwater Fishes | publisher = University of California Press | isbn = 978-0-520-26868-5 | page = 311 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=_Suu7a-ERdMC&pg=PA311 | access-date = 2012-03-09}}</ref>

=== Temperate climate ===
Montane forests in temperate climate are typically one of [[temperate coniferous forest]] or [[temperate broadleaf and mixed forest]], forest types that are well known from [[Europe]] and northeastern [[North America]]. Montane forests outside Europe tend to be more species-rich, because Europe during the Pleistocene offered smaller-area refugia from the glaciers.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Species-Richness in North-Temperate Zone Forests|first=Brian|last=Huntley|journal=Journal of Biogeography|volume=20|number=2|year=1993|pages=163–180|doi=10.2307/2845669|jstor=2845669 |bibcode=1993JBiog..20..163H |url=https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/output/1566936 }}</ref>
[[File:Herbst am Watzmann.jpg|thumb|left|Temperate montane forest in [[Bavaria]], [[Germany]]]]

Montane forests in temperate climate occur in Europe (the [[Alps]], [[Carpathians]], and [[Rhodope Mountains|more]]),<ref>{{cite web
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060215140935/http://www.panda.org/about_wwf/where_we_work/ecoregions/europeanmed_montane_forests.cfm
|url=http://www.panda.org/about_wwf/where_we_work/ecoregions/europeanmed_montane_forests.cfm|archive-date=2006-02-15|title=European-Mediterranean Montane Mixed Forests|publisher=[[World Wildlife Fund]]}}</ref> in [[North America]] (e.g. [[Appalachians]], [[Rocky Mountains]], [[Cascade Range]], and [[Sierra Nevada]]),<ref>{{cite book|last=Billings|first=WD|year=1990|chapter=The Mountain Forests of North America and Their Environments|title=Plant Biology of the Basin and Range|series=Ecological Studies|volume=80|pages=47–86 |publisher=Springer|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-74799-1_3|isbn=978-3-642-74801-1 }}</ref> [[South America]],<ref>{{cite journal|first1=L|last1=Nagy|display-authors=et al|year=2023|title=South American mountain ecosystems and global change – a case study for integrating theory and field observations for land surface modelling and ecosystem management|journal=Plant Ecology & Diversity|volume=16 |issue=1–2 |pages=1–27 |doi=10.1080/17550874.2023.2196966|bibcode=2023PlEcD..16....1N |doi-access=free|hdl=11336/251431|hdl-access=free}}</ref> [[New Zealand]],<ref>{{cite book|title=Forest Vines to Snow Tussocks: The Story of New Zealand Plants|first=John|last=Dawson|publisher=Victoria University Press|location=Wellington|url=https://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-DawFore-t1-body-d11-d3-d3.html}}</ref> and the [[Himalayas]].

[[Climate change]] is predicted to affect temperate montane forests. For example, in the [[Pacific Northwest]] of North America, climate change may cause "potential reduced snowpack, higher levels of evapotranspiration and increased summer drought" which will negatively affect montane wetlands.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=Se-Yeun|last2=Ryan|first2=Maureen E.|last3=Hamlet|first3=Alan F.|last4=Palen|first4=Wendy J.|last5=Lawler|first5=Joshua J.|last6=Halabisky|first6=Meghan|date=2015-09-02|title=Projecting the Hydrologic Impacts of Climate Change on Montane Wetlands|journal=PLOS ONE|language=en|volume=10|issue=9|article-number=e0136385|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0136385|issn=1932-6203|pmc=4557981|pmid=26331850|bibcode=2015PLoSO..1036385L|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Mediterranean climate ===
[[File:Chase khar - چاسه خار (3).jpg|thumb|right|Iranian oak scrub in the [[Zagros Mountains]]]]
Montane forests in [[Mediterranean climate]] are warm and dry except in winter, when they are relatively wet and mild. Montane forests located in Mediterranean climates, known as oro-Mediterranean, exhibit towering trees alongside high biomass.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Anne E|last1=Kelly|first2=Michael L|last2=Goulden|title=A montane Mediterranean climate supports year-round photosynthesis and high forest biomass|journal=Tree Physiology|volume=36|issue=4|date=April 2016|pages=459–468|doi=10.1093/treephys/tpv131|pmid=26764269|doi-access=free}}</ref> These forests are typically mixed conifer and broadleaf forests, with only a few conifer species. [[Pine]] and [[juniper]] are typical trees found in Mediterranean montane forests. The broadleaf trees show more variety and are often evergreen, e.g. [[evergreen oak]].{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

This type of forest is found in the [[Mediterranean Basin]], [[North Africa]], [[Mexico]] and the [[southwestern US]], [[Iran]], [[Pakistan]] and [[Afghanistan]].{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}
{{clear left}}

=== Subtropical and tropical climate ===
{{Main|Tropical montane cloud forest}}
[[File:Forest on Gunung Batu Brinchang, Malaysia.jpg|thumb|right|Tropical montane forest at around 2,000&nbsp;m in [[Malaysia]]]]

In the tropics, montane forests can consist of [[tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests|broadleaf forest]] in addition to [[tropical coniferous forest|coniferous forest]]. One example of a tropical montane forest is a [[cloud forest]], which gains its moisture from clouds and fog.<ref>{{Citation | author1=Tracey, J. G. (John Geoffrey) | author-link=Geoff Tracey | title= The Vegetation of the Humid Tropical Region of North Queensland | publication-date=1982 | pages=34–38| url= https://trove.nla.gov.au/work/23224781?q&versionId=45832425}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last = Mulligan | first = M. | title = Tropical Montane Cloud Forests: Science for Conservation and Management | editor = Bruijnzeel, L. A. |editor2=Scatena, F. N. |editor3=Hamilton, L. S. | year = 2011 | chapter = Modeling the Tropics-Wide Extent and Distribution of Cloud Forest and Cloud Forest Loss, with Implications for Conservation Priority | publisher = Cambridge University Press | isbn = 978-0-521-76035-5 | pages = 15–38 | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=N6FkwMnSX8EC&pg=PA15 | access-date = 2012-03-09}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=A Physiognomic Classification of Australian Rain Forests|first1=Len|last1=Webb| author-link=Leonard Webb (academic) | journal = Journal of Ecology| publisher=British Ecological Society : Journal of Ecology Vol. 47, No. 3, pp. 551–570|date=1 Oct 1959|volume = 47|issue = 3|pages = 551–570|doi = 10.2307/2257290|jstor = 2257290|bibcode=1959JEcol..47..551W }}</ref> Cloud forests often exhibit an abundance of [[moss]]es covering the ground and vegetation, in which case they are also referred to as mossy forests. Mossy forests usually develop on the [[Saddle (landform)|saddles]] of mountains, where moisture introduced by settling clouds is more effectively retained.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clarke|first=C.M.|year=1997|title=[[Nepenthes of Borneo]]|publisher=Natural History Publications (Borneo)|location=Kota Kinabalu|page=29}}</ref> Depending on latitude, the lower limit of montane rainforests on large mountains is generally between {{convert|1500|and|2500|m|ft}} while the upper limit is usually from {{convert|2400|to|3300|m|ft}}.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bruijnzee|first1=L.A.|first2=E. J.|last2=Veneklaas|title=Climatic Conditions and Tropical Montane Forest Productivity: The Fog Has Not Lifted Yet|journal=Ecology|volume=79|number=1|year=1998|page=3|doi=10.2307/176859|jstor=176859}}</ref>

Tropical montane forests might exhibit high sensitivity to climate change.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Loope|first1=Lloyd L.|chapter=Vulnerability of Island Tropical Montane Cloud Forests to Climate Change, with Special Reference to East Maui, Hawaii|date=1998|title=Potential Impacts of Climate Change on Tropical Forest Ecosystems|pages=363–377|editor-last=Markham|editor-first=Adam|place=Dordrecht|publisher=Springer Netherlands|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-94-017-2730-3_18|isbn=978-94-017-2730-3|last2=Giambelluca|first2=Thomas W.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sukumar |first1=R. |last2=Suresh |first2=H. S. |last3=Ramesh |first3=R. |date=1995 |title=Climate Change and Its Impact on Tropical Montane Ecosystems in Southern India |journal=Journal of Biogeography |volume=22 |issue=2/3 |pages=533–536 |doi=10.2307/2845951 |jstor=2845951 |bibcode=1995JBiog..22..533S |issn=0305-0270}}</ref> Climate change may cause variation in temperature, precipitation and humidity, which will cause stress on tropical montane forests. The predicted upcoming impacts of climate change might significantly affect [[biodiversity loss]] and might result in change of species range and community dynamics. [[Global climate model]]s predict reduced cloudiness in the future. Reduction in cloudiness may already be affecting the [[Monteverde Cloud Forest Reserve|Monteverde cloud forest]] in [[Costa Rica]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Karmalkar|first1=A. V.|last2=Bradley|first2=R. S.|last3=Diaz|first3=H. F.|date=2008|title=Climate change scenario for Costa Rican montane forests|journal=Geophysical Research Letters|language=en|volume=35|issue=11|pages=L11702|doi=10.1029/2008GL033940|bibcode=2008GeoRL..3511702K|issn=1944-8007|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Foster|first=Pru|date=2001-10-01|title=The potential negative impacts of global climate change on tropical montane cloud forests|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012825201000563|journal=Earth-Science Reviews|language=en|volume=55|issue=1|pages=73–106|doi=10.1016/S0012-8252(01)00056-3|bibcode=2001ESRv...55...73F|issn=0012-8252|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Subalpine zone==
The subalpine zone is the [[biotic zone]] immediately below the [[tree line]] around the world. In tropical regions of [[Southeast Asia]] the tree line may be above {{convert|4000|m|ft|abbr=on}},<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Blasco |first1=F. |last2=Whitmore |first2=T.C. |last3=Gers |first3=C. |year=2000 |title=A framework for the worldwide comparison of tropical woody vegetation types |journal=Biological Conservation |volume=95 |issue=2 |pages=175–189 |url=http://www.ecolab.ups-tlse.fr/IMG/pdf/BC_Blasco_et_al.2000.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120323203546/http://www.ecolab.ups-tlse.fr/IMG/pdf/BC_Blasco_et_al.2000.pdf |archive-date=2012-03-23 |access-date=2012-03-11 |doi=10.1016/S0006-3207(00)00032-X |bibcode=2000BCons..95..175B }} p. 178.</ref> whereas in Scotland it may be as low as {{convert|450|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Grace |first1=John |last2=Berninger |first2=Frank |last3=Nagy |first3=Laszlo |year=2002 |title=Impacts of Climate Change on the Tree Line |journal=Annals of Botany |volume=90 |issue=4 |pages=537–544 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcf222 |pmid=12324278 |pmc=4240388 }} fig. 1.</ref> Species that occur in this zone depend on the location of the zone on the Earth; for example, ''[[Pinus mugo]]'' (scrub mountain pine) occurs in [[Europe]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.conifers.org/pi/Pinus_mugo.php|title=Pinus mugo|work=Gymnosperm Database|access-date=2024-02-05}}</ref> the [[snow gum]] is found in Australia,<ref>{{cite book|title=Australian Soils and Landscapes|first=Neil|last=McKenzie|year=2004|page=98}}</ref> and the [[subalpine larch]], [[mountain hemlock]], and [[subalpine fir]] occur in western North America.<ref name="wgold">{{Cite web |url=http://faculty.washington.edu/wgold/bis358/012808.pdf |title=BIS258 lecture notes |last=Gold |first=W. |date=2008-01-28 |publisher=University of Washington |access-date=2009-03-15}}</ref>
[[Image:Abies lasiocarpa 7458.jpg|thumb|left|upright|[[Subalpine fir]] in [[Mount Rainier National Park]], Washington, United States]]

Trees in the subalpine zone often become [[krummholz]], that is, crooked wood, stunted and twisted in form. At tree line, tree seedlings may germinate on the [[lee side]] of rocks and grow only as high as the rock provides wind protection. Further growth is more horizontal than vertical, and additional rooting may occur where branches contact the soil. Snow cover may protect krummholz trees during the winter, but branches higher than wind-shelters or snow cover are usually destroyed. Well-established krummholz trees may be several hundred to a thousand years old.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nps.gov/romo/learn/nature/subalpine_ecosystem.htm|title=Subalpine ecosystem|work=Rocky Mountain National Park|publisher=U.S. National Park Service}}</ref>

[[Montane grasslands and shrublands|Meadows]] may be found in the subalpine zone. [[Tuolumne Meadows]] in the [[Sierra Nevada]] of [[California]], is an example of a subalpine meadow.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/tm.htm|title=Tuolumne Meadows and Tioga Road|work=Yosemite National Park|publisher=US National Park Service|access-date=2024-02-05}}</ref>

Example subalpine zones around the world include the [[French Prealps]] in Europe, the [[Sierra Nevada subalpine zone|Sierra Nevada]] and [[Rocky Mountains subalpine zone|Rocky Mountain]] subalpine zones in North America, and subalpine forests in the [[Eastern Himalayan subalpine conifer forests|eastern Himalaya]], [[Western Himalayan subalpine conifer forests|western Himalaya]], and [[Hengduan Mountains subalpine conifer forests|Hengduan mountains]] of Asia.

==Alpine grasslands and tundra==
{{main|Alpine tundra|Alpine plant}}

[[File:The Triplets from Sahale Arm.jpg|right|thumb|Alpine flora near [[Cascade Pass]]]]

Alpine grasslands and tundra lie above the tree line, in a world of intense radiation, wind, cold, snow, and ice. As a consequence, alpine vegetation is close to the ground and consists mainly of [[perennial grass]]es, [[sedges]], and [[forb]]s. Annual plants are rare in this ecosystem and usually are only a few inches tall, with weak root systems.<ref name=blm>{{Include-USGov|agency=Bureau of Land Management|url=http://www.blm.gov/wildlife/plan/WY/Alpine%20Tundra%20Grassland.pdf|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080724070058/http://www.blm.gov/wildlife/plan/WY/Alpine%20Tundra%20Grassland.pdf|archivedate=2008-07-24|article=Grassland Habitat Group}}</ref> Other common [[plant life-form]]s include [[prostrate shrub]]s; [[tussock (grass)|tussock]]-forming [[graminoid]]s; and [[cryptogam]]s, such as [[bryophytes]] and [[lichens]].<ref name=functional/>{{rp|280}}

Plants have adapted to the harsh alpine environment. [[Cushion plant]]s, looking like ground-hugging clumps of moss, escape the strong winds blowing a few inches above them. Many flowering plants of the alpine tundra have dense hairs on stems and leaves to provide wind protection or [[anthocyanin|red-colored pigments]] capable of converting the sun's light rays into heat. Some plants take two or more years to form flower buds, which survive the winter below the surface and then open and produce fruit with seeds in the few weeks of summer.<ref name=rockymtn>{{NPS|url=http://www.nps.gov/romo/naturescience/alpine_tundra_ecosystem.htm|work=Rocky Mountain National Park|title=Alpine Tundra Ecosystem}}</ref> Non-flowering [[lichen]]s cling to rocks and soil. Their enclosed [[algae|algal cells]] can [[photosynthesize]] at temperatures as low as {{convert|-10|C|F}},<ref>{{cite conference|title=Plant Activity under Snow and Ice, with Particular Reference to Lichens|first=Ludger|last=Kappen|journal=Arctic|volume=46|number=4|conference=Circumpolar Ecosystems in Winter II|year=1993|pages=297–302|jstor=40511430}}</ref>  and the outer fungal layers can absorb more than their own weight in water.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://files.dnr.state.mn.us/mcvmagazine/young_naturalists/young-naturalists-article/lichens/lichens.pdf|title=Lichens: two lives in one|first=Todd|last=Whitesel|magazine=Minnesota Conservation Volunteer|year=2006}}</ref>
[[Image:GlarusAlps.jpg|thumb|left|An alpine [[Bog|mire]] in the [[Swiss Alps]]]]

The adaptations for survival of drying winds and cold may make tundra vegetation seem very hardy, but in some respects the tundra is very fragile. Repeated footsteps often destroy tundra plants, leaving exposed soil to blow away, and recovery may take hundreds of years.<ref name=rockymtn/>

Alpine meadows form where sediments from the weathering of rocks has produced soils well-developed enough to support grasses and sedges. Alpine grasslands are common enough around the world to be categorized as a [[biome]] by the [[World Wildlife Fund]]. The biome, called "[[Montane grasslands and shrublands]]", often evolved as virtual islands, separated from other montane regions by warmer, lower elevation regions, and are frequently home to many distinctive and [[endemic]] plants which evolved in response to the cool, wet [[climate]] and abundant sunlight.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}
[[File:Мальовишки дял, Рила 15.JPG|thumb|Alpine landscape below [[Malyovitsa]] Peak, [[Rila]] Mountain, [[Bulgaria]]]]

The most extensive montane grasslands and shrublands occur in the [[Neotropical]] [[páramo]] of the [[Andes Mountains]]. This biome also occurs in the mountains of [[eastern Africa|east]] and [[central Africa]], [[Mount Kinabalu]] of [[Borneo]], the highest elevations of the [[Western Ghats]] in South India and the Central Highlands of [[New Guinea]]. A unique feature of many wet tropical montane regions is the presence of giant rosette plants from a variety of plant families, such as ''[[Lobelia]]'' ([[Afrotropic]]), ''[[Puya (genus)|Puya]]'' ([[Neotropic]]), ''[[Cyathea]]'' (New Guinea), and ''[[Argyroxiphium]]'' ([[Hawaii]]).{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

Where conditions are drier, one finds montane grasslands, [[savanna]]s, and [[woodland]]s, like the [[Ethiopian Highlands]], and montane [[steppe]]s, like the steppes of the [[Tibetan Plateau]].{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Old-growth forest
======================================================================

{{Short description|Forest that has developed over a long period of time without disturbance}}
{{Redirect|Old growth|the Dead Meadow album|Old Growth (album)}}
{{Redirect|Virgin forest}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2022}}
[[File:Biogradska suma.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|Old-growth [[European beech]] forest in [[Biogradska Gora National Park]], Montenegro]]
An '''old-growth forest'''{{Efn|name=aka}} is a [[forest]] that has developed over a long period of time without [[Disturbance (ecology)|disturbance]]. Due to this, old-growth forests exhibit unique ecological features.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.srs.fs.usda.gov/pubs/ja/ja_white002.pdf |title=Defining Old Growth: Implications For Management |last1=White |first1=David |last2=Lloyd |first2=Thomas |journal=Paper Presented at the Eighth Biennial Southern Silvicultural Research Conference, Auburn, al, Nov. L-3, 1994 |year=1994 |access-date=23 November 2009 |location=Eighth Biennial Southern Silvicultural Research Conference}}</ref> The [[Food and Agriculture Organization]] of the [[United Nations]] defines primary forests as naturally regenerated forests of native tree species where there are no clearly visible indications of human activity and the ecological processes are not significantly disturbed. One-third (34%) of the world's forests are primary forests.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://doi.org/10.4060/ca8985en|title=The State of the World's Forests 2020. In brief – Forests, biodiversity and people|publisher=FAO|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132707-4|location=Rome|pages=9|doi=10.4060/ca8985en|s2cid=241416114}}</ref> Old-growth features include diverse tree-related structures that provide diverse wildlife [[habitats]] that increases the [[biodiversity]] of the forested [[ecosystem]].  Virgin or first-growth forests are old-growth forests that have never been logged. The concept of diverse tree structure includes multi-layered canopies and [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] gaps, greatly varying tree heights and diameters, and diverse tree species and classes and sizes of woody debris.[[File:CSIRO ScienceImage 541 Cool Temperate Rainforest Tasmania.jpg|thumb|upright|Cool [[temperate rainforest]] in [[Tasmania]], Australia]] {{as of|2025}}, the world has 11.3 million square kilometers (4.4 million square miles) of primary forest remaining. Brazil, Canada, and Russia have 62% of the world's primary forest. The net area of primary forest has decreased by 1.1 million square kilometers (~424,000 square miles) since 1990, but the rate of loss more than halved in 2010–2020 compared with the previous decade.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 – Key findings|publisher=FAO|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132581-0|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/ca8753en|s2cid=130116768}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book[titled=Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025 – Key findings|publisher=FAO|year=2025|year=978-92-5-140082-1|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/cd6709en}}</ref>

Old-growth forests are valuable for economic reasons and for the [[ecosystem services]] they provide.<ref name="maloof">{{Cite book |last=Maloof |first=Joan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MKiTEAAAQBAJ |title=Nature's Temples: A Natural History of Old-Growth Forests. Princeton University Press |date=4 April 2023 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0-691-23050-4 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Wirth|first1=Christian|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7yF89GGxNmgC&q=old+growth+forest|title=Old-Growth Forests: Function, Fate and Value|last2=Gleixner|first2=Gerd|last3=Heimann|first3=Martin|date=7 July 2009|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-540-92706-8|language=en}}</ref> This can be a point of contention when some in the [[logging industry]] desire to harvest valuable timber from the forests, destroying the forests in the process, to generate short-term profits, while environmentalists seek to preserve the forests in their pristine state for benefits such as [[water purification]], [[flood control]], weather stability, maintenance of biodiversity, and [[nutrient cycling]]. Moreover, old-growth forests are more efficient at [[sequestering carbon]] than newly planted forests and fast-growing [[timber plantations]], thus preserving these forests is vital to [[climate change mitigation]].<ref name="mcgarvey" /><ref name="metz" />

== Characteristics ==
<!-- {{globalize|date=July 2015}}-->
[[File:The Beech Forest.jpg|left|thumb|upright=1.2|[[Nothofagus moorei|Antarctic beech]] old growth in [[Lamington National Park]], Queensland, Australia]]

Old-growth forests tend to have large trees and standing dead trees, multilayered canopies with gaps that result from the deaths of individual trees, and [[coarse woody debris]] on the forest floor.<ref name="naturallywood.com">{{Cite web |url=http://naturallywood.com/uploadedFiles/General/Sustainable_Forests/BC_Forest_Diversity.pdf |title=Naturally: wood British Columbia's Forest Diversity |access-date=25 April 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200408073234/https://www.naturallywood.com/uploadedFiles/General/Sustainable_Forests/BC_Forest_Diversity.pdf |archive-date=8 April 2020 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The trees of old-growth forests develop distinctive attributes not seen in younger trees, such as more complex structures and deeply fissured bark that can harbor rare lichens and mosses.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bolgiano |first1=Chris |title=The Appalachian forest: a search for roots and renewal |date=1998 |publisher=Stackpole Books |location=Mechanicsburg, PA |isbn=0-8117-0126-3 |page=23}}</ref>

A forest regenerated after a severe disturbance, such as wildfire, insect infestation, or harvesting, is often called [[Second growth forest|second-growth]] or 'regeneration' until enough time passes for the effects of the disturbance to be no longer evident. Depending on the forest, this may take from a century to several millennia. [[Hardwood]] forests of the eastern United States can develop old-growth characteristics in 150–500 years. In [[British Columbia]], Canada, old growth is defined as 120 to 140 years of age in the interior of the province where fire is a frequent and natural occurrence. In British Columbia's coastal [[rainforest]]s, old growth is defined as trees more than 250 years, with some trees reaching more than 1,000 years of age.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.llbc.leg.bc.ca/public/pubdocs/bcdocs/360393/old_growth.pdf|title=BC Ministry of Forests 2003 Old Growth Forests}}</ref> In Australia, [[Eucalyptus regnans|eucalypt trees]] rarely exceed 350 years of age due to frequent fire disturbance.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ksymh8ocS5QC&q=Eucalypt+Ecology:+Individuals+to+Ecosystems&pg=PR9|title=Eucalypt Ecology|isbn=9780521497404|last1=Williams|first1=Jann|last2=Woinarski|first2=John|date=13 November 1997|publisher=Cambridge University Press }}</ref>

Forest types have very different development patterns, natural disturbances and appearances. A [[Douglas-fir]] [[Forest stand|stand]] may grow for centuries without disturbance while an old-growth [[ponderosa pine]] forest requires frequent surface fires to reduce the shade-tolerant species and regenerate the canopy species.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hilbert |first1=Jaime |last2=Wiensczyk |first2=Alan |date=2007 |title=Old-growth definitions and management: A literature review |url=http://www.forrex.org/jem/ISS39/vol8_no1_art2.pdf |url-status=dead |journal=BC Journal of Ecosystems and Management |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=15&ndash;31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111003053908/http://www.forrex.org/jem/ISS39/vol8_no1_art2.pdf |archive-date=3 October 2011 |access-date=25 April 2011}}</ref> In the [[boreal forest of Canada]], catastrophic disturbances like wildfires minimize opportunities for major accumulations of dead and downed woody material and other structural legacies associated with old growth conditions.<ref name="Ontario.ca">{{cite web|url=http://www.mnr.gov.on.ca/stdprodconsume/groups/lr/@mnr/@forests/documents/document/mnr_e000252.pdf|title=Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry|work=Ontario.ca |date=8 June 2016 }}</ref> Typical characteristics of old-growth forest include the presence of older trees, minimal signs of human disturbance, mixed-age stands, presence of [[canopy (biology)|canopy]] openings due to tree falls, [[pit-and-mound topography]], down wood in various stages of decay, standing snags (dead trees), multilayered canopies, intact [[soil]]s, a healthy [[fungus|fungal]] ecosystem, and presence of indicator species.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Catanzaro |first1=Paul |url=https://www.umass.edu/arboretum/sites/default/files/2024-04/Restoring-Old-Growth-Characteristics.pdf?1761170156 |title=Restoring old-growth characteristics to New England's and New York's forests |last2=D'Amato |first2=Anthony |page=8 |publisher=[[Vermont Land Trust]]}}</ref>

=== Biodiversity ===
[[File:Northern Spotted Owl.USFWS.jpg|thumb|upright|The [[northern spotted owl]] primarily inhabits old-growth forests in the northern part of its range (Canada to southern [[Oregon]]) and landscapes with a mix of old and younger forest types in the southern part of its range (the [[Klamath Basin|Klamath region]] and California).]]

Old-growth forests are often [[biologically diverse]], and home to many [[rare species]], [[threatened species]], and [[endangered species]] of plants and animals, such as the [[northern spotted owl]], [[marbled murrelet]] and [[Fisher (animal)|fisher]], making them [[ecology|ecologically]] significant. Levels of biodiversity may be higher or lower in old-growth forests compared to second-growth forests, depending on specific circumstances, environmental variables, and geographic variables. Logging in old-growth forests is a contentious issue in many parts of the world. Excessive logging reduces biodiversity, affecting not only the old-growth forest itself, but also indigenous species that rely upon old-growth forest habitat.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ran.org/category/forests/|title=Forests Archives|website=Rainforest Action Network}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/interactive/2007/dec/13/forests|title=The world's remaining great forests|first=Jessica |last=Aldred|website=[[The Guardian]] |date=13 December 2007}}</ref>

Studies in British Columbia's cedar-hemlock forests have shown that certain [[lichen]] species, particularly [[cyanolichen]]s, are almost exclusively found in old-growth forests, being absent from even-aged stands (where all trees grew after a single disturbance event) of the same age (120–140 years). This suggests that true old-growth characteristics, like diverse forest structure and [[microclimate]] conditions, are necessary for some specialist species beyond just forest age.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Radies |first1=David N. |last2=Coxson |first2=Darwyn S. |title=Macrolichen colonization on 120–140 year old ''Tsuga heterophylla'' in wet temperate rainforests of central-interior British Columbia: a comparison of lichen response to even-aged versus old-growth stand structures |journal=The Lichenologist |volume=36 |issue=3–4 |year=2004 |doi=10.1017/S0024282904014227 |pages=235–247|bibcode=2004ThLic..36..235R }}</ref>

[[Inland temperate rainforest]]s of British Columbia illustrate how old-growth structure can shape entire [[food web]]s. Deep winter [[snowpack]]s lift woodland caribou into the lower tree canopy, where their survival depends on heavy accumulations of [[fruticose lichen|fruticose]] "hair" lichens such as ''[[Bryoria]]'' and ''[[Alectoria (fungus)|Alectoria]]''. These lichens reach stand-level "hyperabundance" only in forests older than about 120–150 years, where long-lived canopy architecture and stable microclimates allow sustained growth. Industrial logging and short-rotation [[silviculture]] fail to reproduce these conditions, so the old-growth canopy itself functions as a keystone habitat, underpinning both specialist lichens and the endangered deep-snow mountain caribou that rely on them.<ref name="Goward et al. 2024">{{cite journal |last1=Goward |first1=Trevor |last2=Coxson |first2=Darwyn |last3=Gauslaa |first3=Yngvar |title=The Manna Effect – a review of factors influencing hair lichen abundance for Canada's endangered Deep-Snow Mountain Caribou (''Rangifer arcticus montanus'') |journal=The Lichenologist |volume=56 |issue=4 |year=2024 |doi=10.1017/S0024282924000161 |pages=121–135 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2024ThLic..56..121G }}</ref>

=== Mixed age ===

{{unreferenced section|date=December 2022}}
Some forests in the old-growth stage have a mix of tree ages, due to a distinct [[Regeneration (biology)|regeneration]] pattern for this stage. New trees regenerate at different times from each other, because each of them has a different spatial location relative to the main canopy, hence each one receives a different amount of light. The mixed age of the forest is an important criterion in ensuring that the forest is a relatively stable ecosystem in the long term. A [[climax community|climax]] stand that is uniformly aged becomes [[senescence|senescent]] and degrades within a relatively short time to result in a new cycle of forest [[ecological succession|succession]]. Thus, uniformly aged stands are less stable ecosystems. Boreal forests are more uniformly aged, as they are normally subject to frequent stand-replacing wildfires.

=== Canopy openings ===
[[Forest canopy]] gaps are essential in creating and maintaining mixed-age stands.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Neff |first=Chris |date=2021-11-18 |title=What does 'Old-Growth' really mean? It depends. (Installment 1 of 6) |url=https://njaudubon.org/what-does-old-growth-really-mean-it-depends-installment-1-of-6/#:~:text=Instead,%20old%20growth%20forests%20contain,in%20upcoming%20posts%20%E2%80%93%20stay%20tuned!&text=References:,Long%20Grove,%20Illinois,%202019.&text=Oliver,%20C.%20D.,%20and%20Larson,,11%20pp. |access-date=2024-09-12 |website=New Jersey Audubon |language=en-US}}</ref> Also, some [[herbaceous plant]]s only become established in canopy openings, but persist beneath an understory. Openings are a result of tree death due to small impact disturbances such as wind, low-intensity fires, and tree diseases.<ref name=":1" />

Old-growth forests are unique, usually having multiple horizontal layers of vegetation representing a variety of tree [[species]], age classes, and sizes, as well as "pit and mound" soil shape with well-established [[fungus|fungal nets]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Stamets |first=Paul |author-link=Paul Stamets |url=https://archive.org/details/myceliumrunningh00stam_0/page/35 |title=Mycelium Running |publisher=Ten Speed Press |year=2005 |isbn=978-1-58008-579-3 |pages=35 |url-access=registration}}</ref> As old-growth forest is structurally diverse, it provides higher-diversity habitat than forests in other stages. Thus, sometimes higher biological diversity can be sustained in old-growth forests, or at least a biodiversity that is different from other forest stages.<ref name=":0" />

=== Topography ===
[[File:Shennongjia virgin forest.jpg|thumb|Virgin forest about {{Convert|2500|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level in [[Shennongjia Forestry District]], Hubei<!-- DO NOT LINK, see [[MOS:GEOLINK]] for further guidance -->, China<!-- DO NOT LINK, see [[MOS:GEOLINK]] for further guidance -->]]The characteristic [[topography]] of much old-growth forest consists of pits and mounds. Mounds are caused by decaying fallen trees, and pits ([[tree throw]]s) by the roots pulled out of the ground when trees fall due to natural causes, including being pushed over by animals. Pits expose [[humus]]-poor, mineral-rich soil and often collect moisture and fallen leaves, forming a thick [[organic material|organic]] layer that is able to nurture certain types of organisms. Mounds provide a place free of leaf inundation and saturation, where other types of organisms thrive.<ref name="maloof" />

=== Standing snags ===
Standing [[snag (ecology)|snags]] provide food sources and habitat for many types of organisms. In particular, many species of dead-wood predators, such as [[woodpecker]]s, must have standing snags available for feeding. In North America, the [[spotted owl]] is well known for needing standing snags for nesting habitat.<ref name="maloof" />

=== Decaying ground layer ===
[[File:Hawkwoods1.jpg|thumb|Downed wood replenishes [[topsoil]] as it decays]]
[[File:2005-09 Białowieski Park Narodowy 12.jpg|thumb|upright|Fungus ''[[Climacocystis borealis]]'' on a tree stump in the [[Białowieża Forest]], one of the last largely intact primeval forests in Central Europe]]

Fallen timber, or coarse woody debris, contributes [[carbon]]-rich [[organic matter]] directly to the soil, providing a substrate for [[moss]]es, fungi, and [[seedling]]s, and creating microhabitats by creating relief on the forest floor. In some ecosystems such as the [[temperate rain forest]] of the North American [[Pacific Northwest|Pacific coast]], fallen timber may become [[nurse log]]s, providing a substrate for seedling trees.<ref name="maloof" />

=== Soil ===
Intact soils harbor many life forms that rely on them. Intact soils generally have very well-defined horizons, or [[soil profile]]s. Different organisms may need certain well-defined soil horizons to live, while many trees need well-structured soils free of disturbance to thrive. Some herbaceous plants in northern hardwood forests must have thick duff layers (which are part of the soil profile). Fungal ecosystems are essential for efficient ''[[in-situ]]'' recycling of nutrients back into the entire ecosystem.<ref name="maloof" />

== Definitions ==

=== Ecological definitions ===

==== Stand age definition ====
[[Forest stand|Stand]] age can also be used to categorize a forest as old-growth.<ref>Provincial Non-Spatial Old Growth Order. 2004. Integrated Land Management Bureau, British Columbia, Canada</ref> For any given geographical area, it is possible to determine the average time from disturbance until a forest reaches the old growth stage. This makes it possible to determine [[Forest dynamics#Succession|forest stage]].{{citation needed|date=February 2026}} The drawback of using this method to determine whether forests qualify as old-growth is that it does not account for forest characteristics, meaning that forests with old-growth attributes may be excluded due to being too young while forests without old-growth characteristics may be included solely because they are old.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Dengsheng |last2=Mausel |first2=Paul |last3=Brondizio |first3=Eduardo |last4=Moran |first4=Emilio |date=December 10, 2002 |title=Classification of successful forest stages in the Brazilian Amazon basin |url=https://pdf.sciencedirectassets.com/271259/1-s2.0-S0378112700X03040/1-s2.0-S0378112703000033/main.pdf?X-Amz-Security-Token=IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjELb%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2F%2FwEaCXVzLWVhc3QtMSJHMEUCIQD7OK%2BYdZv22cQWyfNHHMqiGlIrPG8gZFn7dKRf3EJgvAIgFOMdEdDA3Pz42CTHKn66ATwaCgGwQXGIsl6dszU4nOYqsgUIfhAFGgwwNTkwMDM1NDY4NjUiDBhiQNUiVzrE6UPa2yqPBVOncURWS6y7fVQR877aYu%2FpzSBUu5t6EnZJjpsz1GdnLQ0oXhTYUiLZLTgyxRRXrPWfGlQRLjbLi63IHo8%2FiaBL9DV83lUVyWZzNQwCEDK3YcZ4gZtEnDZqVz9iVoYHMBde6CNuaGnM3ubadLIlanpXytEPiqBBNK1%2F0tYHv0jpafRXPgNK3wud85wYmRsw6QQC9DAUjx88ugWNYiTy9RW2kuYOkFgQDUFTNQDl7eqVShUOcavnklfLOalSkeAQI8701zhPY%2BfjwLd%2BoENXAi8reYhyExQphb7uFJFtKRiCNcGEys4wrkiJH1YicKeZ5KudZslDh1e0kgstpViTRzm6SxJvKzEnNdqHMbIeQHgY2wVA9fnNlZWc61ltTQpfD0U7OPlO9Dpd%2FvJeVKt%2FqOTpnnyszkVcBGl8LEKmqRC1aBSORD8I2AjvofVweEs35oaeNH2AANF4gnJ613NEPWkCc6RQl6vYSR0PLizWibBZhlLGXhQMFRH5dbMrpj%2FD8BYaSocSIah%2FOwSZmKBwhvhz%2FoHMCJ1zI3%2FF5%2FwNctmF%2BFyKG7pffwQzhEJFe%2FLDgP8s7UT5wl1lR0UEdPsVyIKGT1bVd6Y7vr4xJK36C31aPVpktlpRV%2BaAu3eiG%2Fp7zV2BvbsF8SzOqfbN0SROBbz4d5VMmnY9IGr%2FTFY8ZIFz%2FR0MSoohUBcMmkwvVx00LifyYwjBCjNcy1hpm3Jkx%2FDrsqwD9ovsVeFssWjBqlqYGE%2FQq1xRob%2BLaSRd6YqkqmiFtA9RilR%2Fu7p1t2jTGXDHNBS2sU0zj5wx05KqksWw4IBvaxf9hS5681glUbcn5WARUnRNkQJeqfqCiZiYzT8hs5ofpi26gwl80izrDFMw6Ji9zgY6sQErmbJLTHAh0Io8zxwVDUMnHDMzaRZSpc32N7nHJrTUJDEqJ%2F%2BY32Cps7YGBj6jmtXTc%2Ba6Hxoue9llRilawdIqhKyKqJYe88xHiZZR7%2FkQqapLpI5oHYKBcHbW6ZO2orkwPwEPweiD0rpOdaYpJcEORS1%2BwtKZbnwOc1nrnn7elWxr1ypxMoVjWPtr9yqR8Vvy5Iar3Xv9DP4raIiC%2FLfGnyzC5f92Ns%2FuRgTTq5PvL5Y%3D&X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Date=20260403T054653Z&X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host&X-Amz-Expires=300&X-Amz-Credential=ASIA_SAMPLE_CREDENTIAL_KEY%2F20260403%2Fus-east-1%2Fs3%2Faws4_request&X-Amz-Signature=6027b29a0629a23d57d0c645549739011a343dc46a3aa98a1daadbaf32fc5990&hash=25cc05320cf3ee54b418811199557552d83111fbfc3649dab520ec506032bb5f&host=68042c943591013ac2b2430a89b270f6af2c76d8dfd086a07176afe7c76c2c61&pii=S0378112703000033&tid=spdf-920a3553-fd49-4e4b-af51-80f8c4
