======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Peatland
======================================================================

{{Short description|Wetland terrain without forest cover, dominated by living, peat-forming plants}}
{{Redirect-several|dab=off|Miring (ritual)|Mire (disambiguation)|Quagmire (disambiguation)}}
{{See also|Floating mat|label 1=Floating mat (quagmire)}}
{{Use British English|date=May 2026}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2026}}

[[File:ARG-2016-Aerial-Tierra del Fuego (Ushuaia)–Valle Carbajal 01.jpg|thumb|A variety of mire types in [[Carbajal Valley]], Argentina]]
[[File:Avaste soo põhjaosa vaated %283%29.JPG|thumb|right|[[Avaste Nature Reserve|Avaste Fen]], one of the largest fens in Estonia]]
[[File:Ruwenzori Upper Bigo Bog.jpg|thumb|right|A valley mire creates a level ground surface in otherwise dramatic topography. Upper Bigo Bog, [[Rwenzori Mountains]], [[Uganda]].]]

A '''peatland''' is a type of [[wetland]] whose soils consist of [[Soil organic matter|organic matter]] from decaying plants, forming layers of [[peat]]. Peatlands arise because of incomplete decomposition of organic matter, usually litter from [[vegetation]], due to [[Waterlogging (agriculture)|water-logging]] and subsequent [[anoxic waters|anoxia]].<ref name="Frolking-2011">{{Cite journal |last1=Frolking |first1=Steve |last2=Talbot |first2=Julie |last3=Jones |first3=Miriam C. |last4=Treat |first4=Claire C. |last5=Kauffman |first5=J. Boone |last6=Tuittila |first6=Eeva-Stiina |last7=Roulet |first7=Nigel |name-list-style=and |date=December 2011 |title=Peatlands in the Earth's 21st century climate system |journal=Environmental Reviews |volume=19 |issue=NA |pages=371–396 |doi=10.1139/a11-014 |bibcode=2011EnvRv..19..371F |issn=1181-8700}}</ref> Peatlands are unusual landforms that derive mostly from biological rather than physical processes, and can take on characteristic shapes and surface patterning.

The formation of peatlands is primarily controlled by climatic conditions such as [[precipitation]] and temperature, although terrain relief is a major factor as waterlogging occurs more easily on flatter ground and in basins.<ref name="Rydin-2013">{{Cite book |last1=Rydin |first1=Håkan |title=The Biology of Peatlands |last2=Jeglum |first2=J. K. |date=2013 |publisher=Oxford University Press |others=Bennett, Keith D. |isbn=978-0-19-960299-5 |edition=2nd |location=Oxford |pages= |oclc=840132559}}</ref> Peat formation typically initiates as a [[paludification]] of a mineral soil forest, terrestrialisation of lakes, or primary peat formation on bare soils on previously glaciated areas.<ref name="Page-2016">{{Cite journal |last1=Page |first1=S.E. |last2=Baird |first2=A.J. |name-list-style=and |date=November 2016 |title=Peatlands and Global Change: Response and Resilience |journal=Annual Review of Environment and Resources |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=35–57 |doi=10.1146/annurev-environ-110615-085520 |issn=1543-5938 |doi-access=free}}</ref> A peatland that is actively forming peat is called a ''mire''. All types of mires share the common characteristic of being saturated with water, at least seasonally with actively forming [[peat]], while having their own ecosystem.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wetlands Types and Classifications |url=http://www.personal.ceu.hu/students/03/nature_conservation/wwddetail/Types_classif.html |access-date=20 May 2019 |archive-date=28 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180928234836/http://www.personal.ceu.hu/students/03/nature_conservation/wwddetail/Types_classif.html }}</ref>

Peatlands are the largest natural [[Carbon sink|carbon store]] on land. Covering around 3 million km<sup>2</sup> globally, they sequester 0.37 [[gigatons]] (Gt) of [[carbon dioxide]] ({{CO2}}) a year. Peat soils store over 600 Gt of carbon, more than the carbon stored in all other vegetation types, including forests.<ref name="Struzik-2021">{{Cite web |last=Struzik |first=Ed |date=2021-09-16 |title=Why Saving World's Peatlands Can Help Stabilise the Climate |url=https://e360.yale.edu/features/why-saving-worlds-peatlands-can-help-stabilize-the-climate |access-date=2024-05-19 |website=Yale E360 |language=en-US}}</ref> In their natural state, peatlands provide a range of [[ecosystem service]]s, including minimising flood risk and erosion, purifying water and regulating climate.<ref name="Page-2016"/><ref name="IUCN-2021">{{Cite web |last=IUCN |date=November 2021 |title=Peatlands and climate change |url=https://www.iucn.org/resources/issues-brief/peatlands-and-climate-change |access-date=2023-10-10 |website=iucn.org |language=en}}</ref>

Peatlands are under threat by commercial peat harvesting, drainage and conversion for agriculture (notably [[palm oil]] in the tropics) and fires, which are predicted to become more frequent with [[climate change]]. The destruction of peatlands results in release of stored [[greenhouse gas]]es into the atmosphere, further exacerbating climate change.

== Types ==
Botanists and ecologists use the word "peatland" as a general term for any terrain dominated by peat to a depth of at least {{convert|30|cm|abbr=on}}, even if it has been completely drained (i.e. a peatland can be dry). A peatland that is still capable of forming new peat is called a '''mire''', while drained and converted peatlands might still have a peat layer but are not considered mires as the formation of new peat has ceased.<ref name="Frolking-2011"/>

There are two types of mire: [[bog]] and [[fen]].<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> A '''bog''' is a mire that, due to its raised location relative to the surrounding landscape, obtains all its water solely from [[precipitation]] ([[ombrotrophic]]).<ref>{{Cite book |last =Craft |first =Christopher |title =Creating and Restoring Wetlands From Theory to Practice |publisher =Elsevier |year=2022 |isbn=978-0-12-823981-0 |edition=2nd}}</ref> A '''fen''' is located on a slope, flat, or in a depression and gets most of its water from the surrounding mineral soil or from groundwater ([[minerotrophic]]). Thus, while a bog is always acidic and nutrient-poor, a fen may be slightly acidic, neutral, or alkaline, and either nutrient-poor or nutrient-rich.<ref>{{Cite book |last =Geist |first =Helmut |url =https://books.google.com/books?id=M9f4oZEFuo8C&pg=PA463 |title =Our Earth's Changing Land: An Encyclopedia of Land-Use and Land-Cover Change |publisher=Greenwood |year =2006 |isbn =978-0-313-32784-1 |volume =2 |page =463}}</ref> All mires are initially fens when the peat starts to form, and may turn into bogs once the height of the peat layer reaches above the surrounding land. A '''{{linktext | quagmire}}''' is a floating (quaking) mire, bog, or any peatland being in a stage of [[hydrosere]] or hydrarch (hydroseral) succession; it yields underfoot<ref>{{cite journal |title=Wetland Restoration: A Survey of Options for Restoring Peatlands |journal =Studia Forestalia Suecica |issue =205 |year =1999 |issn =0039-3150 |isbn =91-576-5557-X |s2cid =199566835 |last =Rode |first =Elve |publisher =[[Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences]] |url =https://pub.epsilon.slu.se/3014/1/SFS205.pdf | access-date = 9 March 2026 | quote = Quagmire - floating (quaking) mire, bog or any peatland being a stage in hydrarch (hydro-seral) succession resulting in pond-filling; yields underfoot.}}</ref><ref>
{{cite book
 |last1                = Van Wirdum
 |first1               = G.
 |last2                = Den Held
 |first2               = A. J.
 |last3                = Schmitz
 |first3               = M.
 |editor-last1         = Verhoeven
 |editor-first1        = Jos T. A.
 |date                 = 9 April 2013
 |orig-date            = 1992
 |chapter              = Terrestrialising fen vegetation in former turbaries in the Netherlands
 |title                = Fens and Bogs in the Netherlands: Vegetation, History, Nutrient Dynamics and Conservation
 |url                  = https://books.google.com/books?id=OjL0CAAAQBAJ
 |series               = Geobotany: 18
 |publication-place    = Dordrecht
 |publisher            = Springer Science & Business Media
 |page                 = 325
 |isbn                 = 9789401579971
 |access-date          = 9 March 2026
 |quote                = A quagmire is any mire yielding underfoot; [...] compare (German) 'Schwingmoor').
}}
</ref> ([[floating mat]]s). Ombrotrophic types of quagmire may be called quaking bogs (quivering bogs); minerotrophic types can be labelled with the term "quagfen".<ref>{{cite journal |title =Wetland Restoration: A Survey of Options for Restoring Peatlands |journal =Studia Forestalia Suecica |issue =205 |year =1999 |issn =0039-3150 |isbn =91-576-5557-X |s2cid =199566835 |last =Rode |first =Elve |publisher =[[Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences]] | quote =  Ombrotrophic types of quagmire may be called quaking bog (quivering bog). Minerotrophic types can be named with the term quagfen. | access-date = 9 March 2026 |url =https://pub.epsilon.slu.se/3014/1/SFS205.pdf}}</ref>

Some [[swamp]]s can also be peatlands (e.g. [[peat swamp forest]]), while [[marsh]]es are generally not considered to be peatlands.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> '''Swamps''' are characterised by their forest canopy or by the presence of other tall and dense vegetation like [[Cyperus papyrus|papyrus]]. Like fens, swamps typically have a higher pH level and higher nutrient availability than bogs. Some bogs and fens can support limited shrub or tree growth on [[hummock]]s. A '''marsh''' is a type of wetland within which vegetation is rooted in mineral soil.

== Global distribution ==
[[File:PEATMAP.jpg|left|thumb|PEATMAP showing the global distribution of peatlands]]

Peatlands are found around the globe, although are at their greatest extent at high latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere. Peatlands are estimated to cover around 3% of the globe's surface,<ref name="IUCN-2021"/> although estimating the extent of their cover worldwide is difficult due to the varying accuracy and methodologies of land surveys from many countries.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> Mires occur wherever conditions are right for peat accumulation: largely where organic matter is constantly waterlogged. Hence the distribution of mires is dependent on [[topography]], climate, parent material, biota and time.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=The Development of Peat Lands |journal=The Quarterly Review of Biology |last=Gorham |first=Eville |year=1857 |volume=32 |issue=2 |pages=145–166 |doi=10.1086/401755 |s2cid=129085635}}</ref> The type of mire—bog, fen, marsh or swamp—depends also on each of these factors.

The largest accumulation of mires constitutes around 64% of global peatlands and is found in the temperate, boreal and subarctic zones of the Northern Hemisphere.<ref name="Page-2011">{{Cite journal |last1=Page |first1=Susan E. |last2=Rieley |first2=John O. |last3=Banks |first3=Christopher J. |date=2011-01-04 |title=Global and regional importance of the tropical peatland carbon pool |journal=Global Change Biology |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=798–818 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2486.2010.02279.x |issn=1354-1013 |bibcode=2011GCBio..17..798P |s2cid=86121682 |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00599518/file/PEER_stage2_10.1111%252Fj.1365-2486.2010.02279.x.pdf}}</ref> Mires are usually shallow in polar regions because of the slow rate of accumulation of dead organic matter, and often contain [[permafrost]] and [[palsa]]s. Very large swathes of Canada, northern Europe and northern Russia are covered by boreal mires. In [[Temperate climate|temperate]] zones mires are typically more scattered due to historical drainage and peat extraction, but can cover large areas. One example is [[blanket bog]] where precipitation is very high i.e., in maritime climates inland near the coasts of the north-east and south Pacific, and the north-west and north-east Atlantic. In the sub-tropics, mires are rare and restricted to the wettest areas.

Mires can be extensive in the tropics, typically underlying tropical rainforest (for example, in [[Kalimantan]], the [[Congo Basin]] and [[Amazon basin]]). Tropical peat formation is known to occur in coastal [[mangrove]]s as well as in areas of high altitude.<ref name="Page-2016"/> Tropical mires largely form where high precipitation is combined with poor conditions for drainage.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> Tropical mires account for around 11% of peatlands globally (more than half of which can be found in Southeast Asia), and are most commonly found at low altitudes, although they can also be found in mountainous regions, for example in South America, Africa and [[Papua New Guinea]].<ref name="Page-2011"/> Indonesia, particularly on the islands of Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua, has one of the largest peatlands in the world, with an area of about 24 million hectares. These peatlands play an important role in global carbon storage and have very high biodiversity. However, peatlands in Indonesia also face major threats from deforestation and forest fires.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Restoring Indonesian peatlands, protecting our planet |url=https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/stories/restoring-indonesian-peatlands-protecting-our-planet |access-date=2024-09-15 |website=UNOPS |language=en-GB}}</ref> In the early 21st century, the world's largest tropical mire was found in the Central Congo Basin, covering 145,500&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup> and storing up to 10<sup>13</sup> kg of carbon.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dargie |first1=Greta C. |last2=Lewis |first2=Simon L. |last3=Lawson |first3=Ian T. |last4=Mitchard |first4=Edward T. A. |last5=Page |first5=Susan E. |last6=Bocko |first6=Yannick E. |last7=Ifo |first7=Suspense A. |s2cid=205253362 |date=2017-01-11 |title=Age, extent and carbon storage of the central Congo Basin peatland complex |journal=Nature |volume=542 |issue=7639 |pages=86–90 |doi=10.1038/nature21048 |pmid=28077869 |issn=0028-0836 |bibcode=2017Natur.542...86D |url=http://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/111018/1/Age%2C%20extent%20and%20carbon%20storage%20of%20the%20central%20Congo.pdf}}</ref>

The total area of mires has declined globally due to drainage for agriculture, forestry and peat harvesting. For example, more than 50% of the original European mire area which is more than 300,000&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup> has been lost.<ref>{{cite book |title=Wise use of mires and peatlands |last1=Joosten |first1=H. |last2=Clarke |first2=D. |year=2002 |publisher=International Mire Conservation Group and International Peat Society}}</ref>{{Clarify|reason=number is original amount or amount lost?|date=October 2023}} Some of the largest losses have been in Russia, Finland, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Poland and Belarus. A catalog of the peat research collection at the University of Minnesota Duluth provides references to research on worldwide peat and peatlands.<ref>{{cite web |title=An Author Catalog of the Peat Research Collection at the University of Minnesota Duluth. |last=Sandy |first=John H. |date=31 October 2022 |url=https://ir.ua.edu/handle/123456789/9811 |access-date=2023-10-29}}</ref>

== Biochemical processes ==
[[File:Carbon Cycle in Peatlands.pdf|thumb|upright=2.5|The carbon cycle within peatlands]]

Peatlands have unusual chemistry that influences, among other things, their biota and water outflow. Peat has very high [[cation-exchange capacity]] due to its high organic matter content: cations such as [[Ca²⁺]] are preferentially [[Adsorption|adsorbed]] onto the peat in exchange for [[H+ Ion|H<sup>+</sup>]] ions. Water passing through peat declines in nutrients and [[pH]]. Therefore, mires are typically nutrient-poor and acidic unless the inflow of [[groundwater]] (bringing in supplementary cations) is high.<ref name="Rydin-2006">{{cite book |title=The Biology of Peatlands |year=2006 |edition=1st |publisher=Oxford University Press |last1=Rydin |first1=Håkan |last2=Jeglum |first2=John}}</ref>

Generally, whenever the inputs of carbon into the soil from dead organic matter exceed the carbon outputs via organic matter [[decomposition]], peat is formed. This occurs due to the anoxic state of water-logged peat, which slows down decomposition.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Belyea |first1=Lisa R. |last2=Malmer |first2=Nils |date=July 2004 |title=Carbon sequestration in peatland: patterns and mechanisms of response to climate change |journal=Global Change Biology |volume=10 |issue=7 |pages=1043–1052 |doi=10.1111/j.1529-8817.2003.00783.x |bibcode=2004GCBio..10.1043B |s2cid=39994255 |url=http://lup.lub.lu.se/record/137465}}</ref> Peat-forming vegetation is typically also recalcitrant (poorly decomposing) due to high [[lignin]] and low nutrient content.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Leng |first1=Lee Yit |last2=Ahmed |first2=Osumanu Haruna |last3=Jalloh |first3=Mohamadu Boyie |date=2019-03-01 |title=Brief review on climate change and tropical peatlands |journal=Geoscience Frontiers |series=Climate change impacts on environmental geosciences |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=373–380 |doi=10.1016/j.gsf.2017.12.018 |issn=1674-9871 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2019GeoFr..10..373L }}</ref> [[Topography|Topographically]], accumulating peat elevates the ground surface above the original topography. Mires can reach considerable heights above the underlying mineral soil or [[bedrock]]: peat depths of above 10&nbsp;m have been commonly recorded in temperate regions (many temperate and most boreal mires were removed by ice sheets in the last Ice Age), and above 25&nbsp;m in tropical regions.<sup>[[Mire#cite note-Rydin2006-7|[7]]]</sup> When the absolute decay rate of peat in the ''catotelm'' (the lower, water-saturated zone of the peat layer) matches the rate of input of new peat into the catotelm, the mire will stop growing in height.<sup>[[Mire#cite note-8|[8]]]</sup>

=== Carbon storage and methanogenesis ===
[[File:Research in to response of northern peatlands to increases in temperature and atmospheric carbon dioxide (9358).jpg|thumb|US scientists use the Spruce and Peatland Responses Under Changing Environments experiment in [[Minnesota]] to assess the response of northern peatlands to increases in temperature and atmospheric carbon dioxide.]]

Despite accounting for just 3% of Earth's land surfaces, peatlands are collectively a major carbon store containing between 500 and 700&nbsp;billion tonnes of carbon.<ref name=ConservLtrs_20250212>{{cite journal |last1=Austin |first1=Kemen G. |last2=Else |first2=Paul R. |last3=Coronado |first3=Euridice N. Honorio |last4=DeGemmis |first4=Alfred |last5=Gallego-Sala |first5=Angela V. |last6=Harris |first6=Lorna |last7=Kretser |first7=Heidi E. |display-authors=4 |title=Mismatch Between Global Importance of Peatlands and the Extent of Their Protection |journal=Conservation Letters |date=12 February 2025 |volume=18 |issue=1 |article-number=e13080 |doi=10.1111/conl.13080|doi-access=free |bibcode=2025ConL...18E3080A }}</ref> Carbon stored within peatlands equates to over half the amount of carbon found in the [[atmosphere]].<ref name="Page-2016"/> Peatlands interact with the atmosphere primarily through the exchange of [[carbon dioxide]], [[methane]] and [[nitrous oxide]],<ref name="Frolking-2011"/> and can be damaged by excess nitrogen from agriculture or rainwater.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-01-25 |title=Northern Ireland's peatlands face 'toxic' nitrogen risk |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-northern-ireland-60117908 |access-date=2022-01-25}}</ref> The [[Carbon sequestration|sequestration]] of carbon dioxide takes place at the surface via the process of [[photosynthesis]], while losses of carbon dioxide occur through living plants via autotrophic [[Respiration (physiology)|respiration]] and from the litter and peat via heterotrophic respiration.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> In their natural state, mires are a small atmospheric carbon dioxide sink through the photosynthesis of peat vegetation, which outweighs their release of greenhouse gases. On the other hand, most mires are generally net emitters of methane and nitrous oxide.<ref name="Scandinavian Journal of Forest Research-2001">{{Cite journal |date=2001-07-01 |title=News and Views |journal=Scandinavian Journal of Forest Research |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=289–294 |doi=10.1080/02827580120112 |bibcode=2001SJFR...16..289. |issn=0000-0000 |s2cid=219716664}}</ref> Due to the continued {{CO2}} sequestration over millennia, and because of the longer atmospheric lifespan of the {{CO2}} molecules compared with methane and nitrous oxide, peatlands have had a net cooling effect on the atmosphere.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Frolking |first1=Steve |last2=Roulet |first2=Nigel T. |title=Holocene radiative forcing impact of northern peatland carbon accumulation and methane emissions |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2486.2007.01339.x |journal=Global Change Biology |language=en |publication-date=25 April 2007 |volume=13 |issue=5 |pages=1079–1088 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2486.2007.01339.x |bibcode=2007GCBio..13.1079F |issn=1354-1013|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The [[water table]] position of a peatland is the main control of its carbon release to the atmosphere. When the water table rises after a rainstorm, the peat and its microbes are submerged under water inhibiting access to oxygen, reducing {{CO2}} release via respiration. Carbon dioxide release increases when the water table falls lower, such as during a drought, as this increases the availability of oxygen to the aerobic [[microbes]] thus accelerating peat decomposition.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brown |first=Alastair |date=2011-12-20 |title=Carbon storage: When peat dries |journal=Nature Climate Change |volume=2 |issue=1 |page=22 |doi=10.1038/nclimate1360 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Levels of methane emissions also vary with the water table position and temperature. A water table near the peat surface gives the opportunity for [[Anaerobic organism|anaerobic microorganisms]] to flourish.

[[Methanogen]]s are strictly anaerobic organisms and produce methane from organic matter in anoxic conditions below the water table level, while some of that methane is oxidised by [[methanotroph]]s above the water table level. Therefore, changes in water table level influence the size of these methane production and consumption zones. Increased soil temperatures also contribute to increased seasonal methane flux. A study in Alaska found that methane may vary by as much as 300% seasonally with wetter and warmer soil conditions due to climate change.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Turetsky |first1=M. R. |last2=Treat |first2=C. C. |last3=Waldrop |first3=M. P. |last4=Waddington |first4=J. M. |last5=Harden |first5=J. W. |last6=McGuire |first6=A. D. |s2cid=18756489 |date=2008-09-01 |title=Short-term response of methane fluxes and methanogen activity to water table and soil warming manipulations in an Alaskan peatland |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |volume=113 |issue=G3 |pages=G00A10 |doi=10.1029/2007jg000496 |issn=2156-2202 |bibcode=2008JGRG..113.0A10T |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Peatlands are important for studying past climate because they are sensitive to changes in the environment and can reveal levels of [[isotope]]s, pollutants, [[macrofossil]]s, metals from the atmosphere and pollen.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Przewodnik do oznaczania torfów i osadów jeziornych |last=Tobolski |first=K |publisher=PWN |year=2000}}</ref> For example, [[Radiocarbon dating|carbon-14 dating]] can reveal the age of the peat. The dredging and destruction of a peatland will release the carbon dioxide that could reveal irreplaceable information about the past climatic conditions. Many kinds of microorganisms inhabit peatlands, due to the regular supply of water and abundance of peat forming vegetation. These microorganisms include but are not limited to [[methanogen]]s, algae, bacteria, [[zoobenthos]], of which ''[[Sphagnum]]'' species are most abundant.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kuske |first1=E |last2=Silamikele |first2=Inese |last3=Kalnina |first3=Laimdota |last4=Klavins |first4=Maris |date=2010-01-01 |title=Peat formation conditions and peat properties: A study of two ombrotrophic bogs in Latvia |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/285748071 |journal=Mires and Peat}}</ref>

=== Humic substances ===
Peat contains substantial organic matter, where [[humic acid]] dominates. [[Humic substance|Humic materials]] can store substantial amounts of water, making them an essential component in the peat environment, contributing to increased carbon storage due to the resulting anaerobic condition. If the peatland is dried from long-term cultivation and agricultural use, it will lower the water table, and the increased aeration will release carbon.<ref>{{cite book |chapter=Impact of drainage on hydrophobicity of fen peat-moor soils |date=2010 |title=Mires and Peat |pages=158–174 |publisher=University of Latvia Press |editor=M. Klavins |first1=L.W. |last1=Szajdak |first2=Jan |last2=Szatylowicz}}</ref> Upon extreme drying, the ecosystem can undergo a state shift, turning the mire into a barren land with lower biodiversity and richness. Humic acid formation occurs during the biogeochemical degradation of vegetation debris and animal residue.<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://agris.fao.org/agris-search/search.do?recordID=LV2010000341 |chapter=Physico-chemical properties of humic acids isolated from an Eriophorum-Sphagnum raised bog |last1=Chemistry |first1=Gierlach-Hladon, T., Karol Marcinkowski Univ. of Medical Sciences, Poznan (Poland). Dept. of Inorganic and Analytical |last2=Environment |first2=Szajdak, L., Polish Academy of Sciences, Poznan (Poland). Inst. for Agricultural and Forest |date=2010 |title=AGRIS: International Information System for the Agricultural Science and Technology |publisher=University of Latvia Press |isbn=978-9984-45-163-3 |language=en}}</ref> The loads of organic matter in the form of humic acid is a source of precursors of coal.{{Clarify|reason=sentence is hard to understand|date=October 2023}} Prematurely exposing the organic matter to the atmosphere promotes the conversion of organics to carbon dioxide to be released in the atmosphere.

== Use by humans ==
[[File:Peat cuttings near Unasary - geograph.org.uk - 176303.jpg|thumb|Extraction of [[peat]] from derelict blanket bog, [[South Uist]], Scotland. This old bog is no longer forming peat because the vegetation has been changed, and therefore it is not a mire.]]
{{See also|Peat}}
Records of past human behaviour and environments can be contained within peatlands. These may take the form of human artefacts, or [[palaeoecological]] and [[geochemical]] records.<ref name="Page-2016"/>

Peatlands are used by humans in modern times for a range of purposes, the most dominant being agriculture and forestry, which accounts for around a quarter of global peatland area.<ref name="Page-2016"/> This involves cutting drainage ditches to lower the water table with the intended purpose of enhancing the productivity of forest cover or for use as pasture or cropland.<ref name="Frolking-2011"/> Agricultural uses for mires include the use of natural vegetation for hay crop or grazing, or the cultivation of crops on a modified surface.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> In addition, the commercial extraction of peat for energy production is widely practiced in Northern European countries, such as Russia, Sweden, Finland, Ireland and the [[Baltic states]].<ref name="Page-2016"/>

Tropical peatlands comprise 0.25% of Earth's terrestrial land surface but store 3% of all soil and forest carbon stocks.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Carbon sequestration in peat bogs as a source of income |work=WUR |url=https://www.wur.nl/en/show/Carbon-sequestration-in-peat-bogs-as-a-source-of-income.htm |access-date=2018-04-09 |archive-date=2018-04-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180409233644/https://www.wur.nl/en/show/Carbon-sequestration-in-peat-bogs-as-a-source-of-income.htm }}</ref> The use of this land by humans, including draining and harvesting of tropical peat forests, results in the emission of large amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. In addition, fires occurring on peatland dried by the draining of peat bogs release even more carbon dioxide. The economic value of a tropical peatland was once derived from raw materials, such as wood, bark, resin and latex, the extraction of which did not contribute to large carbon emissions. In Southeast Asia, peatlands are drained and cleared for human use for a variety of reasons, including the production of [[palm oil]] and timber for export in primarily developing nations.<ref name="Page-2011"/> This releases stored carbon dioxide and prevents the system from sequestering carbon again.

== Tropical peatlands ==
The global distribution of tropical peatlands is concentrated in Southeast Asia where agricultural use of peatlands has been increased in recent decades. Large areas of tropical peatland have been cleared and drained for the production of food and [[cash crop]]s such as palm oil. Large-scale drainage of these plantations often results in [[subsidence]], flooding, fire and deterioration of [[soil quality]]. Small-scale encroachment on the other hand, is linked to poverty and is so widespread that it also has negatively impacts these peatlands.

The biotic and abiotic factors controlling Southeast Asian peatlands are interdependent.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> Its soil, hydrology and morphology are created by the present vegetation through the accumulation of its own organic matter, building a favourable environment for this specific vegetation. This system is therefore vulnerable to changes in hydrology or vegetation cover.<ref name="Hooijer-2006">Hooijer, A., Silvius, M., Wösten, H. and Page, S. 2006. PEAT-CO2, Assessment of CO2 emissions from drained peatlands in SE Asia. Delft Hydraulics report Q3943. [http://np-net.pbworks.com/f/Hooijer%2C+Silvius+et+al+%282006%29+PEAT+CO2+Assement+of+CP2+emissions+from+drained+wetlands+in+SE+Asia.pdf]</ref> These peatlands are mostly located in developing regions with impoverished and rapidly growing populations. These lands have become targets for commercial [[logging]], paper pulp production and conversion to plantations through [[Clearcutting|clear-cutting]], drainage and burning.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> Drainage of tropical peatlands alters the hydrology and increases their susceptibility to fire and soil erosion, as a consequence of changes in physical and chemical compositions.<ref name="UNEP-2008">{{Cite book |title=Assessment on peatlands, biodiversity, and climate change |last=United Nations Environment Programme. Global Environment Facility. Asia Pacific Network for Global Change Research. Global Environment Centre (Malaysia), publisher. Wetlands International, publisher. |year=2008 |publisher=Global Environment Centre |isbn=978-983-43751-0-2 |oclc=933580381}}</ref> The change in soil strongly affects the sensitive vegetation and forest die-off is common. The short-term effect is a decrease in biodiversity but the long-term effect, since these encroachments are hard to reverse, is a loss of habitat. Poor knowledge about peatlands' sensitive hydrology and lack of nutrients often lead to failing plantations, resulting in increasing pressure on remaining peatlands.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/>

=== Biology and peat characteristics ===
Tropical peatland vegetation varies with climate and location. Three different characterisations are [[Mangrove swamp|mangrove woodlands]] present in the littoral zones and deltas of salty water, followed inland by [[Freshwater swamp forest|swamp forests]]. These forests occur on the margin of peatlands with a palm rich flora with trees 70&nbsp;m tall and 8&nbsp;m in girth accompanied by ferns and epiphytes. The third, ''padang'', from the Malay and Indonesian word for forest, consists of shrubs and tall thin trees and appear in the centre of large peatlands.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> The diversity of woody species, like trees and shrubs, are far greater in tropical peatlands than in peatlands of other types. Peat in the tropics is therefore dominated by woody material from trunks of trees and shrubs and contain little to none of the sphagnum moss that dominates in boreal peatlands.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> It's only partly decomposed and the surface consists of a thick layer of leaf litter.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> Forestry in peatlands leads to drainage and rapid carbon losses since it decreases inputs of organic matter and accelerate the decomposition.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Biodiversity and sustainability of tropical peatlands: proceedings of the International Symposium on Biodiversity, Environmental Importance and Sustainability of Tropical Peat and Peatlands, held in Palangka Raya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, 4-8 September 1995 |date=1997 |publisher=Samara Pub |others=Rieley, Jack, 1941–, Page, Susan, 1957– |isbn=1-873692-10-2 |location=Cardigan, UK |oclc=37815652}}</ref> In contrast to temperate wetlands, tropical peatlands are home to several species of fish. Many new, often endemic, species have been discovered but many of them are considered threatened.<ref name="UNEP-2008"/><ref>{{Citation |last1=Ng |first1=Peter K. L. |chapter=Diversity and conservation of blackwater fishes in Peninsular Malaysia, particularly in the North Selangor peat swamp forest |year=1994 |title=Ecology and Conservation of Southeast Asian Marine and Freshwater Environments including Wetlands |pages=203–218 |publisher=Springer Netherlands |doi=10.1007/978-94-011-0958-1_20 |isbn=978-94-010-4414-1 |last2=Tay |first2=J. B. |last3=Lim |first3=Kelvin K. P.}}</ref>

=== Greenhouse gases and fires ===
[[File:Borneo fires and smoke, 2002.jpg|thumb|upright|Satellite image of burning tropical peat swamp, [[Borneo]]. In 1997 alone, 73000&nbsp;ha of swamp [[Borneo peat swamp forests#Recent history|was burned in Borneo]], releasing the same amount of carbon as 13-40% of the mean annual global carbon emissions of [[fossil fuels]]. The majority of this carbon was released from peat rather than overlying tropical rainforest.]]
The tropical peatlands in Southeast Asia only cover 0.2% of Earth's land area but CO<sub>2</sub> emissions are estimated to be 2 Gt per year, equal to 7% of global fossil fuel emissions.<ref name="Hooijer-2006"/> These emissions get bigger with drainage and burning of peatlands and a severe fire can release up to 4,000 t of CO<sub>2</sub>/ha. Burning events in tropical peatlands are becoming more frequent due to large-scale drainage and land clearance and in the past ten years, more than 2&nbsp;million hectares was burnt in Southeast Asia alone. These fires last typically for 1–3 months and release large amounts of CO<sub>2</sub>.
[[File:Burned Peatland in Indonesia.jpg|thumb|Burned peatland due to 2015 El Niño event in South Sumatra, Indonesia.]]
Indonesia is one of the countries suffering from peatland fires, especially during years with [[El Niño–Southern Oscillation|ENSO]]-related drought, an increasing problem since 1982 as a result of developing land use and agriculture.<ref name="UNEP-2008" /> During the [[El Niño]]-event in 1997–1998 more than 24,400&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup><ref name="Rydin-2013" /> of peatland was lost to fires in Indonesia alone from which 10,000&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup> was burnt in Kalimantan and Sumatra. The output of CO<sub>2</sub> was estimated to 0.81–2.57 Gt, equal to 13–40% of that year's global output from fossil fuel burning. Indonesia is now considered the third-biggest contributor to global CO<sub>2</sub> emissions, caused primarily by these fires.<ref>Silvius, M., Kaat, A.H., Van de Bund and Hooijer, A. 2006. Peatland degradation fuels climate change. An unrecognised and alarming source of greenhouse gases. Wetlands International, Wageningen, The Netherlands.[https://www.warum-torf.info/download/peatland-degradation-fuels-climate-change]</ref> The 2015 El Niño event further exacerbated the condition of these peatlands, as wildfires burned approximately 3 million hectares of forests and peatlands on the east coast of Sumatra and in Central Kalimantan, emitting 11.3&nbsp;[[Tera-|Tg]]&nbsp;CO<sub>2</sub> per day during the months of September and October that year.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Murdiyarso |first=Daniel |date=2023-08-14 |title=Indonesia must face up to the heightened risk of drought and fire under El Niño |url=https://forestsnews.cifor.org/83817/el-nino-indonesia-faces-up-to-heightened-risk-of-drought-and-fire?fnl= |access-date=2025-01-09 |website=CIFOR-ICRAF Forests News}}</ref>

With a warming climate, these burnings are expected to increase in intensity and number. This is a result of a dry climate together with an extensive rice farming project, called [[Mega Rice Project|the Mega Rice Project]], started in the 1990s, which converted 1 Mha of peatlands to [[Paddy field|rice paddies]]. Forest and land was cleared by burning and 4000&nbsp;km of channels drained the area.<ref>Boehm, H.-D. V., Siegert, F., Rieley, J. O. ''et al'' (2001). ''Fire impacts and carbon release on tropical peatlands in central Kalimantan, Indonesia''. 22nd Asian Conference on Remote Sensing, 5–9 November 2001, Singapore. Centre for Remote Imaging, Sensing and Processing (CRISP), University of Singapore.  [https://web.archive.org/web/20190508165804/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/4645/74ff3c3f7a2a3fbd1cb4b5e24dd9424f10b5.pdf]</ref> Drought and acidification of the lands led to bad harvest and the project was abandoned in 1999.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Page |first1=Susan |chapter=Tropical peatland fires in Southeast Asia |year=2009 |title=Tropical Fire Ecology |pages=263–287 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-77380-1 |last2=Hoscilo |first2=Agata |last3=Langner |first3=Andreas |last4=Tansey |first4=Kevin |last5=Siegert |first5=Florian |last6=Limin |first6=Suwido |last7=Rieley |first7=Jack |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-77381-8_9}}</ref> Similar projects in China have led to immense loss of tropical marshes and fens due to rice production.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=March 1994 |title='94 International Conference on Wetland Environment and Peatland Utilisation |journal=Chinese Geographical Science |volume=4 |issue=1 |page=95 |doi=10.1007/bf02664953 |bibcode=1994ChGpS...4...95. |issn=1002-0063 |s2cid=195212972}}</ref>

Drainage, which also increases the risk of burning, can cause additional emissions of CO<sub>2</sub> by 30–100 t/ha/year if the water table is lowered by only 1&nbsp;m.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wösten |first1=J. H. M. |last2=Van Den Berg |first2=J. |last3=Van Eijk |first3=P. |last4=Gevers |first4=G. J. M. |last5=Giesen |first5=W. B. J. T. |last6=Hooijer |first6=A. |last7=Idris |first7=Aswandi |last8=Leenman |first8=P. H. |last9=Rais |first9=Dipa Satriadi |s2cid=154223494 |date=March 2006 |title=Interrelationships between Hydrology and Ecology in Fire Degraded Tropical Peat Swamp Forests |journal=International Journal of Water Resources Development |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=157–174 |doi=10.1080/07900620500405973 |bibcode=2006IJWRD..22..157W |issn=0790-0627}}</ref> The draining of peatlands is likely the most important and long-lasting threat to peatlands globally, but is especially prevalent in the tropics.<ref name="UNEP-2008"/>

Peatlands release the greenhouse gas methane which has strong [[global warming potential]]. However, subtropical wetlands have shown high CO<sub>2</sub> binding per mol of released methane, which is a function that counteracts global warming.<ref name="Whiting2001">{{Cite journal |last1=Whiting |first1=Gary J. |last2=Chanton |first2=Jeffrey P. |date=November 2001 |title=Greenhouse carbon balance of wetlands: Methane emission versus carbon sequestration |journal=Tellus B |volume=53 |issue=5 |pages=521–528 |doi=10.1034/j.1600-0889.2001.530501.x |issn=0280-6509 |bibcode=2001TellB..53..521W}}</ref> Tropical peatlands are suggested to contain about 100 Gt carbon,<ref>{{Cite book |title=Peatlands and climate change |date=2008 |publisher=IPS, International Peat Society |others=Strack, Maria., International Peat Society. |isbn=978-952-99401-1-0 |location=Jyväskylä, Finland |oclc=404026180}}</ref><ref name="UNEP-2008"/> corresponding to more than 50% of the carbon present as CO<sub>2</sub> in the atmosphere.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> Accumulation rates of carbon during the last millennium were close to 40&nbsp;g&nbsp;C/m<sup>2</sup>/yr.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yu |first1=Zicheng |last2=Loisel |first2=Julie |last3=Brosseau |first3=Daniel P. |last4=Beilman |first4=David W. |last5=Hunt |first5=Stephanie J. |date=July 2010 |title=Global peatland dynamics since the Last Glacial Maximum |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=37 |issue=13 |pages=n/a |bibcode=2010GeoRL..3713402Y |doi=10.1029/2010gl043584 |issn=0094-8276 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Northern peatlands ==
[[File:EE-Lahemaa-Bagno Viru.jpg|thumb|Wooded bog in [[Lahemaa National Park]], [[Estonia]]. 65% of mires in Estonia have been strongly affected or damaged by human activity in recent years.<ref>{{cite book |title=Mires and Peatlands of Europe |publisher=Schweizerbart Science Publishers. Stuttgart |year=2017 |editor1=Joosten H. |editor2=Tanneberger F. |editor3=Moen, A.}}</ref>]]
Northern peatlands are associated with boreal and subarctic climates.<ref name="Tarnocai-2006">{{cite book |last1=Tarnocai |first1=C. |last2=Stolbovoy |first2=V. |editor-last=Martini |editor-first=I. P. |editor2-last=Martínez Cortizas |editor2-first=A. |editor3-last=Chesworth |editor3-first=W. |title=Developments in Earth Surface Processes |chapter=Chapter 2 Northern Peatlands: their characteristics, development and sensitivity to climate change |publisher=Elsevier |year=2006 |issn=0928-2025 |doi=10.1016/s0928-2025(06)09002-x |volume=9 |pages=17–51 |isbn=978-0-444-52883-4 |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S092820250609002X |access-date=2024-10-17}}</ref> Northern peatlands were mostly built up during the [[Holocene]] after the retreat of [[Pleistocene]] glaciers, but in contrast tropical peatlands are much older. Total northern peat carbon stocks are estimated to be 1055&nbsp;Gt&nbsp;C.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nichols |first1=Jonathan E. |last2=Peteet |first2=Dorothy M. |title=Rapid expansion of northern peatlands and doubled estimate of carbon storage |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-019-0454-z |journal=Nature Geoscience |language=en |publication-date=21 October 2019 |volume=12 |issue=11 |pages=917–921 |doi=10.1038/s41561-019-0454-z |bibcode=2019NatGe..12..917N |s2cid=204812279 |issn=1752-0908|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Of all northern circumpolar countries, Russia has the largest area of peatlands,<ref name="Tarnocai-2006"/> and contains the largest peatland in the world, The [[Vasyugan Swamp|Great Vasyugan Mire]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kirpotin |first1=Sergey N. |last2=Antoshkina |first2=Olga A. |last3=Berezin |first3=Alexandr E. |last4=Elshehawi |first4=Samer |last5=Feurdean |first5=Angelica |last6=Lapshina |first6=Elena D. |last7=Pokrovsky |first7=Oleg S. |last8=Peregon |first8=Anna M. |last9=Semenova |first9=Natalia M. |last10=Tanneberger |first10=Franziska |last11=Volkov |first11=Igor V. |last12=Volkova |first12=Irina I. |last13=Joosten |first13=Hans |date=2021-11-01 |title=Great Vasyugan Mire: How the world's largest peatland helps addressing the world's largest problems |journal=Ambio |language=en |volume=50 |issue=11 |pages=2038–2049 |doi=10.1007/s13280-021-01520-2 |issn=1654-7209 |pmc=8497674 |pmid=33677811|bibcode=2021Ambio..50.2038K }}</ref> Nakaikemi Wetland in southwest Honshu, Japan is more than 50,000 years old and has a depth of 45&nbsp;m.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> The Philippi Peatland in Greece has probably one of the deepest peat layers with a depth of 190&nbsp;m.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Christanis |first=Kimon |date=2016 |title=The Wetland Book: II: Distribution, Description and Conservation |publisher=Springer Netherlands |isbn=978-94-007-6173-5 |editor-last=Finlayson |editor-first=C. Max |pages=1–6 |chapter=The Philippi Peatland (Greece) |doi=10.1007/978-94-007-6173-5_147-1 |editor2-last=Milton |editor2-first=G. Randy |editor3-last=Prentice |editor3-first=R. Crawford |editor4-last=Davidson |editor4-first=Nick C.}}</ref>

== Impacts on global climate ==
According to the [[IPCC Sixth Assessment Report]], the conservation and restoration of wetlands and peatlands has large economic potential to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions, providing benefits for adaptation, mitigation and biodiversity.<ref>{{Cite book |author=IPCC |title=Mitigation of Climate Change |year=2022 |series=Contribution of Working Group III to the [[IPCC Sixth Assessment Report|Sixth Assessment Report]] of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change |chapter=Summary for Policymakers |ref={{harvid|IPCC AR6 WG3 Summary for Policymakers|2022| Sections C.9.1, D.2.2}} |author-link=IPCC |access-date=2022-05-20 |chapter-url=https://report.ipcc.ch/ar6wg3/pdf/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_SummaryForPolicymakers.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220807023536/https://report.ipcc.ch/ar6wg3/pdf/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_SummaryForPolicymakers.pdf |archive-date=2022-08-07 }}</ref>

[[Wetland]]s provide an environment where organic carbon is stored in living plants, dead plants and peat, as well as converted to carbon dioxide and methane. Three main factors give wetlands the ability to sequester and store carbon: high biological productivity, high water table and low decomposition rates. Suitable [[Meteorology|meteorological]] and hydrological conditions are necessary to provide an abundant water source for the wetland. Fully water-saturated wetland soils allow [[Anaerobic oxidation of methane|anaerobic]] conditions to manifest, storing carbon but releasing methane.<ref name="Kayranli-2010">{{Cite journal |last1=Kayranli |first1=Birol |last2=Scholz |first2=Miklas |last3=Mustafa |first3=Atif |last4=Hedmark |first4=Åsa |s2cid=25306339 |date=2010-02-01 |title=Carbon Storage and Fluxes within Freshwater Wetlands: a Critical Review |journal=Wetlands |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=111–124 |doi=10.1007/s13157-009-0003-4 |bibcode=2010Wetl...30..111K |issn=0277-5212}}</ref>

Wetlands make up about 5-8% of Earth's land surface, but contain about 20-30% of the planet's 2500 Gt [[soil carbon]] stores.<ref name="Mitsch-2013">{{Cite journal |last1=Mitsch |first1=William J. |last2=Bernal |first2=Blanca |last3=Nahlik |first3=Amanda M. |last4=Mander |first4=Ülo |last5=Zhang |first5=Li |last6=Anderson |first6=Christopher J. |last7=Jørgensen |first7=Sven E. |last8=Brix |first8=Hans |s2cid=11939685 |date=2013-04-01 |title=Wetlands, carbon, and climate change |journal=Landscape Ecology |volume=28 |issue=4 |pages=583–597 |doi=10.1007/s10980-012-9758-8 |bibcode=2013LaEco..28..583M |issn=0921-2973}}</ref> Peatlands contain the highest amounts of soil organic carbon of all wetland types.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Köchy |first1=M. |last2=Hiederer |first2=R. |last3=Freibauer |first3=A. |date=2015-04-16 |title=Global distribution of soil organic carbon – Part 1: Masses and frequency distributions of SOC stocks for the tropics, permafrost regions, wetlands, and the world |journal=Soil |language=en |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=351–365 |doi=10.5194/soil-1-351-2015 |issn=2199-3971 |bibcode=2015SOIL....1..351K |doi-access=free}}</ref> Wetlands can become sources of carbon, rather than sinks, as the decomposition occurring within the ecosystem emits methane.<ref name="Kayranli-2010"/> Natural peatlands do not always have a measurable cooling effect on the climate in a short time span as the cooling effects of sequestering carbon are offset by the emission of methane, which is a strong greenhouse gas. However, given the short "lifetime" of methane (12 years), it is often said that methane emissions are unimportant within 300 years compared to carbon sequestration in wetlands. Within that time frame or less, most wetlands become both net carbon and [[Radiative flux|radiative]] sinks. Hence, peatlands do result in cooling of the Earth's climate over a longer time period as methane is oxidised quickly and removed from the atmosphere whereas atmospheric carbon dioxide is continuously absorbed.<ref name="ramsar.org-2018">{{Cite web |url=https://www.ramsar.org/document/peatlands-climate-change-mitigation-and-biodiversity-conservation |title=Peatlands, climate change mitigation and biodiversity conservation {{!}} Ramsar|website=ramsar.org|access-date=2018-04-09}}</ref> Throughout the [[Holocene]] (the past 12,000 years), peatlands have been persistent terrestrial [[carbon sink]]s and have had a net cooling effect, sequestering 5.6–38&nbsp;g&nbsp;C/m<sup>2</sup> per year. On average, it has been estimated that today northern peatlands sequester 20–30&nbsp;g&nbsp;C/m<sup>2</sup>/year.<ref name="Frolking-2011"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yu |first1=Zicheng |last2=Beilman |first2=D. W. |last3=Frolking |first3=S. |last4=MacDonald |first4=G. M. |last5=Roulet |first5=N. T. |last6=Camill |first6=P. |last7=Charman |first7=D. J. |year=2011 |title=Peatlands and Their Role in the Global Carbon Cycle |journal=Eos, Transactions American Geophysical Union |volume=92 |issue=12 |pages=97–98 |doi=10.1029/2011EO120001 |issn=2324-9250 |bibcode=2011EOSTr..92...97Y |url=https://digitalcommons.bowdoin.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1061&context=eos-faculty-publications}}</ref>

Peatlands insulate the [[permafrost]] in subarctic regions, thus delaying thawing during summer, as well as inducing the formation of permafrost.<ref name="ramsar.org-2018"/> As the global climate continues to warm, wetlands could become major carbon sources as higher temperatures cause higher carbon dioxide emissions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Turetsky |first1=Merritt R. |last2=Abbott |first2=Benjamin W. |last3=Jones |first3=Miriam C. |last4=Walter Anthony |first4=Katey |last5=Olefeldt |first5=David |last6=Schuur |first6=Edward A. G. |last7=Koven |first7=Charles |last8=McGuire |first8=A. David |last9=Grosse |first9=Guido |date=2019-04-30 |title=Permafrost collapse is accelerating carbon release |journal=Nature |volume=569 |issue=7754 |pages=32–34 |doi=10.1038/d41586-019-01313-4 |pmid=31040419 |issn=0028-0836 |bibcode=2019Natur.569...32T |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Compared with untilled cropland, wetlands can sequester around two times the carbon. Carbon sequestration can occur in constructed wetlands as well as natural ones. Estimates of greenhouse gas fluxes from wetlands indicate that natural wetlands have lower fluxes, but man-made wetlands have a greater carbon sequestration capacity. The carbon sequestration abilities of wetlands can be improved through restoration and protection strategies, but it takes several decades for these restored ecosystems to become comparable in carbon storage to peatlands and other forms of natural wetlands.<ref name="Kayranli-2010"/>

=== Drainage for agriculture and forestry ===
The exchange of carbon between the peatlands and the atmosphere has been of current concern globally in the field of ecology and biogeochemical studies.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/> The drainage of peatlands for agriculture and forestry has resulted in the emission of extensive greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, most notably carbon dioxide and methane. By allowing oxygen to enter the peat column within a mire, drainage disrupts the balance between peat accumulation and decomposition, and the subsequent oxidative degradation results in the release of carbon into the atmosphere.<ref name="Minkkinen-1998">{{Cite journal |last1=Minkkinen |first1=Kari |last2=Laine |first2=Jukka |year=1998 |title=Long-term effect of forest drainage on the peat carbon stores of pine mires in Finland |url=http://www.nrc.ca/cgi-bin/cisti/journals/rp/rp2_abst_e?cjfr_x98-104_28_ns_nf_cjfr28-98 |journal=Canadian Journal of Forest Research |volume=28 |issue=9 |pages=1267–1275 |doi=10.1139/x98-104|bibcode=1998CaJFR..28.1267M |url-access=subscription }}</ref> As such, drainage of mires for agriculture transforms them from net carbon sinks to net carbon emitters.<ref name="Frolking-2011"/> Although the emission of methane from mires has been observed to decrease following drainage,<ref name="Scandinavian Journal of Forest Research-2001"/> the total magnitude of emissions from peatland drainage is often greater as rates of peat accumulation are low. Peatland carbon has been described as "irrecoverable" meaning that, if lost due to drainage, it could not be recovered within time scales relevant to climate mitigation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Goldstein |first1=Allie |last2=Turner |first2=Will R. |last3=Spawn |first3=Seth A. |last4=Anderson-Teixeira |first4=Kristina J. |last5=Cook-Patton |first5=Susan |last6=Fargione |first6=Joseph |last7=Gibbs |first7=Holly K. |last8=Griscom |first8=Bronson |last9=Hewson |first9=Jennifer H. |last10=Howard |first10=Jennifer F. |last11=Ledezma |first11=Juan Carlos |last12=Page |first12=Susan |last13=Koh |first13=Lian Pin |last14=Rockström |first14=Johan |last15=Sanderman |first15=Jonathan |last16=Hole |first16=David G. |title=Protecting irrecoverable carbon in Earth's ecosystems |journal=Nature Climate Change |date=April 2020 |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=287–295 |doi=10.1038/s41558-020-0738-8 |bibcode=2020NatCC..10..287G |s2cid=214718837 |url=https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/12124500|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Noon |first1=Monica L. |last2=Goldstein |first2=Allie |last3=Ledezma |first3=Juan Carlos |last4=Roehrdanz |first4=Patrick R. |last5=Cook-Patton |first5=Susan C. |last6=Spawn-Lee |first6=Seth A. |last7=Wright |first7=Timothy Maxwell |last8=Gonzalez-Roglich |first8=Mariano |last9=Hole |first9=David G. |last10=Rockström |first10=Johan |last11=Turner |first11=Will R. |title=Mapping the irrecoverable carbon in Earth's ecosystems |journal=Nature Sustainability |date=January 2022 |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=37–46 |doi=10.1038/s41893-021-00803-6 |s2cid=244349665 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

When undertaken in such a way that preserves the hydrological state of a mire, the anthropogenic use of mires' resources can avoid significant [[greenhouse gas emissions]]. However, continued drainage will result in increased release of carbon, contributing to global warming. As of 2016, it was estimated that drained peatlands account for around 10% of all greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture and forestry.<ref name="Page-2016"/>

==== Palm oil plantations ====
[[File:Kunak-District Sabah Oil-palm-plantation-01.jpg|thumb|Palm oil plantation in Kunak, Malaysia. Peatlands in South East Asia are being converted to palm oil plantation, releasing as much as 76.6 tonnes of CO<sub>2</sub> per hectare.<ref name="Hashim-2018"/>]]
[[Palm oil]] has increasingly become one of the world's largest crops. In comparison to alternatives, palm oil is considered to be among the most efficient sources of [[vegetable oil]] and [[biofuel]], requiring only 0.26 hectares of land to produce 1 ton of oil.<ref name="Hashim-2018">{{Cite journal |last1=Hashim |first1=Zulkifli |last2=Subramaniam |first2=Vijaya |last3=Harun |first3=Mohd Haniff |last4=Kamarudin |first4=Norman |date=June 2018 |title=Carbon footprint of oil palm planted on peat in Malaysia |journal=The International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment |volume=23 |issue=6 |pages=1201–1217 |doi=10.1007/s11367-017-1367-y |bibcode=2018IJLCA..23.1201H |issn=0948-3349 |s2cid=115328269}}</ref> Palm oil has therefore become a popular [[cash crop]] in many low-income countries and has provided economic opportunities for communities. With palm oil as a leading export in countries such as Indonesia and Malaysia, many smallholders have found economic success in palm oil plantations. However, the land selected for plantations are typically substantial carbon stores that promote biodiverse ecosystems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Laurance |first1=William F. |last2=Koh |first2=Lian P. |last3=Butler |first3=Rhett |last4=Sodhi |first4=Navjot S. |last5=Bradshaw |first5=Corey J. A. |last6=Neidel |first6=J. David |last7=Consunji |first7=Hazel |last8=Mateo Vega |first8=Javier |date=April 2010 |title=Improving the Performance of the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil for Nature Conservation |journal=Conservation Biology |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=377–381 |doi=10.1111/j.1523-1739.2010.01448.x |issn=0888-8892 |pmid=20184655 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2010ConBi..24..377L }}</ref>

Palm oil plantations have replaced much of the forested peatlands in Southeast Asia. Estimates now state that 12.9 Mha or about 47% of peatlands in Southeast Asia were deforested by 2006.<ref name="Hooijer-2010">{{Cite journal |last1=Hooijer |first1=A. |last2=Page |first2=S. |last3=Canadell |first3=J. G. |last4=Silvius |first4=M. |last5=Kwadijk |first5=J. |last6=Wösten |first6=H. |last7=Jauhiainen |first7=J. |date=2010-05-12 |title=Current and future CO2 emissions from drained peatlands in Southeast Asia |journal=Biogeosciences |volume=7 |issue=5 |pages=1505–1514 |bibcode=2010BGeo....7.1505H |doi=10.5194/bg-7-1505-2010 |issn=1726-4189 |doi-access=free|hdl=2381/11179 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> In their natural state, peatlands are [[Waterlogging (agriculture)|waterlogged]] with high water tables making for an inefficient soil.{{Clarify|reason=inefficient soil is unclear in meaning|date=September 2023}}<ref name="Hashim-2018"/> To create viable soil for plantation, the mires in [[Tropics|tropical regions]] of Indonesia and Malaysia are drained and cleared.

The peatland forests harvested for palm oil production serve as above- and below-ground carbon stores, containing at least 42,069 million metric tonnes (Mt) of soil carbon.<ref name="Hooijer-2010"/> Exploitation of this land raises many environmental concerns, namely increased [[greenhouse gas emissions]], risk of fires and a decrease in biodiversity. Greenhouse gas emissions for palm oil planted on peatlands is estimated to be between the equivalent of 12.4 (best case) to 76.6&nbsp;t&nbsp;CO<sub>2</sub>/ha (worst case).<ref name="Hashim-2018"/> Tropical peatland converted to palm oil plantation can remain a net source of carbon to the atmosphere after 12 years.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McCalmont |first1=Jon |last2=Kho |first2=Lip Khoon |last3=Teh |first3=Yit Arn |last4=Lewis |first4=Kennedy |last5=Chocholek |first5=Melanie |last6=Rumpang |first6=Elisa |last7=Hill |first7=Timothy |title=Short- and long-term carbon emissions from oil palm plantations converted from logged tropical peat swamp forest |journal=Global Change Biology |language=en |publication-date=2 February 2021 |volume=27 |issue=11 |pages=2361–2376 |bibcode=2021GCBio..27.2361M |doi=10.1111/gcb.15544 |issn=1354-1013 |pmid=33528067 |s2cid=231757053 |doi-access=free |hdl=2164/17863 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

In their natural state, peatlands are resistant to fire. Drainage of peatlands for palm oil plantations creates a dry layer of flammable peat. As peat is carbon dense, fires occurring in compromised peatlands release extreme amounts of both carbon dioxide and toxic smoke into the air. These fires add to greenhouse gas emissions while also causing thousands of deaths every year.{{Citation needed|date=October 2023}}

Decreased biodiversity due to deforestation and drainage makes these ecosystem more vulnerable and less resilient to change. [[Homogeneity and heterogeneity|Homogenous]] ecosystems are at an increased risk to extreme climate conditions and are less likely to recover from fires.
[[File:Unseasonal peat fire in Russia (Copernicus).jpg|thumb|Satellite image of peat fire in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2021]]

=== Fires ===
Some peatlands are being dried out by [[climate change]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-01-25 |title=Climate change threatening buried UK treasures |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-60091485 |access-date=2022-01-25}}</ref> Drainage of peatlands due to climatic factors may also increase the risk of fires, presenting further risk of [[carbon]] and [[methane]] to release into the atmosphere.<ref name="Page-2016"/> Due to their naturally high moisture content, pristine mires have a generally low risk of fire ignition. The drying of this waterlogged state means that the carbon-dense vegetation becomes vulnerable to fire. In addition, due to the oxygen deficient nature of the vegetation, the peat fires can smoulder beneath the surface causing incomplete combustion of the organic matter and resulting in extreme emissions events.<ref name="Page-2016"/>

In recent years, the occurrence of [[wildfire]]s in peatlands has increased significantly worldwide particularly in the tropical regions. This can be attributed to a combination of drier weather and changes in land use which involve the drainage of water from the landscape.<ref name="Frolking-2011"/> This resulting loss of [[biomass]] through combustion has led to significant emissions of [[greenhouse gas]]ses both in tropical and boreal/temperate peatlands.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Granath |first1=Gustaf |last2=Moore |first2=Paul A. |last3=Lukenbach |first3=Maxwell C. |last4=Waddington |first4=James M. |date=2016-06-27 |title=Mitigating wildfire carbon loss in managed northern peatlands through restoration |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=6 |issue=1 |article-number=28498 |doi=10.1038/srep28498  |doi-access=free|pmid=27346604 |issn=2045-2322 |pmc=4921962 |bibcode=2016NatSR...628498G}}</ref> Fire events are predicted to become more frequent with the warming and drying of the global climate.<ref name="Rydin-2013"/>

== Management and rehabilitation ==
{{See also|Peatland restoration}}

The United Nations [[Convention on Biological Diversity]] highlights peatlands as key ecosystems to be conserved and protected. The convention requires governments at all levels to present action plans for the conservation and management of wetland environments. Wetlands are also protected under the 1971 [[Ramsar Convention]].<ref name="Page-2016"/>

Often, restoration is done by blocking drainage channels in the peatland, and allowing natural vegetation to recover.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 3, 2019 |title=The natural world can help save us from climate catastrophe &#124; George Monbiot |url=http://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2019/apr/03/natural-world-climate-catastrophe-rewilding |website=The Guardian}}</ref> Rehabilitation projects undertaken in North America and Europe usually focus on the rewetting of peatlands and revegetation of native species. This acts to mitigate carbon release in the short term before the new growth of vegetation provides a new source of organic litter to fuel the peat formation in the long term.<ref name="Page-2016"/> [[UNEP]] is supporting peatland restoration in Indonesia.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Environment |first=U. N. |date=2020-08-10 |title=UNEP supports project to restore peatlands in Indonesia |url=http://www.unenvironment.org/news-and-stories/story/unep-supports-project-restore-peatlands-indonesia |access-date=2020-08-11 |website=UN Environment |language=en}}</ref>

Peat extraction is forbidden in Chile since April 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.bcn.cl/leychile/navegar?idNorma=1202472 |title=Ley 21660 sobre protección ambiental de las turberas |year=2024 |access-date=2024-09-11 |website=bcn.cl |publisher=Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional |language=Spanish}}</ref>

'''''Platycerium bifurcatum''''', commonly known as '''elkhorn fern''', is a species of [[epiphyte|epiphytic]] plant in the fern family [[Polypodiaceae]]. It is native to Australia and is widespread on the entire east coast.

==Description==
''Platycerium bifurcatum'' is an epiphytic fern with dimorphic fronds, usually found growing on tree trunks and branches. The rhizome is short-creeping and much-branched. It is covered by the shield-like nest fronds (also called basal fronds or sterile fronds), which are more or less rounded and overlapping, and are appressed to the host tree.{{R|JONES|HOSHIZAKIa}} They can grow to about {{cvt|45|cm}} diameter. Their upper margins are deeply lobed and spreading, such that they trap organic litter which later becomes a nutrient source for the plant.{{R|FOA|ATF}}

The fertile fronds (also known as foliage fronds) are markedly different. They are semi-erect becoming pendant, up to {{cvt|90|cm}} long, very narrow at the base and gradually widening. They fork two or three times, with the final segments being up to {{cvt|30|cm}} long and {{cvt|3|cm}} wide.{{R|JONES}} Spores are produced on the undersides of these final segments.{{R|FOA|ATF}}

===Growth habit===
Elkhorn ferns form a colony, with new plantlets growing from buds on the lower margin of the nest fronds. Nest fronds die back after reaching maturity but remain with the colony, curling inwards and retaining whatever litter they have collected, while roots of the colony members grow into them.{{R|JONES|BURNS}} In this way, with nest leaves building up and new plantlets on the exterior, the colony can grow to huge sizes.{{R|JONES}}

A study published in 2021 attempted to determine whether the individuals in these colonies specialise for different roles. The researchers found that the foliage fronds (called "strap fronds" in the study) of colony members near the bottom are less likely to produce spores than those of members near the top of the colony. They also found evidence that the nest fronds of lower members absorb more water than those of the members above them – in turn those higher members have more hydrophobic nest fronds that channel water to the lower members.{{R|BURNS}}

The researchers also found that colonies are mostly clonal, but occasionally include unrelated individuals. They concluded that their findings, collectively, may constitute the first evidence of [[eusociality]] in plants.{{R|BURNS}} 

==Taxonomy==
This plant was first described in 1799, as ''Acrostichum bifurcatum'', by Spanish botanist [[Antonio José Cavanilles]].{{R|CAV}} It was given its current binomial name by Danish botanist [[Carl Christensen (botanist)|Carl Christensen]] in 1906.

In a 1972 study, botanist [[Barbara Joe Hoshizaki]] published a phylogenic review of ''Platycerium'' in which the known species were ordered into three groups. The ''Afro-American'' and the ''Malayan-Asiatic'' groups both contained seven species, and the ''Javan-Australian'' group four.{{R|HOSHIZAKIa}} The latter group consisted of ''P.&nbsp;bifurcatum'', ''[[Platycerium hillii|P.&nbsp;hillii]]'', ''[[Platycerium veitchii|P.&nbsp;veitchii]]'' and ''[[Platycerium willinckii|P.&nbsp;willinckii]]''. In 1982, [[Elbert Hennipman]] and [[Marco C. Roos]] published a book in which they recognised only ''P.&nbsp;bifurcatum'' of this group, and reduced the other three to subspecies of it.{{R|HENNIPMAN}} This move was criticised by Hoshizaki in 1990 and later by [[Hans-Peter Kreier]] and [[Harald Schneider (botanist)|Harald Schneider]] in 2006.{{R|HOSHIZAKIb|KREIER}} {{As of|2026|8}}, only the [[Global Biodiversity Information Facility]] and [[World Flora Online]] accept some (not all) subspecies.{{R|GBIF|WFO}} No subspecies are recognised by the Australian National Herbarium,{{R|APNI}} [[Plants of the World Online]],{{R|POWO}} or World Ferns.{{R|HASSLER}}

===Etymology===
The genus name ''Platycerium'' comes from the Greek ''platys'' (flat), and ''ceras'' (horn), while the [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''bifurcatum'' means forked. Both names are referring to the morphology of the fertile fronds.{{R|ANBG}}

===Common name===
It is commonly known as elkhorn fern.{{R|PLANTNET|JONES|TOOHEY}}

==Distribution and habitat==
This species is native to eastern Australia, from southern [[New South Wales]] to northern [[Queensland]],{{R|JONES|ATF}} including [[Lord Howe Island]].{{R|PLANTNET}} In the southern areas it grows on trees and boulders in a variety of forest types, including swamp forest and open forest, while in north Queensland it grows mainly on trees in montane rainforest.{{R|JONES|ATF}}

It has been introduced to many countries, including the [[Canary Islands]], Colombia, Hawaii, [[KwaZulu-Natal (National Assembly of South Africa constituency)|KwaZulu-Natal]], New Zealand and Taiwan.{{R|POWO}} The map at the [[Global Biodiversity Information Facility]] website shows occurrences in North and South America, Europe, south eastern Africa and throughout the Asia-Pacific region.{{R|GBIF}}

==Conservation status==
This species has been assessed to be of [[least-concern species|least concern]] by the Queensland Government under its [[Nature Conservation Act 1992|Nature Conservation Act]].{{R|DESQLD}}. It is not listed on either of the New South Wales or Australian Governments' threatened species lists, nor has it been assessed by the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]].

==Cultivation==
''Platycerium bifurcatum'' is commonly cultivated around the world as an ornamental plant.{{R|KREIER|UWIS}} They are easily propagated by division and can be mounted on trees or boards, or grown in baskets.{{R|JONES|UWIS}} With a minimum temperature requirement of {{convert|5|C|F|abbr=on}}, in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions it may be grown outdoors in sheltered locations, otherwise as a houseplant.<ref name=RHSAZ /> It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{R|RHS}}
