'''''Dacrycarpus dacrydioides''''', the '''kahikatea''' (from [[Māori language|Māori]]) or '''white pine''', is a [[Pinophyta|coniferous]] tree in the family [[Podocarpaceae]], [[endemism|endemic]] to [[New Zealand]]. It is New Zealand's tallest tree species, gaining heights of {{convert|60|m|abbr=off}} over a life span of 600 years. It was first described botanically by the French botanist [[Achille Richard]] in 1832 as ''Podocarpus'' ''dacrydioides'', and was given its current [[binomial name]] ''Dacrycarpus dacrydioides'' in 1969 by the American botanist [[David John de Laubenfels|David de Laubenfels]]. Analysis of DNA has confirmed its evolutionary relationship with other species in the genera ''[[Dacrycarpus]]'' and ''[[Dacrydium]]''.

In [[Māori culture]], it is an important source of timber for the building of [[Waka (canoe)|waka]] and making of tools, of food in the form of its berries, and of dye. Its use for timber and its damp fertile habitat, ideal for [[Dairy farming in New Zealand|dairy farming]], have led to its decimation almost everywhere except [[South Westland]].

Kahikatea seeds have fleshy structures called [[Receptacle (botany)|receptacles]] attached to them, which encourage birds such as [[kererū]] and [[tūī]] to eat them and disperse the seeds. The water storage ability of these structures may also act to protect seeds from drying out. It supports many smaller plants in its own branches, which are called [[epiphyte]]s; 100 different species have been recorded on one tree alone.

== Description ==
Kahikatea is a [[conifer]]ous tree reaching a height of {{Convert|50–65|m|ft|abbr=on}}, making it the tallest New Zealand tree,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Benson |first=Nigel |date=23 January 2014 |title=NZ's tallest tree growing ever taller |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/nzs-tallest-tree-growing-ever-taller/72KVQGXUNWX6V3U6NCBZBJXV7U/ |access-date=20 February 2022 |website=[[New Zealand Herald]] |language=en-NZ |archive-date=20 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220220044524/https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/nzs-tallest-tree-growing-ever-taller/72KVQGXUNWX6V3U6NCBZBJXV7U/ |url-status=live }}</ref> with a trunk {{Convert|1–2|m|ft|abbr=on}} through. It has a 600 year life span and gains maturity after between 250 and 450 years.<ref name=":6" /> Near the base of the tree, the roots are typically [[Buttress root|buttressed]] and grooved. Adult trees that grow in clusters develop interlocking root islands that may help prevent individual trees from falling during high winds.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Sukias |first1=James P. S. |last2=Tanner |first2=Chris C. |last3=Clarkson |first3=Beverley R. |last4=Bodmin |first4=Kerry A. |last5=Woodward |first5=Simon |last6=Bartlam |first6=Scott |last7=Costley |first7=Kerry |date=January 2024 |title=Jump-starting podocarp forest establishment in a wetland dominated by invasive willow |journal=Restoration Ecology |language=en |volume=32 |issue=1 |doi=10.1111/rec.14031 |issn=1061-2971|doi-access=free |bibcode=2024ResEc..3214031S }}</ref> The wood itself is odourless and white. The majority of the trunk is branchless—in adults around three quarters—and has grey or dark grey coloured bark which falls off thickly in flakes. Young adults have no branches in a third to a half of the trunk and have a conic shape.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=de Lange |first=P. J. |date=2004 |title=Dacrycarpus dacrydioides |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/dacrycarpus-dacrydioides/ |access-date=12 February 2022 |website=[[New Zealand Plant Conservation Network]] |language=en |archive-date=26 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220126012050/https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/dacrycarpus-dacrydioides/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In juveniles the leaves are 3–7 (reaching {{cvt|4|mm}} in young adults) by {{cvt|0.5–1|mm}} and a dark green to red colour that come to a marked point. They are narrow, arranged in almost opposite pairs spreading away from a wider base, and curved like a [[scythe]]. In adulthood the leaves change dramatically and are a brown-green colour and just {{cvt|1–2|mm}} long, waxy, and grow overlapping one another tightly.<ref name=":0" />

As a conifer, kahikatea has no flowers and instead has [[Conifer cone|cones]]. Male cones, which occur on different trees to female ones, are {{cvt|1|cm}} long and rectangular. The pollen is a pale yellow colour and has a three-pored or trisaccate shape that is distinctive in the New Zealand flora and so can be identified easily.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pocknall |first=D.T. |date=1981 |title=Pollen morphology of the New Zealand species of Dacrydium Selander, Podocarpus L'Heritier, and Dacrycarpus Endlicher (Podocarpaceae) |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/0028825X.1981.10425191 |journal=[[New Zealand Journal of Botany]] |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=67–95 |doi=10.1080/0028825x.1981.10425191 |bibcode=1981NZJB...19...67P |issn=0028-825X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The fruit is highly modified with a yellow-orange fleshy [[Receptacle (botany)|receptacle]] that is {{cvt|2.5–6.5|mm}} long. The purple-black seed is roughly spherical and {{cvt|4–6|mm}} in diameter. Both the seed and the ovary are covered with a thin layer of wax.<ref name=":0" /> Kahikatea has a [[diploid]] chromosome count of 20.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Davies |first1=B. J. |last2=O'Brien |first2=I. E. W. |last3=Murray |first3=B. G. |date=1997 |title=Karyotypes, chromosome bands and genome size variation in New Zealand endemic gymnosperms |journal=[[Plant Systematics and Evolution]] |language=en |volume=208 |issue=3 |pages=169–185 |doi=10.1007/BF00985440 |bibcode=1997PSyEv.208..169D |s2cid=5624551 |issn=1615-6110}}</ref><gallery mode="packed" widths="110" heights="110">
File:Dacrycarpus dacrydioides male cones.jpg|Male cones with pollen
File:Dacrycarpus dacrydioides female cones.jpg|Female cones beginning to fruit
File:Dacrycarpus dacrydioides cones2.jpg|Ripe fruit
File:Dacrycarpus dacrydioides young adult.jpg|Young adult's conical growth habit
</gallery>

=== Phytochemistry ===
Several different [[glycoside]]s have been isolated from the leaves; the [[tricetin]] 3',5'-di-O-/β-glucopyranoside and 3'-0-β-xylopyranoside have been found only in kahikatea.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Markham |first1=Kenneth R. |last2=Whitehouse |first2=Lynley A. |date=1984 |title=Unique flavonoid glycosides from the new zealand white pine, Dacrycarpus dacrydioides |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0031942200849444 |journal=[[Phytochemistry (journal)|Phytochemistry]] |language=en |volume=23 |issue=9 |pages=1931–1936 |doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(00)84944-4 |bibcode=1984PChem..23.1931M |issn=0031-9422|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The receptacles and seeds have been found to contain [[anthocyanin]]s, rare in [[gymnosperm]]s, which it was suggested in one 1988 paper make the fruit as a whole more attractive to prospective animal dispersers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Andersen |first=Øyvind M. |date=1988 |title=Semipreparative Isolation and Structure Determination of Pelargonidin 3-O-alpha-L-rhamnopyranosyl-(1->2)-beta-D-glucopyranoside and Other Anthocyanins from the Tree Dacrycarpus dacrydioides. |journal=[[Acta Chemica Scandinavica]] |language=en |volume=42b |pages=462–468 |doi=10.3891/acta.chem.scand.42b-0462 |issn=0904-213X|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
{{Stack|float=right|
[[File:Standing Straight And Tall - Kahikatea (51236257730) (cropped).jpg|thumb|A stand of kahikatea in the Pohangina Valley.]]
}}
{{Blockquote
| quote = The banks were completely clothed with the finest timber my eyes ever beheld, of a tree we had before seen, but only at a distance [...]. Thick woods of it were everywhere upon the banks, every tree as straight as a pine, and of immense size, and the higher we went the more numerous they were.
| author = [[Joseph Banks]], possibly describing a former stand on the [[Waihou River]], 1769<ref>{{Cite book |last=Banks |first=Joseph |url=https://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-Bea01Bank-t1-body-d7-d4.html#n496 |title=The Endeavour Journal of Joseph Banks 1768–1771 |publisher=[[Angus & Robertson|Angus and Robertson Limited]] |year=1962 |editor-last=Beaglehole |editor-first=John Cawte |pages=435–436 |author-link=Joseph Banks}}</ref>
}}
Kahikatea was first described in 1832 by the French botanist [[Achille Richard]] in his ''Essai d'une Flore de la Nouvelle Zélande'' (Essay on the Flora of New Zealand) as ''Podocarpus dacrydioides''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=d'Urville |first=Jules Dumont |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15395 |title=Voyage de la corvette l'Astrolabe: exécuté par ordre du roi, pendant les années 1826-1827-1828-1829 |date=1832 |publisher=J. Tastu |location=Paris |page=358 |language=Fr |author-link=Dumont D'Urville |via=the [[Biodiversity Heritage Library]]}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=de Laubenfels |first=David J. |author-link=David John de Laubenfels|date=1969 |title=A Revision Of The Melanesian And Pacific Rainforest Conifers, I. Podocarpaceae, In Part |journal=[[Journal of the Arnold Arboretum]] |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=315–369 |doi=10.5962/bhl.part.24691 |jstor=43781661 |s2cid=88784997 |issn=0004-2625|doi-access=free }}</ref> There is an earlier record given in the 1825 issue of ''Mémoires du Muséum d'histoire naturelle'' as ''Podocarpus thujoides'', but it lacks a description.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/84591 |title=Mémoires du Muséum d'histoire naturelle. |date=1825 |publisher=G. Dufour |volume=13 |location=Paris |page=75 |via=the [[Biodiversity Heritage Library]]}}</ref> It was [[Nomen illegitimum|superfluously]] named ''Dacrydium excelsum'' by [[Allan Cunningham (botanist)|Allan Cunningham]] in the 1838 issue of ''[[Annals of Natural History]]'',<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cunningham |first1=Allan |author-link1=Allan Cunningham (botanist) |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/22966 |title=Annals of natural history. |publisher=R. and J.E. Taylor |year=1838 |volume=1 |location=London |page=213 |via=the [[Biodiversity Heritage Library]] |archive-date=21 February 2023 |access-date=3 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230221202700/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/22966 |url-status=live }}</ref> and transferred to the genus ''[[Nageia]]'' by [[Otto Kuntze]] in 1891.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kuntze |first=Otto |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/327 |title=Revisio generum plantarum |date=1891 |publisher=A. Felix [etc.] |location=Leipzig |via=the [[Biodiversity Heritage Library]] |archive-date=9 July 2022 |access-date=3 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220709041607/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/327 |url-status=live }}</ref> It was given its current [[binomial name]], ''Dacrycarpus dacrydioides'', in 1969 by American botanist [[David John de Laubenfels|David de Laubenfels]].<ref name=":1" />

=== Etymology ===
The genus name ''Dacrycarpus'' derives from [[Greek language|Greek]], and means tear shaped fruit, and the [[specific epithet]] ''dacrydioides'' is after its similarity to species in the genus ''[[Dacrydium]]''.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite book |last=Farjon |first=Aljos |title=A Handbook of the World's Conifers |volume=2 |publisher=[[Brill Publishers]] |publication-place=Boston, United States |date=2017 |isbn=978-90-04-32451-0 |page=328}}</ref> Common names include kahikatea, from the [[Māori language]], and white pine. Other Māori names recorded by 19th century [[Ethnography|ethnographers]] include: katea, kaikatea, koroī, kōaka, kahika, and the name kāī (for the young tree).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kahikatea Plant Use Details |url=https://maoriplantuse.landcareresearch.co.nz/WebForms/PeoplePlantsDetails.aspx?firstcome=firstcome&PKey=dcd7a5b7-fdc1-4eb6-9583-014f4bfbe31b |url-status=live |access-date=6 March 2022 |website=Māori Plant Use Database |publisher=[[Landcare Research]] |archive-date=6 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220306093343/https://maoriplantuse.landcareresearch.co.nz/WebForms/PeoplePlantsDetails.aspx?firstcome=firstcome&PKey=dcd7a5b7-fdc1-4eb6-9583-014f4bfbe31b }}</ref> The Māori name kahikatea means "white kahika", with kahika being descended from the [[Proto-Oceanic language|Proto-Oceanic]] word ''*Kapika'', primarily used in other [[Polynesian languages]] to describe ''[[Syzygium malaccense]]'', or the malay apple.<ref>{{cite web|title=Kakiha|work=Te Māra Reo: The Language Garden|year=2022|publisher=Benton Family Trust|url=https://www.temarareo.org/TMR-Kahika.html |access-date=16 June 2025}}</ref> The name white pine was coined by [[James Cook]].<ref name="MeaningTrees">{{cite q|Q118646408|pp=114–119}}</ref>

=== Evolution ===
A 2022 study in ''[[Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution]]'', found a [[phylogeny]], or evolutionary tree, in which kahikatea is found to be within a ''Darcydioid'' [[clade]]. This group of species that share a common ancestor also gave rise to the other ''Dacrycarpus'' species as well as those in the genus ''[[Dacrydium]]''. They suggested it diverged from a common ancestor around 60 million years ago, in the early [[paleogene]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Luo |last2=Jin |first2=Wei-Tao |last3=Liu |first3=Xin-Quan |last4=Wang |first4=Xiao-Quan |date=1 January 2022 |title=New insights into the phylogeny and evolution of Podocarpaceae inferred from transcriptomic data |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1055790321002748 |journal=[[Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution]] |language=en |volume=166 |article-number=107341 |doi=10.1016/j.ympev.2021.107341 |pmid=34740782 |bibcode=2022MolPE.16607341C |s2cid=243482772 |issn=1055-7903|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This is represented in the cladogram below.

== Distribution and habitat ==
{{Multiple image
| image1            = Kahikatea in lake brunner.jpg
| image2            = Dacrycarpus dacrydioides epiphytes.jpg
| caption1          = Kahikatea in [[Lake Brunner]]
| caption2          = The kahikatea can support many other plants, such as those seen here up the trunk and in the higher branches.
| direction         = vertical
}}
Kahikatea is [[Endemism|endemic]] to the [[North Island|North]], [[South Island|South]], and [[Stewart Island|Stewart]] Islands of New Zealand,<ref name=":0" /> and is the only member of the genus ''Dacrycarpus'' found in the country.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/> It inhabits mostly lowland forests between {{cvt|0–600|m}} above sea level, though may in rare cases reach [[Montane ecosystems|montane]] areas. It used to dominate a swamp forest type that now exists almost only on the [[South Westland]] region of the South Island.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Salmon |first=John T. (John Tenison) |url=http://archive.org/details/fieldguidetonati0000salm |title=A field guide to the native trees of New Zealand |date=1986 |publisher=[[Reed Methuen]] |location=Auckland |isbn=978-0-474-00122-2 |page=6 |via=the [[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> Kahikatea prefers flooded or [[Alluvium|alluvial]] soils with low levels of drainage,<ref name=":0" /> which in Westland occur from post glaciation events.<ref name=":2" />

== Ecology ==
Under optimal circumstances a mature kahikatea can produce {{Convert|800|kg|lb}} of fruit, equivalent to 4.5 million seeds, in a year. The fruit contains a special fleshy structure called a receptacle which helps attract birds such as the [[kererū]], [[tūī]], and [[New Zealand bellbird|bellbird]], who then eat the fruit and disperse the seed elsewhere. One 2008 study in the New Zealand Journal of Ecology found a mean retention time of kahikatea seeds in kererū of 44.5 minutes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wotton |first1=Debra M. |last2=Clout |first2=Mick N. |last3=Kelly |first3=Dave |date=2008 |title=Seed retention times in the New Zealand pigeon (Hemiphaga novaezeelandiae novaeseelandiae) |journal=[[New Zealand Journal of Ecology]] |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=1–6 |jstor=24058095 |issn=0110-6465}}</ref>  It was suggested in a 1989 study that the high water content of the receptacle may also help protect the seeds, which are vulnerable to drying out, from dry conditions. It may also serve as a storage vessel for water.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Fountain |first1=David W. |last2=Holdsworth |first2=Jacqueline M. |last3=Outred |first3=Heather A. |date=1989 |title=The dispersal unit of Dacrycarpus dacrydioides (A. Rich.) de Laubenfels (Podocarpaceae) and the significance of the fleshy receptacle |journal=[[Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society]] |volume=99 |issue=3 |pages=197–207 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.1989.tb00399.x |issn=0024-4074}}</ref> The bluish seeds have very strong UV reflectance, which is visible to some species of birds.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=W.G. |last2=Hodgkinson |first2=I.J. |last3=Johnson |first3=P.N. |date=1 January 1990 |title=A test for ultraviolet reflectance from fleshy fruits of New Zealand plant species |journal=[[New Zealand Journal of Botany]] |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=21–24 |doi=10.1080/0028825X.1990.10412340 |issn=0028-825X|doi-access=free |bibcode=1990NZJB...28...21L }}</ref>

Kahikatea can support a vast number of non-parasitic plants that live in its branches, called [[epiphyte]]s. One 2002 study identified between 90 and 100 species occurring on one mature tree. This included 49 [[vascular plant]]s and over 50 [[non-vascular plant]]s, which the authors identified as comparable to the number found on a ''[[Prumnopitys exigua]]'' in Bolivian [[cloud forest]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hofstede |first1=Robert G. M. |last2=Dickinson |first2=Katharine J. M. |last3=Mark |first3=Alan F. |date=2002 |title=Distribution, abundance and biomass of epiphyte-lianoid communities in a New Zealand lowland Nothofagus-podocarp temperate rain forest: tropical comparisons: Epiphytic-lianoid communities in temperate rainforest |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1046/j.1365-2699.2001.00613.x |journal=[[Journal of Biogeography]] |language=en |volume=28 |issue=8 |pages=1033–1049 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-2699.2001.00613.x|s2cid=85726530 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[Intraspecific]] competition between kahikatea trees was found in a 1999 study to be an important factor in their survival and overall success, affecting both the rates of growth and of mortality. Older trees have a particularly large advantage over resources compared to newer ones, and also have higher growth rates.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Duncan |first=Richard P. |date=1991 |title=Competition and the Coexistence of Species in a Mixed Podocarp Stand |journal=[[Journal of Ecology]] |volume=79 |issue=4 |pages=1073–1084 |doi=10.2307/2261099 |jstor=2261099 |bibcode=1991JEcol..79.1073D |issn=0022-0477}}</ref> Following flooding or other natural events, kahikatea has been found to require an open [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] in order to re-establish. Because of the consistency of these events in South Westland however, many forested areas do not progress beyond regaining kahikatea and [[rimu]], as other species, such as [[kāmahi]], need the environment to improve before they can return.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Duncan |first=Richard P. |date=1993 |title=Flood Disturbance and the Coexistence of Species in a Lowland Podocarp Forest, South Westland, New Zealand |journal=[[Journal of Ecology]] |volume=81 |issue=3 |pages=403–416 |doi=10.2307/2261519 |jstor=2261519 |bibcode=1993JEcol..81..403D |issn=0022-0477}}</ref> Kahikatea plays host to the New Zealand endemic beetle ''[[Agapanthida pulchella]]'',<ref>{{Cite Q|Q56166058}}</ref> and is the primary host of the lichen species ''[[Ramalina erumpens]]''.<ref>{{cite Q|Q111484771}}</ref>

== In Māori culture ==
{{Quote box
|align=left
| quote = ''He toa piki rākau kahikatea, he kai na te pakiaka.''

The champion kahikatea climber is food for the roots.

– Māori proverb or {{lang|mi|whakataukī}} about the dangers of gathering the fruit<ref>{{Cite book |last=Park |first=Geoff |title=Ngā Uruora / The Groves of Life: Ecology and History in a New Zealand Landscape |publisher=[[Victoria University Press]] |year=1995 |isbn=0-86473-291-0 |location= Wellington |page=35}}</ref>
| width = 500px
}}
In [[Māori mythology]], kahikatea is a child of [[Tāne]], the god of forests and birds, and Hine-wao-riki. It served as an important source of wood for the making of tools, of dye, and of food from its berries. Māori sometimes climbed more than {{Convert|100|ft|m|abbr=on}} to collect the berries.<ref name=":7" />

The 19th-century British ethnographers [[William Colenso]], [[Richard Taylor (missionary)|Richard Taylor]] and [[Elsdon Best]] recorded the fruit of kahikatea (called {{lang|mi|koroī}}) being eaten.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Colenso |first=William |author-link=William Colenso |date=1868 |title=Essay on the Botany, Geographic and Economic, of the North Island of the New Zealand Group. |url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/periodicals/TPRSNZ1868-1.2.18.1 |journal=[[Transactions and Proceedings of the Royal Society of New Zealand]] |volume=1 |page=31 |via=[[Papers Past]] |archive-date=3 July 2022 |access-date=3 July 2022 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20220703061004/https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/periodicals/TPRSNZ1868-1.2.18.1 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=Taylor_439>{{Cite book |last=Taylor |first=Richard |author-link= Richard Taylor (missionary) |url=http://archive.org/details/teikaamauiornew01taylgoog |title=Te Ika a Maui, or New Zealand, and Its Inhabitants |date=1855 |publisher=Wertheim and Macintosh |page=439 |via=the [[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> Best described climbers collecting berries in a basket, which they lowered on a cord, to be emptied, then hoisted and filled again.<ref name=Best1907>{{Cite journal |last=Best |first=Elsdon |author-link= Elsdon Best |date=1907 |title=Maori Forest Lore: Being some Account of Native Forest Lore and Woodcraft, as also of many Myths, Rites, Customs, and Superstitions connected with the Flora and Fauna of the Tuhoe or Ure-wera District.—Part I. |url= https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/periodicals/TPRSNZ1907-40.2.9.1.15/1 |journal=[[Transactions and Proceedings of the Royal Society of New Zealand]] |volume=40 |pages=210–211 |via=[[Papers Past]]}}</ref> J. H. Kerry-Nicholls and Colenso both recorded a blue or black dye being obtained from the soot of burning kahikatea's resinous heartwood, called {{lang|mi|kāpara}} or {{lang|mi|māpara}}. The dye was then used in tattooing.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kerry-Nicholls |first=J. H. |date=1886 |title=The Origin, Physical Characteristics, and Manners and Customs of the Maori Race, from Data Derived During a Recent Exploration of the King Country, New Zealand. |journal=[[The Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland]] |volume=15 |pages=187–209 |doi=10.2307/2841577 |jstor=2841577 |issn=0959-5295|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Colenso |first=William |date=1891 |title=Art. XLVII.—Vestiges: Reminiscences: Memorabilia of Works, Deeds, and Sayings of the Ancient Maoris. |url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/periodicals/TPRSNZ1891-24.2.4.1.47 |journal=[[Transactions and Proceedings of the Royal Society of New Zealand]] |volume=24 |page=449 |via=[[Papers Past]] |archive-date=3 July 2022 |access-date=3 July 2022 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20220703062250/https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/periodicals/TPRSNZ1891-24.2.4.1.47 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=Best1907 /> The resin of kahikatea was used as chewing gum.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bennett |first=George |date=1860 |title= Gatherings of a Naturalist in Australasia |place=London |publisher=John Van Voorst |url= https://www.google.co.nz/books/edition/Gatherings_of_a_Naturalist_in_Australasi/Vok5AAAAcAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Gatherings+of+a+Naturalist+in+Australasia+excelsum&pg=PA414&printsec=frontcover |page=414 |access-date=18 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Taylor |first=Richard |author-link= Richard Taylor (missionary) |url= http://archive.org/details/teikaamauiornew01taylgoog |title=Te Ika a Maui, or New Zealand, and Its Inhabitants |date=1855 |publisher=Wertheim and Macintosh |via=the [[Internet Archive]]}}</ref>{{Page needed|date=September 2026}}

[[Waka (canoe)|Waka]] (canoes) could be made from kahikatea, but Best recorded that they were far inferior to those made from [[tōtara]], because kahikatea sapwood was not durable.<ref name=Best1907 /> The heartwood was far stronger and R. H. Matthews described it as being used in tools and weapons such as spears.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Matthews |first=R. H. |date=1910 |title=Reminiscences of Maori life fifty years ago. |url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/periodicals/TPRSNZ1910-43.2.2.1.54 |journal=[[Transactions of the New Zealand Institute]] |volume=43 |pages=598–605 |via=[[Papers Past]] |archive-date=3 July 2022 |access-date=3 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220703065429/https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/periodicals/TPRSNZ1910-43.2.2.1.54 |url-status=live }}</ref> Medicinal applications were described by W. H. Goldie, who recorded the leaves being used to cure "internal complaints" as a [[decoction]] or in a steam bath.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goldie |first=W. H. |date=1904 |title=Art. I.—Maori Medical Lore: Notes on the Causes of Disease and Treatment of the Sick among the Maori People of New Zealand, as believed and practised in Former Times, together with some Account of Various Ancient Rites connected with the Same. |url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/periodicals/TPRSNZ1904-37.2.11.1.1 |journal=[[Transactions and Proceedings of the Royal Society of New Zealand]] |volume=37 |pages=1–20 |via=[[Papers Past]]}}</ref>

== Early European uses ==
{{Multiple image
| total_width       = 500
| image1            = Timber_Milling_Gang.tif
| alt1              = Black and white photo of men processing a large kahikatea trunk
| caption1          = A milling gang, employed by Cook's timber mill, likely felling kahikatea
| image2            = Palmerston Cooperage and Box Factory.jpg
| caption2          = The Palmerston Cooperage and Box Factory was one of many factories used to produce boxes from kahikatea wood.
| alt2              = Black and white photo of a wooden building
}}

After visiting the [[Waihou River]] area in November 1769, Captain [[James Cook]] was impressed by the trees, believing that these would be a good source for masts and timber for ships.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/> This led to an early shipbuilding industry in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, where European vessels would visit the Waihou River area to trade for kahikatea timber, despite the timber being easily water logged and not suitable for this purpose. By the 1820s, [[Agathis australis|kauri]] spurs had begun to be used instead.<ref name="MeaningTrees"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://teara.govt.nz/mi/hauraki-coromandel-region/page-5 |title=Hauraki–Coromandel region – Māori and European: 1769 to 1840 |first=Paul |last=Monin |website=[[Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand]] |date= 15 December 2010 |access-date=16 June 2025}}</ref>

During the 19th century, kahikatea wood, due to being soft and odourless, was made into pulp, barrels and boxes, notably butter boxes for butter being exported to the United Kingdom, and occasionally to create furniture.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Park |first=Geoff |title=Ngā Uruora / The Groves of Life: Ecology and History in a New Zealand Landscape |publisher=[[Victoria University Press]] |year=1995 |isbn=0-86473-291-0 |location= Wellington |pages=35, 49}}</ref><ref name="Wassilieff">{{Cite web |last=Wassilieff |first=Maggy |title=Rimu and kahikatea |url=https://teara.govt.nz/en/conifers/page-3 |access-date=2 July 2022 |website=[[Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand|Te Ara]] |archive-date=1 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220701071457/https://teara.govt.nz/en/conifers/page-3 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="MeaningTrees"/>

== Conservation ==

Prior to the arrival of humans in New Zealand around 75% of the country was covered in trees,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wardle |first=Peter |url=http://archive.org/details/vegetationofnewz0000ward |title=Vegetation of New Zealand |date=1991 |publisher=Cambridge [England] : [[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=978-0-521-25873-9 |page=10 |via=the [[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> and kahikatea dominated its own and once widespread kahikatea forest type. Even after the burning of many forests by early [[Māori people|Māori]], there still remained large remnant forests which European settlers came upon in the 18th and 19th centuries. In addition to the wood's use as timber,<ref name=":7"/><ref name="Wassilieff"/> kahikatea's usually flat habitat, with its damp and [[Soil fertility|fertile]] soil, was also a prime location for dairy farming. Together this led to the felling of much of the remaining forests in the North and South Islands during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.<ref name=":0" /> Today they are confined mostly to the [[Westland District|South Westland]] region of the South Island, though small remnants still exist in some places.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Wardle |first=Peter |date=1974 |title=The kahikatea (Dacrycarpus dacrydioides) forest of South Westland. |url=https://newzealandecology.org/nzje/2727.pdf |journal=[[New Zealand Journal of Ecology]] |volume=21 |pages=62–71}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=[[Department of Conservation (New Zealand)|Department of Conservation]] |title=Podocarp-hardwood forests |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/nature/native-plants/podocarp-hardwood-forests/ |access-date=2 July 2022 |website=www.doc.govt.nz |language=en-nz |archive-date=2 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220702115937/https://www.doc.govt.nz/nature/native-plants/podocarp-hardwood-forests/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Conservation efforts have focused on protecting and fencing kahikatea forests around the country.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hadden |first=Peter |url=http://archive.org/details/northnztxtlrepub |title=North New Zealand |publisher=Wairau Press |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-927158-31-9 |pages=229 |language=English |via=the [[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> [[Riccarton Bush]] is one notable example of forest remnant protection. The near {{Convert|16|acre|ha|2|abbr=on|adj=on}} reserve was held in the [[John Deans (pioneer)|Deans]] family for 70 years before it was gifted to [[Christchurch]] by them in 1914,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wigram |first=Henry F. |url=http://archive.org/details/storyofchristchu00wigriala |title=The story of Christchurch, New Zealand |date=1916 |publisher=The Lyttelton Times Co., Ltd. |location=[[Christchurch]] |pages=39–40 |via=the [[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> and subsequently formally protected in the Riccarton Bush Bill.<ref>{{Cite news |date=28 October 1914 |title=City Council. |volume=I |page=3 |work=Sun (Christchurch) |issue=226 |url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/SUNCH19141028.2.9 |access-date=19 July 2022 |via=[[Papers Past]]}}</ref> It is the only surviving kahikatea forest remnant in the entire [[Canterbury Plains]], and contains trees up to 600 years old.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Fletcher |first=Jack |date=13 September 2018 |title=Riccarton Bush a precious remnant of Canterbury's ecological past |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/news/107051099/riccarton-bush-a-precious-remnant-of-canterburys-ecological-past |access-date=19 July 2022 |website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en |archive-date=19 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220719015207/https://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/news/107051099/riccarton-bush-a-precious-remnant-of-canterburys-ecological-past |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Whangamarino Wetland]], a swamp-fen-bog complex south of Auckland on the North Island, was identified as an area of priority restoration as an ecosystem; the wetland is connected to the [[Waikato Tainui|Waikato Tainui iwi]].<ref name=":3" /> Reservation of stands may not totally protect kahikatea, however, because the alluvial plains that they favour are prone to upheaval and erosion and so trees may still become damaged.<ref name=":2" /> Forest remnants outside of South Westland face the threat of never returning to their natural states, as a result of their small size, threats from weed species, and grazing by livestock.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Smale |first1=Mark C. |last2=Ross |first2=Craig W. |last3=Arnold |first3=Gregory C. |date=2005 |title=Vegetation recovery in rural kahikatea (Dacrycarpus dacrydioides) forest fragments in the Waikato region, New Zealand, following retirement from grazing |url=https://newzealandecology.org/nzje/2278.pdf |journal=[[New Zealand Journal of Ecology]] |volume=29 |issue=2 |pages=261–269 |issn=0110-6465 |archive-date=3 November 2022 |access-date=20 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221103221535/https://newzealandecology.org/nzje/2278.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Despite this, kahikatea has been classified as [[Least-concern species|least concern]] by the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]] and "Not Threatened" by the [[New Zealand Threat Classification System]], which gives it an estimated population of above 100,000.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021">{{cite iucn|title=''Dacrycarpus dacrydioides''|article-number=e.T42443A2980535|author=Thomas, P.|date=2013|volume=2013|access-date=19 November 2021|doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2013-1.RLTS.T42443A2980535.en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Assessment Details for Dacrycarpus dacrydioides (A.Rich.) de Laub. |url=https://nztcs.org.nz/assessments/32178 |access-date=2 July 2022 |website=New Zealand Threat Classification System}}</ref>

=== Threats ===
The introduced [[Salix cinerea|grey willow]] and [[Salix × fragilis|crack willow]] have thrived in the deforested areas where kahikatea was previously dominant. The willows are fast-growing and have obstructed streams, displaced native vegetation, and contributed to a loss in native biodiversity.<ref name=":3" /> Kahikatea are considered a light-demanding species that struggles to progress beyond the sapling stage in areas with high willow density. Although the herbicide [[glyphosate]] has been successful in thinning mature grey willow canopies and providing a window for reestablishing native sedges, treated willows can rapidly reestablish their populations in an area due to [[epicormic shoot]]s. Exclusive use of glyphosate to control willow populations would require periodic herbicide application into perpetuity.<ref name=":3" />

The trees are also threatened by diminished seed availability and distribution due to a reduction in native bird species that dispersed the seeds, such as the [[kererū]]. Although some non-native birds, such as the [[common blackbird]], are also prolific seed-spreaders, survival of the kahikatea seeds are further threatened by introduced mice and rats.<ref name=":3" />
