===Deforestation===
{{further|Deforestation}}
[[File:An example of slash and burn agriculture practice Thailand.jpg|thumb|Prehistoric people used [[slash-and-burn]] practices to clear forests and vegetation for cropland. |alt=A landscape being burned by people]]
One of the most consequential impacts of prehistoric and Indigenous human activity was [[deforestation]].{{sfn|Williams|2000|p=28 }}   Techniques used for clearing forests included axes,{{sfn|Williams|2000|pp=30, 32,34  }} animal grazing,{{sfn|Williams|2000|pp=29, 30, 32, 34 }}, fires, and [[Slash-and-burn agriculture|slash-and-burn]].<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Williams|2000|pp=30–34 }}.
|{{harvnb| Roos | 2023 |pp=2029,2033 }}.
|{{harvnb|Ruddiman  |2009 |p= 3012 }}.
|{{harvnb|Roosevelt  |2013 |pp=70, 74,  84}}.
|{{harvnb| Barlow | 2012|pp=47–48  }}.
|{{harvnb|Stahl | 1996|p= 115 }}.
|{{harvnb| Ruddiman| 2003|p=274  }}.
}}</ref>  As early as half a million years ago, fires were used to clear vegetation by ''[[Homo erectus]]''.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Thompson|2021|pp=1–6}}. Cooking by fire: 2 million years ago; Fires became more common: 400 kya;  [[Alluvial fan]]s from fires:  92 kya.
|{{harvnb|Williams|2000|p=28 }}. Anthropogenic fires perhaps half million years ago; ''Homo erectus.''
}}</ref> 

Twelve thousand years ago, more than 90% of Earth's tropical forests and 95% of its temperate forests were inhabited and shaped by Indigenous peoples.{{sfn|Ellis|2021b|p=1}} Ten thousand years ago the world's forest cover was about 6 billion hectares.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Ritchie|2021}}.
}}</ref>  By 5,000 years ago (roughly in the middle of the [[First Agricultural Revolution]]) the coverage had been reduced by 170 million hectares.{{sfn|Ritchie|2021}} In 2023, it was 2 billion hectares below the 10 [[Year#Abbreviations yr and ya|kya]] (thousand years ago) coverage.{{sfn|Ritchie|2021}}{{void|The scientist [[Christopher Doughty]] hypothesized that the Earth's forest cover may have expanded for a brief period in the early [[Holocene]] in the interval ''after'' most megafauna were extirpated and ''before'' the extent of agriculture became significant.{{sfn|Doughty|2013|p=520}}
}}

===Climate change and global warming===

{{Easy CSS image crop
|image = Graph CO2 CH4 and Temperature Graph in English 15 June 2015 by Reg Morrison.jpg
|desired_width = 300
|crop_left_perc = 0
|crop_right_perc = 0
|crop_top_perc = 0
|crop_bottom_perc = 21
|align = right
 |alt= A timeline graph from 400,000 years ago to present, showing three atmospheric values: temperature, methane, and carbon dioxide.
|caption=  [[Greenhouse gas]]es started increasing before the [[Industrial Age]]: [[methane]] (thin dark line) started increasing around 5,000 years ago. [[Carbon dioxide]] (thick line) started increasing around 8,000 years ago.<ref name=Greenhouse/>
}} 

When prehistoric humans began developing large-scale agricultural projects about 7,000 years ago,{{void|{{harvnb|Stephens|2019}} gives a date of about  6000 years ago.{{sfn|Stephens|2019|p=899}}
}} they cleared forests, which may have indirectly caused an increase in the amount of [[greenhouse gases]] (including CO{{Sub|2}} and methane) in the atmosphere.<ref name=Greenhouse>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Ruddiman|2009|p=3011}}.
|{{harvnb|Ruddiman|2003}}.
|{{harvnb|Ruddiman|2005|pp=xiii, 5, 76-83,86-94 }}. CO{{sub|2}} rise began about 8,000 years ago (pp. 5, 86{{nbndash}}88).  Methane rise began about 5,000 years ago  (pp. xiii,  5, 76{{nbndash}}78).
}}</ref>{{efn|Methane increase starting 5,000 years ago may have been due to deforestation, agriculture, and domesticated livestock.{{sfn|Ruddiman|2005|pp= 79-83}} 
}} This may have been the start of humankind's contributions to the modern [[climate change]] crisis.<ref name=Greenhouse/>  The development of technologies such as iron, metal axes, and plows accelerated the impacts.<ref name=AgrAcc>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Stevens|2022| p =273  }}.
|{{harvnb|Ruddiman|2009|p=3012  }}.
|{{harvnb|Ruddiman|2005|pp=73-74 }}. Metal, axes, plows.
|{{harvnb|Ellis|  2021b|p=2}}.
|{{harvnb|Williams|  2000|pp=30-31}}. Metal axes.
}}</ref> 

Before the Industrial Age, humans indirectly changed the climate  through  megafauna extinctions and agriculture.  Extinctions may have slightly increased global warming, but agriculture may have offset that by slightly decreasing global warming.{{sfn|Doughty|2013|pp=505-506,520}}   Changes to the landscape can cause climate change through several mechanisms: [[albedo]] of the Earth's surface, changes to atmospheric [[carbon dioxide]], [[evapotranspiration]], and [[topographic roughness]].{{sfn|Doughty|2013|p=520}}

Although there is extensive evidence for anthropogenic fires, their overall impact on the world's climate may have been small because the world population was relatively small when prehistoric fires were at their peak, and also there is evidence that most fires were non-anthropogenic.{{sfn|Doughty|2013|p=520}}

===Erosion, structures, and fire===
[[File:Dates of First Agricultural Revolution Global Spread Map.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|This map shows when the [[First Agricultural Revolution]] occurred around the world.  Major changes to habitat always accompanied the adoption of agriculture.{{sfn|Ruddiman|2005|pp=65-69}}|alt=A map of the world showing the spread of agriculture, with dates at various locations]]
Long before the start of the [[Neolithic Revolution|First Agricultural Revolution]] (about 11,000 years ago) humans were modifying their habitats with anthropogenic fires.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Thompson|2021|pp=1–2,5–6}}.
|{{harvnb|Doughty|2013|pp=506-507}}.
}}</ref> Human activity altered vegetation patterns, leading to erosion and creating [[alluvial fan]]s.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Thompson|2021|pp=1–2,5–6}}. In Africa, 85,000 to 60,000 years ago.
|{{harvnb|Ruddiman |2005|pp=73-74 }}. Globally, starting around 5,000 years ago.
}}</ref>  The human-driven habitat impacts that came with the agricultural revolution were  an evolution of earlier fire-driven impacts.{{sfn|Thompson|2021|pp=1–2,5–6}}

Agriculture often required the creation of irrigation systems or drainage systems, some of which were so extensive that they left permanent traces in the landscape long after they were abandoned{{snd}}as found in [[Mesopotamia]], Hawaii, and India.{{sfn|Kirch|2005|pp=415,428 }} [[Environmental impact of irrigation|Soil quality]] was heavily impacted by prehistoric humans through processes such as [[erosion]], [[nutrient depletion]], [[Soil_salinity#Salinity_due_to_irrigation|increased salinity]], and [[sedimentation|sediment accumulation]] in ponds and lakes.{{sfn|Kirch|2005|pp=423-427}}  These impacts were significant around 3,000 years ago and accelerated 1,000 years ago.{{sfn|Doughty|2013|p=504}}

===Translocation  of species ===

{{further|Invasive species|Species translocation}}

Beginning in  the Late Pleistocene, humans altered the distributions of various species around the globe, spanning most taxonomic groups.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Boivin|2016|pp=6388}}.  Most taxonomic groups.
|{{harvnb|Kirch |2005|pp=416-418}}.  
|{{harvnb|Roberts|2017|pp=1-2}}.  
|{{harvnb|Stahl |1996|p=115}}.  
}}</ref> Major reorganization of species distributions took place at all scales: local, regional, and intercontinental{{sfn|Boivin|2016|p=6389}}  The archaeological record shows a generally accelerating trend{{snd}}but the rate of change was sporadic and fluctuated.{{sfn|Boivin|2016|p=6389}}  The variety of plants and species that were introduced and cultivated was very broad, and included  domesticated, wild, and [[pathogenic]] species.{{sfn|Boivin|2016|p=6389}} The archaeologist [[Patrick Vinton Kirch]] wrote:  "...the variety of animals moved by human colonists is 'astonishing', including for example lice, beetles, fleas, mites, land snails, geckos, rats, mice, birds, deer, fox, and wolf. Although some translocations were purposeful, many others appear to have been inadvertent."<ref>{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|p=418}}.  Kirch quoting the word "astonishing" from {{harvnb|Grayson|2001}}.</ref>
 
The archaeologists [[Nicole Boivin]] and [[Jon Erlandson]] identified  four developments that played a major role in translocation of species.{{sfn|Boivin|2016|p= 6389}}{{efn|The four developments were not exhaustive, and did not include the most ancient human impacts; they were selected because they demonstrated important trends and patterns.{{sfn|Boivin|2016|p= 6389}}
}} First was the migration of humans around the world, from about  195,000  to 12,000 years ago.{{sfn|Boivin|2016|pp= 6389-6390}} Second was the development of agriculture and pastoralism, from roughly 11,700 to 1,000 years ago.{{sfn|Boivin|2016|pp= 6390-6391}}  Third was the colonization of islands (about 10,600 to 1,000 years ago).{{sfn|Boivin|2016|pp= 6391 -6392}}{{efn|Included in the island-colonization phase was the early colonization of [[Cyprus]] around 10,600 years ago.{{sfn|Boivin|2016|p= 6391}}  Humans may have transported mammals to the [[Bismarck Archipelago]] 20,000 years ago.{{sfn|Rick|2013|pp=34-35}}
}} The final development was urbanization and the creation of trade networks, from roughly 3,000 years ago to the modern era.{{sfn|Boivin|2016|pp=6392-6393}}

===Extinction of animals===

{{further|Extinction|Local extinction|Defaunation}}

[[File:Early migrations mercator.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Map of [[early human migrations]] based on the [[Recent African origin of modern humans|Out of Africa theory]]. Numbers indicate when humans arrived at each location (thousands of years ago{{snd}}kya).|alt=A map of the world showing the spread of humans around the world, with dates given when they arrived at certain locations.]]
 
Over the past 129,000 years many [[megafauna]] species around the world became extinct.{{sfn|Sandom|2014|loc=§§ "Abstract", "Introduction"}}    These extinctions happened during the latter part of the [[Quaternary]] geological period{{snd}}extending from about 129,000 years ago to the present.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|loc=§§ "Abstract", "Introduction"}}.
|{{harvnb|Bartlett|2016|p= 152}}.
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|pp=2–3,6}}.
}}</ref>  These late Quaternary extinctions are sometimes divided into two groups: those during the [[Last Glacial Period|last ice age]] (called the [[Late Pleistocene extinctions]]{{snd}}from 129,000 to 11,700 years ago), and those after [[Holocene glacial retreat|that ice age ended]] (the [[Holocene extinction]]s{{snd}}from 11,700 years ago to the present).<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Burney|2005}}.
|{{harvnb|Whitney-Smith|2004}}.
|{{harvnb|Whitney-Smith|2008}}.
}}</ref>{{efn|Academics use various starting dates for the late Quaternary  extinctions, including: 132,000 years ago,{{sfn|Sandom|2014|loc=§§ "Abstract", "Introduction"}} 129,000 years ago,{{sfn|Svenning|2024|pp=2–3,6}} and 100,000 years ago.{{sfn|Bartlett|2016|p= 152}}
}}

Although extinctions were common in the geological record going back many millions of years, the speed and magnitude of the extinctions since 129,000 years ago are unusual.{{sfn|Sandom|2014|loc=§§ "Abstract", "Introduction"}} 
The extinctions{{snd}}though occurring in a brief time span when considered geologically{{snd}}occurred at different times around the globe.{{sfn|Bartlett|2016|p= 152}}  The loss of hundreds of species of megafauna fundamentally altered the Earth's ecosystem.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Malhi|2016|pp=838-839,844}}.
|{{harvnb|Dirzo|2014|pp=403–405}}.
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|pp=1,12}}.
}}</ref>

Among these extinctions are over 350 mammal species, which reduced the global count of mammal species (of all sizes) to approximately 5,700 in 2020.{{sfn|Andermann|2020|p=1}}   More than half of the [[Megafauna|large land animal]] species alive 100,000 years ago became extinct.{{sfn|Bartlett|2016|p= 152}}   In the Americas, over 66 [[genera]] (over two-thirds) of large{{void|name=large|The definition of "large" animals and "megafauna" varies depending on the context and the geographic area, but 44 kg is a common weight limit.}} mammals became extinct.{{sfn|Harkin|Lewis|2007|p=99}}  In North America alone, about 38 genera of large animals became extinct, including 19 genera of mammals.{{sfn|Meltzer|2020|pp=28555–28556}} Some of the species that became extinct included [[Smilodon|saber-toothed tigers]], [[terror birds]], [[Woolly mammoth|woolly mammoths]], [[Megalochelys|giant tortoises]],{{Efn|''[[Megalochelys]]'' was made extinct by ''[[Homo erectus]]'', not ''Homo sapiens''.{{sfn|Rhodin|2015|p=15}}
}} [[giant ground sloth]]s, and [[glyptodont|huge armadillos]].{{sfn|Vignieri|2014}}{{snd}}human activity was likely a driver in all of those extinctions.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|pp=1-5,18}}.
|{{harvnb|Vignieri|2014}}.
}}</ref>

====Causes of extinctions ====

{{further|Late Pleistocene extinctions|Holocene extinction|Timeline of extinctions in the Holocene}}
[[File:Carbon Dioxide 800kyr.svg|thumb|[[Climate change]] is one of the factors that caused [[megafauna]] extinctions in the Late [[Quaternary]] (from 129,000 years ago to present).|alt=A timeline showing the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere changing over time, and increasing dramatically since 1750]]

Academics have explored the causes of the [[Wiktionary:Late Quaternary|late Quaternary]] extinctions since the early 19th century.{{sfn|Harkin|Lewis|2007|p=96}}  Since the late 20th century, the debate over the cause of the extinctions has been vigorous, focusing on the extent to which humans were responsible for the extinctions.<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Burney|2005|pp= 395–398, 400}}.
|{{harvnb|Harkin|Lewis|2007|pp=96, 101, 109, 111, 114–115}}.
|{{harvnb|Bartlett|2016|p= 152}}.
|{{harvnb|Koch|2006|p= 216}}.
}}</ref>  Causes proposed for the extinctions include:<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Burney|2005|pp= 395–398, 400}}.
|{{harvnb|Koch|2006|p=217}}.
|{{harvnb|Harkin|Lewis|2007|pp=96, 114–115}}.
|{{harvnb|Surovell|2012|p=672}}.
|{{harvnb|Andermann|2020|p=9}} (pollution).
|{{harvnb|Firestone|2007|loc=§§ "Abstract", "Nature of the event", "Conclusions"}}  
}}</ref>
  
* Human causes{{snd}}Over-hunting;<ref name=overkillSources>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Meltzer|2015|pp=33-34}}.
|{{harvnb|Martin|1966}}.
|{{harvnb|Martin|1973}}.
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|p=12}}.
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|pp=1-2 }}.
|{{harvnb|Stewart|2025|loc=§§ "Introduction", "Extinction cause(s)" }}. Includes harvesting of bird eggs.
}}</ref>{{efn|name=overkill|The "overkill hypothesis" is the theory that human over-hunting was the primary cause of megafauna extinctions that occurred soon after humans first arrived on a landmass.<ref name=overkillSources/> 
}} [[Late Pleistocene extinctions#Second-order predation|second-order predation]] (over-hunting a [[predator]] species impacts a prey species: population of prey increases, then crashes);<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Burney|2005|p= 396}}.
|{{harvnb|Whitney-Smith|2008|loc=§ "Results – Step 3"}}  
}}</ref> habitat alterations or reductions;<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Rick|2013|pp=35-36}}.
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|pp=1-2,  7}}.
|{{harvnb|Stewart|2025|loc=§  "Extinction cause(s)" }}. 
}}</ref> introduction of invasive species;<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Rick|2013|pp=35-36}}.
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|pp=10,18}}.
}}</ref> anthropogenic fires (fires set by humans, deliberately or accidentally).<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Rick|2013|pp=35-36}}.
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|p=7}}.
|{{harvnb|Stewart|2025|loc=§  "Extinction cause(s)" }}. 
}}</ref>
* Climatic causes{{snd}}Including gradual [[Climate variability and change|climate changes]], as well as rapid changes<!-- such as [[Younger Dryas]] or [[Clovis culture|Clovis age]] drought-->.<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|p=1 }}.
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|pp=7-8,18}}.
|{{harvnb|Stewart|2025|loc=§  "Extinction cause(s)" }}. 
}}</ref>
* Infectious disease<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|p=1 }}.
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|pp=10,18}}.
}}</ref>
* Impact of an extraterrestrial object<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|p=1 }}.
|{{harvnb|Stewart|2025|loc=§§ "Introduction", "Extinction cause(s)" }}. 
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|p=7}}. 
|{{harvnb|Firestone|2007|loc=§§ "Abstract", "Nature of the event", "Conclusions"}} 
}}</ref>
* Synergistic combination of multiple causes{{snd}}For example, human activities (fire, hunting, agriculture, deforestation) contributing to climate change.<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Doughty|2013|pp=504–505, 519–520}}.
|{{harvnb|Stewart|2025|loc=§  "Extinction cause(s)" }}. 
}}</ref>
 
Researchers consider the two primary causes to be climate change and [[human ecology|human activity]].<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|p=1}}.
|{{harvnb|Bartlett|2016|p=152}}.
}}</ref>{{void|Either together or in combination.}}  Many of the late  Quaternary megafauna extinctions occurred after the arrival of humans, but finding evidence to prove a cause-and-effect relationship is difficult.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Carleton |2020|p=121}}.
|{{harvnb|Fordham|2024|p=1 }}.
|{{harvnb|Allentoft|2014|p=4922}}.
}}</ref> The nature of the extinctions varied between species and locations.{{sfn|Allentoft|2014|p=4922}}

====Human activity as a factor====

[[File:Valltorta (escena de caza).png|thumb|upright=0.9|This cave art from {{ill|Cave of the horses|es|  Cueva de los Caballos}} in Spain depicts humans hunting deer.|alt=A prehistoric cave painting showing humans hunting deer]]

A large number of [[Wiktionary:Late Quaternary|late Quaternary]] megafauna extinctions were a result of human activity.<ref name=AnthroDrivers>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|pp=1–3,18}}.
|{{harvnb|Lemoine|2023|pp=1,8}}.
|{{harvnb|Andermann|2020|pp=1,9 }}
|{{harvnb|Bartlett|2016|pp= 152, 158–159}}.
|{{harvnb|Bergman|2023|pp=1,7–8}}.
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|loc=§§ "Abstract", "Introduction"}} 
}}</ref>  Evidence for human-related causes includes the timing of extinctions following human arrival, the lack of climate change at the time of extinctions, archaeological evidence of hunting and habitat destruction, geographic correlation of human presence and extinction events, and analysis of large fauna that did not go extinct.<ref name=AnthroDrivers/>  Humans were not responsible for ''all'' megafauna extinctions:  a study of extinctions on islands found that while extinctions  during the Holocene were often caused by humans, earlier Pleistocene extinctions often were not.{{sfn|Louys|2021|pp=1–7}}  Some scholars, as of 2020, argue that the extinctions in North America were primarily caused by climate changes.{{sfn|Meltzer|2020|pp=28555–28556, 28559–28560 }}

A 2024 review considered the debate over whether humans or climate change were responsible for late Quaternary large vertebrate extinctions.{{sfn|Svenning|2024|pp=1–3,18}}{{efn|The 2024 review  addressed extinctions that happened in the past  50,000 years.  The author wrote: "The debate on the cause, or causes, of the late-Quaternary extinctions has been ongoing for over 200 years. Though most current work accepts at least a contributory role for modern humans, the topic remains controversial. We ...  conclude the existing evidence strongly supports a dominant role of Homo sapiens and is inconsistent with climate as a substantial cause."{{sfn|Svenning|2024|p=1}}
}}  The study reported strong evidence that human activity was the cause of the extinctions, and only weak evidence for climate change.{{sfn|Svenning|2024|pp=1–3,18}} The study did not find strong support for climate change as a cause in either fine-scale space/time analysis, or in global analysis.{{sfn|Svenning|2024|pp=1–3,18}} The earliest extinctions were likely caused by [[hominin]]s that predated ''[[Homo sapiens]]''.{{sfn|Svenning|2024|pp=1–3, 10–12, 18}}  

Some scientists consider human-driven extinctions to be the first major anthropogenic change to the ecosystem, and thus mark the start of the [[Anthropocene]].<ref name=Anthropo>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|pp=1–3, 12–18}}. Anthropocene starts with major human-driven extinctions, perhaps 50 kya.
|{{harvnb|Rick |2013|pp=33–34, 41–42}}.  Anthropocene starts  at start of Holocene, about 10 kya.
}}</ref>{{efn|Scholars have multiple hypotheses of when the Anthropocene started.  The proposal that it began 10,000 years ago, or more, when humans began extirpating large animals, is a relatively recent proposal.<ref name=Anthropo/>
}} Human activities that contribute to extinctions include hunting, habitat destruction (including anthropogenic fire), and the introduction of invasive species (such as rats, pigs, dogs, and possibly chickens),{{sfn|Grayson|2001|pp=1, 31}} but it is unlikely that small-scale societies caused extinctions by hunting alone.{{sfn|Grayson|2001|p=1}}

====Human arrival dates====
{{further|Early human migrations}}
[[File:Extinctions Africa Austrailia NAmerica Madagascar.gif|thumb|The percentage of [[megafauna]] on different land masses over time, with the arrival of humans indicated.|alt=A timeline showing the number of large animals evolving over time, in four regions (Africa, Australia, North America, and Madagascar).]]

One of the difficulties in determining causes of extinctions is ascertaining when humans arrived in specific locations on Earth.  A technique to estimate arrival time is to measure [[Proxy (statistics)|proxy data]] which is correlated with human arrival.  Proxy data include pollen counts, traces of small invertebrates (such as rats), increase in charcoal particles, and  a decrease in [[Coprophilous fungus|dung-fungus]] spores.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Burney|2005|pp= 398–399}}.
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|pp=414-415}}.
|{{harvnb|Stewart|2025|loc=§ "Types of data used in megafauna extinction research"}}.
}}</ref>  A 2005 study estimated human arrival dates in several locations and identified a common pattern of collapsing animal populations after human arrival.{{sfn|Burney|2005|p= 395}} An argument against climate change as a cause is the fact that extinctions around the world happened at various times, whereas a global climate change would tend to produce extinctions at roughly the same time.{{sfn|Burney|2005|p= 396}}

The primary driver of many extinctions was the arrival of humans, but [[climate variability and change]] also played a role.{{sfn|Bartlett|2016|pp= 152,159}}   The impact on species of climate change was not rapid: the changes could take several thousand years to affect the species.{{sfn|Bartlett|2016|p= 158}}  The study used a model that performed well (corresponded with known data based on archaeological records) in most of the world, including North and South America, Europe, Australia, Japan, Madagascar, Tasmania, and New Zealand.{{sfn|Bartlett|2016|pp= 158–159}}   The model's predictions did not perform well in Africa and Asia.{{sfn|Bartlett|2016|p= 159}}

====Types of animals====
[[File:Svenning 2024 Fig 1A megafauna extinction rate chart.png|thumb|upright=1.2|Larger mammals became extinct to a much larger degree than smaller mammals in the late Quaternary. Vertical axis is percentage of species that became extinct.{{sfn|Svenning|2024|p=3}}{{efn|Values represent number of species in late Quaternary (129,000 years ago to present).}}|alt=A chart showing the percentage of mammals that became extinct, based on size.]]

The majority of mammal extinctions between 50,000 and 10,000 years ago were species that were relatively large or were slow-breeding animals.{{sfn|Koch|2006|pp=215–217, 239–243}}  This preference for large, slow-breeding mammals was not seen in extinctions that happened earlier in the [[Cenozoic]] era.{{sfn|Koch|2006|pp=215–217, 239–243}}   This observation, coupled with the fact that the extinctions happened roughly at the same time that humans spread around the globe, suggests that human activity, particularly hunting, was a contributing factor.{{sfn|Koch|2006|pp=215–217, 239–243}}  Climate change likely played a role in the extinctions: even if precipitated by human activities, climate change may have influenced the timing, location, or magnitude of the [[defaunation]].{{sfn|Koch|2006|pp=215–217, 239–243}} Climate change may have combined synergistically with human activities (hunting, habitat loss, anthropogenic fires) to increase the magnitude of the extinctions.{{sfn|Koch|2006|pp=215–217, 239–243}}

====Extinction rates==== 
{{Easy CSS image crop
|image =  Maximum animal body size during Cenozoic Late Quaternary extinctions.svg
|desired_width = 260

|crop_right_perc = 0
|crop_top_perc = 0
|crop_bottom_perc = 10
|align = right
 |alt=  A graph showing animal size increasing from 60 million years ago to 129,000 years ago, then a sudden drop from then to the present. 
|caption= 129,000 years ago, the largest land animals weighed about 20,000 kg. Then humans began to spread around the world, and most large species became extinct by 1000 CE. The largest land animals today are around 5,000 kg.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|p=9}}. Diagram, mesosoic.
|{{harvnb| Smith  | 2018 |loc=Fig. 3 "Body size and its influence on extinction risk"}}. Approximate values 20,000 and 5,000 from Fig. 3C, 3D.
}}</ref>{{efn|Largest animals in Mesozoic animals were dinosaurs; Cenozoic data is land mammals only.}}
}} 
Scientists used computer models to analyze how extinction rates evolved since the Late Pleistocene.{{sfn|Andermann|2020|p=1}} The models showed that climate change was not a likely factor, because random changes to model conditions produced similar results as conditions that varied climate data.{{sfn|Andermann|2020|p=1 }}  Conversely, the model showed that human impacts were strongly correlated with the extinctions.{{sfn|Andermann|2020|p=1 }} The scientists who ran the models concluded that  humans  caused many extinctions that followed their arrival on new landmasses.{{sfn|Andermann|2020|p=9}}  The models also predicted that continuing human development in the 21st century would cause a new wave of mammal extinctions to begin around 2100 CE in all regions of the world.{{sfn|Andermann|2020|pp=1,9}}

====Geographic distribution====

Late Quaternary megafauna extinctions occurred on all continents except Antarctica.  The portion of large species that went extinct was markedly lower in Eurasia and Africa (where many large mammals survived into the 21st century).{{sfn|Koch|2006|pp=219,231, 242}}  Researchers analyzed the geographic distribution of extinction events and determined that extinctions were closely correlated with the geographical locations of human expansion, and weakly correlated with the severity of climate changes.  The implication of human causation was especially strong in locations where [[Homo sapiens]] were the first [[hominin]]s to arrive.{{sfn|Sandom|2014|loc=§§ "Abstract", "Discussion"}}  The study found significant discrepancies between the locations of climate changes and the locations of extinctions.{{sfn|Sandom|2014|loc=§§ "Abstract", "Discussion"}}{{void|An exception was Eurasia, where there was a potential correlation between extinction and climate change.{{sfn|Sandom|2014|loc=§ "Discussion"}}
}}

====Analysis of surviving megafauna====
{{Easy CSS image crop
|image = Svenning 2024 Fig 3 graph of size vs years ago megafauna.png
|desired_width = 260
|crop_left_perc = 5
|crop_right_perc = 5
|crop_top_perc = 0
|crop_bottom_perc = 34
|align = right
 |alt=  A graph showing the number of animals (per species) over time 
|caption=  Large mammals that did ''not'' go extinct during the late Pleistocene experienced significant population declines.  Each light step-line represents one species. Vertical axis is an estimate of the species' population.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Bergman|2023|p=3}}.
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|p=8}}.
}}</ref>{{efn|Vertical axis is "effective size" of the population, which is the estimated population count.}}
}} 
To answer the question of whether the [[megafauna]] extinctions were caused by human activities or climate change, scientists in 2023 analyzed the megafauna species that did ''not'' go extinct.<ref name=SurvPop>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Bergman|2023|p=1,7}}.
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|p=8}}.
}}</ref>{{void|The surviving species faced two possible futures after the extinctions: their populations could grow due to the elimination of competitors for food and habitat; or their populations could shrink due to same reason (whatever it was) that caused the extinctions.{{sfn|Bergman|2023|p=1}}
}}   The study found that 91% of the species suffered a decline in population, with larger-sized species experiencing larger declines.<ref name=SurvPop/>  The population declines were found on all landmasses on Earth, which is consistent with a cause related to human activities (rather than climate change).<ref name=SurvPop/>{{void|Another factor indicating that the declines were caused by humans is that the megafauna abundance and biomass turnover around the world decreased by 92 to 95%.<ref name=SurvPop/>
}}  Human-related causes of the population declines were also implicated by the fact that the declines were most pronounced in particular temporal periods when humans were expanding into new regions (which would be unlikely if the cause was climate change).<ref name=SurvPop/>

===Cascading impacts===

An environmental change can sometimes produce a cascade of indirect effects.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|p=14}}.  
|{{harvnb|Gretzinger|2019|pp=1-2}}.  
|{{harvnb|Bergman  | 2023 |pp=2,7}}.  
|{{harvnb|Smith  | 2018 |loc="... the extirpation of large mammals led to a fundamental restructuring of energy flow through mammal communities... "}}.  
}}</ref> Extinction of a large herbivorous species can increase the amount of vegetation, alter the region's fire regime, decrease the amount of dung (which in turn impacts biotic [[microhabitat]]s),  or create an empty [[ecological niche]] that other species can fill.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|p=14}}. Vegetation, dung, fire, microhabitats.
|{{harvnb|Gretzinger|2019|pp=1-2}}. Cascading in general.
}}</ref>  Analysis of extinctions occurring after 1500 CE found that they can lead to changes in water quality, pollination, decomposition, pest control, and nutrient cycling.{{sfn|Dirzo|2014|pp=403-405}}   Deforestation caused by humans can increase erosion, impact soil nutrients, and reduce the number of large animals.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Kohler|1988|p=540}}. Erosion, soil.
|{{harvnb|Dirzo|2022|pp=2-3}}.  Decrease in animals.
}}</ref>  Human predation on one species may indirectly cause other species to become extinct.{{sfn|Prates|2021|p=9}}

===Beneficial impacts===

{{further|Ecosystem engineering|Niche construction}}

Human impacts that resulted in the extinction of species or elimination of habitats are generally perceived as detrimental, but impacts can also have beneficial effects.  Historical human activity  reduced exposure to dangers,  improved food supplies, created landscapes that supported denser human population centers, and enabled trade.  Some communities enriched soils, created new habitats, and propagated useful species.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Boivin|2016|p=6393 }}. Danger, food, density, trade.
|{{harvnb|Ellis|2021a|p=1}}.  Soil, new habitats, species propagation.
|{{harvnb|Louys|2021|p=7 }}.
}}</ref>  Identifying historical examples where humans modified their landscape in ways that did not substantially harm other species may provide guidance for modern nature conservation efforts.{{sfn|Louys|2021|p=7}} Historical humans were not the only species that performed significant modifications to their habitat: other species that exhibited [[ecosystem engineering]] behaviors include [[beaver]]s, [[coral]], [[earthworms]], and elephants.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb| Smith| 2000| p=498}}. Beavers, coral, earthworms.
|{{harvnb|Ellis| 2021a| p=3}}. Nest-building insects, beavers.
|{{harvnb|Svenning|2024|pp=14-15}}.  Elephants.
}}</ref>

==Regional impacts==

===Eurasia===
{{further|Category:Extinct animals of Asia|label1=Extinct animals of Asia|Category:Extinct animals of Europe|label2=Extinct animals of Europe}}
[[File:Ice age fauna of northern Spain - Mauricio Antón.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|Artist's rendering of [[Mammoth]]s (left) and [[Woolly rhino]] (right) in Eurasia.|alt=A painting of woolly mammoths and woolly rhinos walking over snow-covered ground.]]

Megafauna in Eurasia{{snd}}such as [[mammoths]], [[Woolly rhinoceros|rhinos]], and [[Megaloceros giganteus|giant deer]]{{snd}}lived contemporaneously with humans for 30,000  years.{{sfn|Surovell|2012|p= 682}}  This is in contrast to Australia, North America, and Pacific islands, where megafauna and flightless birds rapidly became extinct after human arrival.{{sfn|Surovell|2012|p= 682}}{{void|On some islands, the animals became only locally extinct.}}  Many megafauna species in Eurasia were eventually extirpated, due to human hunting in combination with pressures from climate change.{{sfn|Sandom|2014|loc=§§ "Introduction", "Discussion"}}  Between 50 and 10 [[Year#Abbreviations yr and ya|kya]], nine genera (35% of the total) of large mammals became extinct, which is less than in most other continents.{{sfn|Koch|2006|p=219}}

Eurasia is unique among the world's landmasses, because it is the only one that has a significant correlation between climate change and megafauna extinctions.{{sfn|Sandom|2014|loc=§ "Discussion"}}  That fact, coupled with the paucity of direct archaeological evidence of hunting megafauna in Eurasia, has led some researchers to question if hunting played a role in the extinctions.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|loc=§  "Discussion"}}.
|{{harvnb|Surovell|2012|p= 682}}.
}}</ref>  Other scientists suggest that the lack of direct evidence is likely due to the fact that the humans did not live in the same regions of Eurasia as the megafauna for most of the 30,000 years: in some cases, the humans lived primarily in the temperate regions, whereas the megafauna lived farther north.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|loc=§§ "Introduction", "Discussion"}}.
|{{harvnb|Surovell|2012|p= 682}}.
}}</ref> When humans migrated into regions occupied by the megafauna, extinctions followed.{{sfn|Sandom|2014|loc=§ "Discussion"}}

The [[Woolly rhinoceros]] became extinct in Eurasia around 9,800 years ago.  A 2024 study of the causes of the extinction determined that a synergistic combination of [[Climate variability and change|climate change]] (leading to fragmentation and reduction of habitat) and human hunting (low-level, but sustained) caused the extinction, with climate change as the dominant cause.{{sfn|Fordham|2024|pp=1,7}}

A 2022 study focusing on the [[Southern Levant]] examined whether megafauna extinctions were due to climate changes or human hunting.{{sfn|Dembitzer|2022 |pp=1,8}}  The size and mass of hunted animals was studied across a time span ranging from 1.5 million years ago to 10,500 years ago: during that time span, the mean  body mass declined by a factor of about 60.{{sfn|Dembitzer|2022 |pp=1,8}} The changes in hunted animal body size over that time declined at a linear rate, and were not correlated with climate changes.{{sfn|Dembitzer|2022 |pp=1,8}}  The researchers concluded that humans hunted megafauna until they were extirpated, then shifted to the next-largest prey, and repeated that cycle.{{sfn|Dembitzer|2022 |pp=1,8}}  Humans developed new technologies to successfully hunt smaller prey.{{sfn|Dembitzer|2022 |pp=1,8}}  The scientists determined that the extinction of animals in the Southern Levant was due to human hunting, rather than climate change.{{sfn|Dembitzer|2022 |p=8}}

===Africa===
{{further|Category:Extinct animals of Africa |label1=Extinct animals of Africa}}

[[File:Africa Bantu Migration Vegetation Change.svg|thumb| Major vegetation changes followed the migration of [[Bantu peoples]] through central Africa. "ya" = years ago.{{sfn|Bayon|2012|p=1220}}|alt=A map of Africa showing path of Bantu peoples' migration, and correlation with major vegetation changes.]]

Around 2 million years ago, [[hominin]]s in Africa evolved into the [[carnivore]] [[ecological niche]].{{sfn|Hoag|2017|pp=29,41}} Since that time, the ecological diversity of other carnivores in Africa has significantly diminished, leading some scientists to speculate that hominins were partially responsible for the loss in diversity.{{sfn|Hoag|2017|p=41}}{{efn|Some scientists, including [[Lars Werdelin]], speculate that hominins may have begun impacting their environment through hunting as long as 2 million years ago: "... this period also includes the earliest evidence for persistent carnivory among hominins at ∼2 Mya.... carnivorans only saw minimal turnover until the latter part of that period, leading [the scientists] to suggest that the guild’s loss of functional richness and evenness is likely explained by the evolution of hominins into carnivore niche space."{{sfn|Hoag|2017|p=41}}
}} The [[Wiktionary:Late Quaternary|late Quaternary]] extinctions were not as acute in Africa as in other continents, possibly because of the very lengthy and gradual co-evolution of large fauna and hominins.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Hoag|2017|p=41}}.
|{{harvnb|Sandom|2014|loc=§ "The human palaeobiogeography hypothesis"}}.
|{{harvnb|Prates|2021|p=1}}.
}}</ref> Still, 24 African large mammal species became extinct{{sfn|Hoag|2017|p=41}} including ten genera.{{sfn|Koch|2006|p=221}} Humans were the most likely driver in these extinctions, based on the timing of the extinctions in relation to climate changes and human behavioral changes.{{sfn|Hoag|2017|p=41}} Starting in the mid-Holocene, the use of pastoralism and agriculture expanded throughout the continent.{{sfn|Hoag|2017|p=38}} 

Between 3,000 and 2,000 years ago, large parts of the [[rainforest]] in Central Africa became deforested and abruptly changed to [[savanna]].{{sfn|Bayon|2012|pp=1219, 1221}} These changes took place in the modern nations of Gabon, Cameroon, Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Republic of the Congo.{{sfn|Bayon|2012|p=1220}}  Both climate change and human activity have been proposed as hypotheses to explain this transition.{{sfn|Bayon|2012|p=1221}}  <!-- 
Prior to 2012, the scientific consensus was that regional climate oscillations were responsible for the changes to the landscape.{{sfn|Bayon|2012|p=1219}} 
-->  The deforestation coincided with the large-scale movement of [[Bantu languages|Bantu]]-speaking farmers from their original homelands in modern Nigeria and Cameroon, moving south and east through much of Central Africa.{{sfn|Bayon|2012|p=1221}}{{void|It is difficult to determine if the migration of the Bantu followed opportunistically into areas deforested by climate change, or if the Bantu actively cleared the forests.{{sfn|Bayon|2012|pp=1219, 1221}}
}}  Since the Bantu-speaking people required land for crops,  some scientists concluded that human activity was a significant factor in the deforestation.{{sfn|Bayon|2012|pp=1219–1220}}{{void|Additionally, the speed of transition from rainforest to savanna was much faster than other climate-based fluctuations during the [[Holocene]], suggesting that climate change alone may not have been responsible, leading some scientists to conclude that human activity was a significant factor in the deforestation.{{sfn|Bayon|2012|pp=1219–1220}}
}}

In contrast with many Polynesian islands, where Holocene extinctions rapidly followed the arrival of humans, the extinction process on the island of [[Madagascar]] was more gradual.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Dewar|2013| pp =12583,  12587}}.
|{{harvnb|Perry|2014|p=134}}.
}}</ref> After humans arrived around 2,000 BCE, they lived alongside some large animals for hundreds and even thousands of years: some of extinctions did not happen until about 1,500 CE.{{sfn|Dewar|2013| pp =12583,  12587}}  Ultimately, about 45 species of vertebrates (including all large terrestrial animals) became extinct.{{sfn|Dewar|2013| pp =12583,  12587}}  The precise causes of the extinctions are not certain, but hunting and anthropogenic fires{{efn|name=AnthroFire|Anthropogenic fires are fires set by humans, deliberately or accidentally.
}} appear to have played a significant role.{{sfn|Dewar|2013| pp =12583,  12587}}

===North America ===
{{further|Category:Extinct animals of North America|label1=Extinct animals of North America|Deforestation in the United States}}
[[File:United States megafauna human SPDs.webp|thumb|Graph showing decline of megafauna after  human arrival in North America.{{efn|Limited to contiguous United States.}} Time flows from right to left.  The dark gray region of each species shows the estimated population of the species. The thin curved line of each species is the estimated exponential growth (if left undisturbed).{{sfn|Broughton|2018|p=4}}|alt=A timeline showing when humans arrived in North America, and also showing the quantity of certain large animals ]]
<!-- 
Environmental changes have been widespread throughout North America since  the retreat of the [[Last Glacial Period|last glacier cover]] 10,000 years ago.{{sfn|Stahl|1996|pp=105–107,  117–119 }}  The changes varied widely over time and between locations.{{sfn|Stahl|1996|pp=105–107,  117–119 }}{{void|Changes to habitat and biodiversity were in continual flux throughout North America during the Holocene.{{sfn|Stahl|1996|pp=105–107,  117–119 }} 
}}  It is difficult for scientists to conclusively determine the extent to which changes are due to human activities or non-human causes.{{sfn|Stahl|1996|pp=105–107,  117–119 }}{{efn|Although the impacts of the pre-Columbian peoples were certainly far less than those that occurred after European colonization.{{sfn|Stahl|1996|pp=105–107,  117–119 }}
}}
-->
Humans arrived in North America from Asia about 13,500 years ago and migrated southward into South America.{{sfn|Surovell|2016| pp=886–887, 889–900}}  Measurements of the extinction dates of megafauna in the Americas found that the extinctions chronologically proceeded from north to south, corresponding to the migration of humans, suggesting that human activity played a role in the extinctions.{{sfn|Surovell|2016| pp=886–887, 889–900}} After the arrival of humans in North America in the Late Pleistocene, more than half of the large mammal species became extinct{{sfn|Alroy|2001|p=1893 }} including 34 genera and two complete [[order (taxonomy)|orders]].{{sfn|Koch|2006|p=217 }}  The scientist [[Paul Schultz Martin]] proposed in the 1970s that many of the extinctions were due to human hunting.{{sfn|Prates|2021 |loc=§ "Abstract"}}{{efn|name=overkill}}  Whether the extinctions were due to human hunting or other factors (such as climate change) continued to be subject of scientific debate in the early 21st century.{{sfn|Meltzer|2015|p=33}}

A search for direct archaeological  evidence of humans hunting Pleistocene mammals found evidence of hunting for only 5 of 37 [[genera]], leading some researchers to conclude that human hunting may not be a cause of Pleistocene  extinctions of mammals in North America.<ref name="OverkillProof"/>  Other researchers contend that "absence of evidence for kill sites is not evidence of absence",{{sfn|Surovell|2012|p=681|loc=Quoting  Brook and Johnson (2006)}} arguing that the archaeological record is very sparse, and a paucity of direct evidence is not proof that hunting did not occur.<ref name="OverkillProof">{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Grayson|2015|pp=177,188–189}}.
|{{harvnb|Surovell|2012|pp=672–673,681–683 }}.
}}</ref> Researchers in 2001 applied computer models to the question and determined that human hunting, alone, could readily account for the North American mammal extinctions.{{sfn|Alroy|2001|pp=1893, 1896}}{{void|The models indicated that extinctions were unavoidable.{{sfn|Alroy|2001|p=1896}}
}}{{efn|Some researchers questioned the utility of using computer models to analyze the causes of extinctions.{{sfn|Grayson|2015|p=190}}
}}  <!--
 The decline of prey populations may have been so rapid, that the human hunters did not recognize the ecological consequences while they were happening.{{sfn|Alroy|2001|p=1896}}
-->
 
[[File:Victoria.Mammut.P1033804.jpg|thumb|The [[woolly mammoth]] was one of many large mammals that became extinct after humans arrived in North America.|alt=A woolly mammoth]]

The [[Clovis culture]] were peoples living in North America around 12,800 years ago. Scientists have theorized that the Clovis hunted megafauna.{{sfn|Chatters|2024|p=1}}  A 2024 study analyzed the only known Clovis skeletal remains, and compared it to megafauna data. The analysis showed that mammoth was the largest contributor to Clovis diet, supplemented with bison and elk.{{sfn|Chatters|2024|p=1}}{{efn|The diet was comparable to the diet of now-extinct [[Homotherium|saber-toothed cats]].{{sfn|Chatters|2024|p=1}}
}}

Megafauna extinctions in Southern California were partially caused by human activity (fires and hunting),{{void|The 2023 study reporting this did not determine with certainty the cause of the fires, but states that the intense human activity occurring simultaneously with the increase in fires suggests humans may be at least partially at fault.{{sfn|O'Keefe|2023|pp= 5–7}}
}} but those actions were exacerbated by an increasingly arid, dry climate.{{sfn|O'Keefe|2023|pp= 1, 5–7}} Indigenous peoples living in the [[boreal forest]]s of North America used [[controlled fire]]s to manage their habitat.{{sfn|Christianson|2022|p=257}}   The purposes of the fires included controlling [[understory|undergrowth]] vegetation, improving  hunting success, and clearing campsites.{{sfn|Christianson|2022|p=257}}  
 
[[File:Alfred Jacob Miller - Hunting Buffalo - Walters 371940190.jpg | thumb |An artist's depiction of a  [[buffalo jump]]{{snd}} a [[Plains Indian]] hunting technique. |alt= Native Americans on horses, chasing buffalo, causing them to jump and fall down a bluff.]]

The [[Ancestral Puebloans|Ancestral Pueblo peoples]] in southwest North America abandoned their homelands in the 13th century, about the same time that the surrounding areas became deforested.<ref name=Chaco/>  Some scholars hypothesize that the deforestation was due to over-harvesting by the community, which{{snd}}along with other factors such as drought{{snd}}led to a societal collapse.<ref name=Chaco>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Lentz|2021|pp=1-3,12-14}}.
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|p=423}}.
|{{harvnb|Kohler|1988|pp=537-540, 559-560}}.
|{{harvnb|Diamond|2005|pp=136-143, 153-156}}.
}}</ref> Other researchers contend that there is no proof that the Pueblo people were responsible for the deforestation, and no proof that the deforestation was one of the causes of the abandonment of their population centers around [[Mesa Verde]] and [[Chaco Canyon]].{{sfn|Wills|2014|pp=11584, 11590}}

Native Americans hunted [[bison]] in the [[Great Plains#Northern Great Plains|Northern Great Plains]].  Before horses were introduced into North America by Europeans (in the early 1700s) Native Americans hunted on foot.{{sfn|Roos|2018|pp=8143–8144,8146–8147}}  An important technique used for on-foot hunting was [[buffalo jump]]s{{snd}}driving herds of bison over steep [[Bluff (geography)|bluff]]s to their death.{{sfn|Roos|2018|pp=8143–8144,8146–8147}}  Fire was sometimes used during buffalo jumps, used to lure them to the starting location.{{sfn|Roos|2018|p=8145}}  After horses were introduced, Native Americans began to use them for hunting, and the use of fire during the hunts diminished.{{sfn|Roos|2018|pp=8143–8144,8146–8147}}  Archaeological evidence shows  strong correlation between climate and anthropogenic fires:{{efn|name=AnthroFire}} fires were most often used when climate conditions were favorable (wet periods generated more fuel); and the fires influenced the climate.{{sfn|Roos|2018|p=8146}}

===Central America===
{{further|Deforestation in Central America}}
The [[Maya civilization]] flourished in Central America from about 2000 BCE to 1000 CE.{{sfn|Beach|2015|p=8}}  The Maya altered their environment with waterworks (dams, reservoirs, and canals), urban infrastructure (temples, buildings, and roads), [[slash-and-burn]] fires to clear forest, and the establishment of terraces, fields, and orchards for agriculture.{{sfn|Beach|2015|pp=1, 3, 7–8, 10, 17}}{{efn|Although the Maya civilization declined after about 1000 CE, and many forests regrew, impacts of the Mayan culture remain in the early 21st century.{{sfn|Beach|2015|p=1}}
}}  The activities that impacted the environment enabled growth and improvement of the Maya culture, but also caused soil erosion, sedimentation in bodies of water, and mercury pollution{{snd}}and perhaps contributed to the ultimate decline of the civilization.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Beach|2015|p=24}}.   Positive and negative; erosion, mercury.
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|p=422}}.  Contributed to decline.
}}</ref>{{void| The extent of impacts introduced by the Maya civilization  may have exceeded that of the changes in  Amazonia, due to the higher density of sites in Maya territory.{{sfn|Beach|2015|p=9}}
}}

===South America===
{{further|Category:Extinct animals of South America|label1=Extinct animals of South America|Environmental history of Latin America|Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest}}

[[File:Puntas_Cola_de_Pescado_1.jpg|thumb|[[Fishtail projectile point]], such as these from Argentina, were used for hunting.{{sfn|Prates|2021|p=2}}|alt=A photograph of about 20 stones cut into various shapes, some pointed and sharp.]]

{{Easy CSS image crop

|desired_width = 200
