 |alt= A sketch of a large, furry mammal with large claws on its feet
|caption=  An 1884 artist's conception of a [[Megatherium]], an extinct genus of giant sloths that lived in South America.{{sfn|Prates|2021|p=2,5}}
}}

South America{{snd}}like most of the world{{efn|Except Antarctica. The extinctions in Africa were less acute than other continents.{{sfn|Prates|2021|p=2}}
}}{{snd}}experienced Late Pleistocene extinctions, but they were more severe in this continent: over 80% of megafauna species  became extinct, spanning 50 genera and extinguishing three complete [[order (taxonomy)|orders]].<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Koch|2006|p=217}}.
|{{harvnb|Prates|2021|pp=1–2,7–9}}.
}}</ref>  As with many Late Pleistocene extinctions, both human activities and climate change were considered as potential causes.{{sfn|Prates|2021|pp=1–2,7–9}}   A 2021 study of the distribution of [[Fishtail projectile point]]s (often used as weapons) in the continent determined that humans were the primary driver for megafauna extinctions.{{sfn|Prates|2021|pp=1–2,7–9}}{{void|The study found that there were other, less dominant, causes that also contributed to the extinctions.{{sfn|Prates|2021|pp=1–2,7–9}} 
}}  That result was based on a strong correlation{{snd}}in both time and space{{snd}}between megafauna remains and the weapons.{{sfn|Prates|2021|pp=1–2,7–9}}

====Amazonia====
{{further|Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest}}

Although [[Amazonia]] is sometimes viewed in the popular imagination as an untouched wilderness, many parts were heavily impacted by pre-Columbian human settlement.<ref name=AmzSecondary>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Denevan|1992}}.
|{{harvnb|Denevan|2011}}.
|{{harvnb|Clement|2010}}.
|{{harvnb|Heckenberger|2007|p=1}}.
|{{harvnb|Nascimento |2024|pp=803–807}}.
|{{harvnb|Roosevelt|2013|pp=69–70, 84}}
}}</ref>   The first humans to settle in Amazonia arrived around 13,000 years ago.{{sfn|Roosevelt|2013|pp=69–70, 84}}  These pre-Columbian cultures extensively modified the environment, and cleared forests to make room for villages and crops.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Clement|2010}}.
|{{harvnb|Loughlin|2018|pp=1233–1235}}.  
|{{harvnb|Roosevelt|2013|pp=69–70, 84}}
}}</ref> They did not have iron tools, and used fire to make clearings for structures and agriculture, the remains of which are often visible in the modern era as [[Amazonian dark earth]] or ''terra preta''.{{sfn|Clement|2010}}  They also may have contributed to the extinction of some South American [[megafauna]].{{sfn|Clement|2010}} <!-- Megafauna that lived in Amzonia and became extinct include ''[[Notiomastodon]]'' and ''[[Eremotherium]]''.{{citation needed|date=October 2026}}   Indigenous peoples were responsible for extirpating the [[giant otter]] (''Pteronura brasiliensis'') from much of its range in Amazonia.{{citation needed|date=October 2026}}
-->  They introduced crops brought from [[Mesoamerica]] and they abandoned fields which turned into [[secondary forest]]s that were different from the original forests.{{sfn|Clement|2010}}

[[File:Índios isolados no Acre 11.jpg|thumb|When Europeans first visited the Amazon, many believed it was an untouched, [[old growth forest]] and were not aware that much of it was [[secondary forest]] due to habitat alterations by Indigenous peoples.{{sfn|Clement |2010 |pp=534-535}}|alt=An aerial photograph of a dense forest
]]

After the arrival of Europeans in Amazonia, the population of Indigenous peoples there diminished, and during the 18th century, many regions were abandoned and agricultural areas were reclaimed by new sorts of biodiversity.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Clement|2010}}.
|{{harvnb|Loughlin|2018|pp=1233–1235}}.  
}}</ref> In the early 19th century, European scientists{{snd}}such as [[Henry Walter Bates]] and [[Alfred Russel Wallace]]{{snd}}visited Amazonia and erroneously concluded that the secondary forests were in their original, pre-human condition.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Clement|2010}}.
|{{harvnb|Loughlin|2018|p=1235}}. In Ecuador.  
}}</ref>  As late as 2010, some scientists continued to be surprised to find evidence of significant human impacts in certain remote parts of the Amazon basin.{{sfn|Clement|2010}}{{efn|In 2008, some biodiversity  scientists studying the [[Caxiuana National Forest]] were surprised to discover extensive evidence of environmental alterations caused by ancient human cultures.{{sfn|Clement|2010}}
}}

In the [[cloud forests]] of Ecuador, before the arrival of Europeans, prehistoric cultures deforested large amounts of their environment for their own uses.{{sfn|Loughlin|2018|pp=1233–1235}} The intensive management and cultivation of the cleared landscapes continued until arrival of the Europeans caused the Indigenous population to dramatically decrease,{{efn|The population decrease was due to disease, uprisings, and brutal treatment by the Europeans.{{sfn|Loughlin|2018|p=1233}} 
}} leading to a cessation of deforestation around 1588 CE.{{sfn|Loughlin|2018|pp=1233–1235}} During the next 130 years, a [[secondary forest]] grew in the formerly cultivated areas, creating a dense forest that Europeans incorrectly assumed was a pristine wilderness.{{sfn|Loughlin|2018|pp=1233–1235}}  The deforestation performed by the Indigenous peoples was more extensive than the post-1950 deforestation performed by descendants of European colonizers.{{sfn|Loughlin|2018|p=1233}}

Some scholars contend that the impacts of early human inhabitants of Amazonia were sustainable, and even benefited the environment by increasing biodiversity.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Barlow|2012}}.
|{{harvnb|Roosevelt|2013|pp=69–70, 84}}.
}}</ref>  Although pre-Columbian humans made extensive alterations to the environment, the magnitude was generally far less than late 20th-century large-scale agricultural practices.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Clement|2010}}.
|{{harvnb|Roosevelt|2013|pp=69–70, 84}}.
}}</ref>   The agricultural traditions of the prehistoric peoples may offer examples of less-intensive practices that can be used in the modern era to minimize damage to the Amazonian environment.{{sfn|Heckenberger|2007|p=10}}

===Oceania ===
{{further|Category:Extinct animals of Oceania |label1=Extinct animals of Oceania }}
The number of bird species that were exterminated on Pacific islands after the arrival of Indigenous peoples was roughly 2,000{{snd}}most of them flightless.{{sfn|Steadman|1995|pp=1123,1127–1130}}  This was about 20% of the total number of bird species on Earth.  When including species that were [[extirpate]]d (made locally extinct) on Pacific islands, the total is roughly 8,000 populations.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Steadman|1995|pp=1123,1127}}.
|{{harvnb|Duncan|2002 }}.
}}</ref>

====Australia====
{{further|Australian megafauna}}
 
[[File:Megafauna - Genyornis (cropped).png|thumb|upright| ''[[Genyornis newtoni]]'' is a large, flightless bird that became extinct in Australia at roughly the same time humans arrived, but the cause of the extinction is uncertain.<ref name=Genyournis/>|alt=A skeleton of a large bird, inside a museum.]]

Australia experienced a tremendous loss of biodiversity in the late Quaternary: all animals (birds, reptiles, and mammals) weighing more than 100&nbsp;kg became extinct.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Roberts|2001|p=1888}}.
|{{harvnb|Miller|2005|p=287 }}.
}}</ref> Of animals weighing more than 45&nbsp;kg, 23 of 24 genera went extinct.{{sfn|Roberts|2001|p=1888}}  Extinction also claimed all six genera of large reptiles,  a [[Genyornis|giant flightless bird]], three marsupial [[Family (taxonomy)|families]], and two [[guild (ecology)|guilds]].{{sfn|Koch|2006|p= 220}}

Proposed drivers of the extinctions are climate change (in particular, gradual [[aridification]]) and human activity (hunting and anthropogenic fire).<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Roberts|2001|p=1888}}.
|{{harvnb|Archer|2025|p=11 }}.
}}</ref>   Debate about whether the extinctions in Australia were caused by humans or climate change (or both) has been continuing for more than a century.{{sfn|Roberts|2001|p=1888}}{{efn|Causes debated since 1884.{{sfn|Roberts|2001|p=1888}}
}} The debate continued into the 21st century partly because of uncertainties about the dates of the arrival of humans, and the dates of the extinctions.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Roberts|2001|pp=1888, 1892}}.  Page 1888: century of debate
|{{harvnb|Archer|2025|p=11 }}.  Uncertainty about causes in 2025.
|{{harvnb|Wroe|2006|p=1 }}.  Lack of data regarding Australia's extinctions.
}}</ref>{{efn|Scholars that assert human causes include {{harvnb|Brook |2002}}, {{harvnb|Turney|2008}}, {{harvnb|Miller |2005}}, and  {{harvnb |Roberts |2001}}.  Scholars that emphasize climate change causes include  {{harvnb |Archer|2025}} and {{harvnb |Wroe|2006}}.
}} An example of data uncertainty is the human arrival date:{{sfn|Brook|2002 |p=14626}} one researcher put it at between 60 and 52 thousand years ago (kya),{{sfn|Roberts|2001|p=1888}}  another at 50 to 43 kya,{{sfn|Wroe|2006|p=2692}} another at  65 kya,{{sfn|Archer|2025|p =2}} and another at between 55 and 45 kya.{{sfn|Miller|2005|p=287 }}

Both North America and Australia experienced a large number of extinctions, but it has been far harder to draw conclusions about Australian events because of uncertainty about arrival dates and lack of solid evidence of hunting.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Wroe|2006|pp=2692–2693  }}.  
|{{harvnb|Archer|2025|p=13 }}.  
}}</ref>  Some researchers have determined that most of the Australian  extinctions occurred after or contemporaneously with the arrival of humans<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Miller|2005|p=287 }}.
|{{harvnb|Turney  | 2008|pp=12150 –12153  }}.
|{{harvnb|Roberts| 2001  | |pp=1888–1892 }}.
}}</ref> but others have suggested the opposite.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Brook  |2002 |pp=14624, 14627 }}.
|{{harvnb|Wroe|2006|pp=  2602–2693, 2697–2701}}
}}</ref>   A 2006 study determined that human activity was likely not the sole driver of the megafauna extinctions, based on the gradual aridification of the continent  and evidence that most of Australia's extinct megafauna became extinct long before humans arrived.{{sfn|Wroe|2006|pp= 2692–2696, 2701 }}

An example of the confusion surrounding the data for extinctions is a [[Sthenurinae|short-faced kangaroo]] tibia bone which had scratch marks.  Some researchers concluded that they were evidence of butchering by humans, but later analysis determined that the marks were made long after the animal's death, after the bone was fossilized, and hence are not proof of hunting.{{sfn|Archer|2025|pp =1–4, 11–13 }}

One of the few extinct Australian species for which direct evidence of human predation has been found is the large, flightless bird ''[[Genyornis newtoni]]''.{{sfn|Miller|2016|p=2}} Scientists analyzed fragments of its eggshells (up to 140,000 years old) and concluded that humans may have caused the ''[[Genyornis newtoni]]'' extinction due to predation on its eggs.<ref name=Genyournis/>  Scientists also analyzed fragments of eggshells from the extinct large bird  ''[[Dromaius novaehollandiae]]'' and found  a permanent reduction in the variety of its food sources beginning about the time that humans arrived.<ref name=Dromaius>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Miller|2005}}.  ''Dromaius novaehollandiae''.
}}</ref>  The researchers hypothesized that fires set by humans were the most plausible cause of the extinctions, because the isotope record showed that{{snd}}soon after human arrival{{snd}}the available vegetation mixture changed from one adapted to drought to a mixture adapted to fire.<ref name=Dromaius/>{{void|The animals that could adapt to the vegetation change survived; and those that could not became extinct.<ref name=Dromaius/> Another researcher put the results of the eggshell study into doubt, by questioning whether the eggshells were correctly identified.{{sfn|Archer|2025|pp=11–12}}
}}

Data from the island of [[Tasmania]] is consistent with a chronology where the extinctions followed soon after the arrival of humans.{{sfn|Turney|2008|pp=12150, 12153}} The arrival of humans on Tasmania occurred between 43 and 40 kya.{{sfn|Turney|2008|pp=12150,12153}}  Analysis of fossils shows that some Tasmanian megafauna survived  until 41 kya, and so there was overlap between the presence of humans and megafauna on Tasmania.{{sfn|Turney|2008|pp=12150,12153}} In addition, the historical vegetation data of Tasmania does not show any significant climate changes between 43 and 37 kya, indicating that humans are a plausible cause of the extinctions.{{sfn|Turney|2008|pp=12150,12153}}

====New Zealand====
{{further|Māori and conservation|Biodiversity of New Zealand| Deforestation in New Zealand}}
[[File:Dinornithidae SIZE 01.png|thumb|alt= A diagram showing the size of the moa birds, relative to a human|The [[Māori people]] of New Zealand extirpated all species of [[moa]] (large, flightless birds) on the islands.{{efn| 1. ''[[Dinornis novaezealandiae]]'' {{Clear}} 2. ''[[Emeus crassus]]'' {{Clear}} 3. ''[[Anomalopteryx didiformis]]'' {{Clear}} 4. ''[[Dinornis robustus]]''}}
]]

New Zealand provides unique insights into human impacts because it was the last major landmass colonized by humans, it had a diverse set of bird species, and it was the most rapid human-caused megafauna extinction event.{{sfn|Allentoft|2014|p=4922}} Before the arrival of [[Polynesians]] in the 13th century, New Zealand was home to several species of [[moa]] (''Dinornithiformes''){{snd}}large, flightless birds.  All moa species{{snd}}as well as three frog and one reptile species{{snd}}became extinct following the arrival of humans.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Tomlinson|2025|p=2}}
|{{harvnb|Perry|2014|pp=126-127,133-134}}. 
}}</ref> 
The extinction of the moa was the most rapid human-facilitated megafauna extinction, and was one of the final prehistoric [[megafauna]] extinctions of the Holocene.{{sfn|Allentoft|2014|p=4922}}{{efn|Extinctions of large species are continuing in the modern era, including the [[Bluebuck]] (extinct around 1800 CE) and [[Pyrenean ibex]] (a subspecies, extinct 2000 CE).}}

In the mid-20th century, climate change was considered to be a plausible explanation for the New Zealand extinctions but it was eliminated as a possible cause in the latter part of the 20th century.<ref name=MoaExt/>  A scientific analysis of moa [[fossil]]s and habitats indicated that their populations were stable and large prior to the arrival of humans, and there was no evidence of a gradual decline in population, as might be caused by climate change.<ref name=MoaExt>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Allentoft|2014|pp=4922, 4926}}.
|{{harvnb|Tomlinson|2025|p =  2 }}.
|{{harvnb|McGlone|1989|p=126}}.
}}</ref>{{void|The population of the moa increased during the Holocene.{{sfn|Allentoft|2014|p=4926}}}}   It is now widely accepted that Polynesians caused the extinction through hunting and habitat destruction.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Allentoft|2014|pp=4922, 4926}}.
|{{harvnb|Tomlinson|2025|pp = 1–2, 5–8}}.
|{{harvnb|Holdaway|2014|pp=1–2,6–7}}.
|{{harvnb|Holdaway|2000|pp=2250-2253}}.
}}</ref>{{efn|A 2025 study investigated whether the extinction of the moa was inevitable.  Models showed that the moa would become extinct even under low rates of hunting.{{sfn|Tomlinson|2025|pp = 1–2, 5–8}} The only scenarios in which moa survived are those where more than 50% of New Zealand's land was protected from hunting.{{sfn|Tomlinson|2025|pp = 1–2, 5–8}}
}}
 
When Polynesians arrived, the moa population of New Zealand was estimated to be about 9,200 individuals.{{sfn|Allentoft|2014|p=4926}}  Archaeological evidence shows that humans hunted the moa.{{sfn|Allentoft|2014|p=4926}} The moa were extirpated within 100 to 200 years after humans arrived.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Allentoft|2014|p=4926}}.
|{{harvnb|Holdaway|2014|pp=1–2,6–7}}.
|{{harvnb|Perry|2014|pp=126-127,133-134}}.
}}</ref>    At the time the Polynesians extirpated the moa on the South Island, the total human population of New Zealand was less than 2,000.{{sfn|Holdaway|2014|pp=1–2,6–7}}  The human population density at the time of the extinction was very sparse: at most 0.01 humans per km{{super|2}}.{{sfn|Holdaway|2014|pp=1–2,6–7}}  Evidence of moa butchery is found in over 100 sites on [[South Island|New Zealand's South Island]]. Evidence is rarer on the North Island, perhaps because the higher density of Polynesians in the north caused the extinction to proceed rapidly,  thus leaving few traces.{{sfn|Burney|2005|p= 398}}

==== Melanesia====

Islands of [[Melanesia]] experienced dramatic environmental transformations after initial human settlement around 3,000 years ago.{{sfn|Roos|2023|pp=2028–2029, 2031–2033 }}  The islands of [[Fiji]] were studied to assess the impact of prehistoric humans on the environment, particularly the cause of prehistoric deforestation.  Prior to settlement, fires in Fiji caused by [[lightning]] would occasionally occur on the islands, typically during periods of drought.{{sfn|Roos|2023|pp=2028–2029, 2031–2033 }}{{efn|The timing of the  pre-settlement fires may have been influenced by [[El Niño]].{{sfn|Roos|2023|pp=2028, 2031–2033 }} 
}} After settlement, [[slash and burn|slash-and-burn]] anthropogenic fires{{efn|name=AnthroFire}} were used by the humans to prepare land for cultivation, and often led to deforestation.{{sfn|Roos|2023|pp=2028–2029, 2031–2033 }}  Damage to the environment was not solely caused by human activities: [[El Niño]] climate events may have caused droughts which exacerbated deforestation.{{sfn|Roos|2023|pp=2028, 2031–2033 }}

====Polynesia====
Most islands in the Pacific were settled in the late Holocene, and the arrival of humans caused rapid and significant ecological changes.{{sfn|Perry|2014|p=126}} In the eastern Polynesian islands, over 1,000 species of birds became extinct, particularly flightless birds vulnerable to introduced predators and larger birds favored by hunters.{{sfn|Perry|2014|p=126}}  In the eastern Polynesian islands particularly, human activity resulted in extensive deforestation.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Perry|2014|p=126}}.
|{{harvnb|Steadman|1995|pp=1123–1124, 1128–1130}}.
}}</ref> Human activities that led to the extinctions and deforestation included hunting (birds, terrestrial animals, fish, and shellfish), clearing forest with fire (for cultivation as well as driving game), constructing irrigation systems  and other structures, introducing domesticated species (pigs, chickens, and dogs), and  introducing invasive species (rats, skinks,  weeds, and geckos).<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Rick|2013|pp=35–36}}. Hunting, introducing pathogens, clearing forest, fire,  pigs, dogs,
 chickens, construction, irrigation, weeds, geckos, skinks, rats. 
|{{harvnb|Perry|2014|p=126}}. Hunting,  rats,  deforestation, fire.
|{{harvnb|Steadman|1995|pp=1123–1124, 1128–1130}}. Hunting, deforestation, erosion, introduced invasive plants, fire, rats, dogs, pigs.
}}</ref>

In the [[Hawaiian islands]], Polynesian settlers altered the native vegetation by clearing land for agriculture, and the impacts were compounded by the effects of invasive rats introduced by the humans.<ref name=Hawaii>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|pp=423, 428}}. Dryland fields. 
|{{harvnb|Rick|2013|pp=36,37}}. Intensive food production systems; dryland farming.
}}</ref>  The Polynesians also built a [[Dryland farming|dryland field]] system{{snd}}covering 52 km{{super|2}}{{snd}}that left traces that were still visible in the 21st century.<ref name=Hawaii/>  Several animal species became extinct soon after arrival of Polynesians,  including  an [[ibis]] and  four genera of [[Anatidae|geese or ducks]].{{sfn|Rick|2013|p=37}}

Humans settled in [[Tonga]] about 3000 years ago, and soon thereafter the [[Brachylophus gibbonsi|giant iguana]]  and [[Megapodius alimentum|scrubfowl]] became extinct.{{sfn|Perry|2014|p=134}} The extinctions were so rapid that the time interval between the arrival of humans and the extinctions was less than the margin of error of the [[radiocarbon dating]] used to perform the dating.{{sfn|Perry|2014|p=134}}

=====Easter Island=====
{{further|Easter_Island#Ecocide_hypothesis}}
[[File:Easter Island ESA419941 (cropped, lightened).jpg|thumb|alt=An aerial photo of an island, showing trees covering only a small portion of the island|[[Easter Island]] originally had about 20 million [[Easter Island palm|palm trees]], but they are now extinct and most of the island is deforested. Causes include clear-cutting by humans and climate change.<ref name=EI/>]]

Polynesians arrived on [[Easter Island]] between 800 and 1200 CE.{{sfn|Rull|2020|p=124}}{{efn|Europeans first made contact with the Polynesians on Easter Island in 1722.{{sfn|Rull|2020|p=125}}
}}  After their arrival, 18 plant species became extinct including two species of trees: [[Easter Island palm]] and [[Sophora toromiro]] (latter [[extinct in the wild]]).<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb| Rull|2020|p=131}}. Toromiro extinct in the wild.
|{{harvnb|Boivin|2016|p=6392 }}.  18 plant species. 
|{{harvnb| Steadman|1995|p=1126}}.
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|p=423}}.
|{{harvnb|Diamond|2005|pp=103–107 }}.
}}</ref>  Scientists estimate that the island had 20 million palms before the arrival of the Polynesians.{{sfn|Rull|2020|p=130}}   The palm became extinct around 1650.{{sfn|Rull|2020|p=125}}  In addition, several bird species became extinct.<ref name=EIbirds>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb| Steadman|1995|p=1126}}.
|{{harvnb|Diamond|2005|pp= 90, 104–108}}.
}}</ref>{{efn|Birds that became extinct on Easter Island include two species of [[Rail (bird)|rails]], two species of parrots, one species of owl, and one species of heron.<ref name=EIbirds/>
}}

Several causes for the deforestation and animal extinctions have been suggested, primarily anthropogenic:  hunting, deforestation, and introduction of the [[Polynesian rat]].<ref name=EI>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Hunt|2007|pp=485–487, 493–499 }}.
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|p=423}}.
|{{harvnb|Diamond|2005|pp=103–107 }}.
}}</ref>  Climate changes have also been hypothesized as a synergistic, contributory factor.{{sfn|Rull|2020|pp=124–125, 138–139}}{{efn|  [[#CITEREFDiamond2005|Diamond (2005)]] made arguments for an entirely human cause of deforestation, but [[#CITEREFRull2020|Rull (2020)]] concluded that climate change also played a major role.}} The loss of nesting sea birds on the island possibly contributed to deforestation, because the birds' [[guano]] was an important nutrient for the island's vegetation.{{sfn|Kirch|2005|p=420}}<!--

===Island patterns===
{{further|Island ecology|Island syndrome}}
 
Generally, when humans first arrived on an island, impacts on the environment began immediately and accelerated as populations grew.{{sfn|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}} There was no over-arching pattern of human impacts that applied to all islands, but there was some commonality based on whether the cultures were primarily [[hunter-gatherer]]s or [[agriculturalist]]s.{{sfn|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}}   The nature and extent of the human impacts depended on many factors, including island geography, population density, and  subsistence strategies.{{sfn|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}}

Some islands in Polynesia, Caribbean, Mediterranean, and North Atlantic shared some common patterns of human impacts, including anthropogenic burning (to clear landscapes) which led to soil erosion.{{sfn|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}}   In some Caribbean islands, humans are implicated in the extinction of [[sloth]]s.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Surovell|2012|pp=682–683 }}.
|{{harvnb|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}}.
}}</ref>  In the Pacific Ocean, the number of bird species that became extinct was between 559 and 1,696 landbirds.  The total rises to between 820 and 1,960 species when including seabirds, Hawaii, and New Zealand.{{Sfn|Steadman|2006|pp=409–411}}

The [[Channel Islands (California)|California Channel Islands]] were inhabited by hunter-gatherers; the impacts on these islands were less well-defined, but appear to exhibit less landscape clearing and erosion than agriculturalist islands.{{sfn|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}}  Early humans on the Channel Islands impacted the marine environment, and introduced invasive species such as mice and foxes.{{sfn|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}}

-->

==Conservation and Indigenous peoples ==

===The myth of pristine wilderness ===

Beginning in the 19th century, some [[Western world|Western]] scholars and colonizers came to view lands inhabited by Indigenous peoples as a pristine wilderness, largely untouched by human activity prior to European arrival.<ref name=PM>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Denevan|1992|pp=369–370,379–380}}.
|{{harvnb|Denevan|2011|pp=576–578, 580}}.
</ref> This illusion is described as the "myth of pristine wilderness".<ref name=PM/>{{efn|Also called the "pristine myth".<ref name=PM/>}} The concept of pristine wilderness{{snd}}meaning a landscape unchanged by any human activity{{snd}}is primarily a Western notion, encountered primarily in  Scandinavia, the USA, and Australia.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Nelson|Callicott|2008|pp=355–358}}.
|{{harvnb|Callicott|2000|p=24}}. Scandinavia, America, Australia.
|{{harvnb|Denevan|2011|pp=580–581}}. America.
|{{harvnb|Denevan|1992|p=369}}. America.
}}</ref>   The myth was first described in 1992 by several scholars, including [[#CITEREFDenevan1992|a 1992 article]] by the geographer [[William Denevan]].{{sfn|Denevan|2011|p=577}}{{void|Other authors who published writings on the myth are listed in {{harvnb|Denevan|2011|p=577}}.
}} Belief in the myth of the pristine wilderness was widespread in the 19th and 20th centuries, and continued into the early 21st century.{{sfn|Denevan|2011|pp=579–580}}{{efn|Early supporters of the myth of the pristine wilderness in the US included  [[Henry David Thoreau]] and [[James Fenimore Cooper]].{{sfn|Denevan|2011|p=579}}
}}

In the 1990s, Denevan and several other academics published research establishing that the vast majority of lands inhabited by prehistoric cultures were significantly modified by those peoples in virtually all locations on Earth, although the nature and degree of the impact varied widely from location to location.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Denevan|2011|pp=577–578, 580–583}}.
|{{harvnb|Denevan|1992|pp=369–370,379–380}}.
}}</ref>  The consensus of scholars is that there was virtually no pristine wilderness in any of the lands encountered by colonizers or Western peoples, and thus the myth is false.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Denevan|2011|pp=577–578, 580–583}}.
|{{harvnb|Denevan|1992|pp=369–370,379–380}}.
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|pp=411,433}}.
|{{harvnb|Clement|2010|p=534}}.
}}</ref>  According to the geographer and explorer [[Alexander von Humboldt]]:
{{blockquote| If travellers, the moment they set foot in a tropical region and  ... imagine that they are within the precincts of a primeval forest, the misconception must be ascribed to their ardent desire of realizing a long-cherished wish. Every tropical forest is not primeval forest. I have scarcely ever used the latter term in the narrative of my travels.{{snd}} [[#CITEREFHumboldt1850|''Views of Nature'' (1850)]]{{sfn|Stahl|1996|p=105}}
}}

===Attitude towards conservation===
{{further|Ecological anthropology|Ethnoecology|Noble savage#Ecological Noble Savage|label3 =Ecological Noble Savage}}
 
A common view among Westerners was that prehistoric Indigenous cultures universally lived in perfect harmony with nature and endeavored to conserve and protect the environment.{{efn|As early as the 1700s, Europeans were under the mistaken belief that Indigenous peoples (particularly in the New World) had not significantly altered their environment.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|pp=210-211}}.
|{{harvnb|Krech|1999|pp=17-20}}.
}}</ref> 
}} This notion is referred to as the myth of the "[[Noble savage#Ecological Noble Savage|ecological noble savage]]".<ref name=EcoNobSav>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Redford|1993|p=11}}. "Ecologically noble savage".
|{{harvnb|Denevan|2011|pp= 578 "Ecological Indian",  579 "Noble savage", 580 "Environmentally noble savage", 581 "Ecological Indian"}}.
|{{harvnb|Nelson|Callicott|2008|p=410 }}. "Ecological noble savage".
|{{harvnb|Harkin|Lewis|2007}}. "Ecological Indian".
|{{harvnb|Krech|1999}}. "Ecological Indian".
|{{harvnb|Krech|2005|p=78}}. "Ecological Indian".
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|pp=410-412}}. "Myth of the noble savage".
|{{harvnb|Ellingson|2001 |pp=342-358}}. "Ecologically noble savage".
}}</ref>{{efn|The term "ecological Indian" is also used, in a North American context, for the notion of ecological noble savage.<ref name=EcoNobSav/>
}}  This myth is a recent variant of the [[noble savage]] [[cultural stereotype]], which originated several hundred years ago in the Western imagination.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Krech|1999|pp=16–18}}.
|{{harvnb|Nadasdy|2005|pp=292–293}}.
}}</ref>{{efn|The phrase "ecologically noble savage" was first used to describe the myth in 1990.{{sfn|Redford|1993|p=11}}
}} During the [[environmental movement]] of the 1970s, the myth of the ecological noble savage became widespread.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Krech|1999|pp=20–28}}.
|{{harvnb|Krech|2005|p=78}}. 
|{{harvnb|Smith|2000|pp=493–494}}. 
|{{harvnb|Harkin|Lewis|2007|p=52}}. 
}}</ref>{{void|The myth of the ecologically noble savage is often applied in the context of North America, but is also applied in Asia, South America, Australia, and  other places in the world.{{sfn|Buege|1996|p=73}} 
}} The consensus of academics is that the concept of the ecological noble savage was essentially false, and that prehistoric peoples impacted their habitat in virtually all places they inhabited, resulting in significant, permanent changes to the ecosystem, including{{snd}}in some cases{{snd}}extinction of species and deforestation.<ref name=MES>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Hames|2007|pp=181-184}}.
|{{harvnb|Krech|2005|pp=78–84}}. 
|{{harvnb|Smith|2000|pp=494, 510}}. 
|{{harvnb|Nadasdy|2005|p=293}}.
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|pp=410-411}}.
|{{harvnb|Krech|1999|pp=211-213}}.
|{{harvnb|Stahl|1996|p=118}}.
}}</ref>{{efn|
According to the archaeologist [[Patrick Vinton Kirch]]:  "The study of human ecodynamics also needs to confront head on the issue of how past human societies perceived (or failed to perceive) environmental impacts, how social systems themselves adapted or responded to change, and the degree to which such systems could be resilient over long time cycles."{{sfn|Kirch|2005|p=432 }}
}}  

When considering the impacts of Indigenous cultures on the environment, some scholars distinguish cultures that are ecologists from cultures that are conservationists.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Krech|2005|pp=78–79}}. 
|{{harvnb|Smith|2000|pp= 493–496, 500–502, 515–516}}. 
}}</ref> The anthropologist [[Shepard Krech]], in his work [[#CITEREFKrech1999|''The Ecological Indian'']], analyzed the Indigenous peoples of North America and concluded that they  (prior to the 20th century) were ''ecologists'' because they were deeply aware of the interrelationships between humans, animals, and nature; but they were not ''conservationists'' because they did not avoid waste and did not preserve resources for future availability.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Krech|2005|pp=78–79}}. 
|{{harvnb|Krech|1999|pp=22-26}}. 
|{{harvnb|Denevan|2011| pp= 578, 580}}.
|{{harvnb|Clement |2010| p= 535}}.
}}</ref>{{void|According to the anthropologist Peter Stahl, some Native American cultures may have displayed a conservation ethic, but  many did not.{{sfn|Stahl|1996|pp=105–107,  117–119 }}
}}

===Applicability of conservation ethics to historic activities===

Research into the myth of the ecological noble savage generated  new discussions about whether modern values of conservation and sustainability are applicable to prehistoric or Indigenous cultures.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Hames|2007|p=177}}.
|{{harvnb|Smith|2000|pp= 493–496, 500–502, 515–516}}. 
|{{harvnb|Dowie |2009|pp=xv–xxix, 259–269}}. 
|{{harvnb|Buege|1996|pp=71-73, 86-88}}. 
}}</ref>  Analysis was sometimes dependent on the scientific discipline: [[conservation biology|conservation scientists]] and [[ecologist]]s tended to treat major habitat modifications as disturbances or disruptions, whereas [[archaeologist]]s and [[anthropologist]]s tended to view the changes as the natural evolutionary process of [[niche construction]].{{sfn|Ellis|2021a|p=3}}
  
Some scholars contend that  it is inappropriate to apply Western concepts of ecology or conservation to Indigenous peoples or [[Subsistence economy|subsistence cultures]].<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Roosevelt|2013|p=70}}.
|{{harvnb|Nadasdy|2005}}.
|{{harvnb|Smith|2000|pp= 493–496, 500–502, 515–516}}. 
}}</ref>{{void|The anthropologist Eric Alden Smith contends that approaches to conservation that emphasize preserving pristine wilderness are only feasible for urban, wealthy societies, and may not be appropriate for  [[Subsistence economy|subsistence cultures]].{{sfn|Smith|2000|pp=515–516}}
}}  Many modern Native Americans view the Western concept of [[nature conservation]] as inherently flawed, since they view themselves as living within nature.{{sfn|Stahl|1996|pp=105–107,  117–119 }}{{efn| There is no universally accepted definition of "[[nature conservation]]", but two common approaches are (a) focusing on the outcome: maintaining   populations, environments,  and biodiversity in near-original state;  or (b) focusing on processes: implementing practices that prevent or mitigate habitat degradation and species declines.{{sfn|Grayson|2001|pp=1-2}}
}}  
<!--
The myth of the noble savage has been applied to political ends in two ways:  Indigenous peoples have used the myth to support their arguments for equality and self determination.  And conservation organizations have used the myth to generate support for their causes.{{sfn|Hames|2007|p=185}}    The anthropologist [[Mac Chapin]] criticized several major conservation organizations in 2004, claiming their drives to preserve wilderness in an untouched state was harmful to Indigenous communities that lived in or near those preserves.{{sfn|Hames|2007|p=186}}  The philosopher [[Douglas Buege]] contends that the myth of the ecologically noble savage has been applied by Western conservationists in a way that is harmful to modern Indigenous cultures.{{sfn|Buege|1996|pp=71-73, 86-88}}
-->
The suggestion that a pristine wilderness, untouched by humans, is an ideal or desirable condition has been criticized as a racist or ethnocentric [[social construct]].<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Nelson|Callicott|2008|pp=302, 335, 356,358,362,364, 370, 426–427, 446,450 }}. 
}}</ref> In many parts of the world, prehistoric cultures did not (at the time of arrival by [[Western world|Westerners]]) place value on (or, in some cases, even have a word for) the idea of wilderness or "nature untouched by humans".{{sfn|Nelson|Callicott|2008|pp=356–357}}  The philosopher [[J. Baird Callicott]] wrote that the idea of wilderness is "alleged [by various authors] to be ethnocentric, androcentric, phallogocentric, unscientific, unphilosophic, impolitic, outmoded, even genocidal".{{sfn| Callicott| 2000|p=24}} An alternative to the notion of pristine wilderness is a "humanized landscape" or "humanized nature", defined as habitat that has been modified by humans to suit their needs and enable them to survive.<ref>{{multiref
|{{harvnb|Denevan|2011|pp= 577–579,581, 583 }}.
|{{harvnb|Denevan|1992|pp=369–370,374,379}}.
|{{harvnb|Nelson|Callicott|2008|pp=257, 399}}.  
}}</ref>  The historian [[William Cronon]] argues that  humans can only solve environmental problems by applying their culture and civilization to the issues, and that the ideal state of a landscape incorporates those modifications by humans required for their society to grow and thrive.{{sfn|Cronon|1995|pp=18-20}} 
<!--
 Many people in the Chinese culture believe that humanized nature is more beautiful than pristine wilderness.{{sfn|Nelson|Callicott|2008|p=257}}
-->

== The Anthropocene ==
{{further|Anthropocene#Proposed_starting_point}}
[[File:Trinity shot color (cropped).jpg|thumb|alt= A photograph of a nuclear bomb exploding| The 1945 [[Trinity test]] has been proposed as the start of the [[Anthropocene]], but scholars of [[historical ecology]] have proposed far earlier dates, such as the start of the [[Holocene]] around 12,000 years ago.{{sfn|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}}]]

The [[Anthropocene]] is a term used by scientists to refer to the period of  time when human activity has become the dominant influence on the planet's environment and ecosystems.{{sfn|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}}{{efn|In 2024, a proposal to establish a new, official [[geological epoch]] for the Anthropocene (using an epoch start date of around 1950) failed to gain approval from international scientific organizations.{{sfn|Zhong|2024}} In spite of that, the term "Anthropocene" is widely used in the academic community to denote the era in which humans are significantly impacting the Earth.
}}  Scientists do not agree when the Anthropocene began, and several proposals have been made for the start date.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}}.
|{{harvnb|Doughty|2013|pp=504-505}}.
}}</ref> Some proposals put the start date   in the 20th century, but others have suggested that the start date should be about 10,000 years ago{{snd}}based on the fact that human-driven alteration of the environment has been a continuum, extending back at least that far.<ref name=EarlyAntrhoHyp>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Rick|2013|pp= 33–34, 41–42}}.
|{{harvnb|Doughty|2013|pp= 504-505, 516-517}}.
|{{harvnb|Erlandson|2013|pp=1-2,6}}.
}}</ref>  Another proposal puts the start of the Anthropocene even further in the past, when the first human-caused mass extinctions occurred, sometime after 50,000 years ago.{{sfn|Svenning|2024|pp=1–3, 12–18}}

==Informing policy decisions==
 
The study of prehistoric impacts on the environment provides insights that can be used in the modern world to mitigate environmental damage and to inform [[environmental policies]].<ref name=Insights>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Kirch|2005|pp=409, 433}}.
|{{harvnb| Harkin|Lewis |2007| pp= 96,114–116}}.
|{{harvnb|Ellis|2021a|p=24}}. 
|{{harvnb|Rick|2013|pp= 33, 42}}.
|{{harvnb|Roberts|2017|pp=1–2,6}}.
|{{harvnb|Beach|2015|pp=1-2, 24-25}}.
|{{harvnb|Estrada|2022|pp=1-3, 13-14}}.
|{{harvnb|Malhi|2016|pp=843-844}}.
|{{harvnb|Burney|2005|p= 400}} 
}}</ref>   It may also provide incentive to [[List of recovering species|repopulate species]] in regions where they became [[locally extinct]],{{sfn|Svenning|2024|pp=2-3}}{{efn|The population of [[European beaver]] (''Castor fiber'') increased 16,000% in the past century.{{sfn|Svenning|2024|pp=2-3}}}}  to [[De-extinction|revive extinct species]],  or to introduce surrogates{{snd}}such as restoring elephants, cheetahs, or camels to North America.{{sfn|Burney|2005|p= 400}}  Historical examples of environmental damage can also be used in improper ways, for example to demonize modern Indigenous peoples, to justify intensive development of a region because it was already impacted, or to justify new, intensive damage to the environment because Indigenous peoples engaged in similar practices.{{sfn|Hayashida|2005|p=57}}
<!--
==In the modern era==

The environmental impacts of prehistoric cultures and Indigenous peoples continue to be relevant in the modern era in several ways.


===Stewardship===
{{further|Environmental justice|Environmental racism|Ethnoecology}}

In the past, some traditional land use practices produced cascading environmental consequences, sometimes leading to extinctions.{{sfn|Ellis|2021a|p=21 }}  But in the modern era, some of the most biodiverse regions in the world are those managed by Indigenous peoples.{{sfn|Ellis|2021a|p=21 }}  Lands that apply  traditional low-intensity agricultural practices tend to be more biodiverse than lands that use high-intensity methods.{{sfn|Ellis|2021a|p=21}}  Land use practices in the modern era can be shaped in a way that enhances the fertility of soil, enhances biodiversity, and improves hunting sustainability.{{sfn|Ellis|2021a|p=21 }}

In the modern era, Indigenous cultures often play an important role in environmental conservation, providing stewardship of habitats, plants, and animals.{{sfn|Brondízio|2021|p=488}}  Indigenous communities offer unique values, insights, and practices that can help the broader society address environmental issues.<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Brondízio|2021|p=482}}.
|{{harvnb|Sharifian|2022|loc= §§ "Abstract", "Introduction", "Conclusion"  }}.
}}</ref>   
 
The fields of [[ethnoecology]] and [[ethnobiology]] study Indigenous traditions and practices to determine if they may  benefit society in the fields of environment, medicine, and other disciplines.{{sfn|Berkes|2012|pp=2,5, 10–11, 23, 54–59, 279–288}} Indigenous peoples have frequently campaigned against pollution and [[environmental racism]].<ref>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Fernández-Llamazares|2020|pp=330–331}}.
|{{harvnb|Krech|2005|pp=82-83}}.
}}</ref>  Some environmental campaigns by Indigenous peoples are integrated with efforts to promote [[environmental justice]] and [[Indigenous land rights]].{{sfn|Fernández-Llamazares|2020|pp=330–331}} An analysis of Indigenous cultures in South America in the 21st century found that the cultural diversity they provided correlated strongly with biodiversity in the surrounding environment, suggesting that the existence of culturally unique Indigenous communities contributes to conservation efforts.{{sfn|Levis|2024  |pp=866,874}}

===  Clashes between conservationists and Indigenous peoples===
{{see|List of Indigenous peoples actions that conflict with conservation principles}}

In the modern era, some Indigenous communities have been criticized by conservationists for taking actions  that are contrary to [[nature conservation|conservation]] principles.<ref name=ClashConserv>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Krech|2005|p=83}}.
|{{harvnb|Krech|1999|pp=215–228}}.
|{{harvnb|Nadasdy|2005|p=292}}.
}}</ref>  
In these conflicts,  conservationists typically claim that the Indigenous peoples are damaging the environment, and Indigenous peoples sometimes claim that the conservationists do not comprehend their traditional values.{{sfn|Dowie|2009|pp=xv-xxix, 259-269}} Accusations of racism sometimes emerge in these conflicts.{{sfn|Nadasdy|2005|p=292}}{{efn|Some non-Indigenous people protested when [[Chippewa]] Native Americans used modern technologies to exercise their fishing rights.{{sfn|Buege|1996|pp=85–86}}
}}

Examples where environmentalists opposed the actions of Indigenous peoples include the [[Miccosukee]] building modern houses within [[Everglades National Park]],{{sfn|Krech|1999|pp=215–216}}{{sfn| Clary  | 1999 }} and  [[Navajo]] people's [[Uranium mining and the Navajo people|support for]] mining of [[uranium]] on their lands.{{sfn|Krech|1999|pp=215–216}} In water environments, [[Inuit]] hunted [[harp seals]]  in Canada's Arctic,{{sfn|Nadasdy|2005|p=292}} the [[Makah#Whaling|Makah]] tribe hunted [[grey whale]]s,<ref name=Makah>{{Multiref
|{{harvnb|Ellingson|2001|pp=359–370}}.  1999 hunt.
|{{harvnb|"Makah Tribal Whale Hunt", NOAA}}. 1999 and 2007 hunts, and others.
|{{harvnb|Nadasdy|2005|pp=291–292, 313}}. 1990 hunt.
}}</ref>{{efn|The 1999 whale hunt was authorized; the 2007 hunt was unauthorized and the whale sank after being shot.<ref name=Makah/>}} and the  [[Alaskan Athabaskans]] hunted [[beluga whales]] in [[Cook Inlet]] to consume and sell [[muktuk]].{{sfn|Krech|2005|p=83}}   [[Inupiat]] hunted whales wastefully in the 1970s,  fought against a global ban on whaling,{{sfn|Krech|1999|p=222}} and attempted to kill [[grey whale]]s that were trapped in the ice while environmental groups wanted to free them.{{sfn|Krech|1999|p=223}}

-->

An '''oak''' is a [[hardwood]] tree or shrub in the [[genus]] '''''Quercus''''' of the [[Fagaceae|beech family]]. They have spirally arranged leaves, often with lobed edges, and a nut called an [[acorn]], borne within a cup. The genus is widely distributed in the [[Northern Hemisphere]], with some 475 species,<ref name=powo/> both [[deciduous]] and [[evergreen]]. Fossil oaks date back to the Middle [[Eocene]]. [[Molecular phylogeny]] shows that the genus is divided into [[Old World]] and New World [[clade]]s, but many oak species [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridise]] freely, making the genus's history difficult to resolve.<!--Note: lead summaries cited text in body of article: citations are not repeated up here.-->

Ecologically, oaks are [[keystone species]] in habitats from Mediterranean semi-desert to subtropical [[rainforest]]. They live in association with many kinds of [[fungi]], including [[truffle]]s. Oaks support more than 950 species of [[caterpillar]], many kinds of [[gall wasp]] which form distinctive [[gall]]s (roundish woody lumps such as the [[oak apple]]), and a large number of pests and diseases. Oak leaves and acorns contain enough [[tannin]] to be toxic to cattle, but pigs are able to digest them safely. Oak timber is strong and hard, and has found many uses in construction and furniture-making. The bark was traditionally used for [[tanning leather]]. [[Oak (wine)|Wine barrel]]s are made of oak<!--of different species-->; these are used for aging alcoholic beverages such as [[sherry]] and [[whisky]], giving them a range of flavours, colours, and aromas. The spongy bark of the [[cork oak]] is used to make traditional wine bottle corks. Almost a third of oak species are threatened with extinction due to climate change, [[invasive pests]], and [[habitat loss]].<!--per MoS, lead summarizes cited claims in body of article but does not repeat the citations-->

In culture, the oak tree is a symbol of strength and serves as the [[national tree]] of many countries. In Indo-European and related religions, the oak is associated with [[thunder god]]s. Individual oak trees of cultural significance include the [[Royal Oak]] in Britain, the [[Charter Oak]] in the United States, and the [[Gernikako Arbola|Guernica Oak]] in the [[Basque Country (greater region)|Basque Country]].<!--per MoS, lead summarizes cited claims in body of article but does not repeat the citations-->

== Etymology ==

The [[genus|generic]] name ''Quercus'' is [[Latin]] for "oak", derived from [[Proto-Indo-European language|Proto-Indo-European]] ''*kwerkwu-'', "oak", which is also the origin of the name "[[fir]]", another important or sacred tree in [[Indo-European culture]].<ref>{{Cite book|page=407|title=[[Encyclopedia of Indo-European Culture]] |publisher=Fitzroy Dearborn |isbn=1-884964-98-2 |last=Mallory |first=James P. |author1-link=James P. Mallory|author2-link=Douglas Q. Adams |last2=Adams |first2=Douglas Q. |date=1997 |location=Chicago }}</ref> The word "cork", for the bark of the [[cork oak]], similarly derives from ''Quercus''.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Quercus'' (n.) |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/quercus |website=Online Etymology Dictionary |access-date=1 October 2023}}</ref> The common name "oak" is from [[Old English]] ''ac'' (seen in placenames such as [[Acton, London|Acton]], from ''ac'' + ''tun'', "oak town/village"),<ref>{{cite book |last=Mills |first=A. D. |title=A Dictionary of English Place-Names |date=1993 |orig-year=1991 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-283131-6 |page=2}}</ref> which in turn is from [[Proto-Germanic language|Proto-Germanic]] ''*aiks'', "oak".<ref>{{cite web |title=Oak (n.) |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/oak |website=Online Etymology Dictionary |access-date=1 October 2023}}</ref>

== Description ==

Oaks are [[hardwood]] ([[dicotyledon]]ous) trees, [[deciduous]] or [[evergreen]], with spirally arranged leaves, often with [[Dentate leaf|lobate margins]]; some have [[serrated leaves]] or [[Entire (botany)|entire leaves]] with smooth margins. Many deciduous species are [[marcescent]], not dropping dead leaves until spring. Oaks can be grouped into "[[red oak]]s" that have soft bristles on their leaves' lobes, and "[[white oak]]s" that don't have those bristles.<ref name="JCFC"/>

In spring, a single oak tree [[Monoecy|produces both]] male and female flowers. The [[staminate]] (male) flowers are arranged in [[catkin]]s, while the small [[pistillate]] (female) flowers<ref>{{cite web |last=Conrad |first=Jim |url=http://www.backyardnature.net/fl_bloak.htm |title=Oak Flowers |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131104064011/http://www.backyardnature.net/fl_bloak.htm |archive-date=4 November 2013 |website=Backyardnature.com |date=12 December 2011}}</ref> produce an [[acorn]] (a&nbsp;kind of [[Nut (fruit)|nut]]) contained in a capped [[peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] called a [[Calybium and cupule|cupule]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Vázquez |first1=Francisco |title=For Acorns, Size Matters—and So Does Shape |url=https://www.internationaloaksociety.org/content/acorns-size-matters-and-so-does-shape |website=Articles |publisher=International Oak Society |access-date=29 July 2026 |date=March 13, 2015}}</ref> Each acorn usually contains one seed.<ref name="JCFC">{{cite web |last=Busch |first=Mary Jane |title=Go Nuts for Acorns! |url=https://ecosystems.psu.edu/research/centers/private-forests/news/go-nuts-for-acorns |publisher=[[Penn State College of Agricultural Sciences]] |date=23 October 2023}}</ref> The acorns and leaves contain [[tannic acid]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tull |first=Delena |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pnnHgcasN-cC&pg=PA102 |title=Edible and Useful Plants of Texas and the Southwest: A Practical Guide |date=1999 |publisher=[[University of Texas Press]] |isbn=978-0-2927-8164-1 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170215071946/https://books.google.com/books?id=pnnHgcasN-cC&pg=PA102 |archive-date=15 February 2017}}</ref> which helps to guard against fungi and insects.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hipp |first=Andrew |title=Oak Trees |date=2004 |publisher=[[Rosen Publishing]] |isbn=978-0-8239-4206-0 |page=4}}</ref> There are some 500 extant species of oaks.<ref name=powo>{{cite web |title=''Quercus'' L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:325819-2 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |access-date=30 September 2020}}</ref>

Trees in the genus are usually large and slow-growing; ''Q.&nbsp;alba'' can reach an age of 600 years, a diameter of {{convert|4|m|ft}} and a height of {{convert|44|m|ft}}.<ref name="Core">{{cite web |last1=Core |first1=Earl L. |title=Silvical Characteristics of the Five Upland Oaks |url=https://www.nrs.fs.usda.gov/pubs/other/oak_sym/oak_symposium_proceedings_019.pdf |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |access-date=5 October 2023 |pages=19–22}}</ref> The [[Granit oak]] in Bulgaria, a ''Q.&nbsp;robur'' specimen, has an estimated age of 1,637 years, making it the oldest oak in Europe.<ref>{{cite web |last=Todorov |first=Radoslav |title=Знаете ли кои са най-старите живи организми? |url=https://chr.bg/zhivot/znaete-li-koi-sa-naj-starite-zhivi-organizmi/ |trans-title=Do you know which are the oldest living organisms? |website=Chronicle.B |access-date=5 October 2023 |language=Bulgarian |date=30 September 2018}}</ref> The Wi'aaSal tree, a [[live oak]] in the reservation of the [[Pechanga Band of Indians]], California, is at least 1,000 years old, and might be as much as 2,000 years old, which would make it the oldest oak in the US.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Largest Oak Trees in the World |url=https://hardwoodsgroup.com/the-largest-oak-trees-in-the-world/ |website=Hardwoods Group |date=27 July 2021 |access-date=5 October 2023 |archive-date=4 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231204003110/https://hardwoodsgroup.com/the-largest-oak-trees-in-the-world/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Among the smallest oaks is ''[[Quercus acuta|Q.&nbsp;acuta]]'', the Japanese evergreen oak. It forms a bush or small tree to a height of some {{convert|9|m|ft}}.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gilman |first1=Edward F. |last2=Watson |first2=Dennis G. |title=Quercus acuta Japanese Evergreen Oak |url=https://hort.ifas.ufl.edu/trees/QUEACUA.pdf |website=ifas.ufl.edu |publisher=University of Florida |access-date=August 13, 2025 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250813080741/https://hort.ifas.ufl.edu/trees/QUEACUA.pdf |archive-date=August 13, 2025  }}</ref>

== Evolution ==

=== Fossil history ===

Potential records of ''Quercus'' have been reported from [[Late Cretaceous]] deposits in North America and East Asia. These are not considered definitive, as macrofossils older than the [[Paleogene]], and possibly from before the [[Eocene]] are mostly poorly preserved without critical features for certain identification. Amongst the oldest unequivocal records of ''Quercus'' are pollen from Austria, dating to the [[Paleocene]]-Eocene boundary, around 55 million years ago. The oldest records of ''Quercus'' in North America are from [[Oregon]], dating to the Middle Eocene, around 44 million years ago, with the oldest records in Asia from the Middle Eocene of Japan; both forms have affinities to the ''[[Cyclobalanopsis]]'' group.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Barrón |first1=Eduardo |last2=Averyanova |first2=Anna |last3=Kvaček |first3=Zlatko |last4=Momohara |first4=Arata |last5=Pigg |first5=Kathleen B. |last6=Popova |first6=Svetlana |last7=Postigo-Mijarra |first7=José María |last8=Tiffney |first8=Bruce H. |last9=Utescher |first9=Torsten |last10=Zhou |first10=Zhe Kun |title=Oaks Physiological Ecology. Exploring the Functional Diversity of Genus Quercus L |chapter=The Fossil History of Quercus |series=Tree Physiology |date=2017 |volume=7 |pages=39–105 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-69099-5_3 |isbn=978-3-319-69098-8 |hdl=10261/277765 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== External phylogeny ===

''Quercus'' forms part, or rather two parts, of the [[Quercoideae]] subfamily of the [[Fagaceae]], the beech family. Modern [[molecular phylogenetics]] suggests the following relationships:<ref name="Manos Cannon Oh 2008">{{cite journal |last1=Manos |first1=Paul S. |last2=Cannon |first2=Charles H. |last3=Oh |first3=Sang-Hun |title=Phylogenetic Relationships and Taxonomic Status Of the Paleoendemic Fagaceae Of Western North America: Recognition Of A New Genus, Notholithocarpus |journal=Madroño |publisher=California Botanical Society |volume=55 |issue=3 |year=2008 |doi=10.3120/0024-9637-55.3.181 |pages=181–190 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/168898 }}</ref><ref name="Xiang Wang Li 2014">{{cite journal |last1=Xiang |first1=Xiao-Guo |last2=Wang |first2=Wei |last3=Li |first3=Rui-Qi |last4=Lin |first4=Li |last5=Liu |first5=Yang |last6=Zhou |first6=Zhe-Kun |last7=Li |first7=Zhen-Yu |last8=Chen |first8=Zhi-Duan |display-authors=3 |title=Large-scale phylogenetic analyses reveal fagalean diversification promoted by the interplay of diaspores and environments in the Paleogene |journal=Perspectives in Plant Ecology, Evolution and Systematics |publisher=Elsevier BV |volume=16 |issue=3 |year=2014 |doi=10.1016/j.ppees.2014.03.001 |pages=101–110|bibcode=2014PPEES..16..101X }}</ref>

=== Internal phylogeny ===

Molecular techniques for phylogenetic analysis show that the genus ''Quercus'' consisted of [[Old World]] and [[New World]] clades.<ref name=":0"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hipp |first1=Andrew L. |last2=Manos|first2=Paul S. |last3=González-Rodríguez|first3=Antonio |last4=Hahn |first4=Marlene |last5=Kaproth|first5=Matthew |last6=McVay |first6=John D. |last7=Avalos |first7=Susana Valencia origins of Mexican species diversity |journal=New Phytologist |volume=217 |issue=1 |pages=439–452 |doi=10.1111/nph.14773|pmid=28921530 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2018NewPh.217..439H |hdl=10161/15608 been [[DNA sequencing|sequenced]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Plomion |first1=Christophe |last2=Aury |first2=Jean-Marc |last3=Amselem |first3=Joëlle |last4=Alaeitabar |first4=Tina |last5=Barbe
