|date=March 2024 |volume=291 |article-number=110489 |doi=10.1016/j.biocon.2024.110489 |bibcode=2024BCons.29110489V }}</ref> Coyotes, widespread and with a rapidly expanding population, are often the only major nonhuman predator of the species in the Eastern U.S., besides an occasional [[domestic dog]].<ref name= Smith/> In some areas, [[American black bear]]s are also significant predators.<ref name=Mathews/><ref name=Ozoga/> In north-central Pennsylvania, black bears were found to be nearly as common predators of fawns as coyotes.<ref>{{cite web|author=Mulhollem, Jeff|url=http://news.psu.edu/story/186685/2001/12/17/penn-state-study-shows-bears-are-major-predators-fawns|title=Penn State Study Shows Bears Are Major Predators Of Fawns|date=December 17, 2001|access-date=March 25, 2017}}</ref> Bobcats, still fairly widespread, usually only exploit deer as prey when smaller prey is scarce.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Labisky | first1 = Ronald F. | last2 = Boulay | first2 = Margaret C. | year = 1998 | title = Behaviors of Bobcats Preying on White-tailed Deer in the Everglades | journal = The American Midland Naturalist | volume = 139 | issue = 2| pages = 275–281 | doi=10.1674/0003-0031(1998)139[0275:bobpow]2.0.co;2 }}</ref> Discussions have occurred regarding the possible reintroduction of gray wolves and cougars to sections of the eastern United States, largely because of the apparent controlling effect they have through deer predation on local ecosystems, as has been illustrated in the reintroduction of wolves to [[Yellowstone National Park]] and their controlling effect on previously overpopulated [[elk]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nps.gov/yell/naturescience/wolves.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070220051051/http://www.nps.gov/yell/naturescience/wolves.htm |archive-date=February 20, 2007 |title=Wolves of Yellowstone - Yellowstone National Park (U.S. National Park Service) |publisher=Nps.gov |access-date=September 20, 2013}}</ref> However, due to the heavy urban development in much of the Eastern U.S., and fear for livestock and human lives, such ideas have ultimately been rejected by local communities and/or by government services and have not been carried through.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.apnmag.com/natural%20selections/spring03/reintroduction%20of%20wolves.htm |title=Reintroduction of Wolves |publisher=Apnmag.com |access-date=September 20, 2013 |archive-date=September 27, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927134438/http://www.apnmag.com/natural%20selections/spring03/reintroduction%20of%20wolves.htm  }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fws.gov/northeast/graywolf.html |title=Northeast Region, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service - Gray Wolf |publisher=Fws.gov |access-date=September 20, 2013 |archive-date=June 5, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130605002705/http://www.fws.gov/northeast/graywolf.html  }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dec.ny.gov/pubs/42763.html/ |title=Big Cat Tales - NYS Dept. of Environmental Conservation |publisher=Dec.ny.gov |access-date=September 20, 2013 |archive-date=September 21, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921055354/http://www.dec.ny.gov/pubs/42763.html/  }}</ref>

[[File:Deer20210112.webm|thumb|White-tailed deer can jump very far.]]
White-tailed deer can run faster than their predators and have been recorded sprinting at speeds of {{convert|40|mi|km|abbr=on|order=flip|sigfig=1}} per hour and sustaining speeds of {{convert|30|mi|km|abbr=on|order=flip|sigfig=1}} per hour over distances of {{Convert|3-4|mi|km|abbr=on|order=flip|sigfig=1}};<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dagg |first1=Anne Innis |last2=de Vos |first2=Antoon |title=Fast gaits of pecoran species |journal=Journal of Zoology |date=August 1968 |volume=155 |issue=4 |pages=499–506 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-7998.1968.tb03065.x }}</ref> this ranks them amongst the fastest of all deer, alongside the Eurasian [[roe deer]]. They can also jump {{convert|9|ft|m|abbr=on|order=flip|sigfig=1}} high and up to {{convert|30|ft|m|abbr=on|order=flip|sigfig=1}} forward. When shot at, a white-tailed deer will run at high speeds with its tail down. If frightened, the deer will hop in a zig-zag with its tail straight up. If the deer feels extremely threatened, however, it may choose to attack, charging the person or predator posing the threat, using its antlers or, if none are present, its head to fight off its target.

===Forest alteration===
In certain parts of eastern North America, high deer densities have caused large reductions in plant biomass, including the density and heights of certain forest wildflowers, tree seedlings, and shrubs. Although they can be seen as a nuisance species, white-tailed deer also play an important role in biodiversity.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Augustine | first1 = DJ | last2 = Frelich | first2 = LE | year = 1998 | title = Effects of White-Tailed Deer on Populations of an Understory Forb in Fragmented Deciduous Forests | journal = Conservation Biology | volume = 12 | issue = 5| pages = 995–1004 | doi = 10.1046/j.1523-1739.1998.97248.x | bibcode = 1998ConBi..12..995A }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Cote | first1 = S.D. | last2 = Rooney | first2 = T.P. | last3 = Tremblay | first3 = J. | last4 = Dussault | first4 = C. | last5 = Waller | first5 = D.M. | year = 2004 | title = Ecological impacts of deer overabundance | journal = Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics | volume = 35 | pages = 113–47 | doi=10.1146/annurev.ecolsys.35.021103.105725}}</ref> At the same time, increases in browse-tolerant grasses and sedges and unpalatable ferns have often accompanied intensive deer herbivory.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Rooney | first1 = T.P. | year = 2009 | title = High white-tailed deer densities benefit graminoids and contribute to biotic homogenization of forest ground-layer vegetation | journal = Plant Ecology | volume = 202 | issue = 1 | pages = 103–111 | doi=10.1007/s11258-008-9489-8| bibcode = 2009PlEco.202..103R }}</ref> Changes to the structure of forest understories have, in turn, altered the composition and abundance of forest bird communities in some areas.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = McShea | first1 = W.J. | last2 = Rappole | first2 = J.H. | year = 2000 | title = Managing the abundance and diversity of breeding bird populations through manipulation of deer populations | journal = Conservation Biology | volume = 14 | issue = 4| pages = 1161–1170 | doi=10.1046/j.1523-1739.2000.99210.x| bibcode = 2000ConBi..14.1161M }}</ref> In regions of intermediate density, deer activity has also been shown to increase herbaceous plant diversity, particularly in disturbed areas, by reducing competitively dominant plants;<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Royo | first1 = Alejandro A. | last2 = Collins | first2 = Rachel | last3 = Adams | first3 = Mary Beth | last4 = Kirschbaum | first4 = Chad | last5 = Carson | first5 = Walter P. | year = 2010 | title = Pervasive interactions between ungulate browsers and disturbance regimes promote temperate forest herbaceous diversity | journal = Ecology | volume = 91 | issue = 1| pages = 93–105 | doi=10.1890/08-1680.1| pmid = 20380200 | bibcode = 2010Ecol...91...93R }}</ref> and to increase the growth rates of important canopy trees, perhaps by increased nutrient inputs into the soil.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Lucas | first1 = Richard W. | last2 = Salguero-Gómez | first2 = Roberto | last3 = Cobb | first3 = David B. | last4 = Waring | first4 = Bonnie G. | last5 = Anderson | first5 = Frank | last6 = McShea | first6 = William J. | last7 = Casper | first7 = Brenda B. | year = 2013 | title = White-tailed deer (''Odocoileus virginianus'') positively affect the growth of mature northern red oak (''Quercus rubra'') trees | journal = Ecosphere | volume = 4 | issue = 7| page = art84 | doi = 10.1890/ES13-00036.1 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

In northeastern hardwood forests, high-density deer populations affect plant succession, particularly following clear-cuts and patch cuts. In succession without deer, annual herbs and woody plants are followed by commercially valuable, shade-tolerant oak and maple. The shade-tolerant trees prevent the invasion of less commercial cherry and American beech, which are stronger nutrient competitors, but not as shade tolerant. Although deer eat shade-tolerant plants and acorns, this is not the only way deer can shift the balance in favor of nutrient competitors. Deer consuming earlier-succession plants allows in enough light for nutrient competitors to invade. Since slow-growing oaks need several decades to develop root systems sufficient to compete with faster-growing species, removal of the canopy prior to that point amplifies the effect of deer on succession. High-density deer populations possibly could browse eastern hemlock seedlings out of existence in northern hardwood forests;<ref>{{cite book|last=McShea|first=W.J.|title=The Science of Overabundance: Deer Ecology and Population Management|year=1997|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, DC|isbn=978-1-58834-062-7|pages=201–223, 249–279}}</ref> however, this scenario seems unlikely, given that deer browsing is not considered the critical factor preventing hemlock re-establishment at large scales.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Mladenoff | first1 = D.J. | last2 = Stearns | first2 = F. | year = 1993 | title = Easter hemlock regeneration and deer browsing in the northern great lakes region: a re-examination and model simulation | journal = Conservation Biology | volume = 7 | issue = 4| pages = 889–900 | doi=10.1046/j.1523-1739.1993.740889.x| bibcode = 1993ConBi...7..889M }}</ref>

Ecologists have also expressed concern over the facilitative effect high deer populations have on invasions of exotic plant species. In a study of eastern hemlock forests, browsing by white-tailed deer caused populations of three exotic plants to rise faster than they do in the areas which are absent of deer. Seedlings of the three invading species rose exponentially with deer density, while the most common native species fell exponentially with deer density, because deer were preferentially eating the native species. The effects of deer on the invasive and native plants were magnified in cases of canopy disturbance.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Eschtruth |first1=Anne K. |last2=Battles |first2=John J. |title=Acceleration of exotic plant invasion in a forested ecosystem by a generalist herbivore |journal=Conservation Biology: The Journal of the Society for Conservation Biology |date=April 2009 |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=388–399 |doi=10.1111/j.1523-1739.2008.01122.x |pmid=19183209 }}</ref>

===Population and controls===
The white-tailed deer population in North America has declined by several million since 2000, but as of 2017 is considered healthy and is approximately equal to the historical pre-colonization white-tailed population on the continent.<ref name=DF>"[http://www.deerfriendly.com/decline-of-deer-populations Decline of Deer Populations]". DeerFriendly.com. Retrieved March 11, 2021.</ref> The species has rebounded considerably after being overhunted nearly to extinction in the late 1800s and very early 1900s.<ref name=DF /> By contrast, the species' closest cousins ([[blacktail deer]] and [[mule deer]]) have seen their populations cut by more than half in North America after peaking in 1960 and have never regained their pre-colonization numbers.<ref name=DF /> In the 21st century, the loss of natural predators has been more than offset by the ongoing loss of natural habitat to human development, and changes to logging operations.<ref name=DF />

Several methods have been developed to curb the population of white-tailed deer in suburban areas where they are perceived as overabundant, and these can be separated into lethal and nonlethal strategies. Most common in the U.S. is the use of extended hunting as population control, as well as a way to provide meat for humans.<ref name="Population Control">{{cite web|last1=Kammin|first1=Laura|title=Population Control|url=http://web.extension.illinois.edu/deer/damage.cfm?SubCat=8890|website=Living with White Tailed Deer in Illinois|publisher=University of Illinois Extension|access-date=May 27, 2016|archive-date=March 17, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160317005744/http://web.extension.illinois.edu/deer/damage.cfm?SubCat=8890}}</ref> In Maryland and many other states, a state agency sets regulations on bag limits and hunting in the area depending on the deer population levels assessed.<ref>{{cite web|title=2015–2016 White Tailed Deer Seasons and Bag Limits|url=http://www.eregulations.com/maryland/hunting/2015-2016-white-tailed-deer-seasons-bag-limits/|website=Maryland Guide to Hunting & Trapping|publisher=Maryland Department of Natural Resources|access-date=May 27, 2016|archive-date=May 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160520110234/http://www.eregulations.com/maryland/hunting/2015-2016-white-tailed-deer-seasons-bag-limits/}}</ref> Hunting seasons may fluctuate in duration, or restrictions may be set to affect how many deer or what type of deer can be hunted in certain regions. For the 2015–2016 white-tailed deer-hunting season, some areas allowed only the hunting of antlerless white-tailed deer. These included young bucks and females, which encouraged the culling of does, aiding in population control.<ref name="Population Control"/>

A more targeted yet more expensive<ref name=Bloomington>{{cite web|author=The City of Bloomington|title=Deer: Lethal Approaches|date=April 2011 |url=https://bloomington.in.gov/documents/viewDocument.php?document_id=5719|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170609173519/https://bloomington.in.gov/documents/viewDocument.php?document_id=5719|access-date=March 11, 2021|archive-date=June 9, 2017}}</ref> removal strategy than public hunting is a method referred to as sharpshooting. Sharpshooting can be an option when the area inhabited by the deer is unfit for public hunting. This strategy may work in areas close to human populations, since it is done by professional marksmen, and requires a submitted plan of action to the city with details of the time and location of the action, as well as number of deer to be culled.<ref name=Bloomington /> Another controversial method involves trapping the deer in a net or other trap, and then administering a chemical euthanizing agent or extermination by firearm. A main issue in questioning the humaneness of this method is the stress that the deer endure while trapped and awaiting extermination.<ref name=Bloomington />

Nonlethal methods include contraceptive injections, sterilization, and translocation of deer.<ref>{{cite web|author=The City of Bloomington|title=Commonly Discussed Management Options|date=March 16, 2011 |url=https://bloomington.in.gov/sections/viewSection.php?section_id=604#management|access-date=May 27, 2016|archive-date=June 8, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160608200620/http://bloomington.in.gov/sections/viewSection.php?section_id=604#management}}</ref> While lethal methods have municipal support as being the most effective in the short term, some opponents of this view suggest that extermination has no significant impact on deer populations.<ref>{{cite web|author=The Humane Society of the United States|title=Wildlife Fertility Control|url=http://www.humanesociety.org/animals/deer/tips/deer-humane-control.html|website=Controlling Deer Populations Humanely|access-date=May 27, 2016|archive-date=May 23, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160523103651/http://www.humanesociety.org/animals/deer/tips/deer-humane-control.html}}</ref> Opponents of contraceptive methods point out that fertility control cannot provide meat and proves ineffective over time as populations in open-field systems move about. Concerns are voiced that the contraceptives have not been adequately researched for the effect they could have on humans. Fertility control also does nothing to affect the current population and the effects their grazing may be having on the forest plant make-up.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Kammin|first1=Laura|title=Other Control Methods|url=http://web.extension.illinois.edu/deer/damage.cfm?SubCat=8890|website=Living with White Tailed Deer in Illinois|access-date=May 27, 2016|archive-date=March 17, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160317005744/http://web.extension.illinois.edu/deer/damage.cfm?SubCat=8890}}</ref>

Translocation has been considered overly costly for the little benefit it provides. Deer experience high stress and are at high risk of dying in the process, putting into question its humaneness.<ref>{{cite web|author=State of Connecticut|title=White-Tailed Deer|url=https://portal.ct.gov/DEEP/Wildlife/Fact-Sheets/White-tailed-Deer|website=Department of Energy and Environmental Protection|access-date=May 27, 2016}}</ref> Another concern regarding translocation is the possible spreading of [[chronic wasting disease]] to unaffected deer populations and concerns about exposure to human populations.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/10/6/pdfs/03-1082.pdf |title=Chronic Wasting Disease and Potential Transmission to Humans |publisher=[[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] |journal=Emerging Infectious Diseases |volume=10 |issue=6 |date=June 2004 |access-date=March 11, 2021 |first1=Ermias D. |last1=Belay |first2=Ryan A. |last2=Maddox |first3=Elizabeth S. |last3=Williams |first4=Michael W. |last4=Miller |first5=Pierluigi |last5=Gambetti |first6=Lawrence B. |last6=Schonberger |doi=10.3201/eid1006.031082 |doi-access=free |pages=977–984|pmid=15207045 |pmc=3323184 }}</ref>

In addition to the danger of [[#Deer–vehicle collisions|deer-vehicle collisions]] the [[National Agricultural Statistics Service]] (NASS) reported that the estimated loss in field crops, nuts, fruits, and vegetables in 2001 was near $765 million<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://agfuse.com/article/oh-deer-deer-damage-and-what-farmers-can-do-about-it|title=Oh deer! Deer damage and what farmers can do about it|website=AgFuse - Agricultural Social Network|access-date=June 28, 2019|archive-date=June 28, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190628051027/https://agfuse.com/article/oh-deer-deer-damage-and-what-farmers-can-do-about-it}}</ref> (equivalent to ${{formatprice|{{inflation|US-GDP|765000000|2001}}}} in {{inflation/year|US-GDP}}).{{inflation/fn|US-GDP}}

==Behavior==

Males compete for the opportunity to breed with females, with sparring among males determining a [[Dominance (ethology)|dominance hierarchy]].<ref name="Ditchkoff 2001">{{cite journal | last1 = Ditchkoff | first1 = S. S. | last2 = Lochmiller | first2 = Robert L. | last3 = Masters | first3 = Ronald E. | last4 = Hoofer | first4 = Steven R. | last5 = Van Den Bussche | first5 = Ronald A. | year = 2001 | title = Major-Histocompatibility-Complex-Associated Variation In Secondary Sexual Traits Of White-Tailed Deer (''Odocoileus virginianus''): Evidence For Good-Genes Advertisement | journal = Evolution | volume = 55 | issue = 3| pages = 616–625 | doi=10.1111/j.0014-3820.2001.tb00794.x | pmid=11327168 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Bucks attempt to copulate with as many females as possible, gradually losing physical condition since they rarely eat or rest during the rut. The general geographical trend is for the rut to be shorter in duration at increased latitude. Many factors determine how intense the "rutting season" will be; air temperature is a major one. Any time the temperature rises above {{convert|40|F|C|order=flip}}, the males do much less traveling looking for females, else they will be subject to overheating or dehydrating.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024|reason=Specific (and somewhat low) temperature provided for overheating without source.}} Another factor for the strength of rutting activity is competition. If numerous males are in a particular area, then they compete more for the females. If fewer males or more females are present, then the selection process will not need to be as competitive.

===Reproduction===
{{Main|Rut (mammalian reproduction)#White-tailed deer}}
{{multiple image|perrow=1|image1=Mating deer (30951561596).jpg|caption1=Male white-tailed deer mounting a female|
image2=Odocoileus virginianus (white-tailed deer) 8 (8270236202).jpg|caption2=Female white-tailed deer with fawn}}
Females enter [[Estrous cycle|estrus]], colloquially called the [[Rut (mammalian reproduction)|rut]], in the autumn, normally in late October or early November, triggered mainly by the declining [[Photoperiodism|photoperiod]]. Sexual maturation of females depends on [[Population density#Biological population densities|population density]], as well as the availability of food.<ref>{{cite web|title=Forest Foods Deer Eat," Department of Natural Resources website|url= http://www.michigan.gov/dnr/0,1607,7-153-10370_12148-61306--,00.html|publisher=Department of Natural Resources&nbsp;— State of Michigan|year=2008|access-date=February 18, 2011}}</ref> Young females often flee from an area heavily populated with males. Some does may be as young as six months when they reach sexual maturity, but the average age of maturity is 18 months.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.massaudubon.org/learn/nature-wildlife/mammals/deer/about|title = Mass Audubon|access-date = January 20, 2016|website = Mass Audubon (Protecting the Nature of Massachusetts)|archive-date = February 4, 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160204001349/http://www.massaudubon.org/learn/nature-wildlife/mammals/deer/about}}</ref> Copulation consists of a brief copulatory jump.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Warren | first1 = R. J. | display-authors = etal   | year = 1978 | title = Reproductive behaviour of captive white-tailed deer | journal = Animal Behaviour | volume = 26 | pages = 179–183 | doi=10.1016/0003-3472(78)90017-9| bibcode = 1978AnBeh..26N1181W }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author1=David M. Shackleton|author2=Royal British Columbia Museum|title=Hoofed Mammals of British Columbia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iQq2iFktrwoC|year=1999|publisher=UBC Press|isbn=978-0-7748-0728-9}}</ref>
<!-- Further information can be found here: http://www.google.com/#hl=en&tbo=d&sclient=psy-ab&q=white+tailed+deer+mating+ritual&oq=white+tailed+deer+copulation&gs_l=hp.1.3.0i30j0i22l3.0.0.3.15193.1.1.0.0.0.0.158.158.0j1.1.0.les%3Bcrnk_timediscounta..0.0...1c.MQhPyz6zO5c&pbx=1&bav=on.2,or.r_gc.r_pw.r_qf.&fp=86ddbf3dd87f247c&bpcl=38625945&biw=1366&bih=631 -->

Females give birth to one to three spotted young, known as fawns, in mid-to-late spring, generally in May or June. Fawns lose their spots during the first summer and weigh from {{Convert|20|to|35|kg|lb|abbr=on}} by the first winter. Male fawns tend to be slightly larger and heavier than females. For the first four weeks, fawns are hidden in vegetation by their mothers, who nurse them four to five times a day. This strategy keeps scent levels low to avoid predators. After about a month, the fawns<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.georgiawildlife.com/DeerFacts|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905171145/http://www.georgiawildlife.com/DeerFacts|archive-date=September 5, 2015|title=Deer Fact Sheet &#124; Georgia DNR - Wildlife Resources Division|date=September 5, 2015}}</ref> are then able to follow their mothers on foraging trips. They are usually weaned after 8–10 weeks, but cases have been seen where mothers have continued to allow nursing long after the fawns have lost their spots (for several months, or until the end of fall) as seen by rehabilitators and other studies. Males leave their mothers after a year and females leave after two.

Bucks are generally [[sexually mature]] at 1.5 years old and begin to breed even in populations stacked with older bucks.{{citation needed|date=March 2021}}

===Communication===

White-tailed deer have many forms of communication involving sounds, scent, body language, and marking. In addition to the blowing in the presence of danger, all white-tailed deer can produce audible noises unique to each animal. Fawns release a high-pitched squeal, known as a bleat, to call out to their mothers.<ref name=" vocalization">{{cite journal | last1 = Atkeson | first1 = Thomas D. | last2 = Marchinton | first2 = R. Larry | last3 = Miller | first3 = Karl V. | year = 1988 | title = Vocalizations of White-tailed Deer | journal = American Midland Naturalist | volume = 120 | issue = 1| pages = 194–200 | doi=10.2307/2425899| jstor = 2425899 }}</ref> This bleat deepens as the fawn grows until it becomes the grunt of the mature deer, a guttural sound that attracts the attention of any other deer in the area. A doe makes maternal grunts when searching for her bedded fawns.<ref name=" vocalization"/> Bucks also grunt, at a pitch lower than that of the doe; this grunt deepens as the buck matures. In addition to grunting, both does and bucks also snort, a sound that often signals an imminent threat. Mature bucks also produce a grunt-snort-wheeze pattern, unique to each animal, that asserts its dominance, aggression, and hostility.<ref name=" vocalization"/> White-tailed deer also use "tail-flagging", a behavior where the tail is raised when they detect a threat. However, the function of this behavior is disputed, and it appears to be a signal to predators more than an intraspecific communication warning other deer.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bildstein |first=Keith L. |date=1983 |title=Why White-Tailed Deer Flag Their Tails |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=121 |issue=5 |pages=709–715 |doi=10.1086/284096|bibcode=1983ANat..121..709B }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Caro |first1=T.M. |last2=Lombardo |first2=L. |last3=Goldizen |first3=A.W. |last4=Kelly |first4=Marcella |date=1995 |title=Tail-flagging and other antipredator signals in white-tailed deer: new data and synthesis |journal=Behavioral Ecology |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=442–450 |doi=10.1093/beheco/6.4.442}}</ref>

===Marking===
White-tailed deer possess many [[gland]]s that allow them to produce [[scent marking|scent]]s, some of which are so potent they can be detected by the human nose. Four major glands are the preorbital, forehead, tarsal, and metatarsal glands. Secretions from the [[preorbital gland]]s (in front of the eye) were thought to be rubbed on tree branches, but research suggests this is not so.{{Citation needed|date=November 2019}} Scent from the forehead or sudoriferous glands (found on the head, between the antlers and eyes) is used to [[territorial marking|deposit scent]] on branches that overhang [[deer rub|scrapes]] (areas scraped by the deer's front hooves before [[rub-urination]]). The tarsal glands are found on the upper inside of the hock (middle joint) on each hind leg. The scent is deposited from these glands when deer walk through and rub against vegetation. These scrapes are used by bucks as a sort of "sign-post" by which bucks know which other bucks are in the area, and to let does know a buck is regularly passing through the area—for breeding purposes. The scent from the metatarsal glands, found on the outside of each hind leg, between the ankle and hooves, may be used as an alarm scent. The scent from the interdigital glands, which are located between the hooves of each foot, emit a yellow waxy substance with an offensive odor. Deer can be seen stomping their hooves if they sense danger through sight, sound, or smell; this action leaves an excessive amount of odor for warning other deer of possible danger.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://bowsite.com/bowsite/features/armchair_biologist/deerscrapes/deerscrapes.html|title=Whitetail Buck Scrapes|website=bowsite.com}}</ref>

{{anchor|mating}}

[[File:20241125 self anointing white tailed deer cedar hill.webm|thumb|A doe rub-urinating]]
Throughout the year, deer [[rub-urinate]], a process during which a deer squats while urinating so the urine will run down the insides of the deer's legs, over the tarsal glands, and onto the hair covering these glands. Bucks rub-urinate more frequently during the breeding season.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Alexy | first1 = Karen J. | last2 = Gassett | first2 = Jonathan W. | last3 = Osborn | first3 = David A. | last4 = Miller | first4 = Karl V. | year = 2001 | title = White-Tailed Deer Rubs and Scrapes: Spatial, Temporal and Physical Characteristics and Social Role | journal = Wildlife Society Bulletin | volume = 29 | issue = 3| pages = 873–878}}</ref> Secretions from the [[preputial gland]]s<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Odend'hal |first1=S. |last2=Miller |first2=K. V. |last3=Hoffmann |first3=D. M. |title=Preputial Glands in the White-Tailed Deer (Odocoileus virginianus) |journal=Journal of Mammalogy |date=26 May 1992 |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=299–302 |doi=10.2307/1382060|jstor=1382060 }}</ref> and tarsal glands mix with the urine and bacteria to produce a strong-smelling odor.<ref>Osborn, David A., et al. "[http://rcin.org.pl/Content/12996/BI002_27023_Cz-40-2_Acta-T45-nr12-117-122_o.pdf Morphology of the white-tailed deer tarsal gland]." Acta Theriologica 45.1 (2000): 117-122.</ref> During the breeding season, does release hormones and pheromones that tell bucks a doe is in heat and able to breed. Bucks also rub trees and shrubs with their antlers and heads during the breeding season, possibly [[scent rubbing|transferring scent from the forehead glands]] to the tree, leaving a scent other deer can detect.<ref name="marking"/>

Sign-post marking (scrapes and rubs) is a very obvious way white-tailed deer communicate.<ref name=" marking">{{cite journal | last1 = Kile | first1 = Terry L. | last2 = Marchinton | first2 = R. Larry | year = 1977 | title = White-Tailed Deer Rubs and Scrapes: Spatial, Temporal and Physical Characteristics and Social Role | journal = American Midland Naturalist | volume = 97 | issue = 2| pages = 257–266 | doi=10.2307/2425092| jstor = 2425092 }}</ref> Although bucks do most of the marking, does visit these locations often. To make a rub, a buck uses his antlers to strip the bark off small-diameter trees, helping to mark his territory and polish his antlers. To mark areas they regularly pass through, bucks make scrapes. Often occurring in patterns known as scrape lines, scrapes are areas where a buck has used his front hooves to expose bare earth. They often rub-urinate into these scrapes, which are often found under twigs that have been marked with scent from the forehead glands.{{citation needed|date=November 2016}}

== Hunting ==
White-tailed deer have long been hunted as [[game (hunting)|game]], for pure [[trophy hunting|sport]] and for their commodities, and is probably the most hunted native big game species in the [[Americas]]. In Mesoamerica, white-tailed deer (''Odocoileus virginianus'') were hunted from very early times. Rites and rituals in preparation for deer hunting and celebration for an auspicious hunt are still practiced in the area today. Ancient hunters ask their gods for permission to hunt, and some deer rites take place in caves.<ref>Benson, Elizabeth P. "Deer." In [[David Carrasco]] (ed). ''The Oxford Encyclopedia of Mesoamerican Cultures''. : Oxford University Press, 2001.</ref>

[[Venison]], or deer meat, is a nutritious form of lean animal protein that a deer will yield once it has been killed and processed.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aidoo |first1=Kofi E. |last2=Haworth |first2=Richard J. P. |title=Nutritional and chemical composition of farmed venison |journal=Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics |date=December 1995 |volume=8 |issue=6 |pages=441–446 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-277X.1995.tb00339.x }}</ref> In modern times, wild venison is particularly sustainable in areas where deer populations are very high and hunting can be used as a method to control them.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.massaudubon.org/our-work/resilient-lands/land-stewardship/white-tailed-deer-management-plan|title=White-Tailed Deer Management Plan|website=massaudubon.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.maine.gov/ifw/blogs/mdifw-blog/importance-regulated-doe-harvest|title=The Importance of Regulated Doe Harvest|website=maine.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dec.ny.gov/animals/7211.html|title=New York's Deer Management Program|website=dec.ny.gov}}</ref>

In 1884, one of the first hunts of white-tailed deer in Europe was conducted in [[Opočno]] and [[Dobříš]] ([[Brdy|Brdy Mountains]] area), in what is now the [[Czech Republic]]. In the same era, white-tailed deer were hunted to near extinction in North America, but numbers have since rebounded to approximate pre-colonization levels.<ref name="DF" /> In the [[United States]], whitetail hunting is far more popular in some states than others. The top five states for whitetail hunter concentrations are all in the [[Northeastern United States|Northeast]] and [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]] ([[Pennsylvania]], [[Rhode Island]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[Wisconsin]], and [[Ohio]]).<ref name="DA13">Kip Adams. "[https://www.deerassociation.com/hunter-density-across-u-s/ Hunter Density Across the U.S.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210330150124/https://www.deerassociation.com/hunter-density-across-u-s/ |date=March 30, 2021 }}". National Deer Association, January 14, 2013. Accessed March 12, 2021.</ref> The Northeast in particular has twice the hunter density of the Midwest and Southeast and ten times that of the West.<ref name="DA13" />

Since whitetail deer are very adaptable, inhabiting diverse regions ranging from tropical rain forests to high-altitude mountain chains of the Andes Mountains at more than 13,000 feet, different [[Hunting strategy|hunting methods]] as well as types of guns and ammo may be used. Most common cartridges used include the [[.243 Winchester]], [[.308 Winchester]], [[.25-06 Remington]], [[6.5mm Creedmoor]], [[.270 Winchester]], [[7mm Remington Magnum]], [[.30-06 Springfield]], [[.30-30 Winchester|.30-30 Winchester (.30 WCF)]], [[.300 Winchester Magnum]] and [[12-gauge|12 gauge]] shotshells.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Boddington |first=Craig |date=August 29, 2022 |title=Best Old and New Deer Cartridges |url=https://www.rifleshootermag.com/editorial/best-deer-cartridges/463852 |website=www.rifleshooter.com}}</ref> Due to the whitetail deer's frame and weight, cup and core [[bullet]]s are the most recommended for taking clean, ethical shots.

Hunting is a tool that can be used for controlling the whitetail deer population in areas that may not have a strong predator presence and where local ecosystems may be negatively effected by overgrazing.<ref name="Population Control" />

==Human interactions==
[[File:Pet white-tailed deer fawn.JPG|thumb|Fawn being kept as a pet in a farm near [[Cumaral]], [[Colombia]]]]

By the early 20th century, commercial exploitation and unregulated [[hunting]] had severely depressed deer populations in much of their range.<ref>Richard E. McCabe and Thomas R. McCabe (1984). Of Slings and Arrows: An Historical Retrospective. In Lowell K. Halls (ed.), ''White-tailed Deer Ecology and Management'' (Washington: Wildlife Management Institute).</ref> For example, by about 1930, the U.S. population was thought to number about 300,000.<ref>Joel M. Lerner, [http://www.dispatch.com/content/stories/home_and_garden/2009/07/19/NODEER.ART_ART_07-19-09_H1_OSEFNIT.html "Right plants (and fences) can keep deer at bay"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131019080957/http://www.dispatch.com/content/stories/home_and_garden/2009/07/19/NODEER.ART_ART_07-19-09_H1_OSEFNIT.html |date=October 19, 2013 }}, The Columbus Dispatch, July 21, 2009. Accessed December 27, 2012.</ref> After an outcry by hunters and [[conservation biology|conservation ecologists]], commercial exploitation of deer became illegal and conservation programs along with regulated hunting were introduced. In 2005, estimates put the deer population in the United States at around 30''&nbsp;''million.<ref>Mark Johnson, [https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna6835501 Deer eating away at forests nationwide], The Associated Press, January 18, 2005. Accessed December 27, 2012.</ref> Conservation practices have proved so successful, in parts of their range, the white-tailed deer populations currently far exceed their cultural [[carrying capacity]] and the animal may be considered a [[Nuisance wildlife management|nuisance]].<ref>Sinclair, A. R. E. (1997). Carrying capacity and the overabundance of deer: a framework for management.</ref><ref>Mcshea, W. J., Underwood, H. B., Rappole, J. H. (1997). ''The Science Of Overabundance: Deer Ecology and Population Management.'' WA: Smithsonian Institution Press. pp.380–394.</ref> A reduction in non-human predators (which normally cull young, sick, or infirm specimens) has also contributed to locally abundant populations.

At high population densities, farmers can suffer economic damage from deer feeding on cash crops, especially in [[maize|corn]] and [[orchard]]s. It has become nearly impossible to grow some crops in some areas unless very burdensome deer-deterring measures are taken. Deer can easily jump fences, and their fear of motion and sounds meant to scare them away is soon dulled. Timber harvesting and forest clearance have historically resulted in increased deer population densities,<ref>Mattfeld, George F. (1984). Northeastern hardwood and spruce-fir forests. In: Halls, Lowell K., ed. ''White-tailed deer: ecology and management.'' Harrisburg, PA: Stackpole Books: 305–330.</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Whitney | first1 = G.G. | year = 1990 | title = The history and status of the hemlock-northern hardwood forests of the Allegheny Plateau | journal = Journal of Ecology | volume = 78 | issue = 2| pages = 443–458 | doi=10.2307/2261123| jstor = 2261123  }}</ref> which in turn have slowed the rate of reforestation following logging in some areas. High densities of deer can have severe impacts on native plants and animals in parks and natural areas; however, deer browsing can also promote plant and animal diversity in some areas.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Côté | first1 = SD | last2 = Rooney | first2 = TP | last3 = Tremblay | first3 = JP | last4 = Dussault | first4 = C | last5 = Waller | first5 = DM | year = 2004 | title = Ecological impacts of deer overabundance | journal = Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics | volume = 35 | pages = 113–147 | doi=10.1146/annurev.ecolsys.35.021103.105725}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Greenwald | first1 = KR | last2 = Petit | first2 = LJ | last3 = Waite | first3 = TA | year = 2008 | title = Indirect effects of a keystone herbivore elevate local animal diversity | journal = The Journal of Wildlife Management | volume = 72 | issue = 6| pages = 1318–1321 | doi=10.2193/2007-491| bibcode = 2008JWMan..72.1318G }}</ref> Deer can also cause substantial damage to landscape plants in suburban areas, leading to limited hunting or trapping to relocate or sterilize them. In parts of the Eastern US with high deer populations and fragmented woodlands, deer often wander into suburban and urban habitats that are less than ideal for the species.

===Farming===
{{Main|Deer farm}}

Deer farming has expanded into a substantial livestock sector, supplying venison, velvet antlers, hides, and breeding stock.<ref>{{cite web |title=Farming Captive Cervids in Michigan |url=https://www.canr.msu.edu/resources/farming_captive_cervids_in_michigan_wo1026
 |website=Michigan State University Extension
 |publisher=Michigan State University
 |access-date=2025-12-02
}}</ref> Deer are favored in production systems due to their high reproductive efficiency, climatic adaptability, and ability to utilize pasture that is unsuitable for conventional agriculture.<ref name=PSUDeer>{{cite web
 |title=White-tailed Deer Production
 |url=https://extension.psu.edu/white-tailed-deer-production
 |website=Penn State Extension
 |publisher=Pennsylvania State University
 |access-date=2025-12-02
}}</ref>

Producers face strict regulatory requirements to prevent farmed deer from mixing with wild populations. Many jurisdictions mandate tall, reinforced fencing, to reduce the risk of escape, disease transmission, and ecological disruption. High-density operations also require rigorous ecological and veterinary oversight, as unmanaged herds can damage vegetation, alter habitat structure, and increase the spread of diseases such as chronic wasting disease (CWD).<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/cwd-program-standards.pdf |title=CWD Program Standards |publisher=Wildlife Health Institute |year=2024}}</ref>

Most commercial operations fall into two categories:
* Breeding farms, which focus on genetics, herd improvement, and stock sales.
* Hunting ranches, which raise and manage animals for guided hunts and related recreational services.

Both models generate reliable income, supported by sustained demand for venison, specialty antler products, and wildlife-based recreation.<ref name="PSUDeer" />

===Deer–vehicle collisions===
{{Main|Deer–vehicle collisions}}

[[File:Mercury Tracer, whitetail deer hit damage, July 2008.jpg|thumb|right|Car with major damage from striking a white-tailed deer in [[Wisconsin]]]]Motor vehicle collisions with deer are a significant issue in many parts of their range, especially at night and during rutting season, causing injuries and fatalities among both deer and humans. Vehicular damage can be substantial in some cases.<ref>[http://www.iii.org/press_releases/warning-to-motorists-fall-is-peak-season-for-deer-vehicle-collisions.html Warning to Motorists: Fall Is Peak Season for Deer-Vehicle Collisions], Insurance Information Institute, October 1, 2009</ref> In the United States, such collisions increased from 200,000 in 1980 to 500,000 in 1991.<ref name="Côté 2004 113–147">{{Cite journal|title = Ecological Impacts of Deer Overabundance|journal = Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics|date = 2004|pages = 113–147|volume = 35|issue = 1|doi = 10.1146/annurev.ecolsys.35.021103.105725|first1 = Steeve D.|last1 = Côté|first2 = Thomas P.|last2 = Rooney|first3 = Jean-Pierre|last3 = Tremblay|first4 = Christian|last4 = Dussault|first5 = Donald M.|last5 = Waller}}</ref> By 2009, the insurance industry estimated 2.4 million deer–vehicle collisions had occurred over the past two years, estimating damage cost to be over 7 billion dollars and 300 human deaths. Despite the high rate of these accidents, the effect on deer density is still quite low. Vehicle collisions of deer were monitored for two years in Virginia, and the collective annual mortality did not surpass 20% of the estimated deer population.<ref name="doi.wiley.com">{{Cite journal|title = Ecology and management of white-tailed deer in a changing world |journal = Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences|doi = 10.1111/j.1749-6632.2011.06376.x |volume=1249 |issue = 1 |pages=45–56 |pmid=22268688 | last1 = McShea | first1 = WJ|year = 2012|bibcode = 2012NYASA1249...45M }}</ref>

Many techniques have been investigated to prevent roadside mortality. Fences or [[Wildlife crossing|road under- or over- passes]] have been shown to decrease deer-vehicle collisions, but are expensive and difficult to implement on a large scale.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite journal|title = Targeting mitigation efforts: The role of speed limit and road edge clearance for deer–vehicle collisions |doi = 10.1002/jwmg.712|journal = The Journal of Wildlife Management|volume=78|issue = 4|pages=679–688|year = 2014|last1 = Meisingset|first1 = Erling L|last2 = Loe|first2 = Leif E|last3 = Brekkum|first3 = Øystein|last4 = Mysterud|first4 = Atle| bibcode=2014JWMan..78..679M }}</ref><ref name="linkinghub.elsevier.com">{{Cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.jenvman.2011.05.010|pmid=21700381|title=Predicting deer–vehicle collisions in an urban area|journal=Journal of Environmental Management|volume=92|issue=10|pages=2486–2493|year=2011|last1=Found|first1=Rob|last2=Boyce|first2=Mark S.|bibcode=2011JEnvM..92.2486F }}</ref> Roadside habitat modifications could also successfully decrease the number of collisions along roadways.<ref name="linkinghub.elsevier.com"/> An essential procedure in understanding factors resulting in accidents is to quantify risks, which involves the driver's behavior in terms of [[Assured Clear Distance Ahead#ACDA: horizontal line-of-sight|safe speed]] and ability to observe the deer. Some have{{who|date=March 2021}} suggested that reducing speed limits during the winter months when deer density is exceptionally high would likely reduce deer-vehicle collisions, but this may be an impractical solution.<ref name="ReferenceD"/>

===Diseases===
Another issue that exists with high deer density is the spreading of infectious diseases. Increased deer populations lead to increased transmission of tick-borne diseases, which pose a threat to human health, to livestock, and to other deer. White-tailed deer are the primary host for the adult [[black-legged tick|black-legged tick (''Ixodes scapularis'')]], which transmits the [[Lyme disease]] bacterium to humans.<ref>[https://agresearchmag.ars.usda.gov/1998/mar/tick Tackling Ticks That Spread Lyme Disease], Agricultural Research magazine, March 1998</ref> Lyme disease is the most common vector-borne disease in the country with confirmed cases, according to 2019 CDC data, in virtually every state in the U.S. with the highest incidence levels in the states from Maine to Virginia, Minnesota, and Wisconsin. In 2019 the number of confirmed and probable cases totaled about 35,000.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-05-20|title=Lyme Disease Maps: Most Recent Year {{!}} Lyme Disease {{!}} CDC|url=https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/datasurveillance/maps-recent.html|access-date=2022-02-09|website=www.cdc.gov|language=en-us}}</ref> Furthermore, the incidence of Lyme disease seems to reflect deer density in the eastern United States, which suggests a strong correlation. While deer are critical hosts for the tick life cycle, they are not susceptible to infection by the Lyme disease spirochete. The [[white-footed mouse]] (''Peromyscus leucopus'') is the most significant reservoir of ''Borrelia burgdorferi'', the etiologic agent of Lyme disease.<ref>{{Cite journal | url=https://www.caryinstitute.org/science-program/research-projects/lyme-disease | doi=10.1098/rstb.2013.0556| pmid=25688016| pmc=4342961| title=Accelerated phenology of blacklegged ticks under climate warming| journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences| volume=370| issue=1665| article-number=20130556| year=2015| last1=Levi| first1=T.| last2=Keesing| first2=F.| last3=Oggenfuss| first3=K.| last4=Ostfeld| first4=R. S.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://phys.org/news/2018-04-reveals-high-infection-white-footed-mice.html|title=Tick control program reveals high level of infection in white-footed mice|website=phys.org}}</ref>  White-tailed deer also act as hosts for other medically significant tick vectors that transmit diseases including as [[Rocky Mountain spotted fever|Rocky Mountain spotted fever, ''Rickettsia parkeri'' rickettsiosis, and human monotropic ehrlichiosis]].<ref name="Côté 2004 113–147" /><ref name="doi.wiley.com" />

====SARS-CoV-2====
{{Main|SARS-CoV-2 in white-tailed deer}}

Blood samples gathered by [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]] researchers in 2021 also showed that 40% of sampled white-tailed deer demonstrated evidence of [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2|SARS-CoV-2]] antibodies, with the highest percentages in Michigan, at 67%, and Pennsylvania, at 44%.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Fine Maron |first1=Dina |title=Wild U.S. deer found with coronavirus antibodies |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/wild-us-deer-found-with-coronavirus-antibodies |access-date=August 3, 2021 |publisher=National Geographic |date=August 2, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210802183618/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/wild-us-deer-found-with-coronavirus-antibodies |archive-date=August 2, 2021}}</ref> A later study by [[Penn State University]] and wildlife officials in Iowa showed that up to 80 percent of Iowa deer sampled from April 2020 through January 2021 had tested positive for active SARS-CoV-2 infection, rather than solely antibodies from prior infection. This data, confirmed by the [[National Veterinary Services Laboratory]], alerted scientists to the possibility that white-tailed deer had become a [[natural reservoir]] for the coronavirus, serving as a potential "variant factory" for eventual retransmission back into humans.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Jacobs |first1=Andrew |title=Widespread Coronavirus Infection Found in Iowa Deer, New Study Says |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/02/science/deer-covid-infection.html |access-date=5 November 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=2 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211102164643/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/02/science/deer-covid-infection.html |archive-date=2 November 2021}}</ref> An [[Ohio State University]] study further showed that humans had transmitted SARS-CoV-2 to white-tailed deer on at least six separate occasions and that deer possessed six mutations that were uncommon in humans at the time of the study.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bush |first1=Evan |title=Covid is rampant among deer, research shows |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/science/science-news/covid-rampant-deer-research-shows-rcna10181 |access-date=January 2, 2022 |publisher=NBC News |date=January 2, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220102094124/https://www.nbcnews.com/science/science-news/covid-rampant-deer-research-shows-rcna10181 |archive-date=January 2, 2022}}</ref> Infected deer can shed virus via nasal secretions and feces for five to six days and frequently engage in activities conductive to viral spread, such as sniffing food intermingled with waste, nuzzling noses, polygamy, and the sharing of salt licks.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Anthes |first1=Emily |last2=Imbler |first2=Sabrina |title=Is the Coronavirus in Your Backyard? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/07/health/coronavirus-deer-animals.html |access-date=7 February 2022 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=7 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220207100458/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/07/health/coronavirus-deer-animals.html |archive-date=7 February 2022}}</ref> Canadian researchers uncovered an entirely new SARS-CoV-2 variant within a November–December 2021 study of Ontario white-tailed deer. The new COVID variant had also infected a person who had close contact with local deer, potentially marking the first instance of deer-to-human transmission.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Miranda |first1=Gabriela |title=New COVID variant found in deer shows signs of possible deer-to-human transmission |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/health/2022/03/03/variant-coronavirus-found-deer-humans/9356528002/ |access-date=March 5, 2022 |publisher=USA Today |date=March 3, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220305020930/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/health/2022/03/03/variant-coronavirus-found-deer-humans/9356528002/ |archive-date=March 5, 2022}}</ref><ref name="Nature Microbiology">{{cite journal |last1=Pickering |first1=Bradley |last2=Lung |first2=Oliver |last3=Maguire |first3=Finlay |last4=Kruczkiewicz |first4=Peter |last5=Kotwa |first5=Jonathon |last6=Buchanan |first6=Tore |last7=Gagnier |first7=Marianne |last8=Guthrie |first8=Jennifer |last9=Jardine |first9=Claire |last10=Marchand-Austin |first10=Alex |last11=Massé |first11=Ariane |last12=McClinchey |first12=Heather |last13=Nirmalarajah |first13=Kuganya |last14=Aftanas |first14=Patryk |last15=Blais-Savoie |first15=Juliette |last16=Chee |first16=Hsien-Yao |last17=Chien |first17=Emily |last18=Yim |first18=Winfield |last19=Banete |first19=Andra |last20=Griffin |first20=Bryan |last21=Yip |first21=Lily |last22=Goolia |first22=Melissa |last23=Suderman |first23=Matthew |last24=Pinette |first24=Mathieu |last25=Smith |first25=Greg |last26=Sullivan |first26=Daniel |last27=Rudar |first27=Josip |last28=Vernygora |first28=Oksana |last29=Adey |first29=Elizabeth |last30=Nebrokski |first30=Michelle |last31=Goyette |first31=Guillaume |last32=Finzi |first32=Andrés |last33=Laroche |first33=Geneviève |last34=Ariana |first34=Ardeshir |last35=Vahkal |first35=Brett |last36=Côté |first36=Marceline |last37=McGeer |first37=Allison |last38=Nituch |first38=Larissa |last39=Mubareka |first39=Samira |last40=Bowman |first40=Jeff |title=Divergent SARS-CoV-2 variant emerges in white-tailed deer with deer-to-human transmission |journal=Nature Microbiology |date=10 November 2022 |volume=7 |issue=12 |pages=2011–2024 |doi=10.1038/s41564-022-01268-9 |pmid=36357713 |pmc=9712111 }}</ref>

===Cultural significance===
[[File:MAPElNorte017.JPG|thumb|''Odocoileus virginianus'' skull, part of an exhibition on the cultural artifacts of the [[Cora people]] of Western Mexico]]
In the U.S., the species is the [[List of U.S. state animals|state animal]] of [[Arkansas]],<ref>{{cite web |title=State Symbols |work=The Traveler's Guide To Arkansas For Kids |publisher=Arkansas Secretary of State |url=http://www.soskids.arkansas.gov/k-4-history-state-symbols.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050305090357/http://www.soskids.arkansas.gov/k-4-history-state-symbols.html |archive-date=March 5, 2005 |access-date=2011-09-02}}</ref> [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://georgia.gov/blog/2015-05-19/white-tailed-deer-named-state-mammal-georgia |title=White-Tailed Deer Named State Mammal of Georgia |author=Allen, David G. |date=May 19, 2015 |publisher=State of Georgia |access-date=January 23, 2016 |archive-date=January 29, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160129221121/https://georgia.gov/blog/2015-05-19/white-tailed-deer-named-state-mammal-georgia  }}</ref> [[Illinois]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=List of State Mammals |url=https://statesymbolsusa.org/categories/mammal|access-date=2021-01-18|website=State Symbols USA|date=April 23, 2014 }}</ref> [[Michigan]],<ref name="ReferenceD">Shearer, Benjamin F. & Barbara S. Shearer. ''State Names, Seals, Flags, and Symbols: A Historical Guide.'' Westport, CT: Greenwood, 2002. 234.</ref> [[Mississippi]],<ref name="ReferenceC">Shearer, Benjamin F. & Barbara S. Shearer. ''State Names, Seals, Flags, and Symbols: A Historical Guide.'' Westport, CT: Greenwood, 2002. 235.</ref> [[Nebraska]],<ref name="ReferenceD"/> [[New Hampshire]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://statesymbolsusa.org/symbol-official-item/new-hampshire/state-mammal/white-tailed-deer|title=White-tailed Deer State Animal - New Hampshire |website=State Symbols USA|date=September 19, 2014 |access-date=2019-10-17}}</ref> [[Ohio]],<ref name="ReferenceD"/> [[Pennsylvania]], and [[South Carolina]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://statesymbolsusa.org/symbol-official-item/south-carolina/state-mammal/white-tailed-deer|title=White-tailed Deer State Animal - South Carolina |website=State Symbols USA|date=September 27, 2014 |access-date=2019-10-17}}</ref> the game animal of [[Oklahoma]], and the wildlife symbol of [[Wisconsin]]. The white-tailed deer is also the inspiration of the professional basketball team the [[Milwaukee Bucks]]. The profile of a white-tailed deer buck caps the [[coat of arms of Vermont]], is on the [[flag of Vermont]], and is in stained glass at the [[Vermont State House]]. It is the [[List of national animals|national animal]] of [[Honduras]] and [[Costa Rica]] and the provincial animal of Canadian [[Saskatchewan]] and Finnish [[Pirkanmaa]]. It appears on the reverse side of the Costa Rican 1,000 [[Costa Rican colón|colón]] note. The 1942 Disney film adaptation of ''[[Bambi]]'', famously changed Bambi's species from the novel's [[roe deer]] into a white-tailed deer.

== Climate change{{Anchor|Climate Change}} ==

=== Migration patterns ===
[[Climate change]] is affecting the white-tailed deer by changing their [[Animal migration|migration]] patterns and increasing their population size.<ref name="Hushaw-2016">{{Cite journal|last1=Hushaw|first1=Jennifer|last2=Balch|first2=Si|last3=Walberg|first3=Eric|date=March 31, 2016|title=Part II: Species Highlights|url=https://www.manomet.org/wp-content/uploads/old-files/Wildlife_Bulletin_PartII%5b1%5d.pdf|journal=Climate Change and Wildlife}}</ref><ref name="Dawe-2016">{{Cite journal|last1=Dawe|first1=Kimberly|last2=Boutin|first2=Stan|date=August 18, 2016|title=Climate change is the primary driver of white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) range expansion at the northern extent of its range; land use is secondary|journal=Ecology and Evolution|volume=6|issue=18|pages=6435–6451|doi=10.1002/ece3.2316|doi-access=free |pmid=27777720|pmc=5058518|bibcode=2016EcoEv...6.6435D }}</ref> This species of deer is restricted from moving northward due to cold harsh winters.<ref name="Kennedy-Slaney-2018">{{Cite journal|last1=Kennedy-Slaney|first1=Liam|last2=Bowman|first2=Jeff|last3=Walpole|first3=Aaron|last4=Pond|first4=Bruce|date=June 2018|volume=45|issue=3|pages=220–228|doi=10.1071/WR17106|title=Northward bound: The distribution of white-tailed deer in Ontario under a changing climate|journal=Wildlife Research|bibcode=2018WildR..45..220K }}</ref><ref name="Hushaw-2016" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Post|first1=Eric|last2=Stenseth|first2=Nils|date=July 1998|title=Large-Scale Climatic Fluctuation and Population Dynamics of Moose and White-Tailed Deer|journal=Journal of Animal Ecology|volume=67|issue=4|pages=537–543|jstor=2647275|doi=10.1046/j.1365-2656.1998.00216.x|doi-access=free|bibcode=1998JAnEc..67..537P }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=LeDee|first1=Olivia|last2=Hagell|first2=Suzanne|last3=Martin|first3=Karl|last4=MacFarland|first4=David|last5=Meyer|first5=Micheal|last6=Paulios|first6=Andrew|last7=Ribic|first7=Christine|last8=Sample|first8=David|last9=Van Deelen|first9=Timothy|date=2013|title=A Preliminary Assessment|url=https://dnr.wi.gov/files/pdf/pubs/ss/ss0197.pdf|journal=Climate Change Impacts on Wisconsin's Wildlife|access-date=April 19, 2019|archive-date=October 20, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201020035507/https://dnr.wi.gov/files/pdf/pubs/ss/ss0197.pdf}}</ref> Consequently, as climate change warms up Earth, these deer are allowed to migrate further north which will result in the populations of the white-tailed deer increasing.<ref name="Dawe-2016" /><ref name="Kennedy-Slaney-2018" /><ref name="Hushaw-2016" /> Between 1980 and 2000 in a study by Dawe and Boutin, presence of white-tailed deer in [[Alberta|Alberta, Canada]], was driven primarily by changes in the climate.<ref name="Dawe-2016" /> Populations of white-tailed deer have also moved anywhere from {{Convert|50 to 250|km|abbr=on}} north of the eastern Alberta study site. Another study by Kennedy-Slaney, Bowman, Walpole, and Pond found that if current [[Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|CO<sub>2</sub> emissions]] remained the same, global warming resulting from the increased [[greenhouse gas]]es in the atmosphere will allow white-tailed deer to survive further and further north by 2100.<ref name="Kennedy-Slaney-2018" />

=== Food web ===
When species are introduced to foreign [[ecosystem]]s, they could potentially wreak havoc on the existing [[food web]]. For example, when the deer moved north in [[Alberta]], [[Grey Wolf|gray wolf]] populations increased.<ref name="Dawe-2016" /> This [[butterfly effect]] was also demonstrated in [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ysa5OBhXz-Q Yellowstone National Park when the rivers changed because wolves were re-introduced to the ecosystem.] It is also possible that the increasing white-tailed deer populations could result in them becoming an [[invasive species]] for various plants in Alberta, Canada.<ref name="Dawe-2016" />

=== Disease ===
Deer are vulnerable to diseases that are more prevalent in the summer.<ref name="Hushaw-2016" /> Insects carrying these diseases like Lyme are usually killed during the first snowfall. However, as time goes on, they will be able to live longer than they used to meaning the deer are at higher risk of getting sick. It is possible that this will increase the deers' mortality rate from disease.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Changing Climate, Changing Wildlife: A Vulnerability Assessment of 400 Species of Greatest Conservation Need and Game Species in Michigan|last1=Hoving|first1=Christopher|last2=Lee|first2=Yu|last3=Badra|first3=Peter|last4=Klatt|first4=Brian|year=2013|url=https://www.canr.msu.edu/uploads/235/59270/CLIMATE_CHANGE.pdf}}</ref> Examples of these diseases are hemorrhagic disease (HD), [[epizootic hemorrhagic disease]] and [[Bluetongue disease|bluetongue viruses]], which are transmitted by biting [[midge]]s.<ref name="Kennedy-Slaney-2018" /> The hotter summers, longer [[drought]]s, and more intense rains create the perfect [[Biophysical environment|environment]] for the midges to thrive in.<ref name="PennState-2015">{{Cite web|url=https://ecosystems.psu.edu/research/projects/deer/news/2015/weather-and-climate|title=Will Climate Change Change Deer? (Deer-Forest Study)|website=Deer-Forest Study (Penn State University)|date=May 7, 2015 |language=en-us|access-date=2019-04-19}}</ref> Ticks also thrive in warmer weather; heat results in faster development in all of their life stages.<ref name="PennState-2015" /> 18 different species of tick infest white-tailed deer in the United States alone. Ticks parasitic to white-tailed deer transmit diseases causing [[irritation]], [[anemia]], and [[infection]]s.<ref name="PennState-2015" />

=== Parasites ===
Deer are common definitive hosts of the parasite ''[[Parelaphostrongylus tenuis]]'' (also known as menigeal worm or brainworm) and ''[[Fascioloides magna]]'' (also known as giant liver fluke) and contribute to the spread of these parasites among the white-tailed deer population and other cervids.<ref name="Duffy-2002">{{cite journal |last1=Duffy |first1=Michael S. |last2=Greaves |first2=Trent A. |last3=Keppie |first3=Nathan J. |last4=Burt |first4=Michael D. B. |title=Meningeal worm is a long-lived parasitic nematode in white-tailed deer |journal=Journal of Wildlife Diseases |date=April 2002 |volume=38 |issue=2 |pages=448–452 |doi=10.7589/0090-3558-38.2.448 |pmid=12038147 }}</ref> As the climate grows warmer and snow pack density decreases, more deer move into places like northern Minnesota, where the climate had previously been too harsh for a large population to thrive, and spread these parasites to the winter-hardy [[moose]] population.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Murray |first1=Dennis L. |last2=Cox |first2=Eric W. |last3=Ballard |first3=Warren B. |last4=Whitlaw |first4=Heather A. |last5=Lenarz |first5=Mark S. |last6=Custer |first6=Thomas W. |last7=Barnett |first7=Terri |last8=Fuller |first8=Todd K. |title=Pathogens, Nutritional Deficiency, and Climate Influences on a Declining Moose Population |journal=Wildlife Monographs |date=December 2006 |volume=166 |pages=1–30 |doi=10.2193/0084-0173(2006)166[1:PNDACI]2.0.CO;2 }}</ref>

Deer can host an adult brainworm parasite for many years, showing little to no symptoms of infection.<ref name="Duffy-2002" /><ref name="Michigan DNR">{{Cite web |date= |title=Brainworm |url=https://www.michigan.gov/en/dnr/managing-resources/Wildlife/Wildlife-disease/WDM/brainworm |access-date=July 29, 2025 |website=Michigan Department of Natural Resources}}</ref> Moose and other cervid species (like [[elk]]) are dead-end hosts for the [[Parelaphostrongylus tenuis|brainworm]] parasite; where the parasite resides in the brain matter of these cervids and cause severe neurological disease.<ref name="Michigan DNR" /> This parasite eventually causes death, or contributes to an increased likelihood of mortality via predation for dead-end hosts. Factors like infected deer density, climate, and temperature determine transmission levels of this parasite. A warming climate likely increases the rate of transmission due to the migration of deer into moose habitat and favorable weather conditions for transmission occurring more frequently.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lankester |first=Murray Wayne |date=2010 |title=UNDERSTANDING THE IMPACT OF MENINGEAL WORM, PARELAPHOSTRONGYLUS TENUIS, ON MOOSE POPULATIONS |url=https://alcesjournal.org/index.php/alces/article/view/59 |journal=Alces |language=en |volume=46 |pages=53–70 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wasel |first1=Shawn M. |last2=Samuel |first2=W. M. |last3=Crichton |first3=Vince |title=Distribution and ecology of meningeal worm, Parelaphostrongylus tenuis (Nematoda), in northcentral North America |journal=Journal of Wildlife Diseases |date=April 2003 |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=338–346 |doi=10.7589/0090-3558-39.2.338 |pmid=12910761 }}</ref> The [[1854 Treaty Authority]] monitors the density of brainworm and giant liver fluke infection within the deer population of northeastern Minnesota, and uses this information to advise the [[Minnesota Department of Natural Resources|Minnesota DNR]] when making management decisions in the 1854 Ceded Territory.

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Wildlife of Canada
