{{short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
{{If mobile| [[File:American Beaver.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2| Common [[North American beaver]], official national symbol and one of the most iconic species of [[Fauna of Canada|Canada's fauna]].]]|{{WildlifeofCanada}}}}
The '''wildlife of Canada''' or '''biodiversity of Canada''' consist of over 80,000 classified species,{{efn|name=species|"80,000 known species in Canada, excluding viruses and bacteria"<ref name="Olive2019">{{cite book|author=Andrea Olive|title=The Canadian Environment in Political Context, Second Edition|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fsyqDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT36|year=2019|publisher=University of Toronto Press, Higher Education Division|isbn=978-1-4875-7037-8|page=36}}</ref><ref name=Species/>}} and an equal number thought yet to be recognized.<ref name=Animals/> Known [[Fauna of Canada|fauna]] and [[Flora of Canada|flora]] have been identified from five kingdoms:<ref name="auto1">{{cite web|url=https://www.sararegistry.gc.ca/default.asp?lang=En&n=17F0CBCE-1#s1i |title=Wild Species 2000: The General Status of Species in Canada|year=2001|publisher=Conservation Council (CESCC)|work=Minister of Public Works and Government Services Canada}}</ref> [[protozoa]]  represent approximately 1% of recorded species; [[chromist]] (approximately 4); [[fungi]] (approximately 16%); [[plants]] (approximately 11%); and [[animals]] (approximately 68%).<ref name=Species>{{cite web|url=https://wildlife-species.canada.ca/species-risk-registry/virtual_sara/files/reports/Wild%20Species%202015.pdf|title= Wild Species 2015: The General Status of Species in Canada|work= National General Status Working Group: 1|publisher =Canadian Endangered Species Conservation Council|year=2016|page=2}}</ref><ref name="Olive2019"/> Insects account for nearly 70 percent of documented animal species in Canada.<ref name=Species/> More than 300 species are found exclusively in Canada.<ref name="Hayward 2020">{{cite web | last=Hayward | first=Abi | title=Ours to save: the species that can only be found in Canada | website=Canadian Geographic | date=2020-06-05 | url=https://canadiangeographic.ca/articles/ours-to-save-the-species-that-can-only-be-found-in-canada/ | access-date=2023-04-12}}</ref>

[[Ecozones of Canada |There are 20 major ecosystems – ecozones – in Canada: 15 terrestrial and 5 marine]].<ref name="intro1">{{cite web|last=Government of Canada|first=Statistics Canada|date=2018-01-10|title=Introduction to the Ecological Land Classification (ELC) 2017|url=https://www.statcan.gc.ca/eng/subjects/standard/environment/elc/2017-1|access-date=2020-11-09|website=www.statcan.gc.ca}}</ref> Canada's major biomes are the [[tundra]], [[boreal forest]], [[grassland]], and [[temperate deciduous forest]]. Since the end of the last [[glacial period]], Canada has consisted of [[Forests of Canada#Regions|eight distinct forest regions]],<ref>{{Cite book |title=National Atlas of Canada |publisher=[[Natural Resources Canada]] |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-7705-1198-2 |page=1}}</ref> with approximately half of its land area covered by forests (roughly 8 percent of the world's forested land).<ref name="LuckertHaley2011">{{Cite book |last1=Luckert |first1=Martin K. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0Gm-rBnGghcC&pg=PA1 |title=Policies for Sustainably Managing Canada's Forests: Tenure, Stumpage Fees, and Forest Practices |last2=Haley |first2=David |last3=Hoberg |first3=George |publisher=UBC Press |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-7748-2069-1 |page=1}}</ref>

Due to human activities, invasive species and [[Environmental issues in Canada|environmental issues in the country]],<ref name="Welcome page Page daccueil 2022">{{cite web | title=Biodiversity in Canada: Commitments and Trends | publisher=Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada – The Office of the Auditor General of Canada  | date=2022-10-04 | url=https://www.oag-bvg.gc.ca/internet/English/oth_202210_e_44128.html | access-date=2023-04-09}}</ref> there are currently more than [[List of Wildlife Species at Risk (Canada)|800 species at risk of being lost]].<ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/species-risk-public-registry/cosewic-annual-reports/2019-2020.html|publisher=Species at Risk Public Registry|title=COSEWIC Annual Report|year=2019}}</ref> Over 1400 [[Invasive species in Canada|invasive species of fish, plants, insects and invertebrates have been introduced to Canada]] through intentional and unintentional means.<ref name=invasive>{{cite web|url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/invasive-species-in-canada-animals|title=Invasive Species in Canada: Animals &#124; The Canadian Encyclopedia|website=www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca}}</ref> About 65 percent of Canada's resident species are considered ''secure''.<ref name="auto1"/> [[Protected areas of Canada|Protected and conservation areas]] have been established to preserve and restore Canadian flora and fauna species.<ref name="Nature Canada 2022">{{cite web | title=What Are Protected Areas? | website=Nature Canada | date=2022-04-13 | url=https://naturecanada.ca/discover-nature/canadas-different-environments/protected-areas-explained/ | access-date=2023-04-12}}</ref> Approximately 5000 Canadian animal species and 30,000 Canadian plant species are restricted from export for international trade.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/convention-international-trade-endangered-species/list.html|title=Endangered species list|first=Environment and Climate Change|last=Canada|date=May 19, 2017|website=aem}}</ref>

== Biodiversity==
===Habitat===
{{see|Geography of Canada}}
[[File:Terrestrial ecozones and ecoprovinces of Canada, 2017.gif|thumb|right|upright=1.3|[[Ecozones of Canada|Canada's 15 terrestrial ecozones]] are further subdivided into 53 [[ecoprovince]]s, 194 [[ecoregion]]s, and 1,027 [[ecodistrict]]s.<ref name="Biswas 2013 p. 7">{{cite book | last=Biswas | first=A.K. | title=Water Resources of North America | publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg | year=2013 | isbn=978-3-662-10868-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NrztCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA7 | access-date=2023-02-13 | page=7}}</ref>]]

Canada is characterized by a wide range of both [[Temperature in Canada|meteorologic]] and [[Geography of Canada|geological]] regions that are divided into [[Ecozones of Canada|fifteen terrestrial and five marine ecozones]],<ref name="intro">{{cite web |date=January 10, 2018 |title=Introduction to the Ecological Land Classification (ELC) 2017 |url=https://www.statcan.gc.ca/eng/subjects/standard/environment/elc/2017-1 |publisher=Statistics Canada |access-date=November 9, 2020}}</ref> such as the forests of [[British Columbia]] and [[Central Canada]], the [[prairies]] of [[Western Canada]], the [[tundra]] of [[Northern Canada]], and the marine ecosystems of the [[Arctic]], [[Atlantic Canada]] and [[British Columbia Coast|Pacific coast]]. The largest marine ecozone is the [[Arctic Archipelago]] (which covers about 15 percent of Canada, or 1.5 million km2), whereas the largest terrestrial ecozone is the [[Boreal Shield]] (covering 20 percent of Canada, or 1.9 million&nbsp;km<sup>2</sup>).<ref name="ecozone-areas">{{cite web
|url=http://cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/subsite/mx-205/opening
|title=Casting the bottom line on the blue planet
|last=Wiken
|first=Ed
|publisher=[[Natural Resources Canada]]
|access-date=2008-02-13
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080612062616/http://cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/subsite/mx-205/opening
|archive-date=2008-06-12
|url-status=live
}}</ref> 

Canada's major biomes are the [[tundra]], [[boreal forest]], [[grassland]], and [[temperate deciduous forest]].<ref name="BenkeCushing2011"/> [[British Columbia]] has a multitude of smaller biomes, including: a [[subalpine|subalpine forest]] which extends into [[Alberta]], a [[temperate rainforest]] along the coast, a [[Semi-arid climate|semi arid desert]] located in the [[Okanagan Valley]] and [[alpine tundra]] in the higher mountainous regions.<ref name="BenkeCushing2011">{{cite book|author1=Arthur C. Benke|author2=Colbert E. Cushing|title=Rivers of North America|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=faOU1wkiYFIC&pg=PA6|year=2011|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-08-045418-4|pages=6–9}}</ref> 

Over half of Canada's landscape is intact and relatively free of human development.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://naturecanada.ca/news/archived/state-of-canadas-biodiversity-highlighted-in-new-government-report/|title=State of Canada's Biodiversity Highlighted in New Government Report|date=October 22, 2010}}</ref> The [[boreal forest of Canada]] is considered to be the largest [[intact forest landscape|intact forest]] on earth, with around {{convert|3,000,00|km2}} undisturbed by roads, cities or industry.<ref name="RavenBerg2012">{{cite book|author1=Peter H. Raven|author2=Linda R. Berg|author3=David M. Hassenzahl|title=Environment|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QVpO2R51JBIC&pg=RA1-PA361|year=2012|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-0-470-94570-4|pages=1–3}}</ref> The [[Canadian Arctic tundra]] is the second-largest vegetation region in the country consisting of dwarf [[shrubs]], [[Cyperaceae|sedges]] and [[Poaceae|grasses]], [[moss]]es and [[lichen]]s.<ref name="Marsh1999a">{{cite book|author=James H. Marsh|title=The Canadian Encyclopedia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wR_-aSFyvuYC&pg=PA2446|year=1999|publisher=The Canadian Encyclopedia|isbn=978-0-7710-2099-5|page=2446}}</ref> The [[Canadian Prairies]] a [[Aspen parkland|temperate grassland]] with [[shrubland]] and [[northern mixed grasslands]] are used for rearing livestock and cultivating crops.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Quiring |first1=S. M |last2=Papakryiakou |first2=T. N. |title=An evaluation of agricultural drought indices for the Canadian prairies |journal=Agricultural and Forest Meteorology |date=2003 |volume=118 |issue=1–2 |pages=49–62|doi=10.1016/S0168-1923(03)00072-8 |bibcode=2003AgFM..118...49Q }}</ref> Only seven percent of Canada's land is suitable for large scale [[Agriculture in Canada|agricultural production]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hein |first1=Treena |title=Agriculture in Canada |url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/agriculture-in-canada#:~:text=in%20your%20browser.-,Farmland%20and%20Farms,type%20and%20location%20(latitude) |publisher=The Canadian Encyclopedia|year=2020}}</ref>

[[List of lakes of Canada|Canada has over 2,000,000 lakes]]—563 greater than {{convert|100|km2}}—which is more than any other country hosting a multitude of unique ecosystems.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/274077247|title=Status and Trends of Biodiversity of Inland Water Ecosystems|year=2003|publisher=Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity|isbn=92-807-2398-7}}</ref> Canada is home to about twenty five percent (134.6 million ha) of the world's [[wetlands]] that support a vast array of local ecosystems.<ref name="Education1">{{cite book|title=Living in the Environment, Canadian Edition, 4th ed.|date = 16 May 2016|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r5qzDAAAQBAJ&pg=PT404|publisher=Nelson Education|isbn=978-0-17-675682-6|page=404}}</ref> [[List of longest rivers of Canada|Canada's waterways]] have their own ecosystems; with the two longest rivers being the [[Mackenzie River]], that begins at [[Great Slave Lake]] and ends in the [[Arctic Ocean]], with its drainage basin covering a large part of northwestern Canada, and the [[Saint Lawrence River]], which drains the [[Great Lakes]] into the [[Gulf of St. Lawrence]] ending in the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. The Mackenzie, including its tributaries is over {{convert|4200|km2}} in length and lies within the second largest [[Watersheds of North America|drainage basin of North America]], while the St. Lawrence {{convert|3058|km2}} in length, drains the world's [[Great Lakes Basin|largest system of freshwater lakes]].<ref name=Longest >{{cite web | url=https://www.ec.gc.ca/eau-water/default.asp?lang=En&n=45BBB7B8-1#canada | title=Rivers: Longest rivers in Canada | publisher=[[Environment Canada]] | date=22 July 2013 | access-date=28 December 2014}}</ref>{{-}}

===Fauna===
{{main|Fauna of Canada}}
[[File:Perisoreus canadensis mercier2.jpg|thumb|right|The [[Canada jay]] is found in the [[boreal forest of Canada|boreal forest]] north to the [[Arctic treeline|tree line]], and in the [[Rocky Mountains subalpine zone]]. ]]
There are approximately 200 mammal species, over 460 bird species, over 40 amphibian species, over 40 reptile species, and over 1,200 fish species in Canada.<ref name=Animals>{{cite web|url=https://a-z-animals.com/animals/location/north-america/canada/|title=Canada Animals &#124; Canadian Animals &#124; Canada Wildlife &#124; AZ Animals|website=A-Z Animals}}</ref> Invertebrates present include 55,000 species of insects and 11,000 species of mites and spiders.<ref>{{cite web
 | title =Canada's Insect Fauna
 | publisher =Biological Survey of Canada
 | year=2019
 | url = https://biologicalsurvey.ca/pages/read/canadas-insect-fauna}}</ref>

The [[Great Lakes region]] is home to the [[American black bear|black bear]], [[Virginia opossum]], [[American red squirrel]], [[North American beaver]], and [[striped skunk]]; birds include [[eastern bluebird]], [[red-winged blackbird]], [[bush-robin|robin]], [[wood thrush]], [[woodpecker]], [[New World oriole|oriole]], [[bobolink]], [[crow]], [[hawk]], [[bittern]], [[heron]], [[Pacific black duck|black duck]], and [[loon]]. The [[Boreal forest of Canada|boreal forest region]] contains [[moose]], [[caribou]], [[Canada lynx]], [[Subspecies of Canis lupus|timber wolf]], [[marten]], [[porcupine]], [[snowshoe hare]], and [[chipmunk]]. The [[Rocky Mountain region]] fauna included the [[grizzly bear]], [[mountain goat]], [[bighorn sheep]], [[elk]], [[cougar]], and [[flying squirrel]].<ref name=animals/> 

The [[Pacific Maritime Ecozone (CEC)|Pacific ecozone]] is home to the [[mountain goat]], [[mountain beaver]], a vast variety of [[mice]], and [[striped skunk]]; birds include [[Northern pygmy owl|northern pygmy-owl]], [[band-tailed pigeon]], [[black swift]], [[northern flicker]], [[crow]], [[rufous-sided towhee]], and [[black brant]]. Residence species of the [[Great Plains ecoregion]] includes the [[desert cottontail]], [[deer mouse]] [[gophers]], [[plains bison]], and several types of prairie dogs ([[black-tailed prairie dog|black-tailed]], [[white-tailed prairie dog|white-tailed]], and [[Gunnison's prairie dog|gunnison's]]), alongside many [[:Category:Native birds of the Canadian Prairies|prairie birds]]. The [[Arctic]] expanse includes fauna such as the [[musk ox]] and [[reindeer]], [[polar bear]], and [[Arctic fox]], [[arctic hare]], and [[lemming]]; with birds such as the [[snowy owl]], [[willow ptarmigan]], [[snow bunting]] and [[arctic tern]].<ref name=animals/>

[[Walrus]], [[dolphins]], [[Earless seal|seal]]s, [[sea turtle]]s, [[whales]] and [[sharks]] inhabit Canada's coastal waters.<ref name=animals>{{cite book|author1=George A. Feldhamer|author2=Bruce C. Thompson|author3=Joseph A. Chapman|title=Wild Mammals of North America: Biology, Management, and Conservation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-xQalfqP7BcC&pg=PP14|year=2003|publisher=JHU Press|isbn=978-0-8018-7416-1|page=14}}</ref> Seal species include [[harbor seal]], [[harp seal]], [[hooded seal]], [[grey seal]], [[bearded seal]], [[northern fur seal]], [[northern elephant seal]], [[ringed seal]], [[Steller sea lion]], and [[California sea lion]] among others. Salt-water fish including the [[Atlantic cod]], [[Pacific salmon]], [[hake]], [[haddock]] and [[halibut]]; alongside crustaceans such as [[lobster]], [[snow crab]] and [[shrimp]] are the [[Fishing industry in Canada|primary commercial species]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://hillnotes.ca/2020/06/01/statistics-for-canadas-2018-commercial-fisheries/#:~:text=In%202018%2C%20commercial%20fisheries%2C%20including,employed%2026%2C429%20people%20that%20year.|title=Statistics For Canada's 2018 Commercial Fisheries|publisher=Library of Parliament|author=Michael Chalupovitsch |author2=Daniele Lafrance |author3=Thai Nguyen. |year=2019}}</ref> [[Walleye]] (AKA pickerel), [[northern pike]], [[rainbow trout]], [[largemouth bass]] and the [[black crappie]] are common fresh-water fish species found throughout the country.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mongabay.com/data/Canada.htm|title=Freshwater fish of Canada|website=Mongabay.com}}</ref> Canada hosts many [[amphibian]], including [[salamander]]s as well as [[frog]]s and [[toad]]s and many species of [[reptile]], including [[turtle]]s, [[lizard]]s, and [[snake]]s.<ref name=animals/> 

Many of North America's migratory birds, including [[songbirds]], [[waterfowl]] and [[shorebirds]], take up residence in Canada during the spring and summer.<ref name="LebbinParr2010">{{cite book|author1=Daniel J. Lebbin|author2=Michael J. Parr|author3=George H. Fenwick|title=The American Bird Conservancy Guide to Bird Conservation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eYpkN_brmy0C&pg=PA346|year=2010|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-64729-6|page=346}}</ref> In addition to native and migratory mammals, many Eurasian mammals were introduced to Canada either intentionally or accidentally. Among them are domestic mammals, such as the [[horse]], [[pig]], [[sheep]], [[dog]], [[cat]], and [[cattle]], and wild mammals, such as the [[brown rat]] and the [[house mouse]].<ref name=animals/>{{-}}

===Flora===
{{main|Flora of Canada|Forests of Canada}}
[[File:9 - Bunchberry (5207679035).jpg|thumb|right|The [[Canadian bunchberry]] is found in [[montane ecosystems]] and [[boreal forest of Canada|boreal forests]], where it grows along the margins of moist woods.]]
Since the end of the last [[glacial period]], Canada has consisted of [[Forests of Canada#Regions|eight distinct forest regions]].<ref name="Hendee Dawson Sharpe 2012 p. 63">{{cite book | last1=Hendee | first1=J.C. | last2=Dawson | first2=C.P. | last3=Sharpe | first3=W.F. | title=Introduction to Forests and Renewable Resources: Eighth Edition | publisher=Waveland Press | year=2012 | isbn=978-1-4786-0895-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZfMWAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA63 | access-date=2023-04-10 | page=63}}</ref> According to [[Environment and Climate Change Canada]], the nation hosts approximately 17,000 identified species of trees, flowers, herbs, ferns, mosses and other flora.<ref>{{cite web
 | title =Environment Canada – Nature – Flora
 | publisher = Government of Canada
 | date = 2007-03-20
 | url =http://www.ec.gc.ca/default.asp?lang=En&n=D9CE12FB-1
 | access-date = 2008-11-07}}
</ref> Approximately 95 percent of the vascular plants in Canada are of the [[Flowering plant|flowering variety]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/species-risk-public-registry/publications/wild-species-2010/chapter-8.html|title=Wild species 2010: chapter 8|first=Environment and Climate Change|last=Canada|date=February 24, 2017|website=aem}}</ref> Roughly half of Canada is covered by forest, totalling around {{cvt|2.4|sqkm||disp=preunit|million}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/datablog/2009/sep/02/total-forest-area-by-country|title=Total forest coverage by country|date=2 September 2009|website=The Guardian|access-date=23 September 2018}}</ref> Over 90% of Canada's forests are owned by the public ([[crown land]], and the majority being [[provincial forest]]s).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nrcan.gc.ca/our-natural-resources/forests-forestry/sustainable-forest-management/forest-land-ownership/17495|title=Forest land ownership|first=Natural Resources|last=Canada|date=May 25, 2015|website=www.nrcan.gc.ca}}</ref> About half of the forests are allocated for [[logging]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/natureofthings/features/the-worlds-biggest-forest-is-our-own-backyard-and-we-need-to-protect-it|title=The World's Biggest Forest Is In Our Own Backyard And We Need To Protect It|year=2018|publisher=[[The Nature of Things]] (CBC)
|author=Graham Duggan}}</ref> 

The Great Lakes region flora includes [[white pine]], [[Apiaceae|hemlock]] and [[red maple]]s, [[yellow birch]], and [[beech trees]]. [[The Maritimes]] region is dominated by the [[red spruce]], while the [[black spruce]] is prevalent in the [[Canadian Shield|eastern Laurentian]], with [[spruce]] in the [[Canadian Shield|western Laurentian]]. The [[balsam fir]], [[white cedar]] [[tamarack]], [[white birch]], and [[aspen]] and [[jack pine]] are also found in the eastern portion of the country. The tundra is home to the [[aspen]], [[bur oak]], [[balm of Gilead]], [[Celtis conferta subsp. amblyphylla|cottonwood]] and [[Balsam Poplar|balsam poplar]].<ref name=plants/>

The west coast has the [[western hemlock]], [[Juniperus virginiana|red cedar]], [[Douglas fir]], [[Sitka spruce]], and [[western white pine]] being dominate. The Rocky Mountain region consistent of [[alpine fir]], [[Engelmann spruce]], [[lodgepole pine]] and [[mountain hemlock]].<ref>"Canada's Boreal Forest, Forest Products Association of Canada, map, inside front cover.</ref> Other native plants seen across Canada include; [[American ginseng]], [[trillium cernuum]], [[red bearberry]], [[bog Labrador tea]], [[purple prairie clover]], [[sand cherry]], [[Pallas' wallflower]], [[little evening primrose]], [[showy orchis]] and [[common eelgrass]].<ref name=plants>{{cite web|url=https://cwf-fcf.org/en/resources/encyclopedias/native-plant-encyclopedia/?src=blog|title=Native Plant Encyclopedia|website=cwf-fcf.org}}</ref>{{-}}

== Species at risk ==
{{main|List of Wildlife Species at Risk (Canada)}}
[[File:Mustela nigripes 2.jpg|thumb|right|The [[black-footed ferret]] is listed as [[endangered]] primarily as a result of decreases in [[prairie dog]] populations and [[sylvatic plague]].]]
Canada's ''[[Species at Risk Act]]'' (SARA) is the federal government legislation to prevent wildlife species from becoming extinct.<ref name="NEducation">{{cite book|author=Nelson Education|title=Living in the Environment, Canadian Edition, 4th ed.|date=16 May 2016|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r5qzDAAAQBAJ&pg=PT318|publisher=Nelson Education|isbn=978-0-17-675682-6|page=318}}</ref> The goal of the act is to protect endangered or threatened organisms.<ref name="Dorey_2018">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1016/j.biocon.2017.11.018| issn = 0006-3207| volume = 217| pages = 259–268| last1 = Dorey| first1 = Katherine| last2 = Walker| first2 = Tony R.| title = Limitations of threatened species lists in Canada: A federal and provincial perspective| journal = Biological Conservation| access-date = 10 May 2020| date = 1 January 2018| url = http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0006320717312545| url-access = subscription}}</ref> Provinces, territories and large municipalities also have their own species and [[habitat conservation]] regulations.<ref name="Foran2018w">{{cite book|author=Max Foran|title=The Subjugation of Canadian Wildlife: Failures of Principle and Policy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Y5hUDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT137|year=2018|publisher=McGill-Queen's University Press|isbn=978-0-7735-5428-3|pages=137–140}}</ref> 

Although Canada has a low percentage of [[Megadiverse countries|endemic species compared to other countries]]; pollution, [[loss of biodiversity]], over-exploitation of commercial species, invasive species and habitat loss have threatened many species.<ref>Oscar Venter, Nathalie N. Brodeur, Leah Nemiroff, Brenna Belland, Ivan J. Dolinsek, James W. A. Grant. (2006), [https://academic.oup.com/bioscience/article-pdf/56/11/903/26897555/56-11-903.pdf Threats to Endangered Species in Canada], BioScience, Volume 56, Issue 11.</ref> More than 800 species are listed as being at risk of extinction, including 363 classified as [[endangered species]], —190 [[threatened species]], —235 special concern, and 22 extirpated (no longer found in the wild).<ref name="auto"/><ref name="COSEWIC2020pdf">{{cite web |url=https://wildlife-species.canada.ca/species-risk-registry/virtual_sara/files/cosewic/Rapport-Cescc-Report-v00-2020Sept-Eng.pdf |title=COSEWIC Annual Report |publisher=Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada |date=2020-09-02 |access-date=2021-01-01 |page=5}}</ref>

In addition to the extirpated species, at least 19 have become completely extinct,<ref name="COSEWIC2020pdf"/> with 30 species no longer found in Canada.<ref name="Hinterland">{{cite web|url=https://www.hww.ca/en/issues-and-topics/species-at-risk-in-canada.html|publisher=[[Hinterland Who's Who]] |title=Species at Risk in Canada|year=2010|quote= at least 13 of our plant and animal species have disappeared entirely from the Earth and at least 20 others are no longer found in Canada.}}</ref> These include the [[Dawson's caribou]], [[sea mink]], [[great auk]], [[Labrador duck]], [[passenger pigeon]], [[deepwater cisco]], [[longjaw cisco]], [[Banff longnose dace]], and [[blue walleye]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hww.ca/en/issues-and-topics/biodiversity.html|title=Hinterland Who's Who – Biodiversity|publisher=Canadian Wildlife Federation}}</ref>

Species at risk include the [[Canada lynx]], [[polar bear]], [[sea otter]], [[wolverine]], [[black-footed ferret]], [[northern fur seal]], [[steller sea lion]], [[hooded seal]], [[North Atlantic right whale]], [[sei whale]] and [[whooping crane]].<ref name="auto"/>
{{-}}

==Invasive species==
{{Main|Invasive species in Canada|Aquatic invasive species in Canada}}
{{see|List of invasive species in North America}}
[[File:Zebra mussel GLERL 4.jpg|thumb|upright=0.9|[[Zebra mussels]] were first detected in the [[Great Lakes Basin]] in 1988, in [[Lake Saint Clair (North America)|Lake St. Clair]].]]

Over 1400 [[invasive species]] of fish, plants, insects and invertebrates have been introduced to Canada through intentional and unintentional means.<ref name=invasive /> Over 450 invasive flora and over 400 invasive insects have been identified.<ref name="SchlichterMontes2011">{{cite book|author1=Tomás Schlichter|author2=Leopoldo Montes|title=Forests in Development: A Vital Balance|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rE-YG8S46mkC&pg=PA34|year=2011|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-94-007-2576-8|page=34}}</ref> The [[Great Lakes region]] is home to nearly 200 invasive species, making it one of Canada's most heavily affected ecosystems.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theweathernetwork.com/ca/news/article/the-invasive-species-threatening-canada-biodiversity-you-may-not-know-about-giant-hogweed-dog-strangling-vine-purple-loosestrife|title=The invasive species threatening Canada's biodiversity you may not know about|publisher=Pelmorex Weather Networks Inc|website=www.theweathernetwork.com|date=22 May 2020 }}</ref> Freshwater ecosystems are disproportionately more imperilled compared to terrestrial ecosystems.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dextrase |first1=Alan J. |last2=Mandrak |first2=Nicholas E. |title=Impacts of Alien Invasive Species on Freshwater Fauna at Risk in Canada |journal=Biological Invasions |date=January 2006 |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=13–24 |doi=10.1007/s10530-005-0232-2|s2cid=9422553 }}</ref>

Invasive species such as the [[sea lamprey]], [[zebra mussels]], [[European green crab]], the [[mountain pine beetle]], [[round goby]], [[Asian long-horned beetle]], [[emerald ash borer]], [[didymo]], [[spongy moth]], and [[Asian carp]] have altered local habitats and caused essential ecosystems to decline or fail,<ref name="LeeService2004"/> driving native species towards extinction.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Dextrase, Alan|author2=Mandrak, Nicholas|title=Impacts of Alien Invasive Species on Freshwater Fauna at Risk in Canada|journal=Biological Invasions|date=2006-01-01|publisher=Springer Netherlands|issn=1387-3547|pages=13–24|volume=8|issue=1|doi=10.1007/s10530-005-0232-2|s2cid=9422553}}</ref> 

The most invasive flora species are the [[purple loosestrife]], [[yellow iris]], [[dog-strangling vine]], [[knapweed]], and [[leafy spurge]].<ref name="LeeService2004"/> The fungi causing [[Dutch elm disease]] is another notable invasive.<ref name="LeeService2004"/> These species can spread aggressively, outcompete native wild vegetation and overwhelm agricultural crops.<ref name="LeeService2004">{{cite book|author1=Michelle Lee|author2=Canadian Wildlife Service|title=Invasive Alien Species in Canada|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4J-kMHC-irkC|year=2004|publisher=Canadian Wildlife Service|isbn=978-0-662-34262-5}}</ref> 
{{-}}

== Conservation ==
{{Main|Protected areas of Canada}}
Approximately 12.1 percent of the nation's landmass and freshwater are considered [[Wildlife conservation|conservation areas]], including 11.4 percent designated as [[protected areas]].<ref name=conserved/> Approximately 13.8 percent of Canada's territorial waters are conserved, including 8.9 percent designated as protected areas.<ref name=conserved>{{cite web|url=https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/environmental-indicators/conserved-areas.html|title=Canada's conserved areas|publisher=Environment and Climate Canada|year=2020}}</ref> Terrestrial areas conserved have increased by 65 percent in the 21st century, while marine areas conserved have increased by more than 3,800 percent.<ref name=conserved/> Conservation and protected areas have different mandates depending on the organization which manages them, with some areas having a greater focus on ecological integrity, historical preservation, public usage, scientific research, or a combination of usages.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/protected-areas|title=Protected Areas |publisher=The Canadian Encyclopedia|year=2014}}</ref> Some regions within Canada's largest conserved areas are heavily commercialized featuring grand buildings such as the [[Banff Springs Hotel]] and [[Chateau Lake Louise]]. 
{{Canada provinces map|width=285px|map=Canadian National Parks.png|prefix=List of protected areas of|the=the|caption=[[List of national parks of Canada| Canada's national parks and national reserves by provinces and territories]]}}
Canada established the world's first national park management agency the [[Dominion Parks Branch]] now [[Parks Canada]] in 1911.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thestar.com/travel/northamerica/article/990243--parks-canada-celebrates-a-century-of-discovery|title=Parks Canada celebrates a century of discovery|last=Irish|first=Paul|date=May 13, 2011|work=Toronto Star|access-date=May 18, 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110516235956/http://www.thestar.com/travel/northamerica/article/990243--parks-canada-celebrates-a-century-of-discovery|archive-date=May 16, 2011}}</ref> In 1916, Canada and the United States signed the [[Migratory Birds Convention]], which regulates the hunting of transcontinental migratory birds under the ''[[Migratory Birds Convention Act]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/corporate/international-affairs/partnerships-countries-regions/north-america/canada-united-states-protecting-migratory-birds.html|title=Canada-US convention protecting migratory birds|first=Environment and Climate Change|last=Canada|date=February 27, 2015|website=aem}}</ref> The ''[[Canada Wildlife Act]]'' of 1973 goal is research on wildlife with a focus on larger species.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/w-9/FullText.html|title=Consolidated federal laws of canada, Canada Wildlife Act|first=Legislative Services|last=Branch|date=December 12, 2017|website=laws-lois.justice.gc.ca}}</ref> The 1985 ''[[Fisheries Act (Canada)|Fisheries Act]]'' regulates fishing, including the conservation and protection of fish and their spawning grounds.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/f-14/|title=Consolidated federal laws of canada, Fisheries Act|first=Legislative Services|last=Branch|date=August 28, 2019|website=laws-lois.justice.gc.ca}}</ref> The ''[[National Marine Conservation Area|National Marine Conservation Areas Act]]'' established a system of national marine conservation areas in 2002.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/c-7.3/|title=Consolidated federal laws of canada, Canada National Marine Conservation Areas Act|first=Legislative Services|last=Branch|date=August 28, 2019|website=laws-lois.justice.gc.ca}}</ref>

The primary focus of the Canadian national parks system is to preserve ecological integrity.<ref name="Commons2004">{{cite book|author=Canada. Parliament. House of Commons|title=House of Commons Debates|date=November 2004|page=1830}}</ref> [[National Marine Conservation Areas]], while also under federal control, do not afford the same level of protection.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/c-7.3/FullText.html|title=Consolidated federal laws of canada, Canada National Marine Conservation Areas Act|work=Legislative Services|date=August 28, 2019|publisher=Government of Canada}}</ref> The [[Canadian Wildlife Service]], a division of Environment and Climate Change Canada, manages the [[National Wildlife Area]]s and [[Migratory Bird Sanctuary|Migratory Bird Sanctuaries]] for the protection of wildlife.<ref name="Burnett2011">{{cite book|author=J. Alexander Burnett|title=A Passion for Wildlife: The History of the Canadian Wildlife Service|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J30w47u_CGkC&pg=PA170|year=2011|publisher=UBC Press|isbn=978-0-7748-4252-5|page=170}}</ref><ref name="areas">{{cite web
|url=http://www.hww.ca/en/issues-and-topics/environment-canadas.html
|title=Environment Canada's Protected Areas Network
|work=Hinterland Who's Who
|publisher=Canadian Wildlife Service
|access-date=2019-03-14}}</ref> [[List of Canadian protected areas|Provincial and territorial governments also protect areas]] within their boundaries.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/canadian-provinces-territories-by-percentage-of-protected-terrestrial-area.html|title=Canadian Provinces/Territories By Percentage Of Protected Terrestrial Area|website=WorldAtlas|date=25 April 2017 }}</ref> [[Urban parks in Canada]] are operated by [[local government in Canada|municipal governments]] for public recreation and foliage preservation in cities.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/city-parks|title=City parks |publisher=The Canadian Encyclopedia|year=2017}}</ref> Some areas such as the [[Polar Bear Pass National Wildlife Area|Polar Bear Pass]], are [[Comanagement in Canada|co-managed and overseen by government and local indigenous agencies]].<ref name="BeazleyBaldwin2019">{{cite book|author1=Karen Beazley|author2=Robert Baldwin|title=Biodiversity and Protected Areas|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NZ2SDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA112|year=2019|publisher=MDPI|isbn=978-3-03897-732-2|page=112}}</ref>

Canada's 18 [[Biosphere Reserves of Canada|UNESCO Biosphere Reserves]] covers a total area of {{convert|235,000|km2}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.biospherecanada.ca/|title=UNESCO Biosphere Reserves of Canada|publisher=e CanadianBiosphere Reserves Association and the Canadian Commission for UNESCO|year=2018}} [https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5735fdc137013b8eeb217d63/t/5c40d868575d1f41918199a3/1547753580117/Biosphere-brochure-web.pdf PDF]</ref> Canada's first national park, [[Banff National Park]] established in 1885, spans {{convert|6,641|km2}}<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pc.gc.ca/docs/v-g/pm-mp/guidem-mguide/sec15/gm-mg15_e.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060615122147/http://www.pc.gc.ca/docs/v-g/pm-mp/guidem-mguide/sec15/gm-mg15_e.pdf |archive-date=June 15, 2006|title=The Mountain Guide – Banff National Park|publisher=Parks Canada|year=2006}}</ref> of mountainous terrain, with many [[glacier]]s and [[ice field]]s, dense [[pinophyta|coniferous]] forest, and alpine landscapes.<ref name="Price2013">{{cite book|author=Martin F. Price|title=Mountain Area Research and Management: Integrated Approaches|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hNIZihxXTwsC&pg=PA217|year=2013|publisher=Earthscan|isbn=978-1-84977-201-3|pages=217–218}}</ref> Canada's oldest provincial park, [[Algonquin Provincial Park]] established in 1893, covers an area of {{convert|7653.45|km2}} is dominated by [[old-growth forest]] with over 2,400 lakes and 1,200 kilometers of streams and rivers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ontario.ca/page/algonquin-provincial-park-management-plan|title=Algonquin Provincial Park Management Plan|year=1998|publisher=Queen's Printer for Ontario}}</ref> [[Lake Superior National Marine Conservation Area]] is the world's largest freshwater protected area spanning roughly {{convert|10000|km2}} of lakebed, its overlaying freshwater, and associated shoreline on {{convert|60|km2}} of islands and mainland's.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/publications/mpaspotlight-pleinsfeuxzpm/index-eng.html|title=Spotlight on Marine Protected Areas in Canada|first=Fisheries and Oceans Canada|last=Government of Canada|date=December 13, 2017|website=www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca}}</ref> Canada's largest national wildlife region is the [[Scott Islands Marine National Wildlife Area]], which spans {{convert|11570.65|km2}},<ref>{{cite web|title=Scott Islands Marine National Wildlife Area|url=https://www.protectedplanet.net/555695926|access-date=2020-09-25|website=Protected Planet}}</ref> protects critical breeding and nesting habitat for over 40 percent of [[British Columbia]]'s [[seabirds]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-wildlife-areas/locations/scott-islands-marine/regulatory-strategy.html|title=Proposed Scott Islands Marine National Wildlife Area: regulatory strategy|first=Environment and Climate Change|last=Canada|date=February 7, 2013|website=aem}}</ref>{{-}}
